title: Preface
content: Preface Number Systems: From \nN to \nR is volume F3 of the series. It is followed by Algebraic Preliminaries.

title: The ZF Fragment and the von Neumann Natural Numbers
content:
The ZF Fragment and the von Neumann Natural Numbers Logic and Proof, Chapter 3, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2 took the natural numbers as a set 
N inside the familiar real line, with induction as an axiom (@fd1:ax-induction) and with their arithmetic and order borrowed from the real numbers. This volume builds the real numbers, so it cannot borrow from them: where, then, do the natural numbers come from? This chapter starts again from sets alone. Six axioms say how sets are made and when two are equal; with them we build ordered pairs, and so functions, out of sets. Then we build the natural numbers out of nothing but the empty set. Zero is \emptyset, and “one further” is the step x \mapsto x \cup \{x\}, so that 1 = \{0\}, 2 = \{0, 1\}, 3 = \{0, 1, 2\}: each number is the set of the numbers before it. A seventh axiom, Infinity, says that the steps can be completed into a set, and the least such set is \omega. From there, everything that Logic and Proof, Chapter 3, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2 assumed about 
N becomes a theorem about \omega: Peano’s axioms, induction, the recursion theorem, the laws of + and \cdot, and the order with its well-ordering. A final theorem says that any other system satisfying Peano’s axioms is a relabeling of this one, by exactly one matching, and the chapter closes with the rule by which the later chapters of this volume write 
N for \omega and cite Logic and Proof, Chapter 3, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 2 and 3. Two pictures. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1 adopted two working conventions: numbers are not sets (Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 1.1), and a pair is not a number, nor a triple a pair (the remark after @fd2:def-ordered-pair). They belong to the picture of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 1 to 3, in which numbers are given objects. In this chapter every object is a set, so 0 \in 5 and 2 \subseteq 3 are true statements, and the pair (0, 1) is the set \{1, 2\}. The two pictures do not conflict. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 1.1 said that nothing in the main line depends on how numbers are made, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1 used nothing about pairs beyond their characteristic property and that convention; Section 1.2 proves the characteristic property for pairs built from sets. What survives of the conventions becomes a theorem: no pair is a natural number (Section 1.4), and no n-tuple with n \ge 3 is a pair or a natural number (Section 1.6). Statements such as 0 \in 5 are facts about this one construction; the matching of Section 1.7 carries 0, successor, +, \cdot and <, and nothing else. What you need. Logic and Proof, Chapters 1–5, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 1–3, chiefly its Chapters 1 and 2. From Logic and Proof, Chapters 2 and 4: the rules ulename{
eg I} and RAA (@fd1:def-rules-negation, @fd1:def-rule-raa), the rules for equality (@fd1:def-rules-equality), and first-order formulas (@fd1:def-first-order-formula), which are what a “property” in the axiom of Separation means; Section 1.3’s exercises also use De Morgan’s laws and negate quantifiers, bounded ones included (@fd1:prp-de-morgan, @fd1:prp-quantifier-negation, @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation). From Logic and Proof, Chapter 3, the principle of induction (@fd1:ax-induction), which Section 1.3 proves as a theorem about \omega and which is never used on \omega; and, for review exercise R3 of Section 1.7, structural recursion and unique readability (@fd1:thm-structural-recursion, @fd1:thm-unique-readability). From Logic and Proof, Chapter 5, the catalogue of what a proof may not do (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue). From Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1: equality of sets, subsets and sets cut out by a property (@fd2:def-set-equality, @fd2:def-subset, @fd2:def-set-builder), Russell’s theorem (@fd2:thm-russell), unions and intersections, of two sets and of families (@fd2:def-set-operations, @fd2:def-indexed-family, @fd2:def-family-union-intersection), the smallest closed set (@fd2:prp-smallest-closed-set), ordered pairs, products and relations (@fd2:def-ordered-pair, @fd2:def-cartesian-product, @fd2:def-relation), functions and when two are equal (@fd2:def-function, @fd2:prp-function-equality), injective, surjective and bijective maps, composites and inverses (@fd2:def-injective, @fd2:def-surjective, @fd2:def-bijective, @fd2:def-composition, @fd2:thm-composition-injective-surjective, @fd2:def-inverse-function, @fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse), images (@fd2:def-image), and, for review exercise R2 of Section 1.7, left and right inverses (@fd2:def-left-right-inverse, @fd2:prp-right-inverse-surjective, @fd2:thm-left-inverse-iff-injective). From Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2: the recursion theorem and its proof (@fd2:thm-recursion), which Section 1.5 repeats on \omega; and well-ordering (@fd2:thm-well-ordering), induction from a base (@fd2:thm-induction) and the arithmetic of 
N (@fd2:lem-naturals-arithmetic), which Sections 1.6 and 1.7 prove again on \omega and compare with. From Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 3, the axiom of choice (@fd2:ax-choice), only to say that this chapter never uses it; and, for review exercise R1 of Section 1.7, the definition of an infinite set and the theorem that a finite set is not equinumerous with a proper subset (@fd2:def-infinite, @fd2:thm-finite-no-proper-copy, read on \omega through Section 1.7’s dictionary), with Hilbert’s hotel (@fd2:exm-hilbert-hotel). Section 1.7 also names results of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 2 and 3 about finite and countable sets, to say how the later chapters of this volume read them on \omega; apart from R1, it does not use them. Time. About 30 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 40 hours for everything. Roadmap - Axioms for Sets. Six axioms, (Z1)–(Z6), for making sets and telling them apart, why Separation needs a set to cut from, and the sets they name: the empty set, unordered pairs, unions, intersections and differences, each unique by Extensionality. - Ordered Pairs Built from Sets. Kuratowski’s pair \{\{a\}, \{a, b\}\}, three shorter encodings that fail, the proof of the characteristic property with the case a = b on its own, the product A 	imes B as a set, and the working rules (W1)–(W5) of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 1.1 recovered from the axioms. - Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers. The successor \mathrm{S}(x) = x \cup \{x\} and the numerals 0 = \emptyset, 1 = \{0\}, 2 = \{0, 1\}, inductive sets and the axiom of infinity (Z7), \omega as the least inductive set, and induction on \omega proved as a theorem. - The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano’s Axioms. Transitive sets, the facts that no natural number is an element of itself and that every non-zero one is a successor, Peano’s axioms (P1)–(P5) for \omega, Peano systems with a structure for each of (P3)–(P5) that fails it alone, and the theorem that no pair is a natural number. - The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication. The recursion theorem proved on \omega by gluing partial solutions on the sets \mathrm{S}(n), with no order needed; addition and multiplication defined by recursion, n + 1 = \mathrm{S}(n), and the laws of arithmetic, each by an induction on the variable the recursion runs on. - Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers. “Less than” defined as “element of” and proved a strict total order, each number the set of the numbers below it; well-ordering, by an induction on the numbers that contain no element of the set; order tied to arithmetic, with subtraction and induction from any base; powers and parity; and n-tuples and lists of variable length as sets. - All Peano Systems Are Alike. Isomorphisms of Peano systems, the categoricity theorem (every Peano system is a copy of \omega by exactly one isomorphism), addition, multiplication and order carried along it, the identification of \omega with Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2’s 
N, and the dictionary by which the later chapters cite Logic and Proof, Chapter 3, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 2 and 3 on \omega; the review exercises reach back to Logic and Proof, Chapter 3, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 1 and 3. Named moves - Show the set is inductive. To prove P(n) for every n \in \omega, form \{ n \in \omega : P(n) \} and show that it contains 0 and is closed under \mathrm{S}. When the claim fails at 0, carry a disjunction “n = 0 or …” instead. - Fix the others, induct on the recursion variable. In m + n and m \cdot n the recursion runs on the second argument n; fix m (and any third variable) and induct on n. A fact about the first argument, such as 0 + n = n, is a lemma to prove first, not a defining equation. - Build by recursion, compare by induction. A map out of \omega comes from the recursion theorem; facts about it (one-to-one, onto, preserves +) are proved by induction, or by (P5) of the system it maps into.

title: 1.1 Axioms for Sets
content:
Axioms for Sets Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 1 to 3 worked with sets under six working rules, (W1)–(W6) of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 1.1, and took the natural numbers as a given set inside the familiar real line, with induction as an axiom (@fd1:ax-induction). This volume builds the real numbers, so it may not lean on them: we start again from sets alone, and in this chapter every object is a set. This section asks which rules about sets are basic. It states six axioms, shows that they settle when two sets are equal, and produces the first sets from them: the empty set, unordered pairs, unions, intersections and differences. Starting again from sets Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 1.1 listed its working rules and used them without asking where they came from. One of them, specification (@fd2:def-set-builder), was the repair of a rule that fails: “every property defines a set” is contradictory, because the property x 
otin x would define a set that both is and is not an element of itself, and @fd2:thm-russell turns that contradiction into the fact that no set has every set as an element. So rules about sets cannot be chosen by what sounds harmless. They must be chosen with care and stated once, and everything else must then be derived from them. That raises two questions, which this chapter answers in order. Which of the working rules are basic, and which follow from the others? And can the basic rules produce the objects Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 1 to 3 took as given (ordered pairs, functions, the natural numbers), rather than only describe them? Section 1.2 builds ordered pairs out of sets; Section 1.3 builds the natural numbers. To build numbers out of sets we must let sets be the only objects. From here to the end of the chapter, every object is a set, and every element of a set is again a set. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 1.1 used a different picture, in which numbers are given objects that are not sets, and it said that nothing in the main line would depend on how numbers are made. That picture stays valid for Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 1 to 3; this chapter works in the other one, where 0 will be the empty set and 0 \in 1 will be a true statement. The chapter’s introduction says how the two pictures fit together. The language. Statements about sets are written in the first-order language of Logic and Proof, Chapter 4 (@fd1:def-first-order-formula) with one predicate symbol, the two-place \in, together with equality. There are no constant symbols and no function symbols. The variables range over sets. So “x \in y” and “x = y” are the atomic formulas, and everything else is built from them with the connectives and the quantifiers. A property P(x) of sets is a formula of this language in which the variable x may occur free; other free variables, called parameters, are allowed too, and stand for sets fixed in advance. The axioms We want sets that can be built, and we know one way not to build them: by an arbitrary property, with nothing to cut the set out of. So instead of one rule for every property, we list a few specific ways of making a new set from sets we already have, together with one set to start from. A few ways to make sets, and one way to tell them apart. [The Axioms (Z1)–(Z6)] 1. Extensionality. Sets with the same elements are equal: for all sets A and B, if x \in A \leftrightarrow x \in B for every x, then A = B. 2. Empty set. There is a set with no elements. 3. Pairing. For all sets a and b there is a set whose elements are exactly a and b. 4. Union. For every set \sS there is a set whose elements are exactly the elements of members of \sS. 5. Power set. For every set X there is a set whose elements are exactly the subsets of X. 6. Separation. For every set A and every property P(x) there is a set whose elements are exactly the x \in A with P(x). In symbols, with S \subseteq X as an abbreviation of  orall y\, (y \in S 	o y \in X) (@fd2:def-subset):  egin{aligned} &(\mathrm{Z1}) &&  orall A\,  orall B\,  igl( orall x\, (x \in A \leftrightarrow x \in B) 	o A = B igr), \ &(\mathrm{Z2}) && \exists E\,  orall x\, 
eg(x \in E), \ &(\mathrm{Z3}) &&  orall a\,  orall b\, \exists C\,  orall x\,  igl(x \in C \leftrightarrow (x = a \vee x = b) igr), \ &(\mathrm{Z4}) &&  orall \sS\, \exists U\,  orall x\,  igl(x \in U \leftrightarrow \exists S\, (S \in \sS \wedge x \in S) igr), \ &(\mathrm{Z5}) &&  orall X\, \exists Q\,  orall S\, (S \in Q \leftrightarrow S \subseteq X). \end{aligned} (Z6) is not one axiom but one for each property, an axiom schema. For every formula \varphi whose free variables are among x, p_1, \dots, p_k and in which the letter B does not appear,  orall p_1 \cdots  orall p_k\,  orall A\, \exists B\,  orall x\,  igl(x \in B \leftrightarrow (x \in A \wedge \varphi) igr). 	ag{Z6} The letter B here is bound, and may be renamed (Logic and Proof, Section 4.2) to any letter that appears nowhere else in (Z6) (not in \varphi, and neither x nor A). So a property may mention a given set called B, as A \setminus B below does, once the new set is given another letter, say D:  orall B\,  orall A\, \exists D\,  orall x\,  igl(x \in D \leftrightarrow (x \in A \wedge x 
otin B) igr). In words, clause by clause, with what each one licenses. - (Z1) is the only axiom that proves two sets equal by comparing their elements: it turns “same elements” into A = B. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 1.1 stated it as the meaning of equality of sets (@fd2:def-set-equality); here it is an axiom, and only its direction “same elements, hence equal” needs to be assumed. The other direction, from A = B to x \in A \leftrightarrow x \in B, is the equality rule ulename{{=}E} of @fd1:def-rules-equality, a rule of logic. - (Z2) gives the one set we start from. Each of (Z3)–(Z6) makes a set out of sets already given. - (Z3) makes a set out of two given sets a, b. The two need not differ: with b = a its set has the single element a. - (Z4) flattens one level: from a set \sS of sets it makes the set of what lies inside the members of \sS. With (Z3) it gives the union of two sets (below). - (Z5) collects all subsets of X into one set; it is the working rule (W4). - (Z6) cuts a set out of a set A already given, by a property. It is specification (@fd2:def-set-builder), now an axiom. The letter B must not appear in \varphi, or the property could refer to the set being made: with \varphi the formula x 
otin B, and B the very set that (Z6) produces, it would say x \in B \leftrightarrow (x \in A \wedge x 
otin B), which no set B satisfies when A has an element. Properties written with defined symbols. The formulas of (Z6) contain only \in and =. We shall write properties with defined symbols as well (\subseteq, \emptyset, \{a, b\}, and later \cup, pairs and functions), and that is harmless: each defined symbol is shorthand that unwinds into \in and =. For instance “x = \emptyset” unwinds to  orall y\, 
eg(y \in x), and “x = \{a, b\}” to  orall y\,  igl(y \in x \leftrightarrow (y = a \vee y = b) igr). A property is admissible in (Z6) when its unwinding is a formula of the language, which is the case for every property in this chapter. One way to tell sets apart, and one way to make them unique. Each of (Z2)–(Z6) says that there is a set with a certain membership condition. By (Z1) there is then exactly one: two sets with the same membership condition have the same elements, so they are equal. We use this move so often that we state it once: To show that a set is unique, show that any two sets with its membership condition have the same elements, and apply (Z1). The first sets. Here are the axioms at work, each set checked against the membership condition that made it. - The empty set. (Z2) gives a set with no elements; @prp-zf-basic-sets below shows it is unique, and we write it \emptyset. - A singleton. (Z3) with a = b = \emptyset gives a set whose elements are exactly the x with x = \emptyset \vee x = \emptyset, that is, x = \emptyset. This is \{\emptyset\}. It is not \emptyset: it has the element \emptyset, and \emptyset has none. - A two-element set. (Z3) with a = \emptyset and b = \{\emptyset\} gives \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\}, whose elements are exactly \emptyset and \{\emptyset\}. These two are different, by the previous item, so this set has two elements. - A union. (Z4) with \sS = \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\} gives the set of everything that lies in \emptyset or in \{\emptyset\}. Nothing lies in \emptyset, and only \emptyset lies in \{\emptyset\}. So the union is \{\emptyset\}: one element, although \sS has two. - A power set. (Z5) with X = \{\emptyset\} gives the set of subsets of \{\emptyset\}. There are two, \emptyset and \{\emptyset\} itself (the argument of @fd2:exm-power-set-small, which uses only extensionality and excluded middle, applies word for word). So \powerset{\{\emptyset\}} = \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\}, the set of the third item. - A separation. (Z6) with A = \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\} and the property x 
e \emptyset gives \{\{\emptyset\}\}: of the two elements of A, only \{\emptyset\} differs from \emptyset. The degenerate case is the empty set itself, and it matters: each natural number will be built from \emptyset by these axioms, one at a time. The set of all of them needs one more starting point, the Axiom of Infinity (Section 1.3). A non-example by minimal change. Delete the ambient set from (Z6): “for every property P(x) there is a set whose elements are exactly the x with P(x)”. This is the naive rule of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 1.1, and it fails at once. With P(x) the property x 
otin x it gives a set R with R \in R \leftrightarrow R 
otin R, a contradiction; and even with the harmless-looking property x = x it gives a set of which every set is an element, which @fd2:thm-russell rules out. What fails is exactly the clause “x \in A” that was deleted. Every other part of (Z6) survives the change; the ambient set is what makes it safe. Why this list. Each axiom earns its place by something later in the chapter. Pairing and Union give finite sets and the union of two sets; Power set and Separation give the product A 	imes B (Section 1.2) and, with it, relations and functions; Extensionality makes every construction unique. Four further axioms complete the usual system of set theory with choice, and only one of them is needed here: - Infinity says that some set contains \emptyset and is closed under one particular step. It is (Z7), stated in Section 1.3, once there is a step to iterate. Without it, the axioms above produce each finite set we write down, one at a time. That they cannot produce a set holding infinitely many of them is a theorem of set theory, which this book states and does not prove. - Replacement and Foundation are not needed to build the natural numbers, and are left to the volume on set theory, which revisits this chapter. - Choice is @fd2:ax-choice of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 3. Nothing in this chapter uses it. We do not ask whether the axioms are consistent, or (apart from exercise C1) whether one of them follows from the others. Those are questions about the axioms, and this chapter only uses them. Two traps in the list. First, (Z3) gives an unordered pair: \{a, b\} = \{b, a\}, since x = a \vee x = b and x = b \vee x = a say the same thing. So \{a, b\} cannot record which of a, b came first, and Section 1.2 needs a different construction for the ordered pair. Second, (Z6) needs the ambient set A: the rule without it is exactly the one @fd2:thm-russell refutes. The first consequences The existence axioms say “there is a set”; the first proposition says “there is exactly one”, and so lets us give each such set a name. It also rebuilds from the axioms the operations of @fd2:def-set-operations and, for a set of sets \sS, the  igcup \sS and  igcap \sS of @fd2:def-family-union-intersection; indexed families wait for Section 1.2. [The Sets Named by the Axioms] 1. There is exactly one set with no elements. It is written \emptyset. 2. For all sets a and b the set of (Z3) is unique. It is written \{a, b\}, and \{a\} \coloneqq \{a, a\}, the set whose only element is a. 3. For every set \sS the set of (Z4) is unique. It is written  igcup \sS, and A \cup B \coloneqq  igcup \{A, B\} for sets A, B, so that x \in A \cup B if and only if x \in A or x \in B. The sets A \cap B \coloneqq \{ x \in A : x \in B \} and A \setminus B \coloneqq \{ x \in A : x 
otin B \} exist by (Z6). For a non-empty set \sS, the set  igcap \sS \coloneqq \{ x \in A_0 : x \in S 	ext{ for every } S \in \sS \} exists by (Z6) for any A_0 \in \sS, it does not depend on A_0, and x \in  igcap \sS if and only if x \in S for every S \in \sS. 4. For all sets a, b, c, d, \{a, b\} = \{c, d\} \iff (a = c \wedge b = d) \vee (a = d \wedge b = c). In particular \{a\} = \{c, d\} if and only if a = c and c = d. Parts (a)–(c) are the uniqueness move three times: the axiom named gives a set, and any two sets with the same membership condition are equal by (Z1). For  igcap \sS, the condition “x \in A_0” adds nothing, since A_0 is itself one of the S \in \sS; so the condition does not mention A_0 at all. Part (d) is different: it compares elements. From a \in \{a, b\} = \{c, d\} we get a = c or a = d, and each case is finished by locating b and then the remaining element of \{c, d\}. (a) A set with no elements exists by (Z2). If E and E' both have no elements, then for every x, both x \in E and x \in E' are false, so x \in E \leftrightarrow x \in E'; hence E = E' by (Z1). This is the argument of @fd2:prp-empty-set-unique, with (Z1) in place of @fd2:def-set-equality. (b) Let C and C' be sets as in (Z3) for the same a, b. For every x, x \in C and x \in C' are each equivalent to x = a \vee x = b, so C = C' by (Z1). With b = a the condition is x = a \vee x = a, which is equivalent to x = a; so the only element of \{a\} is a. (c) The set of (Z4) is unique by the same argument, its condition being \exists S\, (S \in \sS \wedge x \in S). For \sS = \{A, B\}, an S \in \{A, B\} is A or B, by (b); so x \in A \cup B if and only if x \in A or x \in B. The sets A \cap B and A \setminus B are instances of (Z6), with ambient set A and parameter B (after renaming the bound letter of (Z6)), and are unique by (Z1). Now let \sS be non-empty, and let A_0 \in \sS. By (Z6) with ambient set A_0 and parameter \sS, the set  igcap \sS above exists. Its membership condition simplifies: x \in A_0 \wedge  orall S\, (S \in \sS 	o x \in S) \iff  orall S\, (S \in \sS 	o x \in S). From left to right, drop the first conjunct. From right to left, apply the condition at S = A_0, which is a member of \sS, to get x \in A_0. The right-hand side does not mention A_0. So if A_1 is another member of \sS, the sets built from A_0 and from A_1 have the same elements, and they are equal by (Z1). (d) (\Leftarrow) If a = c and b = d, then \{a, b\} = \{c, d\} by ulename{{=}E}. If a = d and b = c, then \{a, b\} = \{d, c\}, and \{d, c\} = \{c, d\} because x = d \vee x = c is equivalent to x = c \vee x = d, so the two sets have the same elements (Z1). (\Rightarrow) Suppose \{a, b\} = \{c, d\}. Since a \in \{a, b\}, we have a \in \{c, d\}, so a = c or a = d. We take the two cases in turn (ulename{\vee E}). Case 1: a = c. Since b \in \{c, d\}, b = c or b = d. If b = d, then a = c and b = d, the first disjunct. If b = c, then b = c = a, so \{a, b\} = \{a\}. Now d \in \{c, d\} = \{a, b\} = \{a\}, so d = a, and hence b = a = d. Again a = c and b = d. Case 2: a = d. Since b \in \{c, d\}, b = c or b = d. If b = c, then a = d and b = c, the second disjunct. If b = d, then b = d = a, so \{a, b\} = \{a\}. Now c \in \{a\}, so c = a, and b = a = c. So a = d and b = c, the second disjunct again. In each case one of the two disjuncts holds. For the last claim, apply what was just proved with b = a: \{a\} = \{a, a\} = \{c, d\} if and only if (a = c \wedge a = d) \vee (a = d \wedge a = c). Both disjuncts say that a = c and a = d, that is, a = c and c = d. Two consequences of (d) are used constantly. With c = d it says that \{a\} = \{c\} only if a = c: a singleton determines its element. And with c = a it says that \{a, b\} = \{a, d\} only if b = d: in the first disjunct b = d directly, and in the second a = d and b = a, so again b = d. Section 1.2 uses both. The sets of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1, rebuilt. The union A \cup B of part (c) has the membership condition of @fd2:def-set-operations (a), and the intersection and difference are defined exactly as in parts (b) and (c) of that definition; so by (Z1) these are the sets Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1 used. Likewise, if \sS is a non-empty set of subsets of a set X, the  igcap \sS of part (c) and the  igcap \sS of @fd2:def-family-union-intersection, cut out of X, have the same membership condition, “x lies in every member of \sS”, and so they are the same set. The new version needs no ambient X: any member A_0 of \sS does the job. For the empty \sS it would have to contain every set, and no set does (@fd2:thm-russell); exercise B2 returns to this. Compute  igcup \emptyset,  igcup \{\emptyset\} and  igcup \{\{\emptyset\}, \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\}\}.  igcup \emptyset = \emptyset: an element would have to lie in some member of \emptyset, and \emptyset has no members.  igcup \{\emptyset\} = \emptyset: the only member is \emptyset, which has no elements.  igcup \{\{\emptyset\}, \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\}\} = \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\}: the first member contributes \emptyset, the second contributes \emptyset and \{\emptyset\}, and repeats do not count. With @prp-zf-basic-sets every set we have named so far is a set of the axioms, and so are the operations of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 1.2 on sets and on sets of sets: \cup, \cap, \setminus, the power set (Z5),  igcup \sS, and  igcap \sS for non-empty \sS. Unions and intersections of an indexed family (A_i)_{i \in I} need the family as a function, which needs ordered pairs; Section 1.2 returns to them. What is not yet built is an ordered pair; the warning above says why \{a, b\} will not do, and Section 1.2 builds one. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. For each of the sets \{\emptyset\}, \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\}, \powerset{\emptyset},  igcup \{\emptyset\}, and \{ x \in A : x 
otin x \} for a given set A, name the axioms that produce it. 2. True or false: for all sets a and b, \{a\} = \{b\} implies a = b. Justify your answer. 3. Prove that  igcup \{a\} = a for every set a. 4. Is there a set T such that \{x\} \in T for every set x? Justify your answer. (a) \{\emptyset\}: (Z2) for \emptyset, then (Z3) with both inputs \emptyset. \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\}: (Z2), then (Z3) twice, once for \{\emptyset\} and once with the inputs \emptyset and \{\emptyset\}. \powerset{\emptyset}: (Z2), then (Z5); it is \{\emptyset\}, since the only subset of \emptyset is \emptyset.  igcup \{\emptyset\}: (Z2), (Z3), then (Z4); it is \emptyset. \{ x \in A : x 
otin x \}: (Z6) with ambient set A and the property 
eg(x \in x). Uniqueness, in every case, is (Z1). (b) True. Apply @prp-zf-basic-sets (d) with c = d = b: \{a\} = \{b, b\} gives a = b (and b = b). (c) For every x: x \in  igcup \{a\} if and only if x \in S for some S \in \{a\}. The only S \in \{a\} is a (@prp-zf-basic-sets (b)), so this holds if and only if x \in a. The two sets have the same elements, so  igcup \{a\} = a by (Z1). (d) No. Suppose T were such a set. By (Z4),  igcup T is a set. Let x be any set. Then x \in \{x\} and \{x\} \in T, so x \in  igcup T. So every set is an element of  igcup T, which contradicts the second claim of @fd2:thm-russell. Hence no such T exists. B. Practice [B1: Power sets and unions] 1. Compute \powerset{\powerset{\emptyset}}. 2. Prove that  igcup \powerset{X} = X for every set X. (a) \powerset{\emptyset} = \{\emptyset\}, since the only subset of \emptyset is \emptyset. So \powerset{\powerset{\emptyset}} = \powerset{\{\emptyset\}} = \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\}, as computed in the list of first sets after @ax-zf-fragment. (b) We show both inclusions and apply @fd2:prp-subset-antisymmetric (whose proof is (Z1) and logic). (\subseteq) Let x \in  igcup \powerset{X}. Then x \in S for some S \in \powerset{X}, that is, for some S \subseteq X. Hence x \in X. (\supseteq) Let x \in X. The set \{x\} is a subset of X, since its only element is x (@prp-zf-basic-sets (b)). So \{x\} \in \powerset{X}, and x \in \{x\}; hence x \in  igcup \powerset{X}. [B2: Intersections of sets of sets] 1. Let \sS = \{ X, Y \} with X = \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\} and Y = \{\{\emptyset\}, \{\{\emptyset\}\}\}. Compute  igcap \sS twice: once with A_0 = X in @prp-zf-basic-sets (c), once with A_0 = Y. 2. Explain in one or two sentences why the two computations had to agree. 3. Explain why the definition of  igcap \sS makes no sense for \sS = \emptyset. (a) With A_0 = X: of the two elements of X, \emptyset is not in Y (the elements of Y are \{\emptyset\} and \{\{\emptyset\}\}, both non-empty), and \{\emptyset\} is in Y and in X. So  igcap \sS = \{\{\emptyset\}\}. With A_0 = Y: \{\emptyset\} lies in X and in Y; \{\{\emptyset\}\} does not lie in X, since it differs from \emptyset (it has an element) and from \{\emptyset\} (its element \{\emptyset\} is not \emptyset). So again  igcap \sS = \{\{\emptyset\}\}. (b) An element of either set must lie in every member of \sS, and that condition already forces it into A_0, because A_0 is a member. So the condition “x \in A_0” adds nothing, and both computations describe the same elements. (c) There is no A_0 \in \emptyset to cut the set out of. Without an ambient set, the condition “x \in S for every S \in \emptyset” holds for every set x, vacuously; so  igcap \emptyset would be a set of which every set is an element, and there is no such set (@fd2:thm-russell). C. Going deeper [C1: What the empty-set axiom really says; intersections as greatest lower bounds] 1. Show that (Z2) follows from (Z6), once some set A is known to exist. 2. Let \sS be a non-empty set. Show that  igcap \sS \subseteq S for every S \in \sS, and that every set C with C \subseteq S for all S \in \sS satisfies C \subseteq  igcap \sS. Deduce that  igcap \{A, B\} = A \cap B for all sets A, B. [Hint 1] For (a), cut a set out of A by a property that nothing has. For (b), unwind the membership condition of  igcap \sS from @prp-zf-basic-sets (c). [Hint 2] For (a): consider \{ x \in A : x 
e x \}. For (b): let x \in  igcap \sS and S \in \sS; what does the condition say at this S? (a) Let A be a set. By (Z6) with the property 
eg(x = x), the set E \coloneqq \{ x \in A : x 
e x \} exists. If x \in E, then x 
e x, which contradicts x = x (ulename{{=}I}, @fd1:def-rules-equality). So E has no elements, and (Z2) holds. Thus in the presence of (Z6), (Z2) says only “there is a set”. The Axiom of Infinity of Section 1.3 also says that a set exists, so it could replace (Z2) altogether; that is how the full system is often stated, with the clause “\emptyset \in I” of Section 1.3 read as “I has an element with no elements”, so that the symbol \emptyset is not needed before (Z2) is. (In the logic of Logic and Proof, Chapter 4 even “there is a set” can be derived: ulename{{=}I} gives x = x, and ulename{\exists I} gives \exists x\, (x = x), because every domain is non-empty, Logic and Proof, Section 4.11. We keep (Z2) anyway, so that the axioms say plainly where the first set comes from.) (b) Let x \in  igcap \sS and S \in \sS. By the membership condition of @prp-zf-basic-sets (c), x lies in every member of \sS, in particular in S. So  igcap \sS \subseteq S. Now let C be a set with C \subseteq S for every S \in \sS, and let x \in C. Then x \in S for every S \in \sS. Choose A_0 \in \sS (possible, as \sS is non-empty); then x \in A_0 as well, and so x satisfies the defining condition of  igcap \sS. Hence C \subseteq  igcap \sS. For \sS = \{A, B\}, which is non-empty, the members are exactly A and B (@prp-zf-basic-sets (b)). By the first part with S = A and with S = B,  igcap \{A, B\} \subseteq A and  igcap \{A, B\} \subseteq B, so  igcap \{A, B\} \subseteq A \cap B. Conversely, A \cap B \subseteq A and A \cap B \subseteq B, so A \cap B \subseteq S for every S \in \{A, B\}, and the second part gives A \cap B \subseteq  igcap \{A, B\}. Hence  igcap \{A, B\} = A \cap B (@fd2:prp-subset-antisymmetric). In words, (b) says that  igcap \sS is the largest set contained in every member of \sS: it is contained in each of them, and it contains every other set that is. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: (a) produces a set with no elements by (Z6) from a given set, with a property that no set has, and proves it has no elements. - 2: (b) shows  igcap \sS \subseteq S from the membership condition, at the given S. - 3: (b) shows C \subseteq  igcap \sS, placing x in the ambient member A_0 as well as in every S. - 2: deduces  igcap \{A, B\} = A \cap B using that the members of \{A, B\} are exactly A and B: by double inclusion,  igcap \{A, B\} \subseteq A \cap B from the first half of (b) at S = A and S = B, and A \cap B \subseteq  igcap \{A, B\} from the second half with C = A \cap B, then @fd2:prp-subset-antisymmetric (or (Z1)). A solution that compares membership conditions directly earns the same 2. Fatal errors (0 for the step): using a set of all sets, or  igcap \emptyset; in (a), assuming \emptyset exists in order to prove (Z2).

title: 1.2 Ordered Pairs Built from Sets
content:
Ordered Pairs Built from Sets Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 1.3 introduced the ordered pair (@fd2:def-ordered-pair) as an object with one property, the characteristic property, and said that such an object could be built from sets. Section 1.1 has only sets to build with, and its pair \{a, b\} forgets which element came first. This section repairs that with one idea: mark the first coordinate by putting it in a set of its own. It proves that the result has the characteristic property, so that every pair of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 1 to 3 can be read as a set, and then recovers the product A 	imes B and the working rules (W1)–(W5) of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 1.1 from the axioms, in the form proved here: (W2) for lists written out in the text, (W3) for families of subsets of a given set, and (W5) for pairs. The rest of (W2) and (W5) comes in Section 1.6; (W3) for families with no ambient set needs the axiom of Replacement. Order from sets The problem. The set \{a, b\} of @prp-zf-basic-sets (b) is symmetric: \{a, b\} = \{b, a\}. A pair must not be. We want a set, built from a and b by the axioms, from which we can read off which of the two came first, and the second coordinate after that. Here is one way to see what to do. In \{a, b\} the two elements are on an equal footing; we must give a a role that b does not have. Put a into every member of the pair, and b into one member only. The first coordinate is the one in every member. [Ordered Pair as a Set] For sets a and b, the ordered pair of a and b is the set (a, b) \coloneqq \{\{a\}, \{a, b\}\} . Its first coordinate is a and its second coordinate is b. The pair is a set of the axioms: (Z3) gives \{a\} = \{a, a\} and \{a, b\}, and (Z3) once more gives the set whose elements are these two (@prp-zf-basic-sets (b)). In words: the members of (a, b) are the sets \{a\} and \{a, b\}, which coincide when a = b. Sets of this form are called Kuratowski pairs. The first coordinate lies in both members; the second lies in the member \{a, b\}, and in \{a\} only if it equals a. Examples, simplest first. - (a, a) = \{\{a\}, \{a, a\}\} = \{\{a\}, \{a\}\} = \{\{a\}\}. This is the degenerate case: the two members coincide, and the pair has one member. It matters, because a proof that speaks of “the two members of a pair” silently excludes it. - (\{\emptyset\}, \emptyset) = \{\{\{\emptyset\}\}, \{\{\emptyset\}, \emptyset\}\}. Its two members are different: \emptyset lies in the second and not in the first, whose only element is \{\emptyset\}. - Swap the coordinates: (\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}) = \{\{\emptyset\}, \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\}\}. The second member is the same as before, \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\}; the singleton member has changed from \{\{\emptyset\}\} to \{\emptyset\}. So (\{\emptyset\}, \emptyset) 
e (\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}), and the singleton member is what records the order. Why this definition: shorter encodings fail. It is natural to try something simpler first. The next example shows three simpler sets, built from a and b with a written first, none of which is a pair. [Three Encodings That Lose Information] Consider the claim: any set built from a and b in which a is mentioned first is an ordered pair, that is, has the characteristic property. Test it on the three encodings 	ext{(i) } \{a, b\}, \qquad 	ext{(ii) } \{\{a\}, \{b\}\}, \qquad 	ext{(iii) } \{a, \{b\}\} . The claim is false, and each encoding has its own counterexample. (i) With a = \emptyset, b = \{\emptyset\} and with the coordinates swapped, the encoding gives \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\} both times, although \emptyset 
e \{\emptyset\}. The order is lost. (ii) The same two inputs give \{\{\emptyset\}, \{\{\emptyset\}\}\} both times: the encoding is \{\{a\}, \{b\}\} = \{\{b\}, \{a\}\}, again symmetric in a and b. (iii) This one is not symmetric, and it fails in a less obvious way. Take a = \{\{\emptyset\}\}, b = \emptyset, and c = \{\emptyset\}, d = \{\emptyset\}. Then \{a, \{b\}\} = \{\{\{\emptyset\}\}, \{\emptyset\}\}, \qquad \{c, \{d\}\} = \{\{\emptyset\}, \{\{\emptyset\}\}\}, the same set, by (Z1). But a 
e c: the only element of a = \{\{\emptyset\}\} is \{\emptyset\}, which is not \emptyset, so \emptyset \in c and \emptyset 
otin a. So equal encodings do not force equal first coordinates. The trouble is that \{b\} can coincide with a first coordinate, and the encoding cannot tell which of its elements was meant as “a”. The definition avoids both failures. Both of its members are built from a, so neither can be mistaken for a lone coordinate, and the member \{a\} singles out a. Another encoding, often called the Wiener pair, uses \emptyset as a marker; exercise C3 asks you to show that it has the characteristic property. The lesson of (iii) is a habit: a proposed encoding is tested against the characteristic property with all inputs, including inputs that are themselves made of the sets being encoded. “The smaller member” names nothing when a = b. It is tempting to read off the first coordinate as “the element of the smaller member” and the second as “the new element of the larger member”. When a = b, the pair (a, a) = \{\{a\}\} has a single member, and there is no smaller and larger. An argument that compares the two members of (a, b) must treat a = b as a case of its own. The characteristic property Here is what makes the definition the right one: the set (a, b) determines a and b, each in its place. [Characteristic Property of Pairs] For all sets a, b, c, d, (a, b) = (c, d) \iff a = c 	ext{ and } b = d . Try it first (ten minutes): given \{\{a\}, \{a, b\}\} = \{\{c\}, \{c, d\}\}, get a = c first; then ask what changes when a = b. The attempt goes well at first. The member \{a\} of the left side is a member of the right side, so \{a\} = \{c\} or \{a\} = \{c, d\}, and either way @prp-zf-basic-sets (d) gives a = c. Then \{a, b\} must be one of \{c\}, \{c, d\}, and the natural move is to say “it is \{c, d\}, the larger one”, giving \{a, b\} = \{a, d\} and so b = d. That move is where the attempt runs into the warning above. If a = b, then \{a, b\} = \{a\} and it may well equal \{c\}; if c = d, the right side has a single member. So the proof splits: when a = b, the left side is \{\{a\}\}, and both members of the right side must equal \{a\}; when a 
e b, both sides have two different members, and the matching above goes through. Before reading on: where is a 
e b used? (\Leftarrow) If a = c and b = d, then (a, b) = (c, d) by ulename{{=}E}. (\Rightarrow) Suppose (a, b) = (c, d), that is, \{\{a\}, \{a, b\}\} = \{\{c\}, \{c, d\}\}. Either a = b or a 
e b, and we take the cases in turn. Case 1: a = b. Then \{a, b\} = \{a\}, so (a, b) = \{\{a\}\}. The members \{c\} and \{c, d\} of (c, d) are members of \{\{a\}\}, so \{c\} = \{a\} and \{c, d\} = \{a\}. By @prp-zf-basic-sets (d), the second equation gives a = c and c = d. Hence a = c, and b = a = c = d. Case 2: a 
e b. First, c 
e d. Indeed, if c = d, then (c, d) = \{\{c\}\} as in Case 1, so the member \{a, b\} of (a, b) equals \{c\}, and @prp-zf-basic-sets (d) gives c = a and a = b, which contradicts a 
e b. Next, \{a\} \in (a, b) = (c, d), so \{a\} = \{c\} or \{a\} = \{c, d\}. The second would give c = d by @prp-zf-basic-sets (d), which we have excluded. So \{a\} = \{c\}, and a = c by the same proposition. Finally, \{a, b\} \in (c, d), so \{a, b\} = \{c\} or \{a, b\} = \{c, d\}. The first would give a = c and c = b by @prp-zf-basic-sets (d), hence a = b, which is excluded. So \{a, b\} = \{c, d\} = \{a, d\}, using c = a. By @prp-zf-basic-sets (d), (a = a \wedge b = d) \vee (a = d \wedge b = a); in the first disjunct b = d, and in the second b = a = d. So b = d. In both cases a = c and b = d. This proves the theorem. So a 
e b is used twice in Case 2: to exclude c = d, and to exclude \{a, b\} = \{c\}. Once both are excluded, each side has exactly two different members, and they can be matched. Alternatively, the coordinates can be read off a pair p = (a, b) by two set operations. The members of p are \{a\} and \{a, b\} (@prp-zf-basic-sets (b)). An object lies in both if and only if it equals a, since it must lie in \{a\}, and a \in \{a, b\}; so  igcap p = \{a\} (@prp-zf-basic-sets (c)). And  igcup p = \{a\} \cup \{a, b\} = \{a, b\}. So a is the unique element of  igcap p. And  igcup p \setminus  igcap p = \{a, b\} \setminus \{a\} is \{b\} if b 
e a, and \emptyset if b = a; so b is the unique element of  igcup p \setminus  igcap p when that set is non-empty, and b = a when it is empty. Both coordinates are thus determined by the set p alone, which is the characteristic property again. The case split has not gone away here: it is the empty and non-empty cases of  igcup p \setminus  igcap p. Comparing the unions of two pairs directly avoids it: from \{a, b\} = \{c, d\} with c = a, @prp-zf-basic-sets (d) gives b = d in both of its disjuncts. What this pays. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 1.3 took the ordered pair as given, with the characteristic property, and said after @fd2:def-ordered-pair that nothing else about pairs is used in Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1, apart from one working convention. From here on, the pair (a, b) of @fd2:def-ordered-pair is the set of @def-kuratowski-pair, and the property it was assumed to have is @thm-kuratowski-pair. Everything built on pairs becomes a set built by the axioms: a relation from A to B is a subset of A 	imes B (@fd2:def-relation), and a function X 	o Y is the pair (G, Y) of its graph and codomain (@fd2:def-function), now a Kuratowski pair of two sets. The working convention said that a pair is not a number, and that a triple is not a pair. In the picture of this chapter numbers and tuples will be sets too, so both clauses become statements to be checked: Section 1.4 checks the first for the natural numbers (@prp-pair-not-natural), and Section 1.6 checks the second (@prp-tuples-as-sets (c)). Products, and the working rules recovered The working rule (W5) said that the pairs with coordinates in given sets form a set. With pairs built from sets, this is now something to prove. [The Product Exists] For all sets A and B there is exactly one set A 	imes B whose elements are exactly the pairs (a, b) with a \in A and b \in B: p \in A 	imes B \iff \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ \ p = (a, b) . Separation can only cut a set out of a set we already have, so we first need some set containing every pair (a, b) with a \in A and b \in B. The members \{a\} and \{a, b\} of such a pair are subsets of A \cup B, so the pair is a set of subsets of A \cup B: an element of \powerset{\powerset{A \cup B}}. Cut A 	imes B out of that. Let U \coloneqq A \cup B, a set by @prp-zf-basic-sets (c), and let W \coloneqq \powerset{\powerset{U}}, a set by (Z5) twice. Let a \in A and b \in B. Then a, b \in U, so \{a\} \subseteq U and \{a, b\} \subseteq U; that is, \{a\} \in \powerset{U} and \{a, b\} \in \powerset{U}. Hence (a, b) = \{\{a\}, \{a, b\}\} \subseteq \powerset{U}, that is, (a, b) \in W. By (Z6) with ambient set W and parameters A, B, let A 	imes B \coloneqq \{ p \in W : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ \ p = (a, b) \} . (The property is admissible: “p = (a, b)” unwinds into \in and =, as Section 1.1 explained for defined symbols.) If p \in A 	imes B, then p = (a, b) for some a \in A, b \in B. Conversely, if p = (a, b) with a \in A and b \in B, then p \in W by the first paragraph, so p \in A 	imes B. This is the displayed membership condition. Any two sets with this condition are equal by (Z1). The product of @fd2:def-cartesian-product has the same membership condition, so it is this set; and X^2 \coloneqq X 	imes X is a set too. The construction never needed a “set of all pairs”: every pair it collects lies in the set W, which depends on A and B. The working rules of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 1.1 can now be checked against the axioms one by one. [The Working Rules from the Axioms] The axioms (Z1)–(Z6) give the working rules (W1)–(W5) of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 1.1 in the following form. 1. For every set A and every admissible property P(x) (one whose unwinding is a formula of the language, Section 1.1), \{ x \in A : P(x) \} is a set. 2. For each list a_1, \dots, a_n written out in the text, entry by entry, there is a set \{a_1, \dots, a_n\} whose elements are exactly a_1, \dots, a_n. 3. For sets A and B, A \cup B is a set. For a set X and a family (A_i)_{i \in I} of subsets of X, given as a function I 	o \powerset{X} (@fd2:def-indexed-family), the union  igcup_{i \in I} A_i and the intersection  igcap_{i \in I} A_i of @fd2:def-family-union-intersection are sets. 4. For every set X, \powerset{X} is a set. 5. For sets A and B, A 	imes B is a set. Three of the rules are already in hand. For a written list, add one entry at a time with \cup. For a union of a family of subsets of X, the ambient set X is what lets (Z6) apply. (W1) is (Z6), applied to the unwinding of P(x), with the sets P mentions as parameters; (W4) is (Z5), and (W5) is @prp-cartesian-product-exists. (W2) We build the set one entry at a time. The first set is \{a_1\}, by (Z3). If \{a_1, \dots, a_k\} has been built and the list has a further entry a_{k+1}, let \{a_1, \dots, a_{k+1}\} \coloneqq \{a_1, \dots, a_k\} \cup \{a_{k+1}\}, a set by @prp-zf-basic-sets (c). Its elements are those of \{a_1, \dots, a_k\} together with a_{k+1}, that is, the x with x = a_1 \vee \dots \vee x = a_{k+1}. A list written out in the text has a definite number of entries, and the step is applied once for each entry after the first. (W3) A \cup B is a set by @prp-zf-basic-sets (c). Now let f \colon I 	o \powerset{X} be the function with f(i) = A_i, and let G be its graph. By (Z6) with ambient set X and parameters I, G, V \coloneqq \{ x \in X : \exists i \in I\ \, x \in f(i) \} is a set; “x \in f(i)” unwinds to \exists S\,  igl((i, S) \in G \wedge x \in S igr). Every element of every A_i lies in X, since A_i \subseteq X; so x \in V if and only if x \in A_i for some i \in I, the membership condition of @fd2:def-family-union-intersection (a). Hence V is the union. The intersection of @fd2:def-family-union-intersection (b) is defined there by a set-builder inside X, so it exists by (Z6). The proof of (W2) deserves a second look, because of what it does not prove. It is not a proof “for every n \in 
N”: we have no 
N yet, so the number of entries cannot be a variable. It is a recipe which, applied to any list actually written down, produces its set in as many steps as the list has entries. That is all (W2) is used for in Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 1.1, but Chapters 2 and 3 of that volume also write \{x_1, \dots, x_n\} for a variable n, for a function x defined on \{1, \dots, n\} (@fd2:prp-finite-max, @fd2:def-finite). That second half of (W2) needs the natural numbers and \{1, \dots, n\} as sets; it is part (d) of a proposition in Section 1.6, which also builds n-tuples and so gives (W5) for them. The rest of the list is paid elsewhere. A family of sets with no ambient set X needs the axiom of Replacement, which belongs to the volume on set theory. And (W6), “
N, 
Z, 
Q, 
R are sets”, becomes a series of constructions: 
N in Section 1.3, 
Z and 
Q in Chapter 2, and 
R later in this volume, from Cauchy sequences of rationals. Write (\emptyset, \emptyset) and (\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}) as sets, using only braces and \emptyset. (\emptyset, \emptyset) = \{\{\emptyset\}, \{\emptyset, \emptyset\}\} = \{\{\emptyset\}\}, a set with one member, as for every pair (a, a). And (\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}) = \{\{\emptyset\}, \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\}\}, with two different members. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. In the proof of @thm-kuratowski-pair, where is the hypothesis a 
e b of Case 2 used, and what replaces the argument when a = b? 2. Run the proof of @thm-kuratowski-pair on the equation (\{\emptyset\}, \emptyset) = (c, d): which case applies, and what does each step give? 3. Which axioms make (a, b) a set? 4. State the idea of the proof of @thm-kuratowski-pair in two sentences. (a) Twice: to show c 
e d (if c = d, the member \{a, b\} would equal \{c\}, forcing a = b), and to rule out \{a, b\} = \{c\} (which would force a = b). When a = b, the pair (a, b) = \{\{a\}\} has one member, so both members of (c, d) must equal \{a\}, and \{c, d\} = \{a\} gives c = d = a by @prp-zf-basic-sets (d). (b) Here a = \{\emptyset\} and b = \emptyset, and a 
e b because \emptyset \in a and \emptyset 
otin b; so Case 2 applies. Step 1: c 
e d. Step 2: \{a\} = \{\{\emptyset\}\} is a member of (c, d), and it cannot be \{c, d\}, so \{\{\emptyset\}\} = \{c\} and c = \{\emptyset\}. Step 3: \{a, b\} = \{\{\emptyset\}, \emptyset\} is a member of (c, d) and is not \{c\}, so \{\{\emptyset\}, \emptyset\} = \{c, d\} = \{\{\emptyset\}, d\}, which gives d = \emptyset. So (c, d) = (\{\emptyset\}, \emptyset) forces c = \{\emptyset\} and d = \emptyset. (c) (Z3), three times: once for \{a\} = \{a, a\}, once for \{a, b\}, and once for the set with these two elements. Uniqueness of each is (Z1). (d) The singleton member \{a\} of the pair must be one of the members of the other pair, which pins down the first coordinate. When a 
e b the remaining members must match and give the second coordinate; when a = b the pair has a single member, and that case is handled on its own. B. Practice [B1: Coordinates from unions and intersections] Let p = (a, b). Compute  igcap p and  igcup p, and show that, when a 
e b, the set  igcup p \setminus  igcap p has exactly one element, namely b. The members of p are \{a\} and \{a, b\}. An object lies in both if and only if it equals a (it is in \{a\}), and a is in \{a, b\}; so  igcap p = \{a\}. An object lies in at least one member if and only if it equals a or b; so  igcup p = \{a, b\}. Now let a 
e b. Then x \in  igcup p \setminus  igcap p if and only if (x = a or x = b) and x 
e a, that is, if and only if x = b and x 
e a. Since b 
e a, the element b satisfies this, and any x satisfying it equals b. Hence  igcup p \setminus  igcap p = \{b\}. [B2: Nested pairs] Write ((a, b), c) for the pair whose first coordinate is the pair (a, b). 1. Prove that ((a, b), c) = ((a', b'), c') if and only if a = a', b = b' and c = c'. 2. Determine whether ((\emptyset, \emptyset), \emptyset) = (\emptyset, (\emptyset, \emptyset)). Justify your answer. (a) (\Leftarrow) by ulename{{=}E}. (\Rightarrow) By @thm-kuratowski-pair applied to the outer pairs, (a, b) = (a', b') and c = c'. By @thm-kuratowski-pair again, (a, b) = (a', b') gives a = a' and b = b'. (b) No. Both sides are pairs, so by @thm-kuratowski-pair they are equal only if their first coordinates are equal. The first coordinates are (\emptyset, \emptyset) = \{\{\emptyset\}\} and \emptyset, and \{\{\emptyset\}\} 
e \emptyset, since \{\emptyset\} \in \{\{\emptyset\}\}. Hence the two pairs are different. C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: Kuratowski pairs] Prove that for all sets a, b, c, d, \{\{a\}, \{a, b\}\} = \{\{c\}, \{c, d\}\} if and only if a = c and b = d. You may use @prp-zf-basic-sets. This is @thm-kuratowski-pair; its proof above is a complete answer. In outline: (\Leftarrow) is substitution. For (\Rightarrow), if a = b, the left side is \{\{a\}\}, so \{c, d\} = \{a\}, giving c = d = a = b. If a 
e b, then c 
e d (else the left side would have a single member); \{a\} equals \{c\} or \{c, d\}, the second being excluded by c 
e d, so a = c; and \{a, b\} equals \{c\} or \{c, d\}, the first being excluded by a 
e b, so \{a, b\} = \{a, d\} and b = d. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 1: proves (\Leftarrow) by substitution. - 2: in the case a = b, identifies (a, b) = \{\{a\}\} and concludes c = d = a, hence a = c and b = d. - 3: in the case a 
e b, shows \{a\} = \{c\} or \{a\} = \{c, d\}, excludes the second (via c 
e d, itself proved), and concludes a = c. - 3: obtains b = d from the remaining members, excluding \{a, b\} = \{c\} and justifying \{a, b\} = \{a, d\} \Rightarrow b = d. - 1: joins the two cases into the conclusion. Fatal errors (0 for the step): treating \{a, b\} as ordered, or matching “smaller with smaller and larger with larger” without justification; omitting the case a = b in an argument that matches the members of the two pairs (or reads b off  igcup p \setminus  igcap p). Second route (through  igcap p and  igcup p, as in the “Alternatively” paragraph): reading a off  igcap p = \{a\} earns the 3 points for a = c; reading b off  igcup p \setminus  igcap p, with its empty case a = b treated separately, earns the 3 points for b = d and the 2 points of the case a = b. Third route (comparing  igcap and  igcup of the two pairs): showing  igcap (x, y) = \{x\} and  igcup (x, y) = \{x, y\} for every pair (no case split is needed), then getting a = c from \{a\} = \{c\} and b = d from \{a, b\} = \{c, d\} = \{a, d\} by @prp-zf-basic-sets (d), earns the 3 + 3 points and also the 2 + 1 points of the case structure; with (\Leftarrow) this is 10. [C2: Find the error] Here is an argument for @thm-kuratowski-pair, direction (\Rightarrow). (1) Let (a, b) = (c, d). (2) Matching the members of \{\{a\}, \{a, b\}\} and \{\{c\}, \{c, d\}\} in the order written, \{a\} = \{c\} and \{a, b\} = \{c, d\}. (3) From \{a\} = \{c\}, a = c. (4) Then \{a, b\} = \{a, d\}, and so b = d. Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the first line that fails, the rule it breaks, and give a counterexample to that step. The conclusion is true: it is @thm-kuratowski-pair. The argument does not prove it. The first failing line is (2). It uses the rule “if \{P, Q\} = \{P', Q'\}, then P = P' and Q = Q'”, which treats a set with two members as if it were ordered. No result of Section 1.1 gives this rule: @prp-zf-basic-sets (d) allows the crossed matching P = Q' and Q = P' as well. A counterexample to the step: take P = Q' = \emptyset and Q = P' = \{\emptyset\}. Then \{P, Q\} = \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\} = \{P', Q'\} by (Z1), but P 
e P', since \emptyset \in \{\emptyset\} and \emptyset 
otin \emptyset. For pairs the two equations of line (2) happen to be true, since they follow from the theorem. But showing that the members of (a, b) and (c, d) match in this way is the work of the proof: Case 1 handles a = b, where (a, b) = \{\{a\}\} has a single member, and Case 2 rules out c = d and \{a, b\} = \{c\} before matching. So line (2) assumes what is to be proved. This is entry (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue: line (2) cites a general rule that is false, and for pairs the matching it asserts is the goal itself. A second, lesser point concerns line (4). “\{a, b\} = \{a, d\}, so b = d” is true for all a, b, d, but it needs a reason: @prp-zf-basic-sets (d) with c = a. The disjunct a = a \wedge b = d gives b = d directly, and the disjunct a = d \wedge b = a gives b = a = d. No hypothesis b 
e a is needed, and an answer saying so is correct. Repair: split into the cases a = b and a 
e b, as in the proof of the theorem. [C3: Wiener’s encoding] For sets a and b let W(a, b) \coloneqq \{\{\{a\}, \emptyset\}, \{\{b\}\}\}. Prove that W(a, b) = W(c, d) if and only if a = c and b = d. [Hint 1] The empty set is a marker. Which member of W(a, b) has \emptyset as an element? [Hint 2] Let P \coloneqq \{\{a\}, \emptyset\} and Q \coloneqq \{\{b\}\}. Show first that \emptyset \in P and \emptyset 
otin Q. (\Leftarrow) by ulename{{=}E}. (\Rightarrow) Let P \coloneqq \{\{a\}, \emptyset\}, Q \coloneqq \{\{b\}\}, P' \coloneqq \{\{c\}, \emptyset\}, Q' \coloneqq \{\{d\}\}, and suppose \{P, Q\} = \{P', Q'\}. We have \emptyset \in P and \emptyset \in P'. On the other hand \emptyset 
otin Q: the only element of Q is \{b\}, and \{b\} 
e \emptyset because b \in \{b\}. Likewise \emptyset 
otin Q'. So P 
e Q and P' 
e Q', and in each set of members exactly one member has \emptyset as an element. Since P \in \{P', Q'\}, P = P' or P = Q'; the second is impossible, since \emptyset \in P and \emptyset 
otin Q'. So P = P'. Since Q \in \{P', Q'\}, Q = P' or Q = Q'; the first is impossible, since \emptyset \in P' and \emptyset 
otin Q. So Q = Q'. From \{\{a\}, \emptyset\} = \{\{c\}, \emptyset\}, @prp-zf-basic-sets (d) gives \{a\} = \{c\} (and \emptyset = \emptyset), or \{a\} = \emptyset (and \emptyset = \{c\}). The second is impossible, as a \in \{a\}. So \{a\} = \{c\}, and a = c by @prp-zf-basic-sets (d) again. From \{\{b\}\} = \{\{d\}\}, the same proposition gives \{b\} = \{d\} and then b = d. Unlike @thm-kuratowski-pair, this proof needs no case a = b: the marker \emptyset tells the two members apart whatever a and b are. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: shows \emptyset \in P and \emptyset 
otin Q (with the reason \{b\} 
e \emptyset), and likewise for P', Q'. - 3: matches P = P' and Q = Q', excluding the crossed matches by the marker. - 2: derives a = c from P = P', excluding \{a\} = \emptyset. - 2: derives b = d from Q = Q'. Fatal errors (0 for the step): assuming the members match in the order written; using @thm-kuratowski-pair, which is about a different set.

title: 1.3 Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers
content:
Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers Logic and Proof, Chapter 3 described the natural numbers as what we reach from 0 by adding 1, again and again, and nothing else; induction (@fd1:ax-induction) was the precise form of “nothing else”. In this chapter every object is a set, so we need a set to play 0 and an operation on sets to play “add 1”. This section chooses both, adds the one axiom that lets the repetition be completed into a set, and proves induction as a theorem about the set it produces. Going one step further The empty set is the only set we can name without first having another one, so it will be 0. For “add one” we want an operation that, started from \emptyset, keeps producing new sets, never returning to one already met. Putting a set inside itself as an element does that, as we shall see. The successor of a set adds the set itself as an element. [Successor of a set] For every set x, the successor of x is the set \mathrm{S}(x) \coloneqq x \cup \{x\} . In words: the elements of \mathrm{S}(x) are the elements of x, together with x itself. So, for every set y, y \in \mathrm{S}(x) \iff y \in x \ 	ext{ or } \ y = x . The set \mathrm{S}(x) exists and is unique: \{x\} is the set \{x, x\} of Pairing (Z3), and x \cup \{x\} =  igcup \{x, \{x\}\} comes from Union (Z4), both by @prp-zf-basic-sets (b), (c). Two facts are visible at once. First, x \in \mathrm{S}(x) for every x. Second, x \subseteq \mathrm{S}(x): the successor keeps every old element and adds x itself, which is a new element whenever x 
otin x. The next section proves n 
otin n for every natural number n. The letter is an upright \mathrm{S}. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1 used an italic S for a set in @fd2:prp-smallest-closed-set, and we are about to use that proposition with this operation as its step; the two letters never stand for the same thing. Start from \emptyset and apply \mathrm{S} repeatedly. [The first natural numbers as sets] Define  egin{aligned} 0 &\coloneqq \emptyset , & 1 &\coloneqq \mathrm{S}(0) , & 2 &\coloneqq \mathrm{S}(1) , \ 3 &\coloneqq \mathrm{S}(2) , & 4 &\coloneqq \mathrm{S}(3) . \end{aligned} Write each of 1, 2, 3, 4 as a set of the earlier numerals, and then using only \emptyset and braces. Check that 0, 1, 2, 3 are four different sets. Each step adds the previous set as a new element:  egin{aligned} 1 &= \emptyset \cup \{0\} = \{0\} = \{\emptyset\} , \ 2 &= 1 \cup \{1\} = \{0, 1\} = \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\} , \ 3 &= 2 \cup \{2\} = \{0, 1, 2\} =  igl\{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}, \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\} igr\} , \ 4 &= 3 \cup \{3\} = \{0, 1, 2, 3\} =  igl\{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}, \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\}, \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}, \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\}\} igr\} . \end{aligned} Written with \emptyset and braces only, 4 already needs eight pairs of braces and eight copies of \emptyset, which is why the numerals are worth having. The four sets differ, by Extensionality (Z1): two sets are equal only if they have the same elements, so it is enough to find an element of one that is not an element of the other. The set 0 has no elements, while 1, 2 and 3 all have the element 0; so 0 differs from each of them. Next, 1 \in 2 and 1 \in 3, but 1 
otin 1: the only element of 1 = \{0\} is 0, and 1 
e 0. So 1 differs from 2 and from 3. Finally 2 \in 3, but 2 
otin 2: the elements of 2 are 0 and 1, and 2 differs from both, as just shown. So 2 
e 3. Each number is the set of the numbers before it: 3 = \{0, 1, 2\}, and 0 = \emptyset because nothing comes before 0. The picture draws a set as a box and its elements as the boxes directly inside it. The box for 3 holds three boxes, which are copies of the boxes for 0, 1 and 2. In general a natural number n will turn out to be the set of the natural numbers less than n, so that n = \{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\} for n 
e 0. That is a theorem, proved later in this chapter once the order on the natural numbers is defined. For now the pattern is only something we have seen in the first five cases. From here to the end of the chapter, the numerals 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots name these sets. They are not real numbers; where the chapter compares the two pictures, it says so. Other choices of “add one” are possible. The rule x \mapsto \{x\} also starts a list of different sets, \emptyset, \{\emptyset\}, \{\{\emptyset\}\}, \dots. With an axiom of infinity stated for that rule, it too would give a set satisfying Peano’s axioms, but not by the proofs of the next section. What it loses is the pattern above: under it, the set playing 3 has one element, not three, and it does not contain the sets playing 0 and 1. The next section’s proofs rest on that pattern, and one of its results fails outright: under x \mapsto \{x\} the set playing 2 is \{\{\emptyset\}\}, which is the pair (\emptyset, \emptyset) of @def-kuratowski-pair, while the next section shows that no pair is a natural number in our sense. The choice x \cup \{x\} makes the order of the numbers into membership, which the chapter uses repeatedly. The successor is defined for every set, not only for numerals, and its result need not look like a number. For x = \{1\} = \{\{\emptyset\}\}, the successor is \mathrm{S}(x) = \{1, \{1\}\}. It does not contain 0, while every numeral after 0 computed above does. A statement about \mathrm{S}(x) that holds for the numerals may fail for other sets; this is why the results below are stated for elements of one particular set. Inductive sets and the axiom of infinity We want a set whose elements are exactly 0, 1, 2, \dots. The dots are the problem: Pairing and Union make each numeral, one at a time, and no axiom so far collects them all. The way out is to describe the property such a set must have, ask for a set with that property, and then cut it down to size. An inductive set contains 0 and never runs out of successors. [Inductive set] A set I is inductive if \emptyset \in I and, for every x \in I, also \mathrm{S}(x) \in I. In words: the first clause gives the set a starting point, and the second says it is closed under the successor, so that applying \mathrm{S} never leads out of it. In symbols, with bounded quantifiers, \emptyset \in I \ \wedge \  orall x \in I \ \ \mathrm{S}(x) \in I . The word “inductive” has another use in the analysis volume of this series, for subsets of the real numbers that contain the number 0 and are closed under x \mapsto x + 1. The shape is the same, but here the starting point is the set \emptyset, the step is \mathrm{S}, and there is no ambient set of real numbers. An inductive set contains all the numerals: 0 = \emptyset by the first clause, then 1 = \mathrm{S}(0) by the second, then 2 = \mathrm{S}(1), and so on, one application of the second clause per numeral. So an inductive set cannot be finite in any naive sense, and nothing we have so far produces one. Non-examples by minimal change come cheaply. The set 4 = \{0, 1, 2, 3\} contains \emptyset and the successors of 0, 1 and 2; only the last successor is missing, since \mathrm{S}(3) = 4 
otin 4: the set 4 has the element 3, and none of 0, 1, 2, 3 does (0 has no elements, and the elements of 1, 2 and 3 are among 0, 1, 2, each different from 3 by @exm-von-neumann-numerals). And \{1, 2, 3, \dots\}, if we had it, would be closed under \mathrm{S} but would miss the starting point. Both clauses do work. Is \{\emptyset\} inductive? Is \{0, 1, 2\}? Neither. \{\emptyset\} contains \emptyset, but \mathrm{S}(\emptyset) = \{\emptyset\} = 1 is not an element of \{\emptyset\}: its only element is \emptyset = 0, and 1 
e 0 because 0 \in 1. So the closure clause fails at x = \emptyset. \{0, 1, 2\} contains 0 and the successors of 0 and 1, but \mathrm{S}(2) = 3 is not among 0, 1, 2: the set 3 has the element 2, and none of 0, 1, 2 does (0 has no elements, the only element of 1 is 0, and the elements of 2 are 0 and 1, both different from 2 by @exm-von-neumann-numerals). So the closure clause fails at x = 2. Axioms (Z1)–(Z6) of @ax-zf-fragment produce each numeral separately, never all of them at once. That they cannot do better, that is, that no inductive set can be shown to exist from (Z1)–(Z6), is a theorem of set theory proper; we state it without proof, and nothing in this book depends on it. So the existence of an inductive set has to be assumed. [Axiom of Infinity] (Z7) There is an inductive set. Everything else the chapter builds, the natural numbers and their arithmetic included, comes from the inductive set of (Z7) by the six axioms of @ax-zf-fragment. The axiom provides some inductive set and says nothing else about it. It may contain sets other than 0, 1, 2, \dots. We cannot simply call it “the set of natural numbers”; we have to carve that set out of it. The least inductive set An inductive set contains the numerals, and perhaps more. To remove anything extra, keep only what lies in every inductive set: whatever a set must contain merely by being inductive. The natural numbers are what every inductive set is forced to contain. There is one obstacle. Separation (Z6) can only cut a set out of a set already given, so we need an ambient set for the natural numbers; and the smallest-closed-set construction of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1 (@fd2:prp-smallest-closed-set) intersects a set of subsets, but the inductive sets are not handed to us as the elements of any set. So we fix one inductive set I and look only at the inductive subsets of I, which do form a set, by Power set and Separation; the theorem below shows that the choice of I does not matter. [The set of natural numbers] Fix an inductive set I, which exists by (Z7). Define \omega \coloneqq \{ x \in I : x \in J 	ext{ for every inductive set } J \subseteq I \} . The elements of \omega are the natural numbers. In words: a natural number is an element of the fixed inductive set I that survives every attempt to shrink I to a smaller inductive set. The set \omega exists by Separation (Z6), with ambient set I, once the condition is a property in the sense of (Z6): a formula of Logic and Proof, Chapter 4’s first-order language with \in and = (@fd1:def-first-order-formula), with I as a parameter. The condition is “for every J, if J \subseteq I and J is inductive, then x \in J”, and, since J \subseteq I abbreviates  orall y \, (y \in J 	o y \in I) as in (Z5) (@fd2:def-subset), the only part not yet written in that language is “J is inductive”. Written out with no abbreviations it is  egin{aligned} &\exists e \,  igl( e \in J \wedge  orall y \, 
eg (y \in e)  igr) \ &\wedge  orall u \, \Bigl( u \in J 	o \exists z \,  igl( z \in J \wedge  orall w \, ( w \in z \leftrightarrow ( w \in u \vee w = u ) )  igr) \Bigr) . \end{aligned} The first line says that J has an element with no elements, which is \emptyset \in J, because \emptyset is the only set with no elements (@prp-zf-basic-sets (a)). The second says that for each u \in J some element z of J has exactly the elements of u \cup \{u\}, which is \mathrm{S}(u) \in J by (Z1). Here is what “least” means, and why the choice of I is harmless. The Least Inductive Set 1. \omega is inductive. 2. \omega \subseteq J for every inductive set J, whether or not J \subseteq I. 3. \omega is the only set with properties (a) and (b). In particular, \omega does not depend on the inductive set I fixed in @def-omega. Part (a) is Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1’s smallest closed set, with I as the ambient set, \emptyset as the starting element and \mathrm{S} as the step: the closed subsets of I are exactly its inductive subsets, and \omega is their intersection. For (b), an inductive J need not lie inside I, so we cut it down to \omega \cap J, which does; then the definition of \omega applies. Part (c) is two inclusions, each an instance of (b). (a) Apply @fd2:prp-smallest-closed-set with X \coloneqq I, the single starting element \emptyset, which lies in I because I is inductive, and the single step x \mapsto \mathrm{S}(x), which turns elements of I into elements of I for the same reason. A subset J \subseteq I is closed in the sense of that proposition exactly when \emptyset \in J and \mathrm{S}(x) \in J for every x \in J, that is, when J is inductive. So the set of closed subsets is \sS \coloneqq \{ J \in \powerset{I} : J 	ext{ is inductive} \} , a set by Power set (Z5) and Separation (Z6); it is non-empty, since I \in \sS. Its intersection  igcap \sS, formed inside I as in @prp-zf-basic-sets (c), is \{ x \in I : x \in J 	ext{ for every } J \in \sS \}, which is \omega. By @fd2:prp-smallest-closed-set,  igcap \sS is closed; that is, \omega is inductive. (b) Let J be an inductive set. The set \omega \cap J exists by (Z6) (@prp-zf-basic-sets (c)), and \omega \cap J \subseteq \omega \subseteq I. It is inductive: \emptyset \in \omega by (a) and \emptyset \in J because J is inductive; and if x \in \omega \cap J, then \mathrm{S}(x) \in \omega by (a) and \mathrm{S}(x) \in J because J is inductive. So \omega \cap J is an inductive subset of I, and by @def-omega every element of \omega lies in it. Hence \omega \subseteq \omega \cap J \subseteq J. (c) Let W be a set that is inductive and is contained in every inductive set. Then W \subseteq \omega, because \omega is inductive by (a); and \omega \subseteq W by (b), because W is inductive. So W = \omega by @fd2:prp-subset-antisymmetric. Now let I' be another inductive set, and let \omega' be the set that @def-omega produces from I'. The proofs of (a) and (b) used nothing about I except that it is inductive, so they apply to \omega' as well: \omega' is inductive and is contained in every inductive set. By what we just proved, \omega' = \omega. This proves the theorem. So \omega is the least inductive set: it is inductive, and it lies inside every inductive set. From now on we forget I. The numerals 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 of @exm-von-neumann-numerals are natural numbers, since \omega is inductive and contains each of them by the argument given after @def-zf-inductive-set. “An inductive set is the set of natural numbers” is false in general. @thm-omega-least-inductive gives \omega \subseteq J for an inductive J, and nothing more. The set-theory volume of this series, using the axiom of Replacement (not part of this chapter), builds the inductive set \omega \cup \{ \omega, \mathrm{S}(\omega), \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(\omega)), \dots \}; it contains \omega itself as an element, and the next section shows that \omega 
otin \omega. Axiom (Z7) does not say that its I is not a set of this kind. What distinguishes \omega among inductive sets is “least”, and every argument about natural numbers must go through \omega, not through an arbitrary inductive set. Induction on the natural numbers Leastness has an immediate consequence. To show that every natural number belongs to some set A, it is enough to show that A is inductive, since then \omega \subseteq A. [Induction on \omega] 1. (Set form.) Let A \subseteq \omega. If 0 \in A, and \mathrm{S}(n) \in A for every n \in A, then A = \omega. 2. (Property form.) Let P(n) be a property, that is, a formula of the first-order language with \in and =, possibly with other variables as parameters. If P(0) holds and, for every n \in \omega, P(n) implies P(\mathrm{S}(n)), then P(n) holds for every n \in \omega. (a) The hypotheses say that A is inductive. By @thm-omega-least-inductive (b), \omega \subseteq A. With A \subseteq \omega, @fd2:prp-subset-antisymmetric gives A = \omega. (b) Let A \coloneqq \{ n \in \omega : P(n) \}, a set by (Z6). Then 0 \in A, because 0 \in \omega by @thm-omega-least-inductive (a) and P(0) holds. Let n \in A. Then n \in \omega and P(n), so P(\mathrm{S}(n)) by hypothesis, and \mathrm{S}(n) \in \omega because \omega is inductive; hence \mathrm{S}(n) \in A. By (a), A = \omega, which says that P(n) holds for every n \in \omega. Compare part (b) with the principle of induction, @fd1:ax-induction. Read with \omega in place of 
N, and with \mathrm{S}(n) in place of n + 1, the two statements are the same; and once addition is defined, later in this chapter, n + 1 will be \mathrm{S}(n). The difference lies in their status. In Logic and Proof, Chapter 3, induction was an axiom, a basic property of 
N taken on trust. Here it is a theorem, proved from the seven axioms (Z1)–(Z7) about sets, and the proof is three lines long because all the work went into the definition of \omega: the natural numbers were defined as what every inductive set contains, and induction says exactly that. The proof of (b) is the model for the inductions in the rest of this chapter. Show the set is inductive. To prove P(n) for every n \in \omega, form \{ n \in \omega : P(n) \} and show that it has 0 as an element and is closed under \mathrm{S}. Here is the move once, on a statement about the shape of natural numbers: every n \in \omega is 0, or is 1, or has 1 as an element. Let A \coloneqq \{ n \in \omega : n = 0 	ext{ or } n = 1 	ext{ or } 1 \in n \}, a set by (Z6). Then 0 \in A by the first alternative. Let n \in A; there are three cases. If n = 0, then \mathrm{S}(n) = 1, which satisfies the second alternative. If n = 1, then \mathrm{S}(n) = 2 = \{0, 1\}, which has 1 as an element. If 1 \in n, then 1 \in n \subseteq \mathrm{S}(n). In every case \mathrm{S}(n) \in A, since also \mathrm{S}(n) \in \omega because \omega is inductive (@thm-omega-least-inductive (a)). By @thm-omega-induction (a), A = \omega. Two features of this small proof recur. The property carried along is a disjunction, because “1 \in n” alone is false at n = 0 and n = 1, and an induction can only carry a property that holds at the start. And the step is a case split along the disjunction, with one case for each alternative; dropping a case would be the error (N7) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. In the proof just given, which case of the step produces the first natural number that satisfies the third alternative “1 \in n”, and which number is it? The case n = 1. It produces \mathrm{S}(1) = 2 = \{0, 1\}, which has 1 as an element. Neither 0 nor 1 has 1 as an element (0 has no elements, and the only element of 1 is 0 
e 1), so 2 is the first. From then on the third case passes “1 \in n” to \mathrm{S}(n), because n \subseteq \mathrm{S}(n). The next section uses the move five times in a row, to show that \omega satisfies Peano’s axioms. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. List the elements of 3 and of 4 as sets of numerals. 2. Is 2 \subseteq 3? Is 2 \in 3? 3. True or false, with a reason: every inductive set has 5 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(4) as an element. 4. Write “J is not inductive” in symbols, with the negation moved inward until it stands only in front of a membership statement. (a) 3 = \{0, 1, 2\} and 4 = \{0, 1, 2, 3\}, by @exm-von-neumann-numerals. (b) Both are true. The elements of 2 are 0 and 1, and both are elements of 3 = \{0, 1, 2\}; so 2 \subseteq 3 (@fd2:def-subset). And 2 is itself one of the listed elements of 3, so 2 \in 3. A set can be both an element and a subset of another set; for numerals this will turn out to be the rule, not an accident. (c) True. Let J be inductive. Then 0 = \emptyset \in J by the first clause of @def-zf-inductive-set, and the second clause applied five times gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 \in J, each being the successor of the one before. (d) “J is inductive” is \emptyset \in J \wedge  orall x \in J \ \ \mathrm{S}(x) \in J. Its negation is 
eg igl( \emptyset \in J \wedge  orall x \in J \ \ \mathrm{S}(x) \in J  igr) , which by De Morgan’s law @fd1:prp-de-morgan (d) and (c) is equivalent to 
eg(\emptyset \in J) \vee 
eg orall x \in J \ \ \mathrm{S}(x) \in J, and by @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation (a), the bounded form of @fd1:prp-quantifier-negation, to \emptyset 
otin J \ \vee \ \exists x \in J \ \ \mathrm{S}(x) 
otin J . In words: J lacks the starting point, or some element of J has its successor outside J. B. Practice [B1: Intersections and differences] Let J and K be inductive sets.
