Prove that J \cap K is inductive. Is J \setminus \{\emptyset\} inductive? Justify your answer, and say which clause of the definition holds and which fails. The set J \cap K exists by (Z6) (@prp-zf-basic-sets (c)). It contains \emptyset, since \emptyset \in J and \emptyset \in K. If x \in J \cap K, then \mathrm{S}(x) \in J because J is inductive and x \in J, and \mathrm{S}(x) \in K likewise; so \mathrm{S}(x) \in J \cap K. Hence J \cap K is inductive. The set J \setminus \{\emptyset\} is not inductive: it does not contain \emptyset, so the first clause fails. The second clause holds: if x \in J \setminus \{\emptyset\}, then \mathrm{S}(x) \in J, and \mathrm{S}(x) 
e \emptyset because x \in \mathrm{S}(x); so \mathrm{S}(x) \in J \setminus \{\emptyset\}. This is a non-example by minimal change: removing one element breaks exactly one clause. [B2: Zero or a successor] Prove that every n \in \omega is \emptyset or is \mathrm{S}(k) for some k \in \omega, by showing that the set A \coloneqq \{ n \in \omega : n = \emptyset 	ext{ or } n = \mathrm{S}(k) 	ext{ for some } k \in \omega \} is inductive. The set A exists by (Z6), and A \subseteq \omega. It contains 0 = \emptyset by the first alternative. Let n \in A. Then n \in \omega, so \mathrm{S}(n) \in \omega because \omega is inductive (@thm-omega-least-inductive (a)), and \mathrm{S}(n) satisfies the second alternative with k \coloneqq n \in \omega. So \mathrm{S}(n) \in A. By @thm-omega-induction (a), A = \omega, which is the claim. The step never used the hypothesis that n satisfies one of the alternatives, only that n \in \omega. That is legitimate: the step’s conclusion was reached outright, and induction still does the work of saying that every natural number is reached from 0 by successors. C. Going deeper [C1: Two steps back] 1. Prove that every n \in \omega is 0, or is 1, or is \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(k)) for some k \in \omega. 2. Let I be an arbitrary inductive set. Running the argument of (a) on \{ x \in I : x = 0 	ext{ or } x = 1 	ext{ or } x = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(k)) 	ext{ for some } k \in I \}, what does it prove about the elements of I, and what does it not prove? (a) Let A \coloneqq \{ n \in \omega : n = 0 	ext{ or } n = 1 	ext{ or } n = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(k)) 	ext{ for some } k \in \omega \} , a set by (Z6). Then 0 \in A by the first alternative. Let n \in A; we show \mathrm{S}(n) \in A, in three cases along the disjunction. If n = 0, then \mathrm{S}(n) = 1, the second alternative. If n = 1, then \mathrm{S}(n) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(0)), the third alternative with k \coloneqq 0 \in \omega. If n = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(k)) with k \in \omega, then \mathrm{S}(n) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(k))), the third alternative with \mathrm{S}(k) in place of k, and \mathrm{S}(k) \in \omega because \omega is inductive. In each case \mathrm{S}(n) \in \omega, so \mathrm{S}(n) \in A. By @thm-omega-induction (a), A = \omega. (b) Call the set A_I. The same three cases show that A_I has 0 as an element and is closed under \mathrm{S}, so A_I is inductive; by @thm-omega-least-inductive (b), \omega \subseteq A_I. That says only that every natural number is 0, 1 or \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(k)) for some k \in I, which is weaker than (a), whose k lies in \omega. It does not say that every element of I is 0, 1 or \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(k)) for some k \in I. The set form of induction concludes A = \omega only because A \subseteq \omega was given; for A_I \subseteq I the most we get is \omega \subseteq A_I \subseteq I, and the elements of I outside \omega, if any, are not reached. Induction proves statements about \omega, not about arbitrary inductive sets.

title: 1.4 The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano's Axioms
content:
The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano’s Axioms The previous section built \omega and proved induction on it (@thm-omega-induction). Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2 used two further facts about the natural numbers without a second thought: 0 is not of the form n + 1, and m + 1 = n + 1 forces m = n. For the sets of this chapter neither is automatic, and the obvious argument for the second fails, as we shall see. This section proves both for natural numbers, using one property of their membership structure; it then names the list of properties we have reached, Peano’s axioms, and shows that each of its last three items, (P3), (P4) and (P5), does a job that the other two cannot do. Transitive sets We want to prove: if m, n \in \omega and \mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n), then m = n. The tempting move is to cancel, reading m \cup \{m\} = n \cup \{n\} as “the same thing was added to both”. But union does not cancel: \{1\} \cup \{0\} = \{0\} \cup \{1\}, and 0 
e 1. What \mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n) does give is membership. Since m \in \mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n), either m \in n or m = n; and likewise n \in m or n = m. So the one bad case is m \in n and n \in m at once, two sets each inside the other. For the numerals, membership only ever points to earlier numerals, and the elements of an element are earlier still. In 3 = \{0, 1, 2\}, the element 2 has the elements 0 and 1, and both are again elements of 3. This is the property we name. A transitive set contains the elements of its elements. [Transitive set] A set x is transitive if every element of x is a subset of x: for every y \in x, y \subseteq x. In words: unpacking y \subseteq x (@fd2:def-subset), x is transitive when, for all sets y and z, z \in y \ 	ext{ and } \ y \in x \ \Longrightarrow \ z \in x . Membership passes through x in two steps: whatever is an element of an element of x is already an element of x. The name comes from this display, which has the shape of the transitivity of a relation (@fd2:def-relation-properties) with \in as the relation and x fixed at the end. Examples, simplest first. - \emptyset is transitive, vacuously: it has no element y at which the condition could fail. This degenerate case is the base of every induction below. - 1 = \{0\} is transitive: its only element is 0 = \emptyset, and \emptyset \subseteq 1. - 3 = \{0, 1, 2\} is transitive: 0 = \emptyset \subseteq 3, 1 = \{0\} \subseteq 3, and 2 = \{0, 1\} \subseteq 3. A non-example by minimal change: remove 1 from 3. The set \{0, 2\} is not transitive, because its element 2 = \{0, 1\} has the element 1, and 1 
otin \{0, 2\} (1 differs from 0 and from 2, @exm-von-neumann-numerals). Deleting one element broke the property at exactly one place. Transitivity is a property of the set, and it fails for sets that look harmless. The set \{1\} = \{\{\emptyset\}\} is not transitive: 1 \in \{1\}, but 1 = \{0\} is not a subset of \{1\}, since 0 
otin \{1\} (as 0 
e 1). If m is transitive, then n \in m gives n \subseteq m, so m \in n and n \in m together give m \in m. So the bad case above reduces to a set that is an element of itself. The lemma below rules that out for natural numbers, and with it the bad case. [Natural Numbers Are Transitive Sets] 1. Every n \in \omega is a transitive set. 2. \omega is a transitive set: every element of a natural number is a natural number. 3. n 
otin n for every n \in \omega. 4. Every n \in \omega with n 
e 0 is \mathrm{S}(k) for some k \in \omega. 5. 0 \in n for every n \in \omega with n 
e 0. Each part is one use of the move of the previous section, show the set is inductive, in its property form @thm-omega-induction (b). The base is always 0 = \emptyset, where the claim is empty or immediate. The steps of (a)–(c) start from “y \in \mathrm{S}(n) means y \in n or y = n” and treat the two cases. Part (c) is the only one that uses an earlier part: it argues by contradiction inside the step, and transitivity (a) is what turns a membership one level down into the forbidden n \in n. In (d) and (e) the statement is false at 0, so the property carried is a disjunction “n = 0 or …”. Before reading on: in the proof of (c), why does \mathrm{S}(n) \in n give n \in n? Each part is proved by @thm-omega-induction (b), with the property named at its start. (a) Let P(n) be “n is transitive”. P(0) holds because \emptyset has no elements. Let n \in \omega be transitive, and let y \in \mathrm{S}(n). If y \in n, then y \subseteq n because n is transitive, and n \subseteq \mathrm{S}(n); so y \subseteq \mathrm{S}(n). If y = n, then y = n \subseteq \mathrm{S}(n). In both cases y \subseteq \mathrm{S}(n), so \mathrm{S}(n) is transitive. (b) Let P(n) be “n \subseteq \omega”. P(0) holds because \emptyset \subseteq \omega. Let n \in \omega with n \subseteq \omega. The elements of \mathrm{S}(n) = n \cup \{n\} are the elements of n, which lie in \omega by hypothesis, and n itself, which lies in \omega by the choice of n. So \mathrm{S}(n) \subseteq \omega. Hence n \subseteq \omega for every n \in \omega, which says that \omega is transitive. (c) Let P(n) be “n 
otin n”. P(0) holds because \emptyset has no elements. Let n \in \omega with n 
otin n, and suppose \mathrm{S}(n) \in \mathrm{S}(n). Then \mathrm{S}(n) \in n or \mathrm{S}(n) = n. - If \mathrm{S}(n) \in n, then \mathrm{S}(n) \subseteq n, because n is transitive by (a); and n \in \mathrm{S}(n), so n \in n. - If \mathrm{S}(n) = n, then n \in \mathrm{S}(n) = n. Both cases contradict n 
otin n. So \mathrm{S}(n) 
otin \mathrm{S}(n), by ulename{
eg I} (@fd1:def-rules-negation). (d) Let P(n) be “n = 0, or n = \mathrm{S}(k) for some k \in \omega”. P(0) holds by the first alternative. For every n \in \omega, P(\mathrm{S}(n)) holds by the second alternative, with k \coloneqq n. So P(n) holds for every n \in \omega, and for n 
e 0 the second alternative is the claim. (e) Let P(n) be “n = 0 or 0 \in n”. P(0) holds by the first alternative. Let n \in \omega with P(n). If n = 0, then \mathrm{S}(n) = \{0\}, which has 0 as an element. If 0 \in n, then 0 \in n \subseteq \mathrm{S}(n). Either way 0 \in \mathrm{S}(n), so P(\mathrm{S}(n)) holds. So P(n) holds for every n \in \omega, and for n 
e 0 the second alternative is the claim. This proves the lemma. The step of (d) never used P(n). As with the predecessor in Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2 (@fd2:exm-predecessor-no-hypothesis), the step’s conclusion was reached outright, and induction is still what guarantees that 0 and the successors are all there is. Part (b) says that the natural numbers are built only from natural numbers: unwrapping a natural number never leads outside \omega. Part (c) is the fact the bad case needed. Peano’s axioms for the natural numbers Here is the list. Its five items are traditionally called Peano’s axioms; for \omega they are theorems. [Peano’s Axioms Hold in \omega] 1. 0 \in \omega. 2. For every n \in \omega, \mathrm{S}(n) \in \omega. 3. For every n \in \omega, \mathrm{S}(n) 
e 0. 4. For all m, n \in \omega, if \mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n), then m = n. 5. Every A \subseteq \omega with 0 \in A and \mathrm{S}(n) \in A for every n \in A is equal to \omega. Moreover, \{ (n, \mathrm{S}(n)) : n \in \omega \} is a set, and with codomain \omega it is a function \mathrm{S} \colon \omega 	o \omega, which is injective and does not take the value 0. (P1), (P2) and (P5) are the previous section restated: \omega is inductive, and induction holds. (P3) is one line, since n \in \mathrm{S}(n) and nothing is an element of \emptyset. (P4) is the argument of the opening of this section: \mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n) leaves only the case m \in n and n \in m to exclude, and transitivity with m 
otin m excludes it. (P1) and (P2) say that \omega is inductive, which is @thm-omega-least-inductive (a). (P5) is @thm-omega-induction (a). (P3) Let n \in \omega. Then n \in \mathrm{S}(n). If \mathrm{S}(n) = 0, then n \in 0 by ulename{{=}E} (@fd1:def-rules-equality), which is impossible, since 0 = \emptyset has no elements. So \mathrm{S}(n) 
e 0, by ulename{
eg I} (@fd1:def-rules-negation). (P4) Let m, n \in \omega with \mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n). Since m \in \mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n), we have m \in n or m = n; likewise, since n \in \mathrm{S}(n) = \mathrm{S}(m), we have n \in m or n = m. Suppose m 
e n. Then m \in n and n \in m. Since m is transitive (@lem-omega-transitive (a)) and n \in m, we get n \subseteq m; so m \in n \subseteq m, that is, m \in m. This contradicts @lem-omega-transitive (c). Hence m = n, by ulename{RAA} (@fd1:def-rule-raa). For the function: let G \coloneqq \{ p \in \omega 	imes \omega : p = (n, \mathrm{S}(n)) 	ext{ for some } n \in \omega \}, a set by Separation (Z6) inside the product \omega 	imes \omega of @prp-cartesian-product-exists; the pairs (n, \mathrm{S}(n)) lie in that product by (P2). We check the two clauses of @fd2:def-function. (Fn1): for n \in \omega, (n, \mathrm{S}(n)) \in G. (Fn2): if (n, y) \in G and (n, y') \in G, then (n, y) = (k, \mathrm{S}(k)) and (n, y') = (k', \mathrm{S}(k')) for some k, k' \in \omega; by @thm-kuratowski-pair, k = n = k', and then y = \mathrm{S}(n) = y'. So (G, \omega) is a function \omega 	o \omega, whose value at n is \mathrm{S}(n). It is injective by (P4) (@fd2:def-injective), and 0 is not a value by (P3). This proves the theorem. The function \mathrm{S} \colon \omega 	o \omega and the operation x \mapsto \mathrm{S}(x) on all sets share a letter, and they agree wherever both are defined. Only the first is a set. The operation has no graph: a set containing the pair (x, \mathrm{S}(x)) = \{\{x\}, \{x, \mathrm{S}(x)\}\} for every set x would give, after two unions, a set containing every set, which @fd2:thm-russell forbids. One more consequence is used constantly. By @lem-omega-transitive (d), every n \in \omega with n 
e 0 is \mathrm{S}(k) for some k \in \omega, and by (P4) this k is unique: if \mathrm{S}(k) = n = \mathrm{S}(k'), then k = k'. So every non-zero natural number has exactly one predecessor, and 0 has none, by (P3). Is the function \mathrm{S} \colon \omega 	o \omega surjective? Is \omega \in \omega? No to both. \mathrm{S} is not surjective: 0 \in \omega, and by (P3) no n \in \omega has \mathrm{S}(n) = 0. (Every other natural number is a value, by @lem-omega-transitive (d).) If \omega \in \omega, then \omega would be a natural number n with n \in n, which @lem-omega-transitive (c) rules out. So \omega 
otin \omega. In particular \omega is a set that is not a natural number, although all its elements are. Peano systems Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2 worked with a set 
N of real numbers, and this chapter with a set \omega of sets. Both come with a starting element and a step. The last section of the chapter asks whether they are “the same”, and to ask it we need to say what any such structure must satisfy. The answer is the list just proved, with \omega, 0 and \mathrm{S} replaced by letters. A Peano system is a set with a start and a step, where the step is one-to-one, never returns to the start, and reaches everything. [Peano system] A Peano system (M, e, s) consists of a set M, an element e \in M, and a function s \colon M 	o M, such that: - (P3) s(x) 
e e for every x \in M; - (P4) s is injective; - (P5) every subset A \subseteq M with e \in A and s(x) \in A for every x \in A is equal to M. In words: (P1) and (P2) are built into the data, since e \in M and s maps M into M. (P3) says the step never leads back to the start. (P4) says two different elements never step to the same element. (P5) is induction for M: a subset that contains the start and is closed under the step is everything, so every element of M is reached from e by steps. We write (M, e, s) and not (N, e, s), so that the letter never suggests 
N. The notation (M, e, s) lists the three pieces of data; it is not a set built from them (if one object is wanted, take the pair ((M, e), s) of @def-kuratowski-pair). The first example is the one we have, and the second shows that the elements need not be numbers. - (\omega, 0, \mathrm{S}) is a Peano system, by @thm-omega-peano: \mathrm{S} \colon \omega 	o \omega is a function, and (P3)–(P5) are those of the theorem. - Tagged numbers. Let M \coloneqq \omega 	imes \{0\}, a set by @prp-cartesian-product-exists, let e \coloneqq (0, 0), and let s(n, 0) \coloneqq (\mathrm{S}(n), 0). Every element of M is (n, 0) for exactly one n \in \omega (@thm-kuratowski-pair), so s is well defined, and its graph is a set by (Z6) inside M 	imes M. (P3): (\mathrm{S}(n), 0) = (0, 0) would give \mathrm{S}(n) = 0 by @thm-kuratowski-pair, against (P3) for \omega. (P4): (\mathrm{S}(m), 0) = (\mathrm{S}(n), 0) gives \mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n), so m = n by (P4) for \omega. (P5): let A \subseteq M contain e and be closed under s. The set B \coloneqq \{ n \in \omega : (n, 0) \in A \} has 0 as an element and is closed under \mathrm{S}, so B = \omega by @thm-omega-induction (a), and A = M. Here e = (0, 0) = \{\{0\}\} is not \emptyset, and no element of M is a natural number, as we shall see at the end of the section. Why these three clauses and no others? Each one does work that the other two cannot do: for each clause there is a structure satisfying the other two and failing it. [Each axiom is needed] Show that each of the following structures (M, e, s), with s \colon M 	o M, satisfies two of (P3), (P4), (P5) and fails the third. 1. M \coloneqq \{0\}, e \coloneqq 0, s(0) \coloneqq 0. 2. M \coloneqq \{0, 1\}, e \coloneqq 0, s(0) \coloneqq 1, s(1) \coloneqq 1. 3. (The natural numbers beside a two-sided chain.) M \coloneqq \omega 	imes 3, whose elements are the pairs (n, i) with n \in \omega and i \in 3 = \{0, 1, 2\}; e \coloneqq (0, 0); and  egin{aligned} s(n, 0) &\coloneqq (\mathrm{S}(n), 0) , & s(n, 1) &\coloneqq (\mathrm{S}(n), 1) , \ s(0, 2) &\coloneqq (0, 1) , & s(\mathrm{S}(k), 2) &\coloneqq (k, 2) , \end{aligned} for n, k \in \omega. (i) Fails (P3): s(0) = 0 = e. (P4) holds: M has one element, so two inputs with equal outputs are equal. (P5) holds: a subset of \{0\} containing e = 0 is \{0\}. (ii) Fails (P4): s(0) = s(1) with 0 
e 1. (P3) holds: both values are 1 
e 0 = e. (P5) holds: if A \subseteq \{0, 1\} has 0 as an element and is closed under s, then s(0) = 1 \in A, so A = \{0, 1\}. (iii) First, s is a function M 	o M. Each element of M is (n, i) for exactly one n \in \omega and one i \in 3, by @thm-kuratowski-pair. For i = 2, the first coordinate is 0 or \mathrm{S}(k) with k \in \omega (@lem-omega-transitive (d)); never both, by (P3) for \omega; and the k is unique, by (P4) for \omega. So exactly one line of the definition applies to each element, and it names one value. The values lie in M, since \mathrm{S}(n), 0, k \in \omega. The graph is a set by (Z6) inside M 	imes M. To check (P3) and (P4), sort the values by their second coordinates, which are 0, 1 and 2, three different sets (@exm-von-neumann-numerals):  egin{aligned} &	ext{second coordinate } 0 : && s(n, 0) = (\mathrm{S}(n), 0) , \ &	ext{second coordinate } 1 : && s(n, 1) = (\mathrm{S}(n), 1) \ 	ext{ and } \ s(0, 2) = (0, 1) , \ &	ext{second coordinate } 2 : && s(\mathrm{S}(k), 2) = (k, 2) . \end{aligned} (P3) holds. A value equal to e = (0, 0) would have second coordinate 0, so it would be (\mathrm{S}(n), 0) with \mathrm{S}(n) = 0, against (P3) for \omega. (P4) holds. Suppose s(x) = s(x'). The two values have the same second coordinate, so they come from the same row of the display. In the first row, (\mathrm{S}(n), 0) = (\mathrm{S}(n'), 0) gives n = n' by @thm-kuratowski-pair and (P4) for \omega. In the third row, (k, 2) = (k', 2) gives k = k', so \mathrm{S}(k) = \mathrm{S}(k'). In the second row, (\mathrm{S}(n), 1) 
e (0, 1) because \mathrm{S}(n) 
e 0; so either both values are of the form (\mathrm{S}(n), 1), and n = n' as before, or both are (0, 1), and both inputs are (0, 2). In every case x = x'. (P5) fails. Let A \coloneqq \omega 	imes \{0\}, a subset of M (@prp-cartesian-product-exists). It contains e = (0, 0), and it is closed under s, since s(n, 0) = (\mathrm{S}(n), 0) \in A. But (0, 1) \in M is not in A, because its second coordinate 1 is not 0. So A 
e M. The picture shows (iii), with an arrow from each element to its image under s. The top row is a copy of \omega, starting at e. The bottom row is a chain running forever in both directions: read (n, 1) as “n” and (k, 2) as “-(k + 1)”, and s adds one everywhere, with (0, 2), playing -1, stepping to (0, 1), playing 0. Every element has exactly one arrow out and at most one arrow in, which is (P4); only e has no arrow in, which is (P3). What fails is that the bottom row cannot be reached from e. Induction, (P5), is the clause that says “nothing else”. So (P3) and (P4) alone cannot prevent extra elements: in (iii) the whole bottom row is extra. That is why the definition of \omega needed “least”, and why induction is part of the list. Pairs are not natural numbers Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1 adopted a working convention, stated after @fd2:def-ordered-pair: a pair is not a number. In that chapter numbers were given and pairs were postulated, and the convention said they were different kinds of object. Now both are sets: a pair is the set \{\{a\}, \{a, b\}\} of @def-kuratowski-pair, and a natural number is an element of \omega. For natural numbers the convention becomes a theorem. [No Pair Is a Natural Number] For all sets a and b, the pair (a, b) is not an element of \omega. Every natural number other than 0 has \emptyset as an element, by @lem-omega-transitive (e). A pair is not \emptyset, and it does not have \emptyset as an element, because both of its elements contain a. Let a, b be sets, and suppose (a, b) = \{\{a\}, \{a, b\}\} \in \omega (@def-kuratowski-pair). The pair has the element \{a\}, so (a, b) 
e \emptyset = 0. By @lem-omega-transitive (e), 0 = \emptyset \in (a, b), so \emptyset = \{a\} or \emptyset = \{a, b\}. Both are impossible, since a \in \{a\} and a \in \{a, b\}, while \emptyset has no elements. This contradiction shows (a, b) 
otin \omega. So, for instance, the tagged numbers (n, 0) in the second example of a Peano system above are never natural numbers, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1’s answer that ((1, 2), 3) 
e (1, (2, 3)) because “a pair is not a number” is borne out by @prp-pair-not-natural once the numbers 1, 2, 3 are read as elements of \omega, as the later chapters of this volume read 
N (Section 1.7). The same statement for n-tuples with n \ge 3 needs a definition of n-tuples, which comes later in this chapter, together with the order on \omega. The encoding produces true statements that sound absurd. Since \{0\} = 1 and \{0, 1\} = 2, (0, 1) = \{\{0\}, \{0, 1\}\} = \{1, 2\} , so “1 \in (0, 1)” is true of the pair (0, 1), although 1 is not in the open interval (0, 1) of real numbers, and “0 \in (0, 1)” is false of the pair. Such a statement is a fact about how pairs were encoded as sets, not about pairs: with Wiener’s encoding \{\{\{a\}, \emptyset\}, \{\{b\}\}\}, met in Section 1.2 (@exr-pairs-as-sets-c3), the pair of 0 and 1 is \{2, \{\{1\}\}\}, which does not have 1 as an element. A proof about pairs should use only their characteristic property, @thm-kuratowski-pair. The places in this section that look inside a pair (the remark after @thm-omega-peano that the operation x \mapsto \mathrm{S}(x) has no graph, the closing remark of the tagged-numbers example that (0, 0) = \{\{0\}\} is not \emptyset, @prp-pair-not-natural, and this warning) are about the encoding itself. With Peano’s axioms in hand, the next section proves the recursion theorem on \omega and uses it to define addition and multiplication. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. For each of the three structures in @exm-peano-axioms-independent, which of (P3), (P4), (P5) fails? 2. In the proof of (P4) in @thm-omega-peano, where is @lem-omega-transitive (a) used, and where is (c)? 3. Is \omega \cup \{\omega\} inductive? Justify your answer. 4. Is \{0, 1, \{1\}\} a transitive set? Is it an element of \omega? (a) (i) fails (P3); (ii) fails (P4); (iii) fails (P5). Each satisfies the other two (@exm-peano-axioms-independent). (b) Part (a) is used to pass from n \in m to n \subseteq m: m is a natural number, hence a transitive set. Part (c) is used at the end: the argument reaches m \in m, and (c) says m 
otin m, which gives the contradiction. (c) No. The set \omega \cup \{\omega\} = \mathrm{S}(\omega) has \emptyset as an element and is closed under \mathrm{S} on its elements from \omega, but \mathrm{S}(\omega) itself is not an element of \omega \cup \{\omega\}. First, \mathrm{S}(\omega) 
e \omega: \omega \in \mathrm{S}(\omega), while \omega 
otin \omega (the Quick check after @thm-omega-peano). Second, \mathrm{S}(\omega) 
otin \omega: otherwise \mathrm{S}(\omega) \subseteq \omega because \omega is transitive (@lem-omega-transitive (b)), and \omega \in \mathrm{S}(\omega) would give \omega \in \omega. So the closure clause fails at the element \omega. (d) It is transitive: 0 = \emptyset is a subset of every set; 1 = \{0\} is a subset, since 0 is listed; \{1\} is a subset, since 1 is listed. It is not an element of \omega: by @lem-omega-transitive (b), every element of a natural number is a natural number, and \{1\} is not one. Indeed \{1\} 
e 0, and if \{1\} = \mathrm{S}(k) = k \cup \{k\} with k \in \omega, then k \in \{1\}, so k = 1, and \mathrm{S}(1) = \{0, 1\} 
e \{1\} since 0 
otin \{1\}; this contradicts @lem-omega-transitive (d). So being transitive does not make a set a natural number. B. Practice [B1: Put the proof in order] Let m, n \in \omega. The following lines contain a proof that if \mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n), then m = n, shuffled, together with two lines that do not belong. Write the seven correct lines in an order that makes a proof, say which other orders are also admissible, and say why each of the other two lines fails. (i) So m \in n \subseteq m, that is, m \in m. (ii) Suppose \mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n). (iii) We have m \cup \{m\} = n \cup \{n\}, so m = n by canceling {\cup}\{\cdot\} on both sides. (iv) Since n \in \mathrm{S}(n) = \mathrm{S}(m), we have n \in m or n = m. (v) Suppose m 
e n; then m \in n and n \in m. (vi) This contradicts m 
otin m (@lem-omega-transitive (c)); so m = n. (vii) From m \in n and n \in m we get m = n, since \in is antisymmetric. (viii) Since m is transitive (@lem-omega-transitive (a)) and n \in m, we have n \subseteq m. (ix) Since m \in \mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n), we have m \in n or m = n. An admissible order is (ii), (ix), (iv), (v), (viii), (i), (vi): Suppose \mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n). Since m \in \mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n), we have m \in n or m = n. Since n \in \mathrm{S}(n) = \mathrm{S}(m), we have n \in m or n = m. Suppose m 
e n; then m \in n and n \in m. Since m is transitive and n \in m, we have n \subseteq m. So m \in n \subseteq m, that is, m \in m. This contradicts m 
otin m; so m = n. The only other admissible order exchanges (ix) and (iv), which use only (ii) and not each other. Everything else is forced: (v) needs both (ix) and (iv) to reduce each disjunction to its first alternative; (viii) needs the n \in m of (v); (i) needs the m \in n of (v) and the inclusion of (viii); (vi) closes the ulename{RAA} box opened by (v), whose assumption is m 
e n, the negation of the goal (@fd1:def-rule-raa). The distractor (iii) cancels where no cancellation law exists. For sets in general, x \cup \{y\} = x' \cup \{y'\} does not give y = y': \{1\} \cup \{0\} = \{0\} \cup \{1\} with 0 
e 1. For natural numbers the conclusion m = n happens to be true, but that is the statement being proved, not a reason for it. The distractor (vii) cites a “fact” that is not available. No result so far says that m \in n and n \in m cannot both hold, and for natural numbers that is exactly what lines (viii), (i) and (vi) establish. Citing it is the circular step (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue: the line uses, as a reason, what the proof is there to show. [B2: Two steps at a time] Let d \coloneqq \mathrm{S} \circ \mathrm{S} \colon \omega 	o \omega (@fd2:def-composition), so that d(n) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(n)). Show that (\omega, 0, d) satisfies (P3) and (P4) of @def-peano-system, and that it does not satisfy (P5). Hint: look at the set \omega \setminus \{1\}. (P3): for n \in \omega, d(n) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(n)) 
e 0 by (P3) of @thm-omega-peano, applied to \mathrm{S}(n) \in \omega. (P4): if d(m) = d(n), then \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(m)) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(n)), so \mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n) by (P4) of @thm-omega-peano, and then m = n by (P4) again. (Equivalently: d is a composite of two injections, so it is injective by @fd2:thm-composition-injective-surjective (a).) (P5) fails. Let A \coloneqq \omega \setminus \{1\}. It contains 0, since 0 
e 1. It is closed under d: let n \in A; then d(n) \in \omega, and d(n) 
e 1, because \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(n)) = 1 = \mathrm{S}(0) would give \mathrm{S}(n) = 0 by (P4), against (P3). But A 
e \omega, since 1 \in \omega and 1 
otin A. So a subset of \omega with 0 as an element and closed under d need not be all of \omega. The step d skips 1, and starting from 0 it reaches only the “even” numbers. C. Going deeper [C1: A Peano system with a different start] Give an example of a Peano system (M, e, s) with M \subseteq \omega and e 
e 0. Check every clause of @def-peano-system. Any correct answer has: a set M \subseteq \omega; an element e \in M with e 
e 0; a function s \colon M 	o M, so that every value lies in M; and the three clauses (P3), (P4), (P5) for these data. Take M \coloneqq \omega \setminus \{0\}, e \coloneqq 1, and s(n) \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(n) for n \in M. - The data. 1 \in M, since 1 \in \omega and 1 
e 0. For n \in M, \mathrm{S}(n) \in \omega by (P2) and \mathrm{S}(n) 
e 0 by (P3) of @thm-omega-peano, so \mathrm{S}(n) \in M. The graph \{ (n, \mathrm{S}(n)) : n \in M \} is a set by (Z6) inside M 	imes M. (Fn1) holds, since (n, \mathrm{S}(n)) is in the graph for each n \in M; (Fn2) holds as in the proof of @thm-omega-peano, by @thm-kuratowski-pair. So s \colon M 	o M is a function (@fd2:def-function). - (P3). If s(n) = 1 for some n \in M, then \mathrm{S}(n) = \mathrm{S}(0), so n = 0 by (P4) for \omega; but 0 
otin M. - (P4). If \mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n) with m, n \in M, then m = n by (P4) for \omega. - (P5). Let A \subseteq M with 1 \in A and \mathrm{S}(n) \in A for every n \in A. The set A' \coloneqq A \cup \{0\} \subseteq \omega is inductive: 0 \in A'; \mathrm{S}(0) = 1 \in A \subseteq A'; and for n \in A, \mathrm{S}(n) \in A \subseteq A'. By @thm-omega-induction (a), A' = \omega. Every n \in M lies in A' and is not 0, so n \in A. Hence A = M. Other answers can be checked against the four properties at the start. For instance, M \coloneqq \omega \setminus \{0, 1\}, e \coloneqq 2, s(n) \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(n) also works, by the same argument with \{0, 1\} added in (P5). [C2: Closed subsets of the chain] Let (M, e, s) be the structure (iii) of @exm-peano-axioms-independent. Call A \subseteq M good if e \in A and s(x) \in A for every x \in A. 1. Show that every good set contains \omega 	imes \{0\}. 2. Show that each of the following sets is good, where m, k \in \omega:  egin{aligned} G_0 &\coloneqq \omega 	imes \{0\} , \qquad G_\infty \coloneqq M , \ R_m &\coloneqq G_0 \cup \{ (n, 1) : n \in \omega, \ m \in \mathrm{S}(n) \} , \ L_k &\coloneqq G_0 \cup (\omega 	imes \{1\}) \cup \{ (j, 2) : j \in \mathrm{S}(k) \} . \end{aligned} 3. Show that a good set that contains (k, 2) contains L_k. [Hint 1] For (a), apply induction to the set of n \in \omega with (n, 0) \in A. For (c), the arrows of the bottom row point toward (0, 1): from (\mathrm{S}(k), 2) the step goes to (k, 2). [Hint 2] For (c), prove by induction on k \in \omega the property: “for every good A, if (k, 2) \in A, then L_k \subseteq A”. (a) Let A be good, and let B \coloneqq \{ n \in \omega : (n, 0) \in A \}. Then 0 \in B, because (0, 0) = e \in A; and if n \in B, then (\mathrm{S}(n), 0) = s(n, 0) \in A, so \mathrm{S}(n) \in B. By @thm-omega-induction (a), B = \omega, so \omega 	imes \{0\} \subseteq A. (b) All four sets contain e = (0, 0) \in G_0. Closure is checked element by element, using the definition of s. - G_0: s(n, 0) = (\mathrm{S}(n), 0) \in G_0. - G_\infty = M: s maps M into M. - R_m: elements of G_0 are handled as before. If (n, 1) \in R_m with m \in \mathrm{S}(n), then s(n, 1) = (\mathrm{S}(n), 1), and m \in \mathrm{S}(n) \subseteq \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(n)); so s(n, 1) \in R_m. - L_k: elements of G_0 as before; s(n, 1) = (\mathrm{S}(n), 1) \in \omega 	imes \{1\}. Every j \in \mathrm{S}(k) lies in \omega, since \mathrm{S}(k) \in \omega by (P2) of @thm-omega-peano and \omega is transitive (@lem-omega-transitive (b)); so L_k \subseteq M. For (j, 2) with j \in \mathrm{S}(k): if j = 0, then s(0, 2) = (0, 1) \in L_k; if j = \mathrm{S}(i) with i \in \omega (@lem-omega-transitive (d)), then s(j, 2) = (i, 2), and i \in \mathrm{S}(i) = j \in \mathrm{S}(k), so i \in \mathrm{S}(k) because \mathrm{S}(k) is transitive (@lem-omega-transitive (a)); hence (i, 2) \in L_k. (c) We prove by @thm-omega-induction (b) the property P(k): “for every good A, if (k, 2) \in A, then L_k \subseteq A”. Base. Let A be good with (0, 2) \in A. Then (0, 1) = s(0, 2) \in A. The set \{ n \in \omega : (n, 1) \in A \} has 0 as an element and is closed under \mathrm{S}, since s(n, 1) = (\mathrm{S}(n), 1); so it is \omega by @thm-omega-induction (a), and \omega 	imes \{1\} \subseteq A. With (a) and \mathrm{S}(0) = \{0\}, this gives L_0 \subseteq A. Step. Let k \in \omega with P(k), and let A be good with (\mathrm{S}(k), 2) \in A. Then (k, 2) = s(\mathrm{S}(k), 2) \in A, so L_k \subseteq A by P(k). Now L_{\mathrm{S}(k)} = L_k \cup \{ (\mathrm{S}(k), 2) \}, because j \in \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(k)) means j \in \mathrm{S}(k) or j = \mathrm{S}(k). Both parts lie in A, so L_{\mathrm{S}(k)} \subseteq A, which is P(\mathrm{S}(k)). So the good sets include G_0, the sets R_m (whose part in the bottom row starts at (m, 1) and runs to the right), the sets L_k (whose part in the bottom row starts at (k, 2)), and M. Read on the two-sided chain, these are the empty part, the rays starting at some point, and the whole chain. That they are all the good sets is also true, but the proof needs a least element of a non-empty set of natural numbers, which comes later in this chapter with the order on \omega. Part (c) already shows that a good set containing every (k, 2) contains every L_k, hence all of M. Every good set other than M is a witness to the failure of (P5).

title: 1.5 The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication
content:
The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication The set \omega now has a zero, a successor map and an induction theorem, and @thm-omega-peano shows that together they satisfy Peano’s axioms. It has no addition yet. In Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2 the sum m + n of two natural numbers came for free, from the real numbers; in \omega a natural number is a set, and nothing we know about sets adds two of them. This section defines addition and multiplication by recursion, as school does (“m + (n + 1) is one more than m + n”), after first proving, from the axioms, that recursion defines something. Then it proves the laws of arithmetic one by one, most of them by an induction. Recursion on ω Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.3 proved @fd2:thm-recursion: a starting value and a rule for the next value determine exactly one function on 
N. That proof ran inside the familiar real numbers, where 
N is given. Its ingredients, though, were few: induction, and some facts about the sets \{0, \dots, n\} on which the partial solutions live. On \omega there is a natural replacement for \{0, \dots, n\}, namely the set \mathrm{S}(n) = n \cup \{n\} itself. (The next section proves that \mathrm{S}(n) is exactly the set of k \in \omega with k \le n; here we need no order, only \mathrm{S}(n) as a set.) So the proof can be repeated on \omega, with one change, which we point out when we reach it. A starting value and a rule for the next value determine exactly one function on \omega. [Recursion Theorem on \omega] Let X be a set, let a \in X, and let g \colon \omega 	imes X 	o X be a function. Then there is exactly one function f \colon \omega 	o X such that f(0) = a \quad 	ext{and} \quad f igl(\mathrm{S}(n) igr) = g igl(n, f(n) igr) \ 	ext{ for every } n \in \omega . This is the statement of @fd2:thm-recursion word for word, with \omega in place of 
N and \mathrm{S}(n) in place of n + 1. The set \omega 	imes X exists by @prp-cartesian-product-exists. As before, a is the starting value and g turns the stage n and the current value into the next value; the conclusion has an existence half and a uniqueness half. Uniqueness is an induction. For existence, induction cannot build f, so we prove by induction that the finite pieces of f exist and are unique, and then glue them. The roadmap is that of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.3: ① Uniqueness, by @thm-omega-induction. ② Partial solutions. A partial solution up to n is a function on \mathrm{S}(n) obeying the two equations wherever they make sense. A restriction of a partial solution is again one. ③ Claim: for every n there is exactly one partial solution up to n; the next one adds a single pair at the new input \mathrm{S}(n). ④ Glue: the union of all their graphs is the graph of f. The glue step of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.3 compared two indices: if m \le n, the piece up to m lies inside the piece up to n. We have no order on \omega yet, so at each point k where both pieces are defined we cut both down to \mathrm{S}(k): by ② and ③, each restriction is the unique partial solution up to k. Before reading on: where is \mathrm{S}(n) 
otin \mathrm{S}(n) used? Step 0 (facts about \mathrm{S}(n)). Let n, k, m \in \omega. Each of \mathrm{S}(n), \mathrm{S}(m) is an element of \omega by (P2) of @thm-omega-peano. We use five facts. 1. 0 \in \mathrm{S}(n), by @lem-omega-transitive (e), since \mathrm{S}(n) 
e 0 by (P3) of @thm-omega-peano. 2. If \mathrm{S}(k) \in \mathrm{S}(n), then k \in \mathrm{S}(n): we have k \in k \cup \{k\} = \mathrm{S}(k), and \mathrm{S}(k) \subseteq \mathrm{S}(n) because \mathrm{S}(n) is a transitive set (@lem-omega-transitive (a), @def-transitive-set). 3. If k \in \mathrm{S}(m), then \mathrm{S}(k) \subseteq \mathrm{S}(m): k \subseteq \mathrm{S}(m) because \mathrm{S}(m) is transitive, and \{k\} \subseteq \mathrm{S}(m), so k \cup \{k\} \subseteq \mathrm{S}(m). 4. \mathrm{S}(n) 
otin \mathrm{S}(n), by @lem-omega-transitive (c) applied to \mathrm{S}(n) \in \omega. 5. The elements of \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(n)) = \mathrm{S}(n) \cup \{\mathrm{S}(n)\} are the elements of \mathrm{S}(n) and \mathrm{S}(n) itself (@def-set-successor). Every element of \mathrm{S}(n) lies in \omega, by @lem-omega-transitive (b). Step 1 (uniqueness). Let f, f' \colon \omega 	o X both satisfy the two equations, and let P(n) be “f(n) = f'(n)”. P(0) holds, since f(0) = a = f'(0). If P(n) holds, then f igl(\mathrm{S}(n) igr) = g igl(n, f(n) igr) = g igl(n, f'(n) igr) = f' igl(\mathrm{S}(n) igr) , so P(\mathrm{S}(n)) holds. By @thm-omega-induction (b), P(n) holds for every n \in \omega. The two functions have the same domain and codomain, so f = f' by @fd2:prp-function-equality. Step 2 (partial solutions and their restrictions). For n \in \omega, a partial solution up to n is a function h \colon \mathrm{S}(n) 	o X with h(0) = a and h(\mathrm{S}(k)) = g(k, h(k)) for every k \in \omega with \mathrm{S}(k) \in \mathrm{S}(n). The equations make sense: 0 \in \mathrm{S}(n) by (i), and for such k, also k \in \mathrm{S}(n) by (ii). If h is a partial solution up to m and j \in \mathrm{S}(m), then the restriction h|_{\mathrm{S}(j)} is a partial solution up to j. Here j \in \omega by (v), and \mathrm{S}(j) \subseteq \mathrm{S}(m) by (iii), so the restriction (Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 1.4) is a function \mathrm{S}(j) 	o X with the same values as h. Its value at 0 is h(0) = a, since 0 \in \mathrm{S}(j) by (i). Let i \in \omega with \mathrm{S}(i) \in \mathrm{S}(j). Then \mathrm{S}(i) \in \mathrm{S}(m), because \mathrm{S}(j) \subseteq \mathrm{S}(m), and i \in \mathrm{S}(j) by (ii). So the equation at \mathrm{S}(i) is one of the equations of h, and both of its sides are values at points of \mathrm{S}(j): h|_{\mathrm{S}(j)} igl(\mathrm{S}(i) igr) = g igl(i, h(i) igr) = g igl(i, h|_{\mathrm{S}(j)}(i) igr) . Step 3. For every n \in \omega there is exactly one partial solution up to n. We use @thm-omega-induction (b) on n. Base case. \mathrm{S}(0) = \emptyset \cup \{0\} = \{0\}. The graph \{(0, a)\} with codomain X is a function on \{0\}, since a \in X. It is a partial solution up to 0: its value at 0 is a, and the second condition is vacuous, because \mathrm{S}(k) \in \{0\} would mean \mathrm{S}(k) = 0, which (P3) of @thm-omega-peano excludes. Any partial solution up to 0 has the value a at 0, so it equals this one by @fd2:prp-function-equality. Inductive step. Let n \in \omega, and suppose there is exactly one partial solution up to n; call it f_n, with graph G_n \subseteq \mathrm{S}(n) 	imes X. Since n \in \mathrm{S}(n), the value f_n(n) is defined. Let G' \coloneqq G_n \cup \Bigl\{  igl(\mathrm{S}(n), \ g(n, f_n(n)) igr) \Bigr\} . We check @fd2:def-function for G' on \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(n)) with codomain X. By (v) and because g takes values in X, every pair of G' lies in \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(n)) 	imes X. (Fn1): by (v), an input is an element of \mathrm{S}(n), which has an output in G_n, or is \mathrm{S}(n), which has the added output. (Fn2): every first coordinate in G_n lies in \mathrm{S}(n), while \mathrm{S}(n) 
otin \mathrm{S}(n) by (iv). So the added pair is the only pair of G' with first coordinate \mathrm{S}(n), and for an input in \mathrm{S}(n) all pairs of G' lie in G_n, which satisfies (Fn2). Hence f' \coloneqq (G', X) is a function \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(n)) 	o X that agrees with f_n on \mathrm{S}(n). It is a partial solution up to \mathrm{S}(n). Its value at 0 is f_n(0) = a, since 0 \in \mathrm{S}(n). Let k \in \omega with \mathrm{S}(k) \in \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(n)). By (v), there are two cases. Case 1: \mathrm{S}(k) \in \mathrm{S}(n). Then k \in \mathrm{S}(n) by (ii), and since f_n is a partial solution, f' igl(\mathrm{S}(k) igr) = f_n igl(\mathrm{S}(k) igr) = g igl(k, f_n(k) igr) = g igl(k, f'(k) igr) . Case 2: \mathrm{S}(k) = \mathrm{S}(n). Then k = n by (P4) of @thm-omega-peano, so the equation at the new input asks for g(n, f'(n)) and for nothing else; and f'(\mathrm{S}(n)) = g(n, f_n(n)) = g(n, f'(n)) by the choice of the added pair. It is the only one. Let h be a partial solution up to \mathrm{S}(n). Since n \in \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(n)) by (v), the claim of Step 2 (with m = \mathrm{S}(n) and j = n) makes h|_{\mathrm{S}(n)} a partial solution up to n, so it is f_n by the induction hypothesis. Thus h(k) = f_n(k) = f'(k) for every k \in \mathrm{S}(n), and, by the equation of h at \mathrm{S}(n) \in \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(n)), h igl(\mathrm{S}(n) igr) = g igl(n, h(n) igr) = g igl(n, f_n(n) igr) = f' igl(\mathrm{S}(n) igr) . By (v) these are all the inputs, so h = f' by @fd2:prp-function-equality. This proves the claim. For each n \in \omega, let f_n be the partial solution up to n, and G_n its graph. One consequence of the two claims is used below. If k \in \mathrm{S}(m), then f_m|_{\mathrm{S}(k)} is a partial solution up to k (Step 2), hence equals f_k (Step 3), and since k \in \mathrm{S}(k), f_m(k) = f_k(k) \qquad 	ext{whenever } k \in \mathrm{S}(m) . 	ag{$\ast$} Step 4 (glue). Each G_n is a subset of \mathrm{S}(n) 	imes X \subseteq \omega 	imes X (by (v)). Let \sS \coloneqq  igl\{ G \in \powerset{\omega 	imes X} : (G, X) 	ext{ is a partial solution up to some } n \in \omega  igr\} , a set by (Z5) and (Z6) of @ax-zf-fragment. By Step 3, the elements of \sS are exactly the graphs G_n. Let F \coloneqq  igcup \sS, a set by (Z4); a pair lies in F if and only if it lies in some G_n, and F \subseteq \omega 	imes X. We check @fd2:def-function for F. (Fn1): for k \in \omega, the pair (k, f_k(k)) lies in G_k \in \sS, hence in F. (Fn2): let (k, y) \in F and (k, y') \in F, say (k, y) \in G_m and (k, y') \in G_n. Then k lies in the domains of both, k \in \mathrm{S}(m) and k \in \mathrm{S}(n), and by (\ast), y = f_m(k) = f_k(k) = f_n(k) = y' . No comparison of m with n was needed: both pieces were cut down to \mathrm{S}(k), where each is the unique partial solution up to k. So f \coloneqq (F, X) is a function \omega 	o X. If k \in \mathrm{S}(m), then (k, f_m(k)) \in G_m \subseteq F, so f(k) = f_m(k). Hence f(0) = f_0(0) = a. For n \in \omega, both n and \mathrm{S}(n) lie in \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(n)) by (v), and f_{\mathrm{S}(n)} is a partial solution up to \mathrm{S}(n), so f igl(\mathrm{S}(n) igr) = f_{\mathrm{S}(n)} igl(\mathrm{S}(n) igr) = g igl(n, f_{\mathrm{S}(n)}(n) igr) = g igl(n, f(n) igr) . This proves existence, and with Step 1, the theorem. The proof is that of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.3 with \{0, \dots, n\} replaced by \mathrm{S}(n), and with one departure, in (Fn2) of Step 4. There, Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.3 used that two indices m, n satisfy m \le n or n < m, and that \{0, \dots, m\} \subseteq \{0, \dots, n\} when m \le n. On \omega those are facts about order, which the next section proves. Cutting both pieces down to \mathrm{S}(k) avoids the comparison altogether, so the recursion theorem does not have to wait for the order. In Step 3, (P4) did a quiet job: the new input \mathrm{S}(n) is the successor of n and of nothing else, so the added pair had to satisfy exactly one equation. As in Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.3, no choice is made: each partial solution is the only one, and \sS is cut out of a power set by a condition, so no family n \mapsto f_n had to be formed first. From now on a definition “f(0) \coloneqq a, f(\mathrm{S}(n)) \coloneqq g(n, f(n))” on \omega is legitimate whenever a \in X and g \colon \omega 	imes X 	o X is a function, and f is defined by recursion. The functions g that we feed to the theorem are usually given by a formula, such as g(n, x) = \mathrm{S}(x). Such a g is a function as soon as each pair (n, x) gets exactly one value in X: its graph, the set of pairs ((n, x), y) \in (\omega 	imes X) 	imes X such that y is the value the formula assigns to (n, x), is a set by (Z6) of @ax-zf-fragment inside a product (@prp-cartesian-product-exists), and (Fn1), (Fn2) say exactly that the formula gives one value in X for each pair. The hypothesis that g takes its values in X cannot be dropped. Let X = \{0\}, a = 0, and g(n, x) \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(0) for n \in \omega, x \in X, so that g maps \omega 	imes X into \omega but not into X. Any f \colon \omega 	o X with the two equations would need f(\mathrm{S}(0)) = g(0, f(0)) = \mathrm{S}(0), and \mathrm{S}(0) 
otin X since \mathrm{S}(0) 
e 0 by (P3) of @thm-omega-peano; so no such f exists. The proof breaks in Step 3, where the added pair (\mathrm{S}(n), g(n, f_n(n))) must lie in \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(n)) 	imes X. Addition and multiplication With the theorem, addition is the old school definition made official. To add n to m, start at m and take n successor steps: m + 0 is m, and m + \mathrm{S}(n) is one step further than m + n. Multiplication is repeated addition in the same way. Adding n to m is taking n successor steps from m. [Addition and Multiplication on \omega] 1. For each m \in \omega, let A_m \colon \omega 	o \omega be the function given by @thm-omega-recursion with X = \omega, a = m and g(n, x) = \mathrm{S}(x). The sum of m and n is m + n \coloneqq A_m(n). Thus, for all m, n \in \omega, m + 0 = m, \qquad m + \mathrm{S}(n) = \mathrm{S}(m + n) . 2. For each m \in \omega, let M_m \colon \omega 	o \omega be the function given by @thm-omega-recursion with X = \omega, a = 0 and g(n, x) = x + m. The product of m and n is m \cdot n \coloneqq M_m(n), also written mn. Thus, for all m, n \in \omega, m \cdot 0 = 0, \qquad m \cdot \mathrm{S}(n) = m \cdot n + m . 3. The numerals are 0 \coloneqq \emptyset and 1 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(0), 2 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(1), 3 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(2), and so on, as in @exm-von-neumann-numerals. For every n \in \omega, n + 1 = \mathrm{S}(n); in particular 1 + 1 = 2 and k + 2 = (k + 1) + 1 for every k \in \omega. In words: (a) and (b) are the two clauses we would write for a school definition, and the theorem guarantees that they define exactly one function A_m, respectively M_m, for each m. Multiplication binds more tightly than addition, so m \cdot n + m is (m \cdot n) + m. Well-definedness. Three things need checking. First, each g is a function \omega 	imes \omega 	o \omega (the remark above): \mathrm{S}(x) \in \omega for x \in \omega by (P2) of @thm-omega-peano, and x + m \in \omega because A_x maps into \omega. So (b) uses (a), and (a) uses nothing but the successor. Second, + is a function \omega 	imes \omega 	o \omega: its graph is the set of ((m, n), k) \in (\omega 	imes \omega) 	imes \omega such that k = A(n) for some function A \colon \omega 	o \omega with A(0) = m and A(\mathrm{S}(j)) = \mathrm{S}(A(j)) for every j \in \omega; this is a set by (Z6) of @ax-zf-fragment, and each (m, n) gets exactly one k because A_m exists and is unique. The same holds for \cdot. Third, nothing was chosen: each A_m and M_m is the only function with its property. The successor is “plus one”. Proof of the last sentence of (c): for every n \in \omega, n + 1 = n + \mathrm{S}(0) = \mathrm{S}(n + 0) = \mathrm{S}(n) , by (c) and the two equations of (a). From now on we write n + 1 for \mathrm{S}(n) whenever n \in \omega; the defining equations then read as in school:  egin{aligned} m + 0 &= m, & m + (n + 1) &= (m + n) + 1, \ m \cdot 0 &= 0, & m \cdot (n + 1) &= m \cdot n + m . \end{aligned} Two small computations are used repeatedly later: 1 + 1 = \mathrm{S}(1) = 2, and, for every k \in \omega, k + 2 = k + \mathrm{S}(1) = \mathrm{S}(k + 1) = (k + 1) + 1 . A non-example by minimal change: keep a = m in (a), but replace g(n, x) = \mathrm{S}(x) by g(n, x) = \mathrm{S}(n), which ignores the current value. This g is still a function \omega 	imes \omega 	o \omega, so @thm-omega-recursion gives exactly one f \colon \omega 	o \omega with f(0) = m and f(\mathrm{S}(n)) = \mathrm{S}(n). The first equation m + 0 = m still holds for this “sum”, but the second, m + \mathrm{S}(n) = \mathrm{S}(m + n), fails: with m = 2, f(1) = \mathrm{S}(0) = 1, while \mathrm{S}(f(0)) = \mathrm{S}(2) = 3. So it would give 2 + 1 = 1, and it is not addition. The defining equations immediately give the two Peano facts in the “plus one” notation. [Successor Cancellation] For all k, l \in \omega: if k + 1 = l + 1, then k = l; and k + 1 
e 0. By (c) of @def-omega-arithmetic, k + 1 = \mathrm{S}(k) and l + 1 = \mathrm{S}(l). So the first claim is (P4) of @thm-omega-peano, and the second is (P3). Compute 2 + 2 and 2 \cdot 2 from the defining equations alone. By (a) of @def-omega-arithmetic, three times, 2 + 2 = \mathrm{S}(2 + 1) = \mathrm{S} igl(\mathrm{S}(2 + 0) igr) = \mathrm{S} igl(\mathrm{S}(2) igr) = \mathrm{S}(3) = 4 . By (b), twice and then at 0, 2 \cdot 2 = 2 \cdot 1 + 2 = (2 \cdot 0 + 2) + 2 = (0 + 2) + 2 , and 0 + 2 = \mathrm{S}(0 + 1) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(0 + 0)) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(0)) = 2. So 2 \cdot 2 = 2 + 2 = 4. The laws of arithmetic Every law of arithmetic that Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2 took from the real numbers must now be proved, and the only tools are the four defining equations and induction. The equations are lopsided: they say what happens when the second argument goes up by one, and nothing about the first. So in every induction below we fix all variables but one and induct on the variable that the recursion runs on, the second argument of + or \cdot. [Laws of Arithmetic on \omega] For all k, m, n \in \omega: 1. 0 + n = n, and (m + 1) + n = (m + n) + 1; 2. m + n = n + m; 3. (k + m) + n = k + (m + n); 4. m(n + k) = mn + mk and (n + k)m = nm + km; 5. 0 \cdot n = 0, (m + 1) \cdot n = mn + n, and n \cdot 1 = 1 \cdot n = n; 6. mn = nm; 7. (km)n = k(mn). The move is fix the others, induct on the recursion variable: in m + n and m \cdot n the recursion runs on n, so we fix m (and k) and induct on n. Then the base case is a defining equation at 0, and the step can open m + (n + 1) or m \cdot (n + 1) by the other defining equation, apply the induction hypothesis inside, and close up again. The order of the clauses matters: commutativity (b) needs the two facts (a) about the first argument, which no defining equation provides. Each clause except the second half of (d) and the last part of (e), which the table derives from earlier clauses without induction, is proved by @thm-omega-induction (b), applied to the property of n stated in the clause, with the other variables fixed; for the first half of (d) the variable is k, the recursion variable of m(n + k). “Def” refers to the equations of @def-omega-arithmetic, “IH” to the induction hypothesis. We prove (c), associativity of addition, in full. Fix k, m \in \omega, and let P(n) be “(k + m) + n = k + (m + n)”. Base case: by the first equation of (a) of @def-omega-arithmetic, applied twice, (k + m) + 0 = k + m = k + (m + 0) . Inductive step: suppose P(n). Then  egin{aligned} (k + m) + (n + 1) &=  igl((k + m) + n igr) + 1 =  igl(k + (m + n) igr) + 1 \ &= k +  igl((m + n) + 1 igr) = k +  igl(m + (n + 1) igr) , \end{aligned} where the first equality is Def with first argument k + m, the second is P(n), the third is Def with first argument k and second argument m + n, and the fourth is Def with first argument m. So P(n + 1) holds, and by @thm-omega-induction (b), P(n) holds for every n \in \omega. The other clauses follow the same pattern; the table gives, for each, the property inducted on, the base case, the step, and the earlier clauses used. They are proved in the order of the table, so each row uses only rows above it. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Clause, variable Base case Inductive step (IH at the marked equality) Uses ------------------------------------------------ --------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------- (a) 0 + n = n; on n 0 + 0 = 0 (Def) 0 + (n + 1) = (0 + n) + 1 \overset{	ext{IH}}{=} n + 1 Def (a) (m + 1) + n = (m + n) + 1; m fixed, on n both sides are m + 1 (Def) (m + 1) + (n + 1) = ((m + 1) + n) + 1 \overset{	ext{IH}}{=} ((m + n) + 1) + 1 = (m + (n + 1)) + 1 Def (b) m + n = n + m; m fixed, on n m + 0 = m = 0 + m m + (n + 1) = (m + n) + 1 \overset{	ext{IH}}{=} (n + m) + 1 = (n + 1) + m Def; (a), both halves (c) in full above Def (d) m(n + k) = mn + mk; m, n fixed, on k m(n + 0) = mn = mn + 0 = mn + m \cdot 0 m(n + (k + 1)) = m((n + k) + 1) = m(n + k) + m \overset{	ext{IH}}{=} (mn + mk) + m = mn + (mk + m) = mn + m(k + 1) Def; (c) (e) 0 \cdot n = 0; on n 0 \cdot 0 = 0 (Def) 0 \cdot (n + 1) = 0 \cdot n + 0 \overset{	ext{IH}}{=} 0 + 0 = 0 Def (e) (m + 1) n = mn + n; m fixed, on n (m + 1) \cdot 0 = 0 = 0 + 0 = m \cdot 0 + 0 (m + 1)(n + 1) = (m + 1)n + (m + 1) \overset{	ext{IH}}{=} (mn + n) + (m + 1) = mn + (n + (m + 1)) = mn + ((n + m) + 1) = mn + ((m + n) + 1) = mn + (m + (n + 1)) = (mn + m) + (n + 1) = m(n + 1) + (n + 1) Def; (b), (c) (e) n \cdot 1 = n, 1 \cdot n = n; no induction n \cdot 1 = n \cdot 0 + n = 0 + n = n; 1 \cdot n = (0 + 1) \cdot n = 0 \cdot n + n = 0 + n = n Def; (a); first two parts of (e) (f) mn = nm; m fixed, on n m \cdot 0 = 0 = 0 \cdot m m(n + 1) = mn + m \overset{	ext{IH}}{=} nm + m = (n + 1)m Def; (e) (d), second half; no induction (n + k)m = m(n + k) = mn + mk = nm + km (d), first half; (f) (g) (km)n = k(mn); k, m fixed, on n (km) \cdot 0 = 0 = k \cdot 0 = k(m \cdot 0) (km)(n + 1) = (km)n + km \overset{	ext{IH}}{=} k(mn) + km = k(mn + m) = k(m(n + 1)) Def; (d) ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- In the step of (a), second half, the third equality is (m + n) + 1 = m + (n + 1) (Def), read inside the outer + 1; in the step of (b), the last equality is (a), second half, read from right to left. In the long step of (e), the equalities after IH use, in order, (c), Def, (b), Def, (c), Def. In the second half of (e), 1 = 0 + 1 is the first half of (a), and (0 + 1) \cdot n = 0 \cdot n + n is the second part of (e) with m = 0. In (g), k(mn + m) = k(mn) + km is the first half of (d). This proves the theorem. The laws (a)–(g) are the rules of school arithmetic for + and \cdot on the natural numbers, now proved from the seven axioms for sets. The next section defines the order of \omega and ties it to them: m \le n exactly when n = m + j for some j \in \omega. Do not assume 0 + n = n. It is clause (a) of @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws, proved by induction; the defining equation is n + 0 = n. For the same reason, inducting on m in m + n = n + m gets stuck: the step would need (m + 1) + n, and the definition says nothing about a sum whose first argument is a successor until (a) is proved. The order of the table is forced by the lopsided definition. Commutativity, which lets us move a successor from the second place to the first, comes only after the two facts in (a) that move it by hand; once it is available, (e) and (f) follow the same way for multiplication. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These questions are about the proof of @thm-omega-recursion. 1. Where in the proof is \mathrm{S}(n) 
otin \mathrm{S}(n) used, and what would fail without it? 2. Run the construction for X = \omega, a = 0 and g(n, x) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(x)): write the graphs of the partial solutions up to 0, 1 and 2. 3. Why does the uniqueness half need only an induction, while existence needs partial solutions? 4. State the idea of the proof in two sentences. (a) In the inductive step of Step 3, in checking (Fn2) for the extended graph G'. The added pair has first coordinate \mathrm{S}(n), and every first coordinate in G_n lies in \mathrm{S}(n); because \mathrm{S}(n) 
otin \mathrm{S}(n), the input \mathrm{S}(n) is new, so adding the pair cannot give an old input a second output. If \mathrm{S}(n) were an element of \mathrm{S}(n), then G_n would already contain a pair (\mathrm{S}(n), y), and G' would contain both it and (\mathrm{S}(n), g(n, f_n(n))), so G' might fail to be a function. (b) Here g(n, x) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(x)) adds two steps. The partial solution up to 0 has graph \{(0, 0)\}. The next adds the pair at \mathrm{S}(0) = 1 with value g(0, 0) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(0)) = 2: the graph up to 1 is \{(0, 0), (1, 2)\}. The next adds the pair at 2 with value g(1, 2) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(2)) = 4: the graph up to 2 is \{(0, 0), (1, 2), (2, 4)\}. Each graph contains the previous one, as Step 3 says. (c) Uniqueness compares two functions that are given, value by value, and comparing values at n + 1 through the values at n is exactly an induction on n. Existence asks for a function that is not given; induction proves statements and builds nothing. So the proof proves by induction a statement (the claim of Step 3) about finite pieces, and builds f from them as a union, using (Z4). (d) For each n, induction shows that there is exactly one function on \mathrm{S}(n) obeying the equations, and any two of these agree at every point k where both are defined, because on \mathrm{S}(k) each restricts to the unique one up to k. Their union is the required function, and an induction shows there is no other. B. Practice [B1: Small products] Compute 3 \cdot 2 and 2 \cdot 3 from the defining equations of @def-omega-arithmetic alone, without using @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws. Here 5 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(4) and 6 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(5). For 3 \cdot 2, by (b) twice and then at 0: 3 \cdot 2 = 3 \cdot 1 + 3 = (3 \cdot 0 + 3) + 3 = (0 + 3) + 3 . By (a), 0 + 3 = \mathrm{S}(0 + 2) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(0 + 1)) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(0 + 0))) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(0))) = 3. Then 3 + 3 = \mathrm{S}(3 + 2) = \mathrm{S} igl(\mathrm{S}(3 + 1) igr) = \mathrm{S}\Bigl(\mathrm{S} igl(\mathrm{S}(3 + 0) igr)\Bigr) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(3))) = 6 . So 3 \cdot 2 = 6. For 2 \cdot 3, by (b), 2 \cdot 3 = 2 \cdot 2 + 2, and 2 \cdot 2 = 4 by the Quick check above. Then 4 + 2 = \mathrm{S}(4 + 1) = \mathrm{S} igl(\mathrm{S}(4 + 0) igr) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(4)) = 6 . So 2 \cdot 3 = 6 = 3 \cdot 2, as (f) of @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws predicts; but the two computations took different routes, and neither used a law. [B2: Distributivity, last step blank] Here is the proof of m(n + k) = mn + mk for all m, n, k \in \omega, with the last step left blank. Name the move, then complete it. Fix m, n \in \omega and induct on k. Base case: m(n + 0) = mn = mn + 0 = mn + m \cdot 0. Inductive step: suppose m(n + k) = mn + mk. Then m igl(n + (k + 1) igr) = m igl((n + k) + 1 igr) = m(n + k) + m = (mn + mk) + m = \underline{\hspace{6em}} . Justify each equality you add. The move is fix the others, induct on the recursion variable: in m(n + k) the recursion of + runs on k, so m and n are fixed and the induction is on k. The completion is (mn + mk) + m = mn + (mk + m) = mn + m(k + 1) , where the first equality is associativity, (c) of @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws, and the second is the defining equation m(k + 1) = mk + m of @def-omega-arithmetic (b), read from right to left. This is the statement for k + 1, so by @thm-omega-induction (b) it holds for every k \in \omega. (This is clause (d) of @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws, already proved; the exercise practices the move.) C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: addition is commutative] From the two defining equations of addition, m + 0 = m and m + (n + 1) = (m + n) + 1, and @thm-omega-induction alone, prove that m + n = n + m for all m, n \in \omega. Prove every auxiliary fact you need. [Hint 1] The definition says what happens when the second argument is 0 or a successor. To use it on n + m, you need to know the same for the first argument: prove two lemmas first. [Hint 2] The lemmas are 0 + n = n and (m + 1) + n = (m + n) + 1, each by induction on n. All inductions are by @thm-omega-induction (b). Lemma 1: 0 + n = n for every n. Induct on n. Base: 0 + 0 = 0, by the first equation. Step: if 0 + n = n, then 0 + (n + 1) = (0 + n) + 1 = n + 1, by the second equation and the hypothesis. Lemma 2: (m + 1) + n = (m + n) + 1 for all m, n. Fix m and induct on n. Base: (m + 1) + 0 = m + 1 = (m + 0) + 1, by the first equation twice. Step: if (m + 1) + n = (m + n) + 1, then (m + 1) + (n + 1) =  igl((m + 1) + n igr) + 1 =  igl((m + n) + 1 igr) + 1 =  igl(m + (n + 1) igr) + 1 , by the second equation, the hypothesis, and the second equation read from right to left inside the outer + 1. Main induction. Fix m and induct on n for “m + n = n + m”. Base: m + 0 = m = 0 + m, by the first equation and Lemma 1. Step: if m + n = n + m, then m + (n + 1) = (m + n) + 1 = (n + m) + 1 = (n + 1) + m , by the second equation, the hypothesis, and Lemma 2 (with n in the role of m and m in the role of n), read from right to left. Hence m + n = n + m for all m, n \in \omega. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: proves 0 + n = n by induction on n, from the first equation (base) and the second (step). - 3: proves, by an induction with the other variable fixed, a lemma that moves a successor out of the first argument (the book’s (m + 1) + n = (m + n) + 1, or 1 + n = n + 1 together with associativity of addition), base and step both justified. - 2: in the main induction, the base case m + 0 = 0 + m, using the first lemma. - 2: in the main induction, the step, using the second equation, the hypothesis and that lemma. - 1: names the variable inducted on in each induction and fixes the other. Fatal errors (0 for the step): citing commutativity, or any law of @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws, without proving it from the two equations; treating 0 + n = n as if it were a defining equation. A second route inducts on m in the main induction with n fixed; it needs the same two lemmas, and its base and step map to the same 2 + 2 points. A third route proves associativity and 1 + n = n + 1 (each by induction on n, from the equations and 0 + n = n) and then closes the step as m + (n + 1) = (m + n) + 1 = (n + m) + 1 = n + (m + 1) = n + (1 + m) = (n + 1) + m; those two lemmas together earn the 3 points. [C2: Associativity of multiplication, last half blank] Prove that (km)n = k(mn) for all k, m, n \in \omega. The first half is given; name the move, then complete it. Fix k, m \in \omega and induct on n. Base case: (km) \cdot 0 = 0 = k \cdot 0 = k(m \cdot 0). Inductive step: \underline{\hspace{10em}} You may use (a)–(f) of @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws. The move is fix the others, induct on the recursion variable: in (km)n and k(mn) the variable n is the second argument of the outer and the inner product, where the recursion runs, so k and m are fixed. Inductive step. Suppose (km)n = k(mn). Then  egin{aligned} (km)(n + 1) &= (km)n + km = k(mn) + km \ &= k(mn + m) = k igl(m(n + 1) igr) , \end{aligned} where the first equality is the defining equation of @def-omega-arithmetic (b) with first factor km, the second is the induction hypothesis, the third is (d) of @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws read from right to left (k(x + y) = kx + ky with x = mn, y = m), and the fourth is the defining equation with first factor m. By @thm-omega-induction (b), (km)n = k(mn) for every n, and k, m were arbitrary. The base case used the defining equation x \cdot 0 = 0 three times, with x = km, x = k and x = m. Commutativity (f) is not needed for this route; a proof that first rewrites km as mk would need it. [C3: Doubling] Show that there is exactly one function D \colon \omega 	o \omega with D(0) = 0 and D(n + 1) = (D(n) + 1) + 1 for every n \in \omega, and prove that D(n) = n + n for every n \in \omega. Existence and uniqueness. The function g \colon \omega 	imes \omega 	o \omega, g(n, x) \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(x)) = (x + 1) + 1, maps into \omega by (P2) of @thm-omega-peano applied twice. By @thm-omega-recursion with X = \omega and a = 0, there is exactly one D \colon \omega 	o \omega with D(0) = 0 and D(n + 1) = g(n, D(n)) = (D(n) + 1) + 1. (Its partial solutions up to 0, 1, 2 are those of @exr-recursion-and-arithmetic-a1 (b), so D(1) = 2 and D(2) = 4.) The formula. Induct on n by @thm-omega-induction (b) for “D(n) = n + n”. Base: D(0) = 0 = 0 + 0, by the defining equation m + 0 = m. Step: suppose D(n) = n + n. Then  egin{aligned} (n + 1) + (n + 1) &=  igl((n + 1) + n igr) + 1 =  igl((n + n) + 1 igr) + 1 \ &=  igl(D(n) + 1 igr) + 1 = D(n + 1) , \end{aligned} where the first equality is the defining equation of @def-omega-arithmetic (a), the second is (a) of @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws, (m + 1) + n = (m + n) + 1 with m = n, the third is the hypothesis, and the last is the equation of D. Hence D(n) = n + n for every n \in \omega. Alternatively, n \mapsto n + n satisfies the two equations that define D (the computation above, read without the hypothesis, shows (n + 1) + (n + 1) = ((n + n) + 1) + 1), so it is D by the uniqueness half of @thm-omega-recursion. Either way the double n + n is 2n too: 2n = n \cdot 2 = n \cdot 1 + n = n + n by (f), the defining equation of \cdot, and (e) of @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws.

title: 1.6 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers
content:
Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2 compared natural numbers with the order of the real line, and proved that every non-empty set of natural numbers has a least element (@fd2:thm-well-ordering) from that order and induction. In \omega there is no real line to borrow from. But the von Neumann numerals carry their order inside them: 3 = \{0, 1, 2\} is the set of the numbers before it. This section takes “is an element of” as the order, proves that it is a strict total order and a well-ordering, ties it to the arithmetic of the previous section, and then collects three groups of facts about \omega: powers and parity, n-tuples, and lists of variable length. Less than is “element of” The numerals of @exm-von-neumann-numerals were built so that each one collects all the earlier ones: 1 = \{0\}, 2 = \{0, 1\}, 4 = \{0, 1, 2, 3\}. So “m comes before n” can be read off the sets themselves, without any new structure. m is less than n when m is one of the elements of n. [Order on \omega] For m, n \in \omega, we write m < n if m \in n, and m \le n if m < n or m = n. As usual, n > m means m < n, and n \ge m means m \le n. If x_k = y_k for every k, then each element (k, x_k) of G is (k, y_k) \in G', and vice versa, so G = G' by (Z1).
