(c) An n-tuple contains the three pairs (1, x_1), (2, x_2), (3, x_3), which are distinct by @thm-kuratowski-pair, since their first coordinates are. Every element of a pair (a, b) = \{\{a\}, \{a, b\}\} is \{a\} or \{a, b\}. If a pair contained three distinct elements u, v, w, then u and v, being different, would be \{a\} and \{a, b\} in some order, and w, being one of these two, would equal u or v. So a pair has no three distinct elements, and an n-tuple is not a pair. Let 3 \le n < n'. The n'-tuple contains a pair with first coordinate n', since 1 \le n' \le n' (@thm-omega-order (d), with n' 
e 0). Every element of the n-tuple is a pair (k, x_k) with k \le n, and k = n' would give n' \le n, which trichotomy rules out since n < n'. By @thm-kuratowski-pair, no element of the n-tuple has first coordinate n', so the two sets differ. The case n' < n is the same with the roles exchanged. (d) Let n \in \omega and x \colon \{1, \dots, n\} 	o X. The set \{x_1, \dots, x_n\} is cut out of X by a condition, so it is a set by (Z6) of @ax-zf-fragment; by @fd2:def-image it is x(\{1, \dots, n\}). For n = 0 it is \emptyset, since \{1, \dots, 0\} = \emptyset. (e) An n-tuple t contains (1, x_1), so t 
e \emptyset = 0. Each element of t is a pair (k, x_k) = \{\{k\}, \{k, x_k\}\}, which has the element \{k\}, so no element of t is \emptyset. Every m \in \omega with m 
e 0 has 0 = \emptyset as an element (@lem-omega-transitive (e)). So t is neither 0 nor any other element of \omega. Clause (d) is the second half of working rule (W2): @fd2:prp-finite-max and @fd2:def-finite in Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 2 and 3, speak of \{x_1, \dots, x_n\} for a variable n, and this is the set they mean. Clauses (a) and (b) are working rule (W5) for n-tuples. Clause (c) bears out the convention of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1, that a triple is not a pair, and (e), with @prp-pair-not-natural for n = 2, that no pair or n-tuple is a natural number. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. List the elements of \{ k \in \omega : k \le 3 \}. Which natural number is this set? 2. True or false: for m, n \in \omega, m < n implies m \subseteq n. Justify your answer. 3. Find the least element of \{ n \in \omega : n \cdot n > 10 \}, and say why it is least. 4. Which clause of @thm-omega-order says that the notation \{0, \dots, n\} of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2 still means what it meant there, and what set is it on \omega? (a) 0, 1, 2, 3. By @thm-omega-order (c), the set is \mathrm{S}(3) = 4. (b) True. If m < n, then m \in n, and n is a transitive set (@lem-omega-transitive (a)), so m \subseteq n. (c) The least element is 4. From the defining equations, 0 \cdot 0 = 0, 1 \cdot 1 = 1, 2 \cdot 2 = 4, 3 \cdot 3 = 9 and 4 \cdot 4 = 16; and 16 > 10, since 10 \in 16 = \{0, 1, \dots, 15\}, while 0, 1, 4, 9 are all < 10, since each is an element of 10 = \{0, 1, \dots, 9\} (both by @thm-omega-order (c)). So 4 lies in the set. If x lies in the set and x < 4, then x \in 4 = \{0, 1, 2, 3\}, and x \cdot x \in \{0, 1, 4, 9\}, so x \cdot x < 10, and x \cdot x > 10 fails by trichotomy. Hence x < 4 is impossible, and 4 \le x by trichotomy. The set is non-empty, so @thm-omega-well-ordering promised a least element; this is it. (d) Clause (c): \{0, \dots, n\} \coloneqq \{ k \in \omega : k \le n \} is \mathrm{S}(n). (Clause (e) does the same for \{1, \dots, n\} = \mathrm{S}(n) \setminus \{0\}.) B. Practice [B1: Order as inclusion] Prove that for all m, n \in \omega, m \le n if and only if m \subseteq n. (\Rightarrow) If m = n, then m \subseteq n. If m < n, then m \in n, and m \subseteq n because n is a transitive set (@lem-omega-transitive (a)). (\Leftarrow) Let m \subseteq n, and suppose m \le n fails. By trichotomy (@thm-omega-order (a)), n < m, that is, n \in m. Then n \in m \subseteq n, so n \in n, contradicting @lem-omega-transitive (c). Hence m \le n. So on \omega, “\le” can be read as “\subseteq”, just as “<” is “\in”. For arbitrary sets the two readings come apart: \{1\} \subseteq \{0, 1\} = 2, but \{1\} is not a natural number at all: 0 \in 1 \in \{1\} while 0 
otin \{1\} (its only element is 1 
e 0), so \{1\} is not a transitive set, as every natural number is (@lem-omega-transitive (a)). [B2: A product is at least its factor] Prove that for all m, n \in \omega with n \ge 1, m \le mn. Show by an example that the hypothesis n \ge 1 is needed. Since 1 \le n, @prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a) gives n = 1 + j for some j \in \omega. Then mn = m(1 + j) = m \cdot 1 + mj = m + mj , by @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (d) and (e). By @prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a) again, m \le m + mj = mn. The hypothesis is needed: for m = 1 and n = 0, mn = 0, and 1 \le 0 is false, since 0 < 1 (@thm-omega-order (d)) and trichotomy. C. Going deeper [C1: Strong induction on ω] Let P(n) be a property of natural numbers. Suppose that, for every n \in \omega, if P(k) holds for every k \in \omega with k < n, then P(n) holds. Prove that P(n) holds for every n \in \omega. [Hint 1] Consider the set of natural numbers at which P fails. [Hint 2] If that set is non-empty, @thm-omega-well-ordering gives it a least element a. What do you know about P(k) for k < a? Let A \coloneqq \{ n \in \omega : P(n) 	ext{ fails} \}, a set by (Z6) of @ax-zf-fragment, and suppose, for a contradiction, that A 
e \emptyset. By @thm-omega-well-ordering, A has a least element a. Let k \in \omega with k < a. If k \in A, then a \le k, and with k < a this gives k < k (by transitivity, or directly if a = k), contradicting irreflexivity (@thm-omega-order (a)). So k 
otin A, that is, P(k) holds. This holds for every k < a, so the hypothesis gives P(a), contradicting a \in A. Hence A = \emptyset, and P(n) holds for every n \in \omega. This is the statement of @fd1:thm-strong-induction, read on \omega. There it was derived from @fd1:ax-induction directly; here the route goes through well-ordering, which was itself proved from @thm-omega-induction. As there, the hypothesis at n = 0 is vacuous (no k < 0), so it hands us P(0) outright. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: considers the set of failures (or argues by contradiction from a failure) and makes it a set. - 3: applies @thm-omega-well-ordering, with the set non-empty, to obtain a least failure a. - 3: shows P(k) for every k < a, using that a is least and the order facts. - 2: applies the hypothesis at a and reaches the contradiction. Fatal errors (0 for the step): citing @fd1:thm-strong-induction (a statement about Logic and Proof, Chapter 3’s 
N, not proved on \omega) instead of proving the result; taking a least element of a set not shown to be non-empty. A route by @thm-omega-induction (b) on “P(k) for every k < n” earns the same points: 2 for the property, 3 for the base (vacuous) and the use of @thm-omega-order (b) in the step, 3 for the step, 2 for deducing P(n) from the property at n + 1. [C2: Find the error] Here is an attempted proof that any two natural numbers are comparable. Is the conclusion true? Is the proof correct? If not, give the first line that fails, the rule it breaks, and a counterexample to the step. Claim. For all m, n \in \omega: m \in n, m = n or n \in m. (1) We use @thm-omega-induction (b) on n, for the property “for every m \in \omega: m \in n, m = n or n \in m”. (2) For n = 0: every m is 0 or contains 0, by @lem-omega-transitive (e). (3) Suppose the property holds for n, and let m \in \omega. (4) If m \in n or m = n, then m \in n \cup \{n\} = \mathrm{S}(n). (5) If n \in m, then \mathrm{S}(n) \le m, because nothing lies strictly between n and \mathrm{S}(n): no k \in \omega has n \in k \in \mathrm{S}(n). (6) In every case m \in \mathrm{S}(n), m = \mathrm{S}(n) or \mathrm{S}(n) \in m, which is the property for \mathrm{S}(n). (7) By @thm-omega-induction (b), the claim holds. The conclusion is true: it is trichotomy, @thm-omega-order (a). The proof is not correct. The failing line is (5). Its reason, “nothing lies strictly between n and \mathrm{S}(n)”, is true (it follows from irreflexivity and transitivity, as in @thm-omega-order (b)), but it does not give \mathrm{S}(n) \le m. To pass from “m is not strictly between n and \mathrm{S}(n)” to “\mathrm{S}(n) \in m or \mathrm{S}(n) = m”, one must know that if neither holds, then m \in \mathrm{S}(n). That is trichotomy for \mathrm{S}(n) and m: an instance of the claim being proved, at a number the induction has not reached. So the stated reason gives (5) only by assuming the goal (circular). Without that, (5) asserts the general fact “n \in m \Rightarrow \mathrm{S}(n) \le m”, which is true but not yet proved. Either way, line (5) rests on an unavailable fact: entry (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. Counterexample to the step. The inference “x \in y and nothing lies strictly between x and x \cup \{x\}, so x \cup \{x\} \in y or x \cup \{x\} = y” fails for sets in general. Take x = \emptyset and y = \{\emptyset, \{\{\emptyset\}\}\}. Then x \in y, and nothing lies strictly between x and x \cup \{x\} = \{\emptyset\} (the only element of \{\emptyset\} is \emptyset, and \emptyset 
otin \emptyset). But \{\emptyset\} 
otin y, since \{\emptyset\} 
e \emptyset and \{\emptyset\} 
e \{\{\emptyset\}\}; and \{\emptyset\} 
e y, since \{\{\emptyset\}\} \in y is not an element of \{\emptyset\}. So the step needs something about \omega beyond “nothing in between”. Repair. Replace (5) by the claim inside the proof of @thm-omega-order: for all m, n \in \omega, m \in n implies \mathrm{S}(m) \in \mathrm{S}(n), proved by its own induction. Then n \in m gives \mathrm{S}(n) \in \mathrm{S}(m) = m \cup \{m\}, so \mathrm{S}(n) \in m or \mathrm{S}(n) = m. Lines (1)–(4), (6) and (7) are correct. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: says that the conclusion is true and that the proof is not correct. - 3: names line (5) as the failing line and explains why its reason does not give \mathrm{S}(n) \le m (it needs trichotomy for \mathrm{S}(n) and m, or the unproved fact n \in m \Rightarrow \mathrm{S}(n) \le m). - 2: classifies the error as (N9): a line resting on an unavailable fact, either the goal itself (circular) or an unproved general fact. - 2: gives a counterexample to the step on arbitrary sets (any x \in y with x \cup \{x\} neither in nor equal to y). - 1: gives the repair through “m \in n \Rightarrow \mathrm{S}(m) \in \mathrm{S}(n)”. Fatal errors (0 for the step): declaring the conclusion false; blaming line (2) or (4), which are correct.

title: 1.7 All Peano Systems Are Alike
content:
All Peano Systems Are Alike Section 1.4 proved that (\omega, 0, \mathrm{S}) is a Peano system (@thm-omega-peano, @def-peano-system), and Sections 1.5 and 1.6 built +, \cdot and < on it. One question is left. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2 worked with a set 
N inside the familiar real numbers, and this chapter has built a quite different set \omega out of \emptyset. In what sense are they the same? This section answers: any two Peano systems are copies of each other, by exactly one matching, which also carries +, \cdot and < across. Then it says what the later chapters may take from Logic and Proof, Chapter 3, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2 when they write 
N for \omega. Two Peano systems, and what “alike” should mean Here is a second Peano system, inside \omega itself: (\omega \setminus \{0\}, 1, \mathrm{S}), the natural numbers from 1 on, with the same successor. Exercise C1 of Section 1.4 asked you to check it; the check is three lines. - \mathrm{S} maps \omega \setminus \{0\} into itself, since \mathrm{S}(n) 
e 0 by @thm-omega-peano (P3). - (P3) holds with e = 1: if \mathrm{S}(n) = 1 = \mathrm{S}(0), then n = 0 by (P4) of @thm-omega-peano, and 0 
otin \omega \setminus \{0\}. (P4) holds because \mathrm{S} is injective on all of \omega. - (P5) holds: if A \subseteq \omega \setminus \{0\} contains 1 and is closed under \mathrm{S}, then \{0\} \cup A contains 0 and is closed under \mathrm{S} (as \mathrm{S}(0) = 1 \in A), so it is \omega by @thm-omega-induction (a), and A = \omega \setminus \{0\}. Its starting point is 1, not \emptyset, yet it counts the same way: n \mapsto \mathrm{S}(n) pairs 0, 1, 2, \dots with 1, 2, 3, \dots, sends start to start, and turns one step into one step. That is the right meaning of “alike”. For Peano systems (M, e, s) and (M', e', s'), call a bijection \psi \colon M 	o M' an isomorphism if \psi(e) = e' \quad 	ext{and} \quad \psi igl(s(x) igr) = s' igl(\psi(x) igr) \ 	ext{ for every } x \in M . In words: \psi renames the elements, sends the starting point to the starting point, and it does not matter whether we first step and then rename, or first rename and then step. Being equinumerous is not enough. The bijection 	au \colon \omega 	o \omega that exchanges 1 and 2 and fixes every other number satisfies 	au(0) = 0, but 	au(\mathrm{S}(0)) = 	au(1) = 2, while \mathrm{S}(	au(0)) = \mathrm{S}(0) = 1. So 	au is a bijection from a Peano system to itself that is not an isomorphism: it does not respect the successor. Categoricity, below, is a statement about isomorphisms, and it says much more than “same size”. The categoricity theorem The theorem says that every Peano system is an isomorphic copy of \omega, and so any two are copies of each other, in only one way. [Categoricity of the Peano Axioms] Let (M, e, s) be a Peano system. 1. There is exactly one function \varphi \colon \omega 	o M with \varphi(0) = e and \varphi(\mathrm{S}(n)) = s(\varphi(n)) for every n \in \omega. 2. This \varphi is a bijection. 3. For any two Peano systems (M, e, s) and (M', e', s') there is exactly one bijection \psi \colon M 	o M' with \psi(e) = e' and \psi(s(x)) = s'(\psi(x)) for every x \in M. Try it first (ten minutes): given a Peano system (M, e, s), which map \omega 	o M would you build, with which theorem, and how would you show that it is onto? The attempt meets three obstacles, one for each part. ① Which map. It is forced: 0 must go to e, then 1 to s(e), then 2 to s(s(e)), and so on. But “and so on” is not a definition. @thm-omega-recursion turns it into one, with X = M, starting value e and step x \mapsto s(x); it gives existence and uniqueness at once. ② Onto. We know nothing about the elements of M one by one, so we cannot show “each x \in M is s(\dots s(e))” directly. What we have is (P5) for M, which speaks about subsets. So look at the image of \varphi: it contains e and is closed under s, and (P5) does the rest. ③ One-to-one. Prove “\varphi(m) = \varphi(n) \Rightarrow m = n” by induction on n. If m is fixed before the induction, the hypothesis at n speaks about that one m, while the step needs it at the predecessor of m. So “for every m” goes inside the property. The base and the step then use (P3) and (P4) for M: a successor is never e, and equal successors have equal predecessors. For (c), compose: go back from M to \omega along \varphi^{-1}, then forward to M' along \varphi'. Before reading on: which axiom of M gives surjectivity, and which give injectivity? (a) Let g \colon \omega 	imes M 	o M be g(n, x) \coloneqq s(x); its graph \{ ((n, x), y) \in (\omega 	imes M) 	imes M : y = s(x) \} is a set by (Z6) inside the product of @prp-cartesian-product-exists, and each (n, x) has exactly one partner s(x) because s is a function. By @thm-omega-recursion with X = M and a = e, there is exactly one \varphi \colon \omega 	o M with \varphi(0) = e and \varphi(\mathrm{S}(n)) = g(n, \varphi(n)) = s(\varphi(n)) for every n \in \omega. (b), onto. Let B \coloneqq \varphi(\omega) \subseteq M, the image of \omega under \varphi (@fd2:def-image). Then e = \varphi(0) \in B. If x \in B, say x = \varphi(n) with n \in \omega, then \mathrm{S}(n) \in \omega by @thm-omega-peano (P2), and s(x) = s(\varphi(n)) = \varphi(\mathrm{S}(n)) \in B. So B contains e and is closed under s, and (P5) for M gives B = M. Hence \varphi is surjective (@fd2:def-surjective). (b), one-to-one. Let Q(n) be “for every m \in \omega, if \varphi(m) = \varphi(n), then m = n”. We prove Q(n) for every n \in \omega by @thm-omega-induction (b). Base case. Let m \in \omega with \varphi(m) = \varphi(0) = e. Suppose m 
e 0. Then m = \mathrm{S}(k) for some k \in \omega (@lem-omega-transitive (d)), and \varphi(m) = s(\varphi(k)) 
e e by (P3) for M, a contradiction. So m = 0. Inductive step. Let n \in \omega with Q(n), and let m \in \omega with \varphi(m) = \varphi(\mathrm{S}(n)) = s(\varphi(n)). If m = 0, then s(\varphi(n)) = \varphi(0) = e, against (P3) for M. So m 
e 0, and m = \mathrm{S}(k) for some k \in \omega (@lem-omega-transitive (d)). Then s(\varphi(k)) = \varphi(m) = s(\varphi(n)), so \varphi(k) = \varphi(n) by (P4) for M, and k = n by Q(n), applied to k in the place of m. Hence m = \mathrm{S}(k) = \mathrm{S}(n), which is Q(\mathrm{S}(n)). So \varphi is injective (@fd2:def-injective), and with the first half it is a bijection (@fd2:def-bijective). (c) Let \varphi \colon \omega 	o M and \varphi' \colon \omega 	o M' be the maps of (a) for the two systems; both are bijections by (b). By @fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse, \varphi has an inverse \varphi^{-1} \colon M 	o \omega, and we set \psi \coloneqq \varphi' \circ \varphi^{-1} (@fd2:def-composition). The two equations \varphi \circ \varphi^{-1} = \id_M and \varphi^{-1} \circ \varphi = \id_\omega of @fd2:def-inverse-function also say that \varphi is an inverse of \varphi^{-1}, so \varphi^{-1} is a bijection by @fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse. Hence \psi is a bijection as a composite of bijections (@fd2:thm-composition-injective-surjective (c)). \psi has the two properties. Since \varphi(0) = e, we have \varphi^{-1}(e) = 0, so \psi(e) = \varphi'(0) = e'. Let x \in M and n \coloneqq \varphi^{-1}(x), so x = \varphi(n). Then s(x) = \varphi(\mathrm{S}(n)), so \varphi^{-1}(s(x)) = \mathrm{S}(n), and \psi igl(s(x) igr) = \varphi' igl(\mathrm{S}(n) igr) = s' igl(\varphi'(n) igr) = s' igl(\psi(x) igr) . Uniqueness. Let \chi \colon M 	o M' be any function with \chi(e) = e' and \chi(s(x)) = s'(\chi(x)) for every x \in M. Then \chi \circ \varphi \colon \omega 	o M' satisfies (\chi \circ \varphi)(0) = \chi(e) = e' and (\chi \circ \varphi) igl(\mathrm{S}(n) igr) = \chi igl(s(\varphi(n)) igr) = s' igl((\chi \circ \varphi)(n) igr) for every n \in \omega. By the uniqueness in (a), for the system M', \chi \circ \varphi = \varphi'. So for every x \in M, \chi(x) = \chi(\varphi(\varphi^{-1}(x))) = \varphi'(\varphi^{-1}(x)) = \psi(x), and \chi = \psi by @fd2:prp-function-equality. This proves the theorem. The proof is the third named move of the chapter, build by recursion, compare by induction: the map out of \omega came from the recursion theorem, and every fact about it (onto, one-to-one) came from an induction or from (P5). The uniqueness in (c) is stronger than stated: no function at all, bijective or not, other than \psi respects e and s. Each axiom of M has a job in (b), and the structures of @exm-peano-axioms-independent show each job failing. These are not Peano systems, so the theorem does not apply to them. But for each of them @thm-omega-recursion, with X = M, a = e and g(n, x) = s(x) exactly as in the proof of (a), still gives exactly one \varphi \colon \omega 	o M with \varphi(0) = e and \varphi(\mathrm{S}(n)) = s(\varphi(n)). - In structure (i), M = \{0\} with s(0) = 0, which fails (P3) only, \varphi is the constant map 0, not injective: \varphi(1) = s(\varphi(0)) = 0 = \varphi(0). - In structure (ii), M = \{0, 1\} with s(0) = s(1) = 1, which fails (P4) only, \varphi(1) = \varphi(2) = 1, again not injective. - In the natural numbers beside a two-sided chain, structure (iii), which fails (P5) only, \varphi is n \mapsto (n, 0) (remark below), which is injective by @thm-kuratowski-pair, but not onto, as the remark below shows. What induction buys. In structure (iii) of @exm-peano-axioms-independent, the natural numbers beside a two-sided chain (a copy of \omega next to a copy of 
Z), M = \omega 	imes 3 with e = (0, 0), the map \varphi still exists, by @thm-omega-recursion as above. It is \varphi(n) = (n, 0), by the uniqueness half of @thm-omega-recursion: n \mapsto (n, 0) sends 0 to e and satisfies the recursion, as s(n, 0) = (\mathrm{S}(n), 0). Its image \omega 	imes \{0\} misses (0, 1), so \varphi is not onto. Exercise C2 asks the reverse question: is there a map M 	o \omega that respects the two structures? For the Peano system (\omega \setminus \{0\}, 1, \mathrm{S}) of the first subsection, what is the map \varphi of @thm-peano-categoricity (a)? What is \varphi(3)? \varphi(n) = \mathrm{S}(n) = n + 1. Indeed n \mapsto \mathrm{S}(n) maps \omega into \omega \setminus \{0\} by (P3), sends 0 to \mathrm{S}(0) = 1, and satisfies \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(n)) = \mathrm{S}(\varphi(n)); by the uniqueness in (a), it is \varphi. So \varphi(3) = \mathrm{S}(3) = 4. Step by step: \varphi(0) = 1, \varphi(1) = \mathrm{S}(1) = 2, \varphi(2) = 3, \varphi(3) = 4. Arithmetic and order travel along the isomorphism An isomorphism matches e and s. Addition and multiplication on \omega were built from 0 and \mathrm{S} alone, by recursion (@def-omega-arithmetic), and < can be described by + (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a)). So we expect the matching to carry them across, as long as the other system has operations defined by the same equations. [Isomorphisms Preserve Arithmetic and Order] Let (M, e, s) be a Peano system, and let \oplus, \otimes \colon M 	imes M 	o M be functions such that, for all x, y \in M,  egin{aligned} x \oplus e &= x, & x \oplus s(y) &= s(x \oplus y), \ x \otimes e &= e, & x \otimes s(y) &= (x \otimes y) \oplus x . \end{aligned} Let \varphi \colon \omega 	o M be the bijection of @thm-peano-categoricity. Then for all m, n \in \omega: 1. \varphi(m + n) = \varphi(m) \oplus \varphi(n); 2. \varphi(m n) = \varphi(m) \otimes \varphi(n); 3. m < n if and only if \varphi(n) = \varphi(m) \oplus z for some z \in M with z 
e e. For (a) and (b), fix m and induct on n, the variable the recursions run on: each side obeys the same two equations, the base from 0 and the step from \mathrm{S}, and \varphi turns one set of equations into the other. For (c), translate @prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a), “m < n iff n = m + j with j 
e 0”, through (a), using that \varphi is a bijection with \varphi(0) = e. (a) Fix m \in \omega; we induct on n (@thm-omega-induction (b)). Base case: \varphi(m + 0) = \varphi(m) = \varphi(m) \oplus e = \varphi(m) \oplus \varphi(0), by @def-omega-arithmetic (a) and the first equation for \oplus. Step: if \varphi(m + n) = \varphi(m) \oplus \varphi(n), then  egin{aligned} \varphi igl(m + \mathrm{S}(n) igr) &= \varphi igl(\mathrm{S}(m + n) igr) = s igl(\varphi(m + n) igr) \ &= s igl(\varphi(m) \oplus \varphi(n) igr) = \varphi(m) \oplus s igl(\varphi(n) igr) = \varphi(m) \oplus \varphi igl(\mathrm{S}(n) igr) , \end{aligned} by @def-omega-arithmetic (a), the equation of \varphi, the hypothesis, the second equation for \oplus, and the equation of \varphi again. Let L \colon \omega 	o \omega have the graph G \coloneqq  igl\{ (n, k) \in \omega 	imes \omega : (n = 0 	ext{ and } k = 0) 	ext{ or } n = \mathrm{S}(k)  igr\}, a set by (Z6). Each n \in \omega has exactly one partner. If n = 0, the partner k = 0 works, and no k has 0 = \mathrm{S}(k), by (P3). If n 
e 0, then n = \mathrm{S}(k) for some k (@lem-omega-transitive (d)), and only one, by (P4). So L is a function (@fd2:def-function) with L(0) = 0 and L(\mathrm{S}(k)) = k. Hence L(\mathrm{S}(n)) = n for every n \in \omega, that is, L \circ \mathrm{S} = \id_\omega: L is a left inverse of \mathrm{S} (@fd2:def-left-right-inverse (a)). This matches @fd2:thm-left-inverse-iff-injective: \mathrm{S} is injective and \omega 
e \emptyset. Not unique. The value of a left inverse at 0 is never used, since 0 is not of the form \mathrm{S}(n); setting L'(0) \coloneqq 5 and L'(\mathrm{S}(k)) \coloneqq k gives another left inverse. [R3] Let M = \{0, 1\}, e = 0 and s(0) = s(1) = 1. Show that there is no function f \colon M 	o \omega with f(0) = 0 and f(s(x)) = \mathrm{S}(f(x)) for every x \in M. Which of the Peano axioms play the part, for definitions on \omega, that a theorem about reading formulas plays for definitions on formulas? Suppose f exists. Taking x = 1, f(1) = f(s(1)) = \mathrm{S}(f(1)). But no n \in \omega has n = \mathrm{S}(n): n \in \mathrm{S}(n) (@def-set-successor), so n = \mathrm{S}(n) would give n \in n, against @lem-omega-transitive (c). So no such f exists. (Taking x = 0 instead gives f(1) = \mathrm{S}(0) = 1, so the two equations at the input 1 also contradict each other.) The trouble is that 1 is built in two ways, as s(0) and as s(1), and the two ways ask for different values. In Logic and Proof, Chapter 3, @fd1:thm-structural-recursion defines functions on formulas, and what makes it work is @fd1:thm-unique-readability: each compound formula is built from its parts in exactly one way. On \omega the same job is done by (P3) and (P4): 0 is not a successor, so its value is not asked for twice, and a successor is the successor of exactly one number, so the equation at \mathrm{S}(n) asks for one thing. The structure M fails (P4), since s(0) = s(1), though it satisfies (P5). [R4] For n \in \omega, compute  igcup \mathrm{S}(n) and  igcup n. Then find a set x with  igcup \mathrm{S}(x) 
e x. A formula for every set. For any set x,  igcup \mathrm{S}(x) =  igcup (x \cup \{x\}) =  igcup x \cup x: an element of a member of x \cup \{x\} is an element of a member of x, or an element of x itself. For n \in \omega. The tool is transitivity. By @lem-omega-transitive (a), n is transitive, so every element of a member of n is a member of n, that is,  igcup n \subseteq n. Hence  igcup \mathrm{S}(n) =  igcup n \cup n = n. For  igcup n itself:  igcup 0 =  igcup \emptyset = \emptyset = 0; and if n 
e 0, then n = \mathrm{S}(k) (@lem-omega-transitive (d)), and  igcup n =  igcup \mathrm{S}(k) = k by what we just proved. So  igcup undoes the successor: it is the “predecessor” on \omega, with 0 sent to 0. A set where it fails. Let x \coloneqq \{1\} = \{\{\emptyset\}\}. Then  igcup x = 1 = \{\emptyset\}, and  igcup \mathrm{S}(x) = \{\emptyset\} \cup \{\{\emptyset\}\} = \{0, 1\} = 2. This is not x: 0 = \emptyset \in 2, but \emptyset 
otin x, since the only element of x is \{\emptyset\} 
e \emptyset. Why the identity alone is not enough. The look-alike tool is the identity  igcup \mathrm{S}(x) =  igcup x \cup x, which holds for every set. On its own it does not give x: it gives  igcup \mathrm{S}(x) = x exactly when  igcup x \subseteq x, that is, when x is transitive (@def-transitive-set), and \{1\}, which is not transitive, is a witness that this can fail. Nor is an induction on n a route that avoids transitivity: its step  igcup \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(n)) =  igcup \mathrm{S}(n) \cup \mathrm{S}(n) = n \cup \mathrm{S}(n) = \mathrm{S}(n) proves  igcup \mathrm{S}(n) = n, which is equivalent to transitivity of n, so it proves @lem-omega-transitive (a) again along the way.

title: Building the Integers and the Rationals from Equivalence Classes
content:
Building the Integers and the Rationals from Equivalence Classes “Subtract 5 from 3” has no answer in 
N, and “halve 1” has none among the integers. School answers by inventing -2 and 	frac12. This chapter builds them, from pairs and nothing else. The pairs (3, 5) and (0, 2) both record “two less than nothing”, and the integer -2 is the set of all pairs that record it; the pairs (1, 2) and (2, 4) both record “one divided by two”, and the rational 	frac12 is the set of all pairs that record that. The tool is the quotient of a set by an equivalence relation, from Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.5, used twice: once on 
N 	imes 
N to make 
Z, once on 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0} to make 
Q. The one thing that can go wrong is an operation that depends on which pair was used to name a class, and the chapter’s central skill is checking that it does not. At the end, 
Q is an ordered field, every rule for inequalities used in this chapter is proved from the order axioms, and every rational lies below a natural number. Yet 
Q still has a hole where \sqrt 2 should be: no rational squares to 2, and the rationals whose square is below 2 have no least upper bound in 
Q. Later chapters of this volume fill the hole. The school picture. Logic and Proof, Chapters 1–5, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 1–3 treated 
Z and 
Q as known subsets of the familiar real line (Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.1), and used their arithmetic and order as school facts. From this chapter on they are the sets built here, and the familiar facts are theorems. Section 2.2 proves 
Z = 
N \cup \{ -n : n \in 
N \}, the description that Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.1 took as a definition, and Section 2.4 proves 
Q = \{ m/n : m \in 
Z, \ n \in 
Z_{>0} \} in the same way. Nothing earlier was circular: Logic and Proof, Chapters 1–5, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 1–3 used these facts as stated facts, never as proved ones. No proof in this chapter uses a school fact about the integers, the rationals or the real numbers; school decimals appear once, in a table in Section 2.6 marked as being for orientation only. The results of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 2 and 3 about their integers, such as the division algorithm and congruences, are not cited for the constructed 
Z; a later chapter of this volume rebuilds them. What you need. Chapter 1 and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 1 and 2, chiefly Chapter 1 and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.5. From Chapter 1, the natural numbers \omega with the citing rule of Section 1.7 (@cor-omega-identification), by which 
N means \omega and induction (@fd1:ax-induction) and the recursion theorem (@fd2:thm-recursion) of Logic and Proof, Chapter 3, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2 apply to it; the arithmetic of \omega (@def-omega-arithmetic, @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws, @cor-omega-successor-cancellation), its order, cancellation and subtraction (@thm-omega-order, @prp-omega-order-arithmetic), well-ordering (@thm-omega-well-ordering), induction and recursion on \omega (@thm-omega-induction, @thm-omega-recursion), and the theorem that no pair is a natural number (@prp-pair-not-natural). From Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.5: equivalence relations, classes and quotient sets (@fd2:def-equivalence-relation, @fd2:def-equivalence-class, @fd2:def-quotient-set, @fd2:thm-classes-partition), and the two examples that this chapter generalizes, arithmetic modulo n (@fd2:prp-congruence-arithmetic) and a rule on classes that is not a function (@fd2:exm-ill-defined-class-map). From Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.6: partial orders, upper bounds and suprema (@fd2:def-partial-order, @fd2:def-order-bounds, @fd2:def-order-supremum). From Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1: sets cut out by a property (@fd2:def-set-builder), ordered pairs, products and relations (@fd2:def-ordered-pair, @fd2:def-cartesian-product, @fd2:def-relation), and functions, their equality and injectivity (@fd2:def-function, @fd2:prp-function-equality, @fd2:def-injective). From Logic and Proof, Chapter 5, the catalogue of what a proof may not do (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue), for the find-the-error exercises. Section 2.6 compares its proof with Logic and Proof, Chapter 2’s parity proof that \sqrt 2 is irrational (@fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational), which it does not use, and names the rule ulename{
eg I} (@fd1:def-rules-negation, @fd1:def-rule-raa). A few exercises reach further back: the negation laws of Logic and Proof, Chapters 2 and 4 (@fd1:prp-de-morgan, @fd1:prp-quantifier-negation, @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation, @fd1:prp-negated-implication) in Section 2.5’s A1 and in review exercise R3; finite and infinite sets (@fd2:def-finite, @fd2:def-infinite, @fd2:cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets, @fd2:prp-subset-finite) in Section 2.3’s C1; a quotient by the fibres of a function (@fd2:exm-fibres-of-function) in Section 2.2’s C1; and countable sets (@fd2:thm-product-countable, @fd2:cor-product-countable, @fd2:prp-countable-subset, @fd2:prp-countable-image) in review exercise R2, read on \omega through Section 1.7 (@prp-omega-powers-parity). Time. About 25 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 35 hours for everything. Roadmap - The Integers as Classes of Pairs. Pairs (a, b) of natural numbers as notes saying “a minus b”, the cross-sum relation a + d = b + c proved an equivalence relation by cancellation in 
N, 
Z as its quotient set, the classes drawn as diagonals of the quarter plane, and the normal form [(n, 0)] or [(0, n)] of each integer. - Well-Definedness, and the Arithmetic of the Integers. The lemma that a rule on classes is a function as soon as equivalent inputs give equivalent outputs (for maps, for binary operations one argument at a time, and for properties), the sum, product and negative of integers checked against it, rules that fail it, and the copy of 
N inside 
Z that makes 
Z = 
N \cup \{ -n : n \in 
N \} a theorem. - The Integers as an Ordered Ring. The axioms (F1)–(F9) of a commutative ring and of a field, 
Z a commutative ring by reduction of each law to 
N, ordered rings and the orders that come from a positive set, the order of 
Z and its discreteness, the rules for inequalities in every ordered ring, least elements of bounded sets of integers, and a field with two elements that cannot be ordered. - The Rationals as Classes of Fractions. Pairs (p, q) with q > 0 identified by cross-multiplication, 
Q as their quotient set with a well-defined sum and product, the proof that 
Q is a field, the copy of 
Z inside it that turns the class [(p, q)] into the quotient p/q, and why non-zero denominators would give the same set but spoil the order. - The Rationals as an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property. The positive rationals as the classes with a positive numerator, 
Q an ordered field with the comparison formula p/q < r/s \iff ps < rq, reciprocals reversing order, a midpoint between any two rationals, the Archimedean property proved from the construction with no supremum in sight, its form 1/n < \varepsilon for rational \varepsilon > 0, and the integer part  loor{x}. - The Gaps in the Rationals. No rational squares to 2, proved by descent on a least denominator rather than by parity, the set \{ x \in 
Q : x^2 < 2 \} bounded above with no supremum in 
Q, and the rational sequence 2, 	frac32, 	frac{17}{12}, 	frac{577}{408}, \dots that closes in on the gap from above; the review exercises reach back to Chapter 1, Logic and Proof, Chapters 2, 4, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 2, 3. Named moves - Check on representatives, one argument at a time. To show that [x] \ast [y] \coloneqq [g(x, y)] is well defined, change x to an equivalent x' with y fixed, then y to an equivalent y' with x' fixed, and join the two changes by transitivity, as the lemma of Section 2.2 does. Each change is one computation at the level below. When the formula is symmetric in its two inputs, the second change comes free. A formula that merely looks right is not yet a definition. - Reduce to the level below. A law about classes, written on representatives, becomes an identity in 
N (for 
Z) or in 
Z (for 
Q), which is already proved. The two sides are either the same pair or two related pairs, and in both cases the classes agree. - Order from a positive set. To order a commutative ring, say which elements are positive, check that they are closed under + and \cdot and that every element is exactly one of positive, zero or minus a positive, and let a < b mean that b - a is positive. Every rule for inequalities then follows by turning the comparison into one positive element.

title: 2.1 The Integers as Classes of Pairs
content:
The Integers as Classes of Pairs Chapter 1 built the natural numbers as the set \omega, with its 0, +, \cdot and <, and proved the laws of arithmetic, the order and well-ordering from the axioms for sets. From this chapter on, 
N means that set (@cor-omega-identification and the citing rule of Section 1.7). In 
N the equation 5 + x = 3 has no solution: 5 \le 5 + x for every x \in 
N by @prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a), while 3 < 5 by the same result, as 5 = 3 + 2 with 2 
e 0. So 5 + x = 3 would give 5 \le 3 < 5, hence 5 < 5, which @thm-omega-order (a) rules out. This section builds a larger set 
Z, out of 
N alone, with the one tool of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.5: the quotient of a set by an equivalence relation. What we use about the natural numbers Every fact about 
N in this section and the next is one of the following results of Chapter 1, and each is cited where a proof uses it. The defining equation n + 0 = n and the evaluation of numeral sums and comparisons such as 2 + 3 = 5 and 0 
e 2 rest on @def-omega-arithmetic and @thm-omega-order and are not cited each time. - Defining equations (@def-omega-arithmetic): n + 0 = n, m + \mathrm{S}(n) = \mathrm{S}(m + n) and n \cdot 0 = 0, and the numerals 0 \coloneqq \emptyset, 1, 2, …, with n + 1 = \mathrm{S}(n). - Laws of arithmetic (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws): + and \cdot are commutative and associative, \cdot distributes over +, and 0 + n = n, 1 \cdot n = n, 0 \cdot n = 0. - Cancellation (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (b), (f)): m + k = n + k gives m = n; and mk = nk with k 
e 0 gives m = n. - Order (@thm-omega-order (a)): < is a strict total order, so for all m, n exactly one of m < n, m = n, n < m holds, and < is transitive and irreflexive. - Order and addition (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a)): m \le n if and only if n = m + j for some j \in 
N; and m < n if and only if n = m + j for some j 
e 0. Adding preserves < (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (c)). - Small facts and well-ordering: 0 < 1 (@thm-omega-order (d)); no k satisfies n < k < \mathrm{S}(n) (@thm-omega-order (b)); every non-empty subset of 
N has a least element (@thm-omega-well-ordering). That is the whole list for now. Nothing about the integers or the rationals of school enters a proof: from here on they are the sets this chapter builds, and their familiar properties become theorems. A naive attempt The school picture of an integer is “a natural number with a sign”: +3, -2, 0. It is tempting to take that literally and let an integer be a pair (s, n) with a sign s \in \{0, 1\} (read 0 as “plus” and 1 as “minus”) and a size n \in 
N. Two things go wrong at once. First, zero gets two names, (0, 0) and (1, 0): a “plus zero” and a “minus zero”. Either both stay, and every theorem must treat them as the same, or one is banned, and every definition must check that it never produces the banned one. Second, addition needs cases. Adding +m and -n should give +(m - n) when n \le m and -(n - m) when m < n, where m - n is the subtraction of @prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a), defined on 
N only when n \le m. There are four sign patterns for a sum, and two of them split again by the order of the sizes. A proof that addition is associative would split by the signs of all three terms and then by the order of their sizes, and every case would subtract in 
N in its own direction. The trouble in both is the same: the definition performs a subtraction that 
N can only do one way round. The construction below never performs it. It records the subtraction as a pair, and lets an equivalence relation decide when two recorded subtractions should count as equal. Pairs that record a difference Think of a pair (a, b) \in 
N 	imes 
N as a note saying “a minus b”, to be computed later or never. The note (3, 5) is legitimate even though 3 - 5 is not a natural number. Many notes say the same thing: (3, 5), (0, 2) and (10, 12) all describe “two less than nothing”, which school calls -2. When do two notes (a, b) and (c, d) describe the same thing? School would write a - b = c - d, and then add b + d to both sides to get a + d = b + c. That last equation is the one we keep, because it uses only addition, which 
N has for all inputs. The computation with minus signs is a heuristic, borrowed from school to find the definition; the definition does not depend on it. An integer is a difference you have not computed yet. [The Integers] For (a, b), (c, d) \in 
N 	imes 
N, let (a, b) \sim (c, d) \iff a + d = b + c . The set of integers is the quotient set 
Z \coloneqq (
N 	imes 
N)/{\sim} of @fd2:def-quotient-set, and an integer is an element of 
Z. The class of the pair (a, b) is written [(a, b)]: [(a, b)] = \{ (c, d) \in 
N 	imes 
N : (c, d) \sim (a, b) \} . In words: two pairs are related when their cross sums agree, the first coordinate of each added to the second coordinate of the other. The relation is a subset of (
N 	imes 
N) 	imes (
N 	imes 
N), described by a property (@fd2:def-relation, @fd2:def-cartesian-product). An integer is one whole class: the set of all pairs that record the same difference. The notation [(a, b)] is the class notation [x] of @fd2:def-equivalence-class with x = (a, b); no new bracket is introduced. Well-definedness. @fd2:def-quotient-set is stated for an equivalence relation. Until \sim is shown to be one, the definition of 
Z is a plan, not a definition. The next proposition supplies the missing check, and it is placed directly after the definition for that reason. An integer is a set of pairs. It is not a natural number with a sign, and it is not a pair. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1 adopted the convention that a pair is not a number (after @fd2:def-ordered-pair), and on \omega that became a theorem, @prp-pair-not-natural. The same care is needed here: [(0, 2)] is the set \{ (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 4), \dots \}, and the school -2 is what those pairs have in common. The construction takes “what they have in common” to be the set of them. [The Relation Behind the Integers] The relation \sim of @def-integers-as-classes is an equivalence relation on 
N 	imes 
N (@fd2:def-equivalence-relation). Reflexivity and symmetry are rearrangements of one equation, by commutativity. Transitivity has two hypotheses, a + d = b + c and c + f = d + e, and a goal a + f = b + e in which c and d do not appear. In school one would subtract them. In 
N we add the two equations, so that c + d appears on both sides, and then remove it by cancellation. Before reading on: which line uses cancellation in 
N, and why is it more direct than subtracting c + d? We check (Eq1)–(Eq3) of @fd2:def-equivalence-relation. Let (a, b), (c, d), (e, f) \in 
N 	imes 
N. (Eq1) a + b = b + a by commutativity (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (b)), so (a, b) \sim (a, b). (Eq2) Suppose (a, b) \sim (c, d), that is, a + d = b + c. By commutativity, c + b = b + c = a + d = d + a, and c + b = d + a says (c, d) \sim (a, b). (Eq3) Suppose (a, b) \sim (c, d) and (c, d) \sim (e, f), that is, a + d = b + c \quad 	ext{and} \quad c + f = d + e . Adding the two equations gives (a + d) + (c + f) = (b + c) + (d + e). By associativity and commutativity (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (b), (c)), the left side is (a + f) + (c + d) and the right side is (b + e) + (c + d), so (a + f) + (c + d) = (b + e) + (c + d) . By cancellation (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (b)) with k = c + d, a + f = b + e. That is (a, b) \sim (e, f). This proves that \sim is an equivalence relation. The answer to the prompt is the last line of (Eq3). It is tempting to “subtract c + d from both sides” at the end. In 
N the difference n - m of @prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a) exists only when m \le n. Here it does exist, since c + d \le (a + f) + (c + d) and c + d \le (b + e) + (c + d) by the same result and commutativity, but only after that check; and reading off ((a + f) + (c + d)) - (c + d) = a + f uses the uniqueness in (a), which is itself proved by cancellation. Cancellation removes c + d directly, and it holds for all k, with no size check. So 
Z = (
N 	imes 
N)/{\sim} is now defined, and by @fd2:thm-classes-partition its elements partition 
N 	imes 
N: every pair lies in exactly one integer, and [(a, b)] = [(c, d)] if and only if a + d = b + c. Pictures of classes The quarter plane 
N 	imes 
N is a grid of lattice points, and the classes are easy to see in it. [Three classes, listed and drawn] List the elements (x, y) with x \le 4 of each of the classes [(3, 5)], [(0, 0)] and [(4, 1)], and describe each class as a set of lattice points. The class [(3, 5)]. A pair (x, y) lies in it when x + 5 = y + 3. This holds if and only if y = x + 2. Indeed, if y = x + 2, then y + 3 = x + (2 + 3) = x + 5 by associativity (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (c)). Conversely, x + 5 = (x + 2) + 3, so x + 5 = y + 3 gives (x + 2) + 3 = y + 3, and cancellation (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (b)) gives y = x + 2. So [(3, 5)] = \{ (x, x + 2) : x \in 
N \} , and the elements with x \le 4 are (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 6). The class [(0, 0)]. Here the condition is x + 0 = y + 0, that is, x = y, since n + 0 = n (@def-omega-arithmetic (a)). So [(0, 0)] = \{ (x, x) : x \in 
N \}, the diagonal, and the elements with x \le 4 are (0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (4, 4). The class [(4, 1)]. The condition x + 1 = y + 4 holds if and only if x = y + 3, by the same two steps as for [(3, 5)]. So [(4, 1)] = \{ (y + 3, y) : y \in 
N \}. Its elements with x \le 4 are (3, 0) and (4, 1) only: x = y + 3 = 3 + y (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (b)) gives 3 \le x (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a)); with x \le 4 = \mathrm{S}(3), x is 3 or 4, since no natural number lies strictly between 3 and \mathrm{S}(3) (@thm-omega-order (b)); and then y + 3 = 3 = 0 + 3 or y + 3 = 4 = 1 + 3, so y is 0 or 1 by cancellation (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (b)). Each of these three classes is the set of lattice points on one diagonal line y = x + k or x = y + k of the quarter plane, starting on an axis and running up and to the right. The picture shows the three classes as three diagonals: [(3, 5)] solid with filled dots, [(0, 0)] dashed with open dots, [(4, 1)] dotted with squares. Every pair lies in exactly one class (@fd2:thm-classes-partition), so no two of these diagonals share a lattice point; after the normal form below we see that every class is a diagonal of this kind, so every lattice point lies on exactly one of them. The class [(0, 0)] is the degenerate case: it is the integer zero, and it is the only class whose line passes through the origin. A non-example by minimal change. Replace the sums in the definition by products: on 
N 	imes 
N, let (a, b) \approx (c, d) mean ad = bc. This is still reflexive (ab = ba) and symmetric (ad = bc gives cb = da), both by commutativity of \cdot (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (f)). It is not transitive: (1, 1) \approx (0, 0), \qquad (0, 0) \approx (2, 1), \qquad 	ext{but} \qquad (1, 1) 
ot\approx (2, 1) , since 1 \cdot 0 = 1 \cdot 0, 0 \cdot 1 = 0 \cdot 2 and 1 \cdot 1 
e 1 \cdot 2. The clause that fails is (Eq3), and the line of the proof above that has no counterpart is cancellation. Additive cancellation holds for every k; multiplicative cancellation (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (f)) needs k 
e 0, and the pair (0, 0) supplies a middle factor that is 0. When Section 2.4 builds fractions with this product relation, it excludes zero second coordinates for exactly this reason. Why this definition Why cross sums. “a - b = c - d” cannot be the definition, because a - b is defined in 
N only when b \le a. The cross-sum equation a + d = b + c says the same thing whenever both differences exist, and it makes sense for every two pairs. Why whole classes. Each class has a simplest pair, one with a coordinate 0, as the next proposition shows. One could define 
Z as the set of these simplest pairs instead. But then the sum of (3, 0) and (0, 5) would have to be brought back to a simplest pair, (0, 2), by a subtraction in 
N in the right direction: the case analysis of the naive attempt returns. With classes, any representatives may be combined, and the equivalence relation absorbs the bookkeeping. The price is the check of the next section: a definition through representatives must not depend on which ones were used. The degenerate class and the name. The class of (0, 0) is the diagonal; it will be the zero of 
Z. The word “integer” is Latin for “whole” or “untouched”, a number not broken into fractions; Section 2.4 builds those. The first result about the new set says that each class has exactly one simplest name. [Normal Form of an Integer] 1. Every class [(a, b)] \in 
Z contains exactly one pair of the form (n, 0) or (0, n) with n \in 
N (the pair (0, 0) has both forms and counts once). Precisely, for each (a, b) \in 
N 	imes 
N exactly one of the following holds: - a = b + k for some k 
e 0, and then [(a, b)] = [(k, 0)]; - a = b, and then [(a, b)] = [(0, 0)]; - b = a + k for some k 
e 0, and then [(a, b)] = [(0, k)]. 2. For all m, n \in 
N: if [(m, 0)] = [(n, 0)], then m = n; and if [(0, m)] = [(0, n)], then m = n. The three cases are the three cases of trichotomy for a and b, and @prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a) turns each inequality into an equation with a non-zero k. In each case one line of arithmetic shows that (a, b) is related to the simplest pair. For “exactly one pair”, two simplest pairs of the same form are handled by (b), so we prove (b) first. Two of opposite forms, (k, 0) and (0, l) with k, l 
e 0, would need k + l = 0, which the order forbids. (b) Suppose [(m, 0)] = [(n, 0)]. By @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b), (m, 0) \sim (n, 0), that is, m + 0 = 0 + n. Since m + 0 = m (@def-omega-arithmetic (a)) and 0 + n = n (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (a)), m = n. Likewise [(0, m)] = [(0, n)] gives 0 + n = m + 0, so n = m. (a), the three cases. Let (a, b) \in 
N 	imes 
N. By @thm-omega-order (a), exactly one of b < a, a = b, a < b holds. By @prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a), b < a holds if and only if a = b + k for some k 
e 0, and a < b if and only if b = a + k for some k 
e 0. So exactly one of the three listed conditions holds. In each case the stated equality of classes follows from @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b), once the two pairs are shown to be related: - if a = b + k, then a + 0 = a = b + k (@def-omega-arithmetic (a)), so (a, b) \sim (k, 0); - if a = b, then a + 0 = b + 0, so (a, b) \sim (0, 0); - if b = a + k, then a + k = b = b + 0 (@def-omega-arithmetic (a)), so (a, b) \sim (0, k). In particular every class contains a pair of the form (n, 0) or (0, n). (a), only one such pair. Let C be a class containing two such pairs p and p'. Since both lie in C, [p] = C = [p'] by @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b). If p = (m, 0) and p' = (n, 0), then m = n by (b), so p = p'; likewise if both have the form (0, \cdot). This covers every case in which one of the pairs is (0, 0), since (0, 0) has both forms. There remains p = (k, 0) and p' = (0, l) with k 
e 0 and l 
e 0. Then p \sim p' says k + l = 0 + 0 = 0. Since l 
e 0, @prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a) gives k < 0; and since k = 0 + k (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (a)) with k 
e 0, it also gives 0 < k. By transitivity k < k, which @thm-omega-order (a) rules out. So this case cannot occur, and the pair is unique. So every integer has a normal form: it is [(n, 0)] for a unique n \in 
N, or [(0, n)] for a unique n \in 
N with n 
e 0. In the picture, every class is a diagonal: (x, y) \sim (n, 0) means x + 0 = y + n, that is, x = y + n, and (x, y) \sim (0, n) means x + n = y + 0, that is, y = x + n (@def-omega-arithmetic (a)), so [(n, 0)] = \{ (y + n, y) : y \in 
N \} \quad 	ext{and} \quad [(0, n)] = \{ (x, x + n) : x \in 
N \} . The normal form is where the class’s diagonal meets an axis. The next section reads [(n, 0)] as the natural number n and [(0, n)] as its negative; this is how the description of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.1, “an integer is a natural number or the negative of one”, becomes a theorem about the constructed 
Z. A property of a class must not be read off one representative. “The integer [(a, b)] is small when a \le 3” sounds like a property of integers and is not one: [(3, 3)] = [(5, 5)], the first pair has a = 3 \le 3, and the second has a = 5. The class is “small” or not according to the name we happened to use. The property “[(a, b)] is positive when b < a” looks the same and happens to be safe: if (a, b) \sim (a', b') and b < a, then b' < a'. That needs a proof, and Section 2.3 gives it before it calls any integer positive. Is (2, 7) \sim (10, 15)? Is (2, 7) \sim (15, 10)? Yes: the cross sums are 2 + 15 = 17 and 7 + 10 = 17. No: the cross sums are 2 + 10 = 12 and 7 + 15 = 22, and 12 
e 22. In school terms, (2, 7) and (10, 15) both record “five less”, while (15, 10) records “five more”. The normal forms agree: 7 = 2 + 5 and 15 = 10 + 5, so [(2, 7)] = [(0, 5)] = [(10, 15)], while [(15, 10)] = [(5, 0)], a different class by @prp-integer-normal-form (a). The set 
Z exists, and each element has a simplest name. It has no arithmetic yet. The next section defines the sum and product of two integers by formulas on representatives, and the warning above is the question it must answer for each formula. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the relation \sim and the set 
Z of @def-integers-as-classes in symbols. 2. Which pairs with a coordinate equal to 0 lie in [(6, 9)]? 3. Why does the proof of @prp-integer-pairs-equivalence cancel c + d rather than subtract it? 4. True or false, with a reason: [(1, 1)] = [(5, 5)]. (a) For (a, b), (c, d) \in 
N 	imes 
N: (a, b) \sim (c, d) \iff a + d = b + c; and 
Z \coloneqq (
N 	imes 
N)/{\sim} = \{ [(a, b)] : (a, b) \in 
N 	imes 
N \}. (b) Only (0, 3). A pair (x, 0) in the class would need x + 9 = 0 + 6 = 6 (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (a)); but 9 \le x + 9 by @prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a) (with @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (b) to write x + 9 = 9 + x), and 6 < 9, so x + 9 = 6 would give 9 \le 6 < 9, and then 9 < 9, which @thm-omega-order (a) excludes. A pair (0, y) needs 0 + 9 = y + 6, that is, 3 + 6 = y + 6, so y = 3 by cancellation (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (b)). This agrees with @prp-integer-normal-form (a): 9 = 6 + 3, so [(6, 9)] = [(0, 3)], and the class has exactly one pair with a coordinate 0. (c) Subtraction in 
N is defined only when the number subtracted is at most the other (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a)). Here c + d is at most both sides, so subtracting would be possible, but only after that check, and reading off the differences uses the uniqueness in (a), which is itself proved by cancellation. Cancellation (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (b)) holds for every k \in 
N with no check, so the proof uses it directly. (d) True. (1, 1) \sim (5, 5) because 1 + 5 = 1 + 5, so the classes are equal by @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b). Both are the zero class [(0, 0)]. B. Practice [B1: Three look-alike relations] On 
N 	imes 
N, determine which of the following relations are equivalence relations. For each one, decide which of (Eq1)–(Eq3) hold. Justify your answer. 1. (a, b) \approx_1 (c, d) if and only if a + c = b + d. 2. (a, b) \approx_2 (c, d) if and only if a + 2d = 2b + c. 3. (a, b) \approx_3 (c, d) if and only if a + d \le b + c. (a) Symmetric, but neither reflexive nor transitive. Symmetric: a + c = b + d gives c + a = d + b by commutativity (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (b)). Not reflexive: (0, 1) \approx_1 (0, 1) would need 0 + 0 = 1 + 1, that is, 0 = 2, which is false. Not transitive: (0, 1) \approx_1 (1, 0) since 0 + 1 = 1 + 0, and (1, 0) \approx_1 (0, 1) since 1 + 0 = 0 + 1; transitivity would give (0, 1) \approx_1 (0, 1), which we just saw is false. Notice that every pair is related to something, since (a, b) \approx_1 (b, a) by commutativity. A symmetric relation in which every element is related to something still need not be reflexive: “x related to y, so y related to x, so x related to x” uses transitivity, and that is what fails here. (b) An equivalence relation. (Eq1) a + 2b = 2b + a. (Eq2) a + 2d = 2b + c gives c + 2b = 2d + a, by commutativity. (Eq3) Suppose a + 2d = 2b + c and c + 2f = 2d + e. Adding, and rearranging by @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (b), (c), (a + 2f) + (2d + c) = (2b + e) + (2d + c) , and cancellation (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (b)) gives a + 2f = 2b + e. In school terms the pair (a, b) records a - 2b, and the relation says a - 2b = c - 2d. (c) Reflexive and transitive, not symmetric. (Eq1) a + b \le b + a, since the two sides are equal. (Eq3) First, for x, y, u, v \in 
N, x \le y and u \le v give x + u \le y + v: by @prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a), y = x + i and v = u + j for some i, j \in 
N, so y + v = (x + u) + (i + j) by @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (b), (c), and (a) again gives x + u \le y + v. Now let a + d \le b + c and c + f \le d + e. Adding and rearranging, (a + f) + (c + d) \le (b + e) + (c + d) . If b + e < a + f, then (b + e) + (c + d) < (a + f) + (c + d) by @prp-omega-order-arithmetic (c), contradicting the display by trichotomy (@thm-omega-order (a)). So a + f \le b + e, by trichotomy again. Not symmetric: (0, 1) \approx_3 (0, 0) since 0 + 0 \le 1 + 0, that is, 0 \le 1; but (0, 0) \approx_3 (0, 1) would need 0 + 1 \le 0 + 0, that is, 1 \le 0, which is false since 0 < 1 (@thm-omega-order (d)). [B2: A class in set-builder form] Let (a, b) \in 
N 	imes 
N. Describe the class [(a, b)] by a set-builder expression, in the two cases b \le a and a \le b. Hence describe [(7, 2)] and [(2, 7)]. Case b \le a. Write a = b + k with k \in 
N (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a)). We claim [(a, b)] = \{ (y + k, y) : y \in 
N \} . A pair (x, y) lies in [(a, b)] when x + b = y + a, that is, x + b = (y + k) + b by @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (c), (b). By cancellation (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (b)) this holds if and only if x = y + k; the converse direction is substitution. So the elements of the class are exactly the pairs (y + k, y), y \in 
N. Case a \le b. Write b = a + k (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a)). In the same way, (x, y) \sim (a, b) means x + (a + k) = y + a, which by rearranging and canceling a holds if and only if y = x + k. So [(a, b)] = \{ (x, x + k) : x \in 
N \}. The two descriptions agree when a = b (then k = 0), as they must. For the examples, 7 = 2 + 5, so [(7, 2)] = \{ (y + 5, y) : y \in 
N \}, and [(2, 7)] = \{ (x, x + 5) : x \in 
N \}. C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: the relation that builds 
Z] Let \sim be the relation of @def-integers-as-classes on 
N 	imes 
N. 1. Prove that \sim is an equivalence relation. 2. Prove that if (a, b) \sim (a', b') and (c, d) \sim (c', d'), then (a + c, b + d) \sim (a' + c', b' + d'). 3. Say in one sentence what (b) means for a rule that adds two integers by adding representatives coordinatewise. Name the property of 
N behind each step. (a) This is @prp-integer-pairs-equivalence; here is the proof once more. Reflexive: a + b = b + a by commutativity. Symmetric: if a + d = b + c, then c + b = d + a by commutativity. Transitive: let a + d = b + c and c + f = d + e. Adding the two equations and rearranging by associativity and commutativity gives (a + f) + (c + d) = (b + e) + (c + d), and cancellation of c + d (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (b)) gives a + f = b + e. (b) The hypotheses are a + b' = b + a' and c + d' = d + c'. Adding them, (a + b') + (c + d') = (b + a') + (d + c') . By associativity and commutativity (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (b), (c)), the left side is (a + c) + (b' + d') and the right side is (b + d) + (a' + c'). So (a + c) + (b' + d') = (b + d) + (a' + c') , which is the cross-sum equation for (a + c, b + d) \sim (a' + c', b' + d'). (c) The class of (a + c, b + d) does not depend on which representatives of [(a, b)] and [(c, d)] were used, so “add representatives coordinatewise, then take the class” is well defined: it assigns exactly one integer to each pair of integers. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: reflexive and symmetric, each citing commutativity of + in 
N. - 3: transitivity: combines the two hypotheses into one equation with a common summand on both sides (by adding them, or by substituting one into the other) and removes that summand by cancellation in 
N, named as such. - 2: in (b), combines the two hypotheses (by adding them, or by substituting both into a rearranged sum). - 2: in (b), rearranges by associativity and commutativity to the cross-sum equation for the two sums. - 1: (c) concludes that the coordinatewise sum is well defined on classes. A proof of (b) that changes one argument at a time (first (a, b) to (a', b') with (c, d) fixed, then the other) and joins the two by transitivity earns the four points of (b) if each step is justified. Fatal errors (0 for the step): subtracting in 
N (for instance “subtract d from both sides”) without showing that the difference exists; proving only reflexivity and symmetry and calling the relation an equivalence relation.

title: 2.2 Well-Definedness, and the Arithmetic of the Integers
content:
Well-Definedness, and the Arithmetic of the Integers Section 2.1 built 
Z as the set of classes of \sim on 
N 	imes 
N, and gave each integer a normal form (@prp-integer-normal-form). The integers cannot yet be added. Every operation on classes will be defined by a formula on representatives, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.5 showed what can go wrong: a formula that gives two answers for one class (@fd2:exm-ill-defined-class-map). This section proves, once and for all, the lemma that says when such a formula defines a function. It then uses the lemma for the sum, product and negative of integers, and finds a copy of 
N inside 
Z. Definitions through representatives In Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.5 the addition of 
Z/n was defined by [a] + [b] \coloneqq [a + b], and @fd2:prp-congruence-arithmetic checked that the right side depends only on the classes, not on the integers a and b used to name them. In @fd2:exm-ill-defined-class-map the same kind of formula, [a]_6 \mapsto [a]_4, gave one class two values, and so defined no function. The same situation will recur throughout this volume: for 
Z in this section, for 
Q in Section 2.4, and for 
R later in this volume. Each time, a set is a quotient X/{\sim}, and something is defined on it by a formula on elements of X. Rather than repeat the argument of @fd2:prp-congruence-arithmetic for every formula, we separate it into two parts: a general lemma, proved here once, which turns a check on representatives into a function on classes; and the check itself, which is different for each formula and is all that remains to do each time. A rule “[x] \mapsto something computed from x” is called well defined when representatives of the same class always give the same result. The lemma below says that being well defined is enough, in three settings: a map from one quotient to another, a binary operation on a quotient, and a property of classes. The lemma A rule on classes is a function as soon as equivalent inputs give equivalent outputs. [Functions on Classes] Let \sim be an equivalence relation on a set X, and \approx an equivalence relation on a set Y. Classes are taken for \sim in X and for \approx in Y. 1. Let f \colon X 	o Y be a function such that, for all x, x' \in X, x \sim x' implies f(x) \approx f(x'). Then there is exactly one function F \colon X/{\sim} 	o Y/{\approx} with F([x]) = [f(x)] for every x \in X. 2. Let g \colon X 	imes X 	o X be a function such that, for all x, x', y, y' \in X,  egin{aligned} x \sim x' &\implies g(x, y) \sim g(x', y) , \ y \sim y' &\implies g(x, y) \sim g(x, y') . \end{aligned} Then there is exactly one function G \colon (X/{\sim}) 	imes (X/{\sim}) 	o X/{\sim} with G([x], [y]) = [g(x, y)] for all x, y \in X. 3. Let S \subseteq X be such that, for all x, x' \in X, x \sim x' and x \in S imply x' \in S. Let  ar S \coloneqq \{ [x] : x \in S \} \subseteq X/{\sim}. Then, for every x \in X, [x] \in  ar S if and only if x \in S. In words: (a) says that a map on elements that respects the two relations passes to a map on classes; (b) says that a binary operation that respects \sim in each argument separately passes to an operation on classes; (c) says that a property that respects \sim can be asked of a class, and the answer is the answer for any of its representatives. Clause (a) will give the negative of an integer, (b) its sum and product, and (c) the positive integers in Section 2.3. A function is a graph with exactly one output for each input (@fd2:def-function). The obvious graph is the set of all pairs ([x], [f(x)]). It has at least one output for each class, because every class is some [x]. The only danger is two outputs for one class, coming from two representatives x and x' of it; @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b) turns “same class” into x \sim x', the hypothesis turns that into f(x) \approx f(x'), and @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b) turns it back into “same output”. For (b) the same plan works, once the two one-argument hypotheses are chained into one statement about both arguments by transitivity. (a) Let G_F \coloneqq \{ (C, D) \in (X/{\sim}) 	imes (Y/{\approx}) : C = [x] 	ext{ and } D = [f(x)] 	ext{ for some } x \in X \} , a set by specification (@fd2:def-set-builder). We check the two clauses of @fd2:def-function. (Fn1): every C \in X/{\sim} is [x] for some x \in X (@fd2:def-quotient-set), and then (C, [f(x)]) \in G_F. (Fn2): suppose (C, D) \in G_F and (C, D') \in G_F, say C = [x], D = [f(x)], and C = [x'], D' = [f(x')]. Then [x] = [x'], so x \sim x' by @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b). By the hypothesis, f(x) \approx f(x'), so [f(x)] = [f(x')] by @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b), that is, D = D'. So F, the function with graph G_F and codomain Y/{\approx}, is a function X/{\sim} 	o Y/{\approx}, and F([x]) = [f(x)] because ([x], [f(x)]) \in G_F. For uniqueness, let F' \colon X/{\sim} 	o Y/{\approx} also satisfy F'([x]) = [f(x)] for every x. Every C \in X/{\sim} is some [x], and then F'(C) = [f(x)] = F(C). The two functions have the same domain and codomain, so F' = F by @fd2:prp-function-equality. (b) First, for all x, x', y, y' \in X with x \sim x' and y \sim y', g(x, y) \sim g(x', y) \quad 	ext{and} \quad g(x', y) \sim g(x', y') , by the first hypothesis (with y fixed) and the second (with x' fixed). By transitivity, (Eq3) of @fd2:def-equivalence-relation, g(x, y) \sim g(x', y'). Now let G_G be the set of (P, E) \in  igl((X/{\sim}) 	imes (X/{\sim}) igr) 	imes (X/{\sim}) such that P = ([x], [y]) and E = [g(x, y)] for some x, y \in X, a set by specification. (Fn1): an element of (X/{\sim}) 	imes (X/{\sim}) is a pair (C, D) of classes (@fd2:def-cartesian-product), and C = [x], D = [y] for some x, y \in X (@fd2:def-quotient-set); then ((C, D), [g(x, y)]) \in G_G. (Fn2): suppose (P, E) and (P, E') lie in G_G, with P = ([x], [y]), E = [g(x, y)], and P = ([x'], [y']), E' = [g(x', y')]. From ([x], [y]) = ([x'], [y']) the characteristic property of pairs (@fd2:def-ordered-pair) gives [x] = [x'] and [y] = [y'], so x \sim x' and y \sim y' by @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b). By the first paragraph, g(x, y) \sim g(x', y'), so E = E' by @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b). So G_G, with codomain X/{\sim}, defines a function G with G([x], [y]) = [g(x, y)]. Uniqueness is as in (a), by @fd2:prp-function-equality. (c) (\Leftarrow) If x \in S, then [x] \in  ar S by the definition of  ar S. (\Rightarrow) If [x] \in  ar S, then [x] = [x'] for some x' \in S. By @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b), x \sim x', so x' \sim x by (Eq2). The hypothesis, applied to x' \sim x and x' \in S, gives x \in S. This proves the theorem. The functions F and G are said to be induced by f and g. In practice we write the conclusion of (a) as “the rule [x] \mapsto [f(x)] is well defined”, and of (b) as “the operation [x] \ast [y] \coloneqq [g(x, y)] is well defined”, and the work is always the check of the hypotheses. Each hypothesis has a job. Without the hypothesis of (c) the conclusion fails. On 
N 	imes 
N with the relation \sim of @def-integers-as-classes, let S \coloneqq \{ (a, b) : 0 < a \}. Then (1, 1) \in S, so [(1, 1)] \in  ar S; and [(0, 0)] = [(1, 1)], so [(0, 0)] \in  ar S, while (0, 0) 
otin S. Membership in  ar S does not tell us whether a particular representative lies in S. The hypotheses of (a) and (b) are needed in the same way, and the examples below show them failing. Sum, product and negative of integers To guess the formulas, borrow the school picture once more. If (a, b) records “a - b” and (c, d) records “c - d”, then school algebra gives  egin{aligned} (a - b) + (c - d) &= (a + c) - (b + d) , \ (a - b)(c - d) &= (ac + bd) - (ad + bc) , \ -(a - b) &= b - a . \end{aligned} These identities are a heuristic: they come from the school integers, which this chapter does not assume, and they are used only to find the definition. Each right side is again a difference of two natural numbers, so it can be recorded as a pair. Sum, Product and Negative of Integers For all (a, b), (c, d) \in 
N 	imes 
N, let  egin{aligned} [(a, b)] + [(c, d)] &\coloneqq [(a + c, \ b + d)] , \ [(a, b)] \cdot [(c, d)] &\coloneqq [(ac + bd, \ ad + bc)] , \ -[(a, b)] &\coloneqq [(b, a)] . \end{aligned} The sum + \colon 
Z 	imes 
Z 	o 
Z and product \cdot \colon 
Z 	imes 
Z 	o 
Z are the functions that @thm-well-defined-on-classes (b), with X = 
N 	imes 
N and the equivalence relation \sim of @prp-integer-pairs-equivalence, induces from the maps g_+, g_\cdot \colon (
N 	imes 
N) 	imes (
N 	imes 
N) 	o 
N 	imes 
N given by the pairs on the right; the negative - \colon 
Z 	o 
Z is the function that @thm-well-defined-on-classes (a) induces from (a, b) \mapsto (b, a). We also write xy for x \cdot y. In words: to add integers, add representatives coordinatewise; to multiply, use the cross formula; to negate, swap the coordinates. All the arithmetic on the right happens in 
N, where it is always possible. The definition is legitimate only if the hypotheses of @thm-well-defined-on-classes hold for the three maps on pairs; the next proposition checks them, and until then the three formulas are rules, not yet functions. The move used in the proof is the one this chapter is built on. Check on representatives, one argument at a time. To show that [x] \ast [y] \coloneqq [g(x, y)] is well defined, change x to an equivalent x' with y fixed, then change y to an equivalent y' with x' fixed. Each change is a computation at the level below, in 
N here; @thm-well-defined-on-classes (b) joins the two by transitivity. [The Operations on Integers Are Well Defined] The maps g_+ and g_\cdot of @def-integer-operations satisfy the hypotheses of @thm-well-defined-on-classes (b), and the map (a, b) \mapsto (b, a) satisfies those of @thm-well-defined-on-classes (a), with \sim on both sides. Hence the sum, product and negative of @def-integer-operations are well-defined functions. Each hypothesis is an equation in 
N to be derived from another. The given equation is the cross-sum equation for (a, b) \sim (a', b'); the target is the cross-sum equation for the two outputs. For the sum, adding c + d to both sides of the given equation and rearranging is enough. For the product, the target has c and d in every term, so we multiply the given equation by c, and separately by d, and add the results; the rest is rearranging. Both formulas are unchanged when the two input pairs are swapped, so the second argument costs nothing. Before reading on: why may we change one argument at a time, rather than both at once? Let (a, b), (a', b'), (c, d) \in 
N 	imes 
N with (a, b) \sim (a', b'), that is, a + b' = b + a' . {#eq-integer-rep-change} All rearrangements below use @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws: commutativity and associativity of +, commutativity of \cdot, and distributivity. Sum, first argument. We need (a + c, b + d) \sim (a' + c, b' + d), that is, (a + c) + (b' + d) = (b + d) + (a' + c). The left side is (a + b') + (c + d), which by @eq-integer-rep-change equals (b + a') + (c + d), and that is the right side rearranged. Product, first argument. We need (ac + bd, \ ad + bc) \sim (a'c + b'd, \ a'd + b'c) , that is, the cross-sum equation (ac + bd) + (a'd + b'c) = (ad + bc) + (a'c + b'd) . {#eq-integer-product-target} Multiply both sides of @eq-integer-rep-change by c and use distributivity: ac + b'c = bc + a'c. Multiply both sides of @eq-integer-rep-change, read from right to left, by d: bd + a'd = ad + b'd. Adding these two equations, (ac + b'c) + (bd + a'd) = (bc + a'c) + (ad + b'd) . The Integers as an Ordered Ring Sections 2.1 and 2.2 built 
Z as a set of classes with well-defined operations +, \cdot and -, but we do not yet know which laws they obey. This section collects the laws of school algebra into one definition, a commutative ring, and checks them for 
Z by reducing each to a law of 
N. Then it orders 
Z and derives the rules for inequalities from axioms alone: from here on, an inequality about integers is proved, never read off a picture. The laws of a ring Expanding brackets or moving a term across an equation uses a short list of laws: sums and products may be reordered and regrouped, 0 and 1 do nothing, every element has a negative, and products distribute over sums. The list holds in 
Z, it will hold in 
Q, and a result proved from the list alone holds wherever the list does. It deserves a name. A commutative ring is a set where you may add, subtract and multiply by the usual rules; a field is one where you may also divide by anything non-zero. [Commutative Ring, Field] A commutative ring is a set R with two functions, addition + \colon R 	imes R 	o R and multiplication \cdot \colon R 	imes R 	o R (written a \cdot b = ab), such that clauses (F1)–(F7) and (F9) of the following list hold; clause (F8) is used only for fields. 1. a + b = b + a for all a, b \in R. 2. (a + b) + c = a + (b + c) for all a, b, c \in R. 3. There is an element 0 \in R with a + 0 = a for every a \in R. 4. For every a \in R there is an element -a \in R with a + (-a) = 0. 5. (ab)c = a(bc) for all a, b, c \in R. 6. ab = ba for all a, b \in R. 7. There is an element 1 \in R with a \cdot 1 = a for every a \in R. 8. For every non-zero a \in R there is an element a^{-1} \in R with a a^{-1} = 1. 9. a(b + c) = ab + ac for all a, b, c \in R. A field is a commutative ring in which, in addition, 1 
e 0 and (F8) holds. We write a - b \coloneqq a + (-b), and in a field a / b \coloneqq a b^{-1} for b 
e 0. In words: (F1)–(F4) say that addition is commutative and associative, with a neutral element 0 and negatives; (F5)–(F7) say the first three things about multiplication; (F9) links the two and lets us expand brackets. (F8) asks for inverses of non-zero elements only, and only in a field. The notations -a and a^{-1} anticipate that these elements are unique, which we prove below. These are the axioms (F1)–(F9) of the linear-algebra companion, Chapter 0, and of the ordered fields of Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1, in the same numbering, except that there (F7) includes 1
