Z, then S has a greatest element. Let b be a lower bound and T \coloneqq \{ s - b : s \in S \}, a non-empty set. For s \in S, s \ge b gives s - b \ge 0 by (O3), so T \subseteq \{ x \in 
Z : x \ge 0 \} = 
N by @thm-integers-ordered-ring (b). By @thm-omega-well-ordering, T has an element m with m \le t for every t \in T, in the order of 
N and so in that of 
Z (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (a)). Then m = s_0 - b for some s_0 \in S, so m + b = s_0 \in S; and for s \in S, s - b \ge m gives s \ge m + b by (O3). So m + b is least in S. If c is an upper bound, then -S \coloneqq \{ -s : s \in S \} has the lower bound -c (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a)), so by the first part it has a least element, which is -s_1 for some s_1 \in S, by the definition of -S. For s \in S, -s_1 \le -s gives s \le s_1, by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), or by -(-s) = s (@prp-ring-algebra (a)) when -s_1 = -s. So s_1 is greatest in S. This proves the proposition. Both hypotheses are needed: 
Z has no least element, and neither has \emptyset, which every integer bounds. The rules of @prp-ordered-ring-rules also show that some rings carry no order at all. [A field with two elements that cannot be ordered] Let R \coloneqq \{0, 1\}, two distinct elements, with addition and multiplication given by the tables  egin{array}{c|cc} {+} & 0 & 1 \ \hline 0 & 0 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{array} \qquad\qquad  egin{array}{c|cc} \cdot & 0 & 1 \ \hline 0 & 0 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{array} Check that R satisfies (F1)–(F9), so that it is a field, and show that no relation < on R makes it an ordered commutative ring. The axioms. (F1), (F6): both tables are symmetric. (F3), (F7): the row of 0 in the first table and of 1 in the second repeat the headings. (F4): -0 = 0 and -1 = 1, since 1 + 1 = 0. (F8): 1 has inverse 1, since the second table gives the product of 1 and 1 as 1. And 1 
e 0. The three laws with three variables can be checked over the eight triples (a, b, c), or by cases. From the tables, 0x = 0 and 1x = x, and x + y = 1 exactly when exactly one of x, y is 1. (F2): both sides are 1 exactly when an odd number of a, b, c (one or three) are 1. (F5): both sides are 1 exactly when a = b = c = 1. (F9): if a = 0, both sides are 0; if a = 1, both sides are b + c. So R is a field. No order. If < made R an ordered commutative ring, then, as 1 
e 0, @prp-ordered-ring-rules (h) would give 2 \cdot 1 > 0. But 2 \cdot 1 = 1 \cdot 1 + 1 = (0 + 1) + 1 = 0 by the definition of multiples, and 0 > 0 is forbidden by (O1). The argument uses only 1 
e 0 and n \cdot 1 = 0 for some n \ge 1. So no commutative ring with 1 
e 0 in which n \cdot 1 = 0 for some n \in 
N, n \ge 1, can be ordered. The integers modulo n \ge 2 of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.5 are such rings (their ring laws taken for granted, as in the warning after @def-commutative-ring-and-field), since n \cdot [1] = [n] = [0]; a later chapter of this volume rebuilds them on the constructed 
Z. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Let R be an ordered commutative ring. 1. Here is a proof that if a < 0 < b, then ab < a^2 + b^2. Name the axiom, rule or result that justifies each of the five steps. (1) ab < 0b. (2) 0b = 0. (3) a^2 > 0 and b^2 > 0. (4) a^2 + b^2 > 0 + 0 = 0. (5) ab < a^2 + b^2. 2. True or false: “R has no zero divisors.” Give a reason. 3. True or false: “1 > 0 in every ordered commutative ring.” Give a reason. 4. Name the move by which @thm-integers-commutative-ring was proved, and say which row of its table needed the relation \sim rather than equality of pairs. (a) (1) @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), with a < 0 and b > 0. (2) @prp-ring-algebra (b) and (F6). (3) @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), as a, b 
e 0 by (O1). (4) @prp-ordered-ring-rules (b), strict, and (F3). (5) (O2). (b) True, by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (f); a general commutative ring may have zero divisors (the warning after @def-commutative-ring-and-field). (c) False: in the zero ring with the empty relation, 1 = 0. It is true when 1 
e 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)). (d) Reduce to the level below: on representatives, each axiom becomes an identity in 
N. Only (F4) needed \sim: (a + b, b + a) is related to (0, 0) but is not that pair. B. Practice [B1: Three rows in detail] Let x = [(a, b)], y = [(c, d)], z = [(e, f)] be integers. Verify in detail, naming the law of 
N used at each step, the rows (F9), (F4) and (F6) of the table in the proof of @thm-integers-commutative-ring. All operations are those of @def-integer-operations, and “Law” refers to @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws. (F9). Since y + z = [(c + e, d + f)], x(y + z) = [(a(c + e) + b(d + f), \ a(d + f) + b(c + e))], whose coordinates are ac + ae + bd + bf and ad + af + bc + be by Law (d). And xy + xz = [((ac + bd) + (ae + bf), \ (ad + bc) + (af + be))], whose coordinates are the same sums by Laws (b), (c). So both sides are the class of one pair. (F4). x + (-x) = [(a + b, b + a)], and (a + b, b + a) \sim (0, 0) means (a + b) + 0 = (b + a) + 0 (@def-integers-as-classes), true by @def-omega-arithmetic (a) and Law (b). So x + (-x) = [(0, 0)] by @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b). (F6). yx = [(ca + db, cb + da)]. By Law (f), ca = ac, db = bd, cb = bc, da = ad, and by Law (b), bc + ad = ad + bc; so the pair is (ac + bd, ad + bc), the pair of xy. [B2: The wrong positive set] Let P' \coloneqq \{ [(a, b)] : a < b \} \subseteq 
Z. Show that membership in P' does not depend on the representative, that P' satisfies (P2) of @prp-order-from-positives, and that it does not satisfy (P1). Which part of (P1) fails? Independence of representatives. If (a, b) \sim (a', b') and b = a + k with k 
e 0, then b' + a = a + b' = b + a' = (a + k) + a' = (a' + k) + a (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (b), (c)), so b' = a' + k by cancellation (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (b)), and a' < b' by @prp-omega-order-arithmetic (a). By @thm-well-defined-on-classes (c), [(a, b)] \in P' if and only if a < b. (P2). For x = [(a, b)]: x \in P' iff a < b; x = 0 iff a = b (as in the proof of @thm-integers-ordered-ring); -x \in P' iff b < a. By trichotomy in 
N (@thm-omega-order (a)), exactly one holds. (P1) fails for products. [(0, 1)] \in P', but, by @def-integer-operations with a = c = 0 and b = d = 1 in [(ac + bd, \ ad + bc)], [(0, 1)][(0, 1)] = [(1, 0)] , and [(1, 0)] 
otin P', since 1 < 0 is false. The sum half of (P1) holds, as in the proof of @thm-integers-ordered-ring. So P', the negative integers, fails only closure under products; it would define the reversed order, which breaks exactly (O4). C. Going deeper [C1: Ordered rings with 1 
e 0 are infinite] 1. Prove the sum law of @prp-ordered-ring-rules (h) in full: for every ordered commutative ring R, every a \in R and all m, k \in 
N, (m + k) \cdot a = m \cdot a + k \cdot a. State the property you induct on and justify every equality. 2. Deduce that every ordered commutative ring with 1 
e 0 is infinite (@fd2:def-infinite). 3. The set \{0, 1, 2\} with addition and multiplication “modulo 3”, given by the tables below, is a commutative ring with 1 
e 0 (you may take this for granted). Show that it cannot be ordered.  egin{array}{c|ccc} {+} & 0 & 1 & 2 \ \hline 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \ 1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \ 2 & 2 & 0 & 1 \end{array} \qquad\qquad  egin{array}{c|ccc} \cdot & 0 & 1 & 2 \ \hline 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \ 2 & 0 & 2 & 1 \end{array} [Hint 1] For (b): what does (h) say about k \mapsto k \cdot 1? [Hint 2] Suppose R has m elements; consider k \mapsto k \cdot 1 on \{1, \dots, m + 1\}. (a) Fix R, a \in R, m \in 
N, and use @fd1:ax-induction (through @cor-omega-identification (b)) on k, for P(k): “(m + k) \cdot a = m \cdot a + k \cdot a”. Base: (m + 0) \cdot a = m \cdot a = m \cdot a + 0 = m \cdot a + 0 \cdot a, by @def-omega-arithmetic (a), (F3) and 0 \cdot a = 0. Step: assume P(k). Then  egin{aligned} (m + (k + 1)) \cdot a &= ((m + k) + 1) \cdot a = (m + k) \cdot a + a \ &= (m \cdot a + k \cdot a) + a = m \cdot a + (k \cdot a + a) \ &= m \cdot a + (k + 1) \cdot a , \end{aligned} by associativity in 
N (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (c)), the recursion for multiples, P(k), (F2), and the recursion again. So P(k + 1) holds, and P(k) holds for every k. (b) Let 1 
e 0 in R, and suppose R has m elements for some m \in 
N (@fd2:def-finite). Let f \colon \{1, \dots, m + 1\} 	o R, f(k) \coloneqq k \cdot 1. If k < l, then k \cdot 1 < l \cdot 1 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (h), so k \cdot 1 
e l \cdot 1 by (O1): f is injective. But \{1, \dots, m + 1\} has m + 1 > m elements (by its identity map), so @fd2:cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets (a) forbids an injection into R. This contradiction shows that R is infinite (@fd2:def-infinite). (c) By the definition of multiples and the tables, 1 \cdot 1 = 0 + 1 = 1, 2 \cdot 1 = 1 + 1 = 2 and 3 \cdot 1 = 2 + 1 = 0. An order would give 3 \cdot 1 > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (h), since 1 
e 0, that is, 0 > 0, against (O1). (Alternatively, (b) applies to this finite ring.) Marking scheme. (10 points) - 1: (a) states the induction property with m and a fixed and k the induction variable. - 2: (a) base case, citing m + 0 = m, 0 \cdot a = 0 and (F3). - 2: (a) inductive step, with associativity in 
N, the recursion, the hypothesis and (F2) each named. - 2: (b) shows that k \mapsto k \cdot 1 is injective, citing (h) and (O1). - 2: (b) derives the contradiction from @fd2:cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets (a) with m + 1 > m elements (or any correct count). - 1: (c) computes 3 \cdot 1 = 0 and concludes. Fatal errors (0 for the step): inducting on m and k at once without fixing one; using 1 > 0 without 1 
e 0; in (b), “the multiples are all different, so there are infinitely many” with no finiteness result cited (@fd2:cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets, @fd2:prp-subset-finite with 
N infinite, or equivalent). A route for (b) composing the inverse of a bijection \{1, \dots, m\} 	o R with f earns the same 4 points. So does a route that shows k \mapsto k \cdot 1 is an injection 
N 	o R (2 points, as above), so that its image is an infinite subset of R, and concludes with @fd2:prp-subset-finite (2 points).

title: 2.4 The Rationals as Classes of Fractions
content:
The Rationals as Classes of Fractions Section 2.3 made 
Z an ordered commutative ring and showed, in a Quick check, that 
Z is not a field, because 2x = 1 has no solution in it. This section repairs that defect the way Section 2.1 repaired the missing subtraction in 
N. There, a pair (a, b) recorded “a - b” without performing it; here a pair (p, q) records “p divided by q” without performing it. We define 
Q as a set of classes of such pairs, give it addition and multiplication through representatives, check that they are well defined, and prove that 
Q is a field containing a copy of 
Z. Fractions as pairs At school, 	frac12, 	frac24 and 	frac36 are “the same number”, and the test for sameness is cross-multiplication: 	frac pq = 	frac rs when ps = rq. The test is the useful part. It mentions only multiplication of integers, which we have, and not division, which we do not. So we keep the test and let a rational number be what the equivalent fractions have in common: the class of all of them. A rational number is a quotient you have not computed yet: the set of all fractions that would compute to it. Signs need a decision. The fractions 	frac{1}{-2} and 	frac{-1}{2} name the same number, and allowing both would put a sign in two places. We require the denominator to be positive, so that a sign can sit only in the numerator. This is the convention Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.5 already used for its fractions, and Section 2.5 below will profit from it: there, the order of 
Q is read off a single inequality between integers. Recall that 
Z_{>0} = \{ n \in 
Z : n > 0 \}, by @thm-integers-ordered-ring (b). On 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0}, let (p, q) \sim (r, s) mean ps = rq. We reuse the symbol \sim of Section 2.1; which relation is meant is always clear from the pairs, natural numbers there and an integer with a positive integer here. [Cross-Multiplication Is an Equivalence Relation] The relation \sim on 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0} given by (p, q) \sim (r, s) \iff ps = rq is an equivalence relation (@fd2:def-equivalence-relation). Reflexivity and symmetry are just reflexivity and symmetry of =: with this form of the test, (p, q) \sim (p, q) reads pq = pq. For transitivity we are given ps = rq and ru = ts, and want pu = tq. Multiply the first equation by u and use the second to replace ru: this gives (pu)s = (tq)s. We cannot divide by s, but 
Z has no zero divisors, so a factor s 
e 0 can be canceled. Let (p, q), (r, s), (t, u) \in 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0}. All computations are in the commutative ring 
Z (@thm-integers-commutative-ring). (Eq1) pq = pq, so (p, q) \sim (p, q). (Eq2) If ps = rq, then rq = ps, so (r, s) \sim (p, q). (Eq3) Let ps = rq and ru = ts. Then, using (F5), (F6) and the two hypotheses, (pu)s = (ps)u = (rq)u = (ru)q = (ts)q = (tq)s . Hence (pu - tq)s = (pu)s - (tq)s = 0, by (F9) and @prp-ring-algebra (c). Since s \in 
Z_{>0}, s > 0, so s 
e 0 by (O1). By @prp-ordered-ring-rules (f), pu - tq = 0, that is, pu = tq. So (p, q) \sim (t, u). This proves the proposition. The hypothesis that denominators are non-zero is used once, for the middle pair (r, s), and it is needed there. On 
Z 	imes 
N, with the same formula, (1, 0) \sim (0, 0) (since 1 \cdot 0 = 0 \cdot 0) and (0, 0) \sim (1, 1) (since 0 \cdot 1 = 1 \cdot 0), but (1, 0) 
ot\sim (1, 1) (since 1 \cdot 1 
e 1 \cdot 0). The pair (0, 0) is related to everything, and transitivity collapses through it. [The Rational Numbers] Let \sim be the equivalence relation of @prp-rational-pairs-equivalence on 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0}. The set of rational numbers is the quotient set (@fd2:def-quotient-set) 
Q \coloneqq (
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0})/{\sim} . A rational number is an element of 
Q: a class [(p, q)] with p \in 
Z and q \in 
Z_{>0}. We call p a numerator and q a denominator of the representative (p, q). In words: a rational number is a set of pairs, all the pairs (r, s) with positive s that cross-multiply with (p, q). It is not a pair, and it is not a number with a sign and a bar. Numerators and denominators belong to representatives, not to the class: (1, 2) and (2, 4) represent the same rational number with different denominators. Nothing in the definition needs checking beyond @prp-rational-pairs-equivalence, which makes the quotient set meaningful. By @fd2:thm-classes-partition, every pair lies in exactly one class, and [(p, q)] = [(r, s)] holds exactly when ps = rq. Examples. - [(1, 2)] = \{ (k, 2k) : k \in 
Z_{>0} \}. Indeed, (r, s) \sim (1, 2) means 2r = s. Then 2r > 0, and r \le 0 would give 2r = r + r \le 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)), so r > 0. Conversely each (k, 2k) with k > 0 has 2k > 0 and k \cdot 2 = 2k \cdot 1. Its elements with denominator at most 6 are (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6). - [(-2, 1)] = \{ (-2s, s) : s \in 
Z_{>0} \}, since (r, s) \sim (-2, 1) means r = -2s. This is the class that will be the integer -2. - The degenerate case: [(0, 1)] = \{ (0, s) : s \in 
Z_{>0} \}, since (r, s) \sim (0, 1) means r \cdot 1 = 0 \cdot s = 0. Every fraction with numerator 0 lies in this one class, whatever its denominator; it will be the zero of 
Q. - [(2, 3)] contains (4, 6) and (6, 9), since 2 \cdot 6 = 4 \cdot 3 and 2 \cdot 9 = 6 \cdot 3. It does not contain (-4, -6), which is not even an element of 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0}. Describing the whole class needs divisibility, which a later chapter of this volume develops on the constructed 
Z. A non-example by minimal change. Allow the denominator 0: take 
Z 	imes 
N instead of 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0}, with the same formula. Reflexivity and symmetry survive, by the same lines. Transitivity fails, as the triple (1, 0), (0, 0), (1, 1) above shows, so there is no quotient set. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.5 met the same failure in an exercise; it is the reason denominators must be non-zero. Why positive and not merely non-zero denominators? Non-zero denominators would also give an equivalence relation, and, as the last example of this section shows, essentially the same set 
Q. The difference appears with the order. With positive denominators, “[(p, q)] is positive” can mean “p > 0”, one inequality in 
Z; with non-zero denominators, it would have to say “p and q have the same sign”, and a naive comparison of two fractions breaks, as the warning at the end of this section shows. Do not read [(p, q)] as the number p/q. There is no division in 
Z, and 
Q has no multiplication yet, so “p/q” means nothing at this point. The class is a set of pairs, and any statement made with one representative, such as “the denominator of [(1, 2)] is 2”, must be checked against all of them (here it fails: (2, 4) is also in the class). The fraction notation becomes honest once 
Z is placed inside 
Q, in @prp-integers-embed-rationals and the identification that follows it. Is (3, 4) \sim (-6, -8) in 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0}? The question is malformed: -8 
otin 
Z_{>0}, so (-6, -8) is not an element of 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0}, and \sim says nothing about it. In the variant with non-zero denominators (the last example of this section), the answer is yes: 3 \cdot (-8) = -24 = (-6) \cdot 4. This construction pays a debt. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.5 described 
Q as the quotient of 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0} by cross-multiplication while 
Z was still the school integers; now 
Z is the ring of Section 2.3, and the quotient is the definition of 
Q. Adding and multiplying classes The school rules 	frac pq + 	frac rs = 	frac{ps + rq}{qs} and 	frac pq \cdot 	frac rs = 	frac{pr}{qs} are a heuristic for the definition, nothing more; the definition below does not depend on them, and the proofs never use them. [Operations on the Rationals] For [(p, q)], [(r, s)] \in 
Q, define  egin{aligned} [(p, q)] + [(r, s)] &\coloneqq [(ps + rq, \ qs)] , \ [(p, q)] \cdot [(r, s)] &\coloneqq [(pr, \ qs)] , \ -[(p, q)] &\coloneqq [(-p, \ q)] . \end{aligned} The right-hand sides are classes of elements of 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0}: since q > 0 and s > 0, qs > 0 by (O4), so qs \in 
Z_{>0} by @thm-integers-ordered-ring (b). Each formula is computed from chosen representatives, so the definition is legitimate only once we know that other representatives give the same class. That is the next proposition. [The Operations on the Rationals Are Well Defined] Let X \coloneqq 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0}, with \sim as in @prp-rational-pairs-equivalence. The maps  egin{aligned} g_+ igl((p, q), (r, s) igr) &\coloneqq (ps + rq, \ qs) , \ g_\cdot igl((p, q), (r, s) igr) &\coloneqq (pr, \ qs) \end{aligned} from X 	imes X to X satisfy the hypotheses of @thm-well-defined-on-classes (b), and f(p, q) \coloneqq (-p, q) satisfies the hypothesis of @thm-well-defined-on-classes (a). Hence +, \cdot and - of @def-rational-operations are functions 
Q 	imes 
Q 	o 
Q, 
Q 	imes 
Q 	o 
Q and 
Q 	o 
Q. This is the move of Section 2.2, check on representatives, one argument at a time. Change the first pair to an equivalent one with the second fixed, then the second with the first fixed; @thm-well-defined-on-classes (b) joins the two changes by transitivity. Each change is one identity in 
Z: expand both cross-products and use the hypothesis pq' = p'q (or rs' = r's) once. All computations are in the commutative ring 
Z (@thm-integers-commutative-ring), and we reorder products by (F5), (F6) without comment. Multiplication, first argument. Let (p, q) \sim (p', q'), so pq' = p'q, and let (r, s) \in X. We need (pr, qs) \sim (p'r, q's), that is, (pr)(q's) = (p'r)(qs). Indeed (pr)(q's) = (pq')(rs) = (p'q)(rs) = (p'r)(qs) . Multiplication, second argument. Let (r, s) \sim (r', s'), so rs' = r's, and let (p, q) \in X. We need (pr)(qs') = (pr')(qs). Indeed (pr)(qs') = (pq)(rs') = (pq)(r's) = (pr')(qs) . Addition, first argument. Let pq' = p'q. We need (ps + rq, qs) \sim (p's + rq', q's), that is, (ps + rq)(q's) = (p's + rq')(qs). By (F9),  egin{aligned} (ps + rq)(q's) &= (pq')s^2 + rqq's , \ (p's + rq')(qs) &= (p'q)s^2 + rqq's , \end{aligned} and the right-hand sides are equal because pq' = p'q. Addition, second argument. Let rs' = r's. We need (ps + rq, qs) \sim (ps' + r'q, qs'), that is, (ps + rq)(qs') = (ps' + r'q)(qs). By (F9),  egin{aligned} (ps + rq)(qs') &= pqss' + (rs')q^2 , \ (ps' + r'q)(qs) &= pqss' + (r's)q^2 , \end{aligned} and the right-hand sides are equal because rs' = r's. Negation. If pq' = p'q, then (-p)q' = -(pq') = -(p'q) = (-p')q by @prp-ring-algebra (c), so (-p, q) \sim (-p', q'). So g_+ and g_\cdot satisfy the hypotheses of @thm-well-defined-on-classes (b): for a change of both arguments, g(x, y) \sim g(x', y) \sim g(x', y'), and transitivity joins the two steps, which is what the proof of that lemma does. By its conclusion, there is exactly one function 
Q 	imes 
Q 	o 
Q with [x] + [y] = [g_+(x, y)], and likewise for \cdot. By @thm-well-defined-on-classes (a), -[(p, q)] \coloneqq [(-p, q)] is a function 
Q 	o 
Q. This proves the proposition. Not every formula in representatives passes this test, and the failures are instructive. [Formulas that ignore the class] Decide which of the following rules define a function on 
Q. 1. [(p, q)] \mapsto p + q \in 
Z. 2. [(p, q)] \mapsto p \in 
Z. 3. [(p, q)] \mapsto [(p^2, q^2)] \in 
Q. (a) Not a function. [(1, 2)] = [(2, 4)], since 1 \cdot 4 = 2 \cdot 2, yet the rule gives 1 + 2 = 3 for one representative and 2 + 4 = 6 for the other. A function has one value at each argument (@fd2:def-function), and this rule offers two at the same class. (b) Not a function, for the same pair: the outputs are 1 and 2. (c) A function. First, q^2 > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), as q 
e 0, so (p^2, q^2) \in 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0}. If pq' = p'q, then p^2 (q')^2 = (pq')^2 = (p'q)^2 = (p')^2 q^2 , by (F5), (F6), so (p^2, q^2) \sim (p'^2, q'^2), and @thm-well-defined-on-classes (a) applies. The function is x \mapsto x \cdot x, since [(p, q)] \cdot [(p, q)] = [(p^2, q^2)] by @def-rational-operations. The tempting argument for (a) runs: “a rational number x is p/q, so p and q are determined by x, and so is p + q”. Its conclusion is false, and the flaw is the word “is”: (p, q) is a representative of x, and (2p, 2q) is another, just as legitimate. A rule defined through representatives is a function on classes only when every representative gives the same value, and that has to be proved, as in (c). The rationals form a field The ring axioms for 
Q are checked by the move of Section 2.3, reduce to the level below: each side of an axiom, written on representatives, is the class of an explicit pair in 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0}, and the two pairs are compared by an identity in 
Z. One small observation recurs: for every (p, q) \in 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0} and k \in 
Z_{>0}, (p, q) \sim (kp, kq) , \quad 	ext{since } p(kq) = (kp)q ; here kq > 0 by (O4), so (kp, kq) \in 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0} by @thm-integers-ordered-ring (b), and the relation makes sense. Scaling both entries by the same positive integer does not change the class. The Rationals Form a Field 
Q, with the operations of @def-rational-operations, is a field (@def-commutative-ring-and-field), with zero [(0, 1)] and one [(1, 1)]. A rational number [(p, q)] is zero if and only if p = 0. title: 2.5 The Rationals as an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property
content:
The Rationals as an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property Section 2.4 built 
Q as a set of classes of fractions and proved that it is a field (@thm-rationals-field): we can add, subtract, multiply, and divide by anything non-zero. What it did not give us is an order. In school one “sees” that -3/5 < -7/12 by placing both on a line, but the line is the school picture this volume has set aside, so the order must be defined on the classes and its rules proved. This section does that, by the method of Section 2.3: name the positive rationals, check two closure properties, and let @prp-order-from-positives produce the rest. Then we prove the first fact about 
Q that later chapters of this volume lean on at every turn: every rational is exceeded by a natural number, and so 1/n eventually drops below any positive rational. Finally every rational gets an integer part. Which fractions are positive Throughout, a rational is written as in Section 2.4. By @prp-integers-embed-rationals (b), every x \in 
Q is p/q for some p \in 
Z and q \in 
Z_{>0}, where p/q is the class [(p, q)], and p/q = r/s if and only if ps = rq. The integers sit inside 
Q as m = m/1, and the natural numbers inside the integers. The order of 
Z came from its positive set P_{
Z} (@def-integer-order), and @prp-order-from-positives turned closure under + and \cdot, together with a trichotomy, into all of (O1)–(O4). We do the same for 
Q, so the whole question is: which fractions should count as positive? A first guess from school is “numerator and denominator have the same sign”. But in 
Q the denominator is always positive. That was the decision recorded with @def-rationals-as-classes, and here it pays: the sign of a fraction is the sign of its numerator. A fraction with a positive denominator is positive exactly when its numerator is. [The Order on 
Q] Let P_{
Q} \coloneqq  igl\{ [(p, q)] : (p, q) \in 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0} 	ext{ and } p > 0  igr\} . For x, y \in 
Q, we write x < y if y - x \in P_{
Q}. As in @def-ordered-ring-and-field, x > y means y < x, and x \le y means x < y or x = y. In words: a rational is in P_{
Q} if it has a representative (p, q) with p > 0, the inequality being the order of 
Z; and x < y means that the difference y - x, computed in the field 
Q, lies in P_{
Q}. Well-definedness. The definition says “has a representative with p > 0”. To use it we want more: that every representative of a class in P_{
Q} has a positive numerator, so that the test can be run on whichever representative is at hand. This is the situation of @thm-well-defined-on-classes (c), with X = 
Z 	imes
