First argument: let (p, q) \sim (p', q') and ps < rq; we must show p's < rq'. … Name the move, then complete it. The move is check on representatives, one argument at a time: change the first pair with the second fixed, then the second with the first fixed, and join the two by transitivity of \iff. First argument. Let pq' = p'q and ps < rq. Multiply by q' > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)): psq' < rqq'. The left side is (pq')s = (p'q)s = (p's)q, and the right side is (rq')q. So (p's)q < (rq')q. If p's \ge rq', then multiplying by q > 0 would give (p's)q \ge (rq')q (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), or equality), against (O1). So p's < rq'. Since \sim is symmetric, the same argument with the roles of (p, q) and (p', q') exchanged gives the converse: ps < rq \iff p's < rq'. Second argument. Let rs' = r's, and fix (p', q'). If p's < rq', multiply by s' > 0: p'ss' < rq's', and rs' = r's turns the right side into (r's)q' = (r'q')s. So (p's')s < (r'q')s, and canceling s > 0 as above gives p's' < r'q'. By symmetry again, p's < rq' \iff p's' < r'q'. Join. Chaining the two equivalences, ps < rq \iff p's < rq' \iff p's' < r'q' . This proves the claim. By @thm-rationals-ordered-field (a) both sides also mean p/q < r/s; the point of the exercise is that the integer relation alone is already independent of the representatives, and positivity of q, q', s, s' is used at every multiplication and cancellation. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: names the move (check on representatives, one argument at a time, joined by transitivity of \iff). - 3: first argument: multiplies ps < rq by q' > 0, uses pq' = p'q to reach (p's)q < (rq')q, cancels q > 0 (by contradiction via trichotomy), and gets the converse from symmetry of \sim. - 3: second argument: the same with s' > 0, rs' = r's and cancellation of s > 0, with the converse by symmetry. - 2: chains ps < rq \iff p's < rq' \iff p's' < r'q' and says where positivity of q, q', s, s' is used. Fatal errors (0 for the step): multiplying or canceling by a denominator without using its sign; proving only one direction of an equivalence without invoking symmetry; using p/q < r/s (the comparison formula of @thm-rationals-ordered-field (a)) instead of working on the integer relation. [C3: Find the error] Here is an argument for @thm-rationals-archimedean. Is the conclusion true? Is the argument correct? If not, name the first line that fails, say what makes it illegal, and give a counterexample to the step. (1) Let x \in 
Q, and write x = p/q with p \in 
Z and q \in 
Z_{>0}. (2) Then q \ge 1, by discreteness of 
Z. (3) So x = p/q \le p, since dividing by a number at least 1 cannot increase it. (4) Hence n \coloneqq p + 1 is a natural number with n > x. The conclusion is true: it is @thm-rationals-archimedean. The argument is not correct. The failing line is (3). It cites the general “fact” that p/q \le p whenever q \ge 1. That is neither proved in this chapter nor true, so the line rests on nothing: entry (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. What is true, and what the proof of the theorem uses, is the special case p \ge 0. Counterexample to the step. p = -3, q = 2: then q \ge 1, but x = -3/2 > -3 = p. Indeed the comparison formula gives -3/1 < -3/2, because (-3) \cdot 2 = -6 < -3 = (-3) \cdot 1. There is no counterexample to the conclusion. A second failing line. Line (4) also fails for p \le -2: then p + 1 \le -1, which is not in 
N = \{ n \in 
Z : n \ge 0 \} (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)). For p = -1, n = 0 happens to work, because x < 0; but the stated reason “x \le p” still fails there once q \ge 2. Repair. Split on the sign of p, as the proof of @thm-rationals-archimedean does: for p \le 0, x \le 0 < 1; for p > 0, line (3) is correct, with the comparison formula as its reason (p \cdot 1 \le p \cdot q). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: says that the conclusion is true and the argument is not correct. - 3: names line (3), and the unproved general claim “p/q \le p for q \ge 1” (entry (N9)) as what makes it illegal. - 2: gives a counterexample to the step with p < 0 and q \ge 2, checked by the comparison formula. - 1: notes that line (4) fails as well for p \le -2. - 2: repairs the argument by a case split on the sign of p. Fatal errors (0 for the step): declaring the conclusion false; offering a counterexample to the conclusion.

title: 2.6 The Gaps in the Rationals
content:
The Gaps in the Rationals The rationals now have everything Section 2.5 asked of them: they form an ordered field (@thm-rationals-ordered-field), every rational lies below a natural number (@thm-rationals-archimedean), and no two rationals are neighbors, since their midpoint lies between them. Is anything missing? School geometry suggests an answer. The diagonal of a square with side 1 has a length whose square is 2, and no fraction seems to measure it. That picture is motivation only. This section proves the two facts behind it from the construction: no rational squares to 2, and the set of rationals whose square is below 2 has no least upper bound in 
Q. We also build a sequence of rationals that closes in on the gap from above without ever landing in it. A later chapter of this volume fills the gap. No rational squares to two Throughout, x^2 \coloneqq x \cdot x and 2 \coloneqq 1 + 1, with 4 = 2 \cdot 2 and so on; by the identifications of Sections 2.2 and 2.4 these are the natural numbers of the same names. Their sums and products may be computed in 
N, since the maps \iota and j preserve + and \cdot (@prp-naturals-embed-integers, @prp-integers-embed-rationals), and so may their comparisons (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (a), @thm-rationals-ordered-field (b)). Logic and Proof, Chapter 2 proved that “\sqrt 2 is irrational” (@fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational), about the school rationals, by parity: an argument about even and odd integers. Parity is available here too, from @prp-omega-powers-parity (d) for positive integers or from the integer part (@prp-rational-integer-part; see Exercise R4). We prove the statement for the constructed 
Q by a different route, one that needs only the order and the least-element property of 
Z, and that adapts to other non-squares (Exercise C2). No Rational Squares to Two There is no x \in 
Q with x^2 = 2. Work backwards from a supposed square root x = p/q. From x^2 = 2 we get 2 - x = x^2 - x = x(x - 1), so x =  rac{2 - x}{x - 1} =  rac{2 - p/q}{p/q - 1} =  rac{2q - p}{p - q} . Since 1 < x < 2 (as 1^2 < 2 < 2^2), the new denominator p - q is positive and smaller than q. So no fraction for x can have a least positive denominator, while @prp-integer-least-element says some fraction must. The written proof checks the descent with integers only: it never divides, and it verifies (2q - p)^2 = 2(p - q)^2 by expanding. Before reading on: using only integers, why is the new denominator q' \coloneqq p - q positive, and why is q' < q? Suppose, for a contradiction, that x \in 
Q and x^2 = 2. Then x 
e 0, since 0^2 = 0 (@prp-ring-algebra (b)) and 2 > 0. By (O1), x > 0 or x < 0; let y \coloneqq x in the first case and y \coloneqq -x in the second. Then y > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a)) and y^2 = x^2 = 2, because (-x)(-x) = x x (@prp-ring-algebra (c)). By @prp-integers-embed-rationals (b), y = a/b with a \in 
Z and b \in 
Z_{>0}, and a > 0 by @thm-rationals-ordered-field (a). By @def-rational-operations, y^2 = a^2/b^2, and 2 = 2/1, so y^2 = 2 says a^2 \cdot 1 = 2 b^2 (@prp-integers-embed-rationals (b)). Hence the set D \coloneqq \{ q \in 
Z_{>0} : p^2 = 2q^2 	ext{ for some } p \in 
Z_{>0} \} contains b, so it is non-empty, and 0 is a lower bound of it. By @prp-integer-least-element, D has a least element q. Choose p \in 
Z_{>0} with p^2 = 2q^2. q < p. Suppose p \le q. Since p, q \ge 0, @prp-ordered-ring-rules (g) gives p^2 < q^2 if p < q, and p^2 = q^2 if p = q; so p^2 \le q^2, that is, q^2 + q^2 \le q^2, and adding -q^2 (O3) gives q^2 \le 0. But q 
e 0, so q^2 > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e). This contradicts (O1), so p \le q fails, and q < p by totality (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)). p < 2q. Suppose 2q \le p. Since 2q, p \ge 0, (g) (or equality, if 2q = p) gives (2q)^2 \le p^2, that is, 2q^2 + 2q^2 = 4q^2 \le 2q^2, so 2q^2 \le 0. But 2q^2 > 0 by (O4). As before, p < 2q. Descent. Let p' \coloneqq 2q - p and q' \coloneqq p - q, integers. By @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), p < 2q gives p' > 0, and q < p gives q' > 0; so p', q' \in 
Z_{>0} (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)). Adding -q to p < 2q (O3) gives q' = p - q < q. Expanding with @prp-ring-algebra (c) and (d),  egin{aligned} p'^2 - 2q'^2 &= (4q^2 - 4pq + p^2) - (2p^2 - 4pq + 2q^2) \ &= 2q^2 - p^2 = 0 . \end{aligned} So p'^2 = 2q'^2 with p' \in 
Z_{>0}, that is, q' \in D. But q' < q, and q is the least element of D. This contradiction shows that no x \in 
Q has x^2 = 2. The answer to the prompt: q' = p - q > 0 because q < p, and q' < q because p < 2q. These are the two inequalities “1 < x < 2” of the Idea, written for integers. The hypothesis p^2 = 2q^2 is used in each of the three steps, and the minimality of q only once, in the final contradiction. The proof assumes x^2 = 2, reaches a contradiction, and concludes 
eg(\exists x \in 
Q \; x^2 = 2): its last step is ulename{
eg I} (@fd1:def-rules-negation), not RAA (@fd1:def-rule-raa), since what is refuted is the assumption and the conclusion is its negation. The steps “q < p” and “p < 2q” refute p \le q and 2q \le p and then read the remaining case off trichotomy. The set below the gap Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.6 stated, without proof, that the set of positive rationals with square below 2 has no least upper bound in 
Q, and pointed out that the ambient set decides whether a supremum exists. We now prove it. By @prp-ordered-ring-rules (i) and @thm-rationals-ordered-field, \le is a total order on 
Q, so (
Q, \le) is a partially ordered set and the words of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.6 apply: upper bounds (@fd2:def-order-bounds) and a supremum, an upper bound s with (S1) x \le s for every x in the set and (S2) s \le u for every upper bound u (@fd2:def-order-supremum). [A Bounded Set of Rationals with No Rational Supremum] Let A \coloneqq \{ x \in 
Q : x^2 < 2 \} , \qquad A^+ \coloneqq \{ x \in A : x > 0 \} = \{ x \in 
Q : x > 0, \ x^2 < 2 \} . 1. A is non-empty and bounded above in (
Q, \le), but A has no supremum in 
Q. 2. A and A^+ have the same upper bounds in 
Q. Hence A^+ is also non-empty and bounded above, and has no supremum in 
Q. Try it first (ten minutes): a rational s > 0 is offered as \sup A. Find a rational that proves the offer wrong, once in the case s^2 < 2 and once in the case s^2 > 2. If s^2 < 2, we need an element of A above s. The obvious try is s + h with h > 0 small, but (s + h)^2 = s^2 + 2sh + h^2 has an h^2 in it, and taming that needs a separate size estimate on h. If s^2 > 2, we need a smaller upper bound, and a guess s - h runs into the same algebra. A cleaner idea finds the new rational in one formula. If s^2 > 2, then 2/s < s and (2/s)^2 = 4/s^2 < 2: the gap lies between 2/s and s. Their average t(s) \coloneqq  rac{1}{2}\Bigl( s +  rac{2}{s} \Bigr) =  rac{s^2 + 2}{2s} is smaller than s, and its square is still above 2; that is the smaller upper bound. If s^2 < 2, apply the same trick from the other side: t(s) overshoots, so u(s) \coloneqq 2/t(s) = 4s/(s^2 + 2) undershoots, and it lands above s. Each claim is an identity in the field 
Q, checked by clearing denominators. The proof uses @thm-no-rational-square-two exactly once, to rule out the third case s^2 = 2. (a) Non-empty: 1^2 = 1 < 2, so 1 \in A. Bounded above: 2 is an upper bound. Indeed, let x \in A, and suppose x > 2. Then 0 \le 2 < x, so 4 = 2^2 < x^2 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (g), and 2 < 4, so 2 < x^2, against x^2 < 2 by (O1). So x \le 2, by totality. Two maps. For s \in 
Q_{>0}, we have 2s > 0 by (O4), and s^2 + 2 > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e) and (b); both are non-zero. Let t(s) \coloneqq  rac{s^2 + 2}{2s} , \qquad u(s) \coloneqq  rac{4s}{s^2 + 2} . Both are rationals, and both are positive, by @prp-reciprocal-order (a) and (O4). They satisfy  egin{aligned} t(s)^2 - 2 &=  rac{(s^2 - 2)^2}{4s^2} , & s - t(s) &=  rac{s^2 - 2}{2s} , \ u(s) - s &=  rac{s(2 - s^2)}{s^2 + 2} , & 2 - u(s)^2 &=  rac{2(s^2 - 2)^2}{(s^2 + 2)^2} . \end{aligned} {#eq-newton-identities} Each identity is checked by multiplying both sides by its denominator, which is non-zero, so that the multiplication can be undone with the inverse. For the first, 2s \cdot t(s) = s^2 + 2, so 4s^2 (t(s)^2 - 2) = (s^2 + 2)^2 - 8s^2 = s^4 - 4s^2 + 4 = (s^2 - 2)^2. For the second, 2s(s - t(s)) = 2s^2 - (s^2 + 2) = s^2 - 2. For the third, (s^2 + 2)(u(s) - s) = 4s - s^3 - 2s = s(2 - s^2). For the fourth, (s^2 + 2)^2 (2 - u(s)^2) = 2(s^2 + 2)^2 - 16s^2 = 2(s^2 - 2)^2. No supremum. Suppose, for a contradiction, that s \in 
Q is a supremum of A. By (S1) and 1 \in A, s \ge 1 > 0, so s \in 
Q_{>0}. By @thm-no-rational-square-two, s^2 
e 2, so by (O1), s^2 < 2 or s^2 > 2. In both cases s^2 - 2 
e 0, so (s^2 - 2)^2 > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e). Case 1: s^2 < 2. Then 2 - s^2 > 0, and the third identity of @eq-newton-identities exhibits u(s) - s as a product of positive elements (with @prp-reciprocal-order (a) for the reciprocal), so u(s) > s. The fourth gives 2 - u(s)^2 > 0, so u(s)^2 < 2 and u(s) \in A. So A has an element u(s) > s, and s is not an upper bound of A, against (S1). Case 2: s^2 > 2. The first identity gives t(s)^2 - 2 > 0, so t(s)^2 > 2. Then t(s) is an upper bound of A: if some x \in A had x > t(s), then 0 < t(s) < x would give 2 < t(s)^2 < x^2 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (g), against x^2 < 2; so x \le t(s) for every x \in A. By (S2), s \le t(s). But the second identity, with s^2 - 2 > 0 and 2s > 0, gives s - t(s) > 0, that is, t(s) < s. Then t(s) < s \le t(s), so t(s) < t(s), against (O1). Both cases are impossible, so A has no supremum in 
Q. (b) Since A^+ \subseteq A, every upper bound of A is an upper bound of A^+. Conversely, let u be an upper bound of A^+. Since 1 > 0 and 1^2 < 2, 1 \in A^+, so u \ge 1 > 0. Let x \in A. If x > 0, then x \in A^+ and x \le u. Otherwise x \le 0 < u (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)). So u is an upper bound of A. Conditions (S1) and (S2) for a set mention only the set of its upper bounds: (S1) says that s is one, and (S2) that it lies below all of them. So s is a supremum of A^+ if and only if it is a supremum of A, and by (a), A^+ has none. It is non-empty, since 1 \in A^+, and bounded above, by 2. The set A^+ is the set of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.6, so clause (b) is the statement left unproved there. The two descriptions differ only by the non-positive elements of A, which lie below every upper bound anyway. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 proves the same conclusion for A^+ in 
Q, as part of its motivation for the axioms of the real numbers, and then shows that A^+ does have a supremum in the real numbers. That is the sense of “gap”: a bounded set of rationals whose least upper bound, if it is anywhere, is not a rational. “A has no supremum in 
Q, so A is unbounded” mixes up the two conditions a supremum needs. A is bounded above, by 2 for instance; what fails is (S2): among the rational upper bounds there is no least one, because every upper bound s is beaten by the smaller upper bound t(s). A rational sequence aimed at the gap The map t does more than refute a candidate. Started at an upper bound, it produces a smaller one, and it can be applied again. Iterating it gives a sequence of rationals that approaches the gap from above. A Rational Sequence Aimed at the Gap For s \in 
Q_{>0} let t(s) \coloneqq (s^2 + 2)/(2s). Define x_0 \coloneqq 2 and x_{n+1} \coloneqq t(x_n) for n \in 
N, and let e_n \coloneqq x_n^2 - 2. Show that this defines a sequence with x_n \in 
Q_{>0} for every n \in 
N, and that for every n \in 
N: 1. e_n > 0, that is, x_n^2 > 2; 2. e_{n+1} = e_n^2/(4x_n^2) \le e_n^2/8; 3. x_n - x_{n+1} = e_n/(2x_n) > 0, so x_{n+1} < x_n. Compute x_0, \dots, x_3 and e_0, \dots, e_3. The sequence. For s \in 
Q_{>0}, s^2 + 2 > 0 and 2s > 0, so t(s) \in 
Q_{>0} by (O4) and @prp-reciprocal-order (a): t maps 
Q_{>0} to 
Q_{>0}. The recursion theorem (@fd2:thm-recursion, read on 
N = \omega as @thm-omega-recursion by @cor-omega-identification (b)), with X = 
Q_{>0}, starting value 2 and g(n, s) \coloneqq t(s), gives exactly one function n \mapsto x_n from 
N to 
Q_{>0} with x_0 = 2 and x_{n+1} = t(x_n). So every x_n is a positive rational, with no further argument. Two identities. For s \in 
Q_{>0}, 2s \cdot t(s) = s^2 + 2. Hence 4s^2 (t(s)^2 - 2) = (s^2 + 2)^2 - 8s^2 = (s^2 - 2)^2 and 2s (s - t(s)) = 2s^2 - s^2 - 2 = s^2 - 2. Multiplying by the inverses of 4s^2 
e 0 and 2s 
e 0, t(s)^2 - 2 =  rac{(s^2 - 2)^2}{4s^2} , \qquad s - t(s) =  rac{s^2 - 2}{2s} . {#eq-newton-step} (i). We use @fd1:ax-induction (read on \omega as @thm-omega-induction (b), by @cor-omega-identification (b)) for P(n): e_n > 0. Base P(0): e_0 = 2^2 - 2 = 2 > 0. Step: suppose e_n > 0. By @eq-newton-step with s = x_n, e_{n+1} = t(x_n)^2 - 2 =  rac{e_n^2}{4x_n^2} . Here e_n^2 > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), since e_n 
e 0, and 1/(4x_n^2) > 0 by @prp-reciprocal-order (a); so e_{n+1} > 0 by (O4). This proves (i) for every n. (ii). The equation was just shown, for every n. By (i), x_n^2 > 2, so 4x_n^2 > 4 \cdot 2 = 8 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c). From 0 < 8 < 4x_n^2, @prp-reciprocal-order (b) gives 1/(4x_n^2) < 1/8, and multiplying by e_n^2 > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)) gives e_{n+1} < e_n^2/8; in particular e_{n+1} \le e_n^2/8. (iii). By @eq-newton-step with s = x_n, x_n - x_{n+1} = e_n/(2x_n), a product of the positive elements e_n and 1/(2x_n); so it is positive, and x_{n+1} < x_n by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a). The first terms. By the definition of t, x_1 =  rac{4 + 2}{4} =  rac{3}{2} , \quad x_2 =  rac{9/4 + 2}{3} =  rac{17}{12} , \quad x_3 =  rac{289/144 + 2}{17/6} =  rac{577}{408} . The errors are e_0 = 2, e_1 = 9/4 - 2 = 1/4, e_2 = 289/144 - 2 = 1/144 and e_3 = 577^2/408^2 - 2 = 1/166464, since 577^2 = 332929 = 2 \cdot 166464 + 1 and 408^2 = 166464. As a check on (ii): e_1 = 2^2/(4 \cdot 4) = 1/4, e_2 = (1/16)/9 = 1/144, and e_3 = (1/144)^2 / (4 \cdot 289/144) = 1/(144 \cdot 1156) = 1/166464. For orientation only (decimals are not part of this volume’s toolkit), here are the terms in school decimals: n x_n e_n = x_n^2 - 2 x_n, roughly --- --------- ----------------- -------------- 0 2 2 2 1 3/2 1/4 1.5 2 17/12 1/144 1.41667 3 577/408 1/166464 1.414216 The terms decrease, every one of them is an upper bound of A (a positive rational whose square exceeds 2, as in Case 2 of the proof above), and by (ii) the error is roughly squared at each step: after three steps, e_3 = 1/166464 is already below 1/100000. The terms crowd together. Yet no rational L can be “the number they approach”, for if they approached L, their squares would approach L^2, and the errors e_n force L^2 = 2, which @thm-no-rational-square-two forbids. This paragraph is a picture, not a proof: limits in 
Q have not been defined. A later chapter of this volume defines them, with \varepsilon \in 
Q_{>0}, and proves that this sequence is Cauchy in 
Q yet has no limit in 
Q, citing (i)–(iii) from this example. Is 3/2 an upper bound of A = \{ x \in 
Q : x^2 < 2 \}? Is 17/12? Is 4/3? The first two are. Each is positive, and (3/2)^2 = 9/4 > 2 because 9 > 8, while (17/12)^2 = 289/144 > 2 because 289 > 288 (the comparison formula, @thm-rationals-ordered-field (a)). A positive rational b with b^2 > 2 bounds A: if x \in A had x > b, then x^2 > b^2 > 2 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (g), against x^2 < 2. (These are x_1 and x_2 of @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2, and 17/12 = t(3/2) is the smaller upper bound that Case 2 of the proof of @thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2 produces from s = 3/2.) But 4/3 is not, although it is positive: (4/3)^2 = 16/9 < 2 because 16 < 18, so the hypothesis b^2 > 2 fails, and indeed 7/5 \in A, as (7/5)^2 = 49/25 < 2 (49 < 50), while 7/5 > 4/3 (21 > 20). This chapter built two number systems by one method. From 
N to 
Z: pairs (a, b), identified when a + d = b + c, so that subtraction becomes possible. From 
Z to 
Q: pairs (p, q) with q > 0, identified when ps = rq, so that division becomes possible. Each time an operation was defined on representatives and checked to be well defined (@thm-well-defined-on-classes), and each axiom was reduced to the level below. The third step, from 
Q to the real numbers, takes the same route in a later chapter of this volume: the representatives are sequences of rationals like the one above, identified when their difference tends to 0, so that the gap found in this section, and every other gap of 
Q, is filled. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These questions are about the proof of @thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2. 1. Where is @thm-no-rational-square-two used, and what would go wrong without it? 2. Run the proof on s = 3/2 and on s = 7/5: which case applies, which rational does the proof produce, and why does it refute s? 3. Let F be an ordered field containing an element r > 0 with r^2 = 2, and let A_F \coloneqq \{ x \in F : x^2 < 2 \}. Which step of the proof fails for A_F, and what happens to t(r) and u(r)? 4. State the idea of the proof in two sentences. (a) Once, right after a supposed supremum s is fixed: it excludes s^2 = 2, so that trichotomy leaves the two cases s^2 < 2 and s^2 > 2. Without it there is a third case, in which neither map helps: (s^2 - 2)^2 = 0, so the identities give u(s) = s and t(s) = s. (b) For s = 3/2: s^2 = 9/4 > 2 (as 9 > 8), so Case 2. The proof produces t(3/2) = (9/4 + 2)/3 = 17/12, an upper bound of A, since (17/12)^2 = 289/144 > 2; and 17/12 < 3/2, since 17 \cdot 2 = 34 < 36 = 3 \cdot 12. So 3/2 is not the least upper bound. For s = 7/5: s^2 = 49/25 < 2 (as 49 < 50), so Case 1. The proof produces u(7/5) =  rac{28/5}{49/25 + 2} =  rac{28/5}{99/25} =  rac{140}{99} , which lies in A, since 140^2 = 19600 < 19602 = 2 \cdot 99^2, and exceeds 7/5, since 140 \cdot 5 = 700 > 693 = 7 \cdot 99. So 7/5 is not an upper bound. (c) The step “s^2 
e 2”: in F the candidate s = r satisfies r^2 = 2, and it falls in neither case. Indeed r is the supremum of A_F in F: it is an upper bound (if x > r > 0, then x^2 > 2), and an upper bound v < r would have v > 0 (as 1 \in A_F) and v^2 < 2, and then u(v) \in A_F with u(v) > v, as in Case 1. The maps fix r: t(r) = (2 + 2)/(2r) = 2/r = r, since r \cdot r = 2, and u(r) = 4r/4 = r. (d) Suppose a rational s were the supremum; since no rational squares to 2, either s^2 < 2 or s^2 > 2. The explicit rationals u(s) and t(s) then give, respectively, an element of the set above s or an upper bound below s, so s fails (S1) or (S2). B. Practice [B1: Put the proof in order] Here are lines of a proof of @thm-no-rational-square-two, shuffled, together with two lines that do not belong. Write the lines of a correct proof in a correct order, and say what is wrong with each line you leave out. (i) Set p' \coloneqq 2q - p and q' \coloneqq p - q; both are positive integers, by the two inequalities between p and q. (ii) Write x = a/b with a, b \in 
Z_{>0}; then a^2 = 2b^2. (iii) Since p^2 = 2q^2, we have p < q. (iv) Since q' = p - q < q, this contradicts the choice of q; so no rational squares to 2. (v) Suppose x \in 
Q has x^2 = 2; replacing x by -x if necessary, take x > 0. (vi) p < 2q, since p \ge 2q would give p^2 \ge 4q^2 > 2q^2. (vii) Choose such an x with the least positive value. (viii) Among all pairs (p, q) of positive integers with p^2 = 2q^2, choose one with q least (@prp-integer-least-element; b is such a q). (ix) Expanding, p'^2 - 2q'^2 = 2q^2 - p^2 = 0, so p'^2 = 2q'^2. (x) q < p, since p \le q would give 2q^2 = p^2 \le q^2, that is, q^2 \le 0. An admissible order is 	ext{(v)}, \ 	ext{(ii)}, \ 	ext{(viii)}, \ 	ext{(x)}, \ 	ext{(vi)}, \ 	ext{(i)}, \ 	ext{(ix)}, \ 	ext{(iv)} . Lines (x) and (vi) may be exchanged, since neither uses the other. Otherwise the order is forced by what each line uses: (ii) needs the x > 0 of (v); (viii) needs the pair (a, b) of (ii), which makes the set of such q non-empty; (x) and (vi) are about the pair fixed in (viii), and if they came before it, the pair might change afterwards; (i) needs both inequalities; (ix) needs the definitions in (i); and (iv) needs q' \in 
Z_{>0} with p'^2 = 2q'^2, from (i) and (ix), and q' < q, which comes from (vi). Line (vii) is legal but does no work. There is only one positive rational x with x^2 = 2: if 0 < x < y had x^2 = y^2 = 2, then @prp-ordered-ring-rules (g) would give 2 = x^2 < y^2 = 2, against (O1). So “the least” just picks out the x of (v) and gives nothing new. The descent does not produce a smaller x: it keeps the number and shrinks its denominator, p'/q' = p/q, so choosing x least never leads to a contradiction. What must be least is the denominator q, as in (viii). Line (iii) fails. Its conclusion is false: from p^2 = 2q^2 and q > 0 we get p^2 > q^2, hence q < p by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (g), the opposite of (iii). It also clashes with (x). [B2] Let A \coloneqq \{ x \in 
Q : x^2 < 2 \} and A^+ \coloneqq \{ x \in 
Q : x > 0, \ x^2 < 2 \}. Without looking back, prove that A and A^+ have the same upper bounds in 
Q, and deduce from @thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2 (a) that A^+ has no supremum in 
Q. (\subseteq) for upper bounds: if u bounds A, it bounds the subset A^+ \subseteq A. Conversely, let u bound A^+. Since 1 > 0 and 1^2 = 1 < 2, 1 \in A^+, so 1 \le u and u > 0. Let x \in A. If x > 0, then x \in A^+, so x \le u. If x \le 0, then x \le 0 < u. So u bounds A. Now suppose s were a supremum of A^+. Then s is an upper bound of A^+, hence of A (S1), and s \le u for every upper bound u of A^+, which are exactly the upper bounds of A (S2). So s would be a supremum of A, which @thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2 (a) excludes. Hence A^+ has no supremum in 
Q. [B3] Compute x_4 of @exm-newton-rationals-sqrt2, as a fraction of integers, and e_4 = x_4^2 - 2. Check your value of e_4 against (ii) of the example. Hence x_4 is an upper bound of \{ x \in 
Q : x^2 < 2 \} below x_3. With x_3 = 577/408, x_4 = t(x_3) =  rac{577^2 + 2 \cdot 408^2}{2 \cdot 577 \cdot 408} =  rac{332929 + 332928}{470832} =  rac{665857}{470832} . Then 665857^2 = 443365544449 and 470832^2 = 221682772224, and 443365544449 - 2 \cdot 221682772224 = 1, so e_4 =  rac{1}{221682772224} . By (ii), e_4 = e_3^2/(4x_3^2) = 1/(166464 \cdot 4 \cdot 332929), and 4 \cdot 166464 \cdot 332929 = 221682772224, which agrees. Since x_4 > 0 and e_4 > 0, x_4 bounds the set (the argument of the Quick check), and x_4 < x_3 by (iii). C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: the gap at \sqrt 2] Prove that no rational number squares to 2, and that the set \{ x \in 
Q : x^2 < 2 \} has no supremum in 
Q. No rational squares to 2. Suppose x \in 
Q with x^2 = 2. Then x 
e 0, and replacing x by -x if needed ((-x)^2 = x^2), x > 0. Write x = a/b with a, b \in 
Z_{>0} (@prp-integers-embed-rationals (b), @thm-rationals-ordered-field (a)); then a^2 = 2b^2. Among all q \in 
Z_{>0} for which some p \in 
Z_{>0} has p^2 = 2q^2, take the least (@prp-integer-least-element; the set contains b and is bounded below by 0), with its p. Then q < p (else p^2 \le q^2 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (g), so q^2 \le 0, against q^2 > 0) and p < 2q (else 4q^2 \le p^2 = 2q^2, so 2q^2 \le 0). So p' \coloneqq 2q - p and q' \coloneqq p - q are positive integers with q' < q, and p'^2 - 2q'^2 = 2q^2 - p^2 = 0 by expanding. This contradicts the choice of q. Bounded above. 2 bounds the set A: x > 2 would give x^2 > 4 > 2 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (g)). And 1 \in A. No supremum. Suppose s \in 
Q is a supremum of A. As 1 \in A, s \ge 1 > 0, and s^2 
e 2 by the first part. If s^2 < 2, let u \coloneqq 4s/(s^2 + 2) \in 
Q_{>0}. Clearing denominators, u - s = s(2 - s^2)/(s^2 + 2) > 0 and 2 - u^2 = 2(s^2 - 2)^2/(s^2 + 2)^2 > 0. So u \in A and u > s: s is not an upper bound. If s^2 > 2, let t \coloneqq (s^2 + 2)/(2s) \in 
Q_{>0}. Clearing denominators, t^2 - 2 = (s^2 - 2)^2/(4s^2) > 0 and s - t = (s^2 - 2)/(2s) > 0. So t^2 > 2, and t bounds A (an x \in A with x > t > 0 would have x^2 > t^2 > 2); and t < s. So s is not the least upper bound. By trichotomy one of the two cases holds, and each contradicts the choice of s. So A has no supremum in 
Q. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 4: no rational squares to 2: sets up a least denominator, or any other correct route (1); proves the key inequalities q < p < 2q, or the parity step of another route (2); reaches the contradiction (1). - 1: shows that A is bounded above, with an explicit upper bound, and non-empty. - 2: the case s^2 < 2: an explicit element of A larger than s, with both properties verified. - 2: the case s^2 > 2: an explicit smaller rational, verified to be an upper bound of A. - 1: concludes by trichotomy, with s^2 = 2 excluded by the first part. Fatal errors (0 for the step): assuming that \sqrt 2 exists (in 
Q or in a larger field) and comparing s with it; “s^2 < 2, so s + \varepsilon \in A for small \varepsilon” with no \varepsilon exhibited and checked. A second route for the first part, by parity (every integer is 2m or 2m + 1, with m =  loor{a/2} from @prp-rational-integer-part, and not both), earns the same 4 points: 1 for the least denominator, 2 for “p even, then q even”, 1 for the contradiction. [C2: Which integers have a rational square root?] For which n \in 
Z_{>0} does the set A_n \coloneqq \{ x \in 
Q : x^2 < n \} have a supremum in 
Q? Prove your answer. [Hint 1] First find k \in 
N with k^2 \le n < (k + 1)^2, and treat n = k^2 on its own. For k^2 < n, adapt both proofs of this section: the descent, and then the two maps. [Hint 2] Let T \coloneqq \{ m \in 
Z : m \ge 0, \ n < m^2 \}. It contains n + 1, it is bounded below by 0, and 0 
otin T; so its least element is k + 1 for some k \in 
N. In the descent for k^2 < n, try q' \coloneqq p - kq. Answer: exactly when n = k^2 for some k \in 
N, and then the supremum is k. Finding k. Let T \coloneqq \{ m \in 
Z : m \ge 0, \ n < m^2 \}. Since n + 1 \ge 1, (n + 1)^2 \ge n + 1 > n (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)), so n + 1 \in T; 0 is a lower bound of T; and 0 
otin T, as 0^2 = 0 < n. By @prp-integer-least-element, T has a least element l. Since 0 
otin T and l \ge 0, we have l > 0, so l \ge 1 by discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)); then l - 1 \ge 0 by (O3), so k \coloneqq l - 1 \in 
N by @thm-integers-ordered-ring (b). Then n < (k + 1)^2, and k 
otin T with k \ge 0 gives k^2 \le n. So either n = k^2 or k^2 < n < (k + 1)^2. Case n = k^2. Here k \ge 1, since n \ge 1. We show k = \sup A_n. (S1): if x \in A_n had x > k, then x > k \ge 0 would give x^2 > k^2 = n (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (g)), against x^2 < n; so x \le k. (S2): let v be an upper bound of A_n, and suppose v < k. Let w \coloneqq v if v \ge 0 and w \coloneqq 0 otherwise; then v \le w and 0 \le w < k. Let c be the midpoint of w and k (Section 2.5): w < c < k. Then c > 0 and c^2 < k^2 = n by (g), so c \in A_n, and c > w \ge v, so v is not an upper bound. Hence k \le v for every upper bound v, and k is the supremum. Case k^2 < n < (k + 1)^2. Then n \ge 2, since n = 1 = 1^2 is the other case; so 1 \in A_n. (i) No rational squares to n. Suppose x^2 = n with x \in 
Q; as in @thm-no-rational-square-two, we may take x > 0, and then p^2 = nq^2 for some p, q \in 
Z_{>0}, with q least among all such denominators (@prp-integer-least-element). Multiplying k^2 < n < (k + 1)^2 by q^2 > 0 gives (kq)^2 < p^2 < ((k + 1)q)^2, so kq < p < (k + 1)q by (g). Let p' \coloneqq nq - kp , \qquad q' \coloneqq p - kq . Then 0 < q' < q. For p', expand: q \cdot p' = nq^2 - kpq = p^2 - kpq = p(p - kq) > 0 by (O4); since q > 0, p' \le 0 would give q p' \le 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)), so p' > 0. (The bounds alone do not give this: for n = 5, k = 2, q = 10, p = 28, we have kq < p < (k + 1)q, but nq - kp = -6. It is p^2 = nq^2 that forces the sign.) Finally, expanding, p'^2 - n q'^2 = (k^2 - n)(p^2 - nq^2) = 0 , so q' is a smaller admissible denominator, a contradiction. (ii) No supremum. The proof of @thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2 (a) goes through with n in place of 2, using (i) where it used @thm-no-rational-square-two. The set A_n contains 1 and is bounded above by n (if x > n \ge 1, then x^2 > n^2 \ge n). For s \in 
Q_{>0}, let t(s) \coloneqq  rac{s^2 + n}{2s} , \qquad u(s) \coloneqq  rac{2ns}{s^2 + n} . Clearing denominators as before,  egin{aligned} t(s)^2 - n &=  rac{(s^2 - n)^2}{4s^2} , & s - t(s) &=  rac{s^2 - n}{2s} , \ u(s) - s &=  rac{s(n - s^2)}{s^2 + n} , & n - u(s)^2 &=  rac{n(s^2 - n)^2}{(s^2 + n)^2} . \end{aligned} A supremum s would satisfy s \ge 1 > 0 and s^2 
e n by (i). If s^2 < n, then u(s) \in A_n and u(s) > s; if s^2 > n, then t(s) is an upper bound of A_n with t(s) < s. Either way s is not the supremum. So A_n has a supremum in 
Q exactly when n is the square of a natural number. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: produces k \in 
N with k^2 \le n < (k + 1)^2, from a least element. - 2: the case n = k^2: checks (S1) and (S2) for k. - 3: the case k^2 < n: no rational squares to n, by a descent with a least denominator (or another correct route), including a proof that the new numerator is positive. - 2: the two maps (or any explicit rationals) and the two cases, as in the proof for 2. - 1: states the answer: exactly the squares of natural numbers. Fatal errors (0 for the step): using a square root of n, or the floor of one, as if it existed; deducing nq - kp > 0 from kq < p < (k + 1)q alone. R. Review [R1] Prove, by induction on m, that for all m, n \in 
N: if m + n = m, then n = 0. Use only the equations of addition (m + 0 = m, m + (n + 1) = (m + n) + 1, 0 + n = n, (m + 1) + n = (m + n) + 1) and the fact that k + 1 = l + 1 implies k = l. Do not use cancellation or any fact about the order: cancellation gives the claim in one line (m + n = m + 0), and it is itself proved from the facts this exercise asks you to use. We use @thm-omega-induction (b) (the form of @fd1:ax-induction on \omega = 
N, by @cor-omega-identification (b)) on m, for the property P(m): “for every n \in 
N, if m + n = m, then n = 0”. Keeping “for every n” inside P(m) lets the step use the hypothesis for the same n. Base P(0). Let 0 + n = 0. Since 0 + n = n (@thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (a)), n = 0. Step. Assume P(m), and let (m + 1) + n = m + 1. By @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (a), (m + 1) + n = (m + n) + 1, so (m + n) + 1 = m + 1. By @cor-omega-successor-cancellation, m + n = m. By P(m), n = 0. This proves P(m + 1). By induction, P(m) holds for every m \in 
N. Cancellation (@prp-omega-order-arithmetic (b)) and the order facts are deliberately not used: each gives a one-line proof, and cancellation is itself proved by peeling off one successor at a time with @cor-omega-successor-cancellation, the move of the step above. [R2] Show that the set 
Q, as constructed in this chapter, is countable. The tools are the results on countable sets of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 3, read on 
N = \omega through the dictionary of Section 1.7 (@cor-omega-identification and the table after it). 
Z is countable. 
N 	imes 
N is countable (@fd2:thm-product-countable). The map a \mapsto [a], from 
N 	imes 
N to 
Z = (
N 	imes 
N)/{\sim}, is surjective, since every class is the class of each of its elements (@fd2:def-quotient-set). By @fd2:prp-countable-image, 
Z is countable. 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0} is countable. 
Z_{>0} \subseteq 
Z is countable by @fd2:prp-countable-subset, and the product of two countable sets is countable (@fd2:cor-product-countable (a)). 
Q is countable. The map (p, q) \mapsto [(p, q)], from 
Z 	imes 
Z_{>0} to 
Q, is surjective (@fd2:def-quotient-set), so 
Q is countable by @fd2:prp-countable-image. (Section 1.7 lets a review exercise cite @fd2:thm-product-countable and @fd2:cor-product-countable (a), which run on \omega through @prp-omega-powers-parity.) The conclusion is @fd2:thm-integers-rationals-countable for the constructed 
Q; that theorem, about the school rationals, is not used. [R3] Let A \coloneqq \{ x \in 
Q : x^2 < 2 \} and s \in 
Q. Write “s is a supremum of A in 
Q” in symbols, with bounded quantifiers. Then write its negation, moving 
eg inward as far as it goes and naming the law used at each step. The proof that A has no supremum in 
Q has two cases; which half of the negation does each case establish, and with which witness? By @fd2:def-order-supremum, “s is a supremum of A” is the conjunction of (S1) and (S2):  igl(  orall x \in A \ \ x \le s  igr) \ \wedge \  orall v \in 
Q \  igl( ( orall x \in A \ \ x \le v) 	o s \le v  igr) . Its negation is, by @fd1:prp-de-morgan (d), 
eg  igl(  orall x \in A \ \ x \le s  igr) \ \vee \ 
eg  orall v \in 
Q \  igl( ( orall x \in A \ \ x \le v) 	o s \le v  igr) . By @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation (a), the first disjunct becomes \exists x \in A \ 
eg(x \le s), that is, \exists x \in A \ \ s < x (totality of \le, @prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)). By @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation (a) and then @fd1:prp-negated-implication, the second becomes \exists v \in 
Q \  igl( ( orall x \in A \ \ x \le v) \wedge 
eg(s \le v)  igr) , that is, there is an upper bound v of A with v < s. In words: s fails to be the supremum when some element of A lies above s, or some upper bound lies below s. In the proof of @thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2, Case 1 (s^2 < 2) establishes the first disjunct, with witness x = u(s) = 4s/(s^2 + 2). Case 2 (s^2 > 2) establishes the second, with witness v = t(s) = (s^2 + 2)/(2s). (The proof itself needs no negation law: it derives a contradiction from (S1) in Case 1 and from (S2) in Case 2.) [R4] Is there a rational number x with x^3 = 2, where x^3 \coloneqq x^2 \cdot x? Prove your answer. No. The tool is descent on the denominator, as in @thm-no-rational-square-two, but run with parity, which @prp-rational-integer-part supplies. Parity. For every a \in 
Z there is m \in 
Z with a = 2m or a = 2m + 1, and not both forms occur. Indeed, let m \coloneqq  loor{a/2} (@prp-rational-integer-part): m \le a/2 < m + 1, so 2m \le a < 2m + 2 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)). The integer r \coloneqq a - 2m has 0 \le r < 2; if r > 0, then r \ge 1, and if r > 1, then r \ge 2, by discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)); so r = 0 or r = 1. If 2m = 2m' + 1, then d \coloneqq m - m' has 2d = 1; but d \le 0 gives 2d \le 0, and d \ge 1 gives 2d \ge 2, and by discreteness one of these holds. Moreover an odd cube is odd: (2m + 1)^3 = 2(4m^3 + 6m^2 + 3m) + 1 . Descent. Suppose x \in 
Q and x^3 = 2. Then x > 0: x = 0 gives x^3 = 0, and x < 0 gives x^2 > 0 and x^3 = x^2 \cdot x < 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), (c)). So x = p/q with p, q \in 
Z_{>0} and p^3 = 2q^3 (@prp-integers-embed-rationals (b), @def-rational-operations). Take q least among such denominators (@prp-integer-least-element), with its p. Since p^3 = 2q^3 has the even form, p is not odd (its cube would be odd), so p = 2m with m \in 
Z, and m > 0 because p > 0 (m \le 0 would give 2m \le 0). Then 2q^3 = 8m^3, and canceling the non-zero factor 2 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (f)), q^3 = 2(2m^3). So q is not odd either: q = 2l with l \in 
Z_{>0}. Then 8m^3 = 2 \cdot 8l^3, so m^3 = 2l^3, and l < l + l = q. So l is a smaller admissible denominator, with m \in 
Z_{>0}: a contradiction. Why the look-alike fails. The substitution p' \coloneqq 2q - p, q' \coloneqq p - q of the square-root proof came from x = (2 - x)/(x - 1), which used x^2 = 2. For cubes the same algebra fails: expanding, (2q - p)^3 - 2(p - q)^3 = -3p^3 + 12p^2 q - 18pq^2 + 10q^3 , which is not a constant multiple of p^3 - 2q^3 (it has a p^2 q term), so this identity gives no way to derive p'^3 = 2q'^3 from p^3 = 2q^3, and the descent has no smaller pair to move to. Parity, by contrast, works for every power: “even cube, so even base” is the same argument for squares and cubes.

title: Divisibility, Division with Remainder, and the Integers Modulo n
content:
Divisibility, Division with Remainder, and the Integers Modulo n Chapter 2 built 
Z out of pairs of natural numbers and proved it an ordered ring, but it said nothing about which integers divide which. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.2 did, for the school integers: it proved division with remainder, showed that every integer from 2 on has a prime factor, and set the uniqueness of prime factorization aside as a fact it neither proved nor used. This chapter proves that arithmetic again for the constructed 
Z, and goes further, using only the ordered-ring axioms and one property of the order: a non-empty set of integers with a lower bound has a least element (@prp-integer-least-element). That property gives division with remainder at once. Then one move does most of the work. In a set of integers closed under sums and under multiplication by any integer, the least positive element divides every element, and dividing by it with remainder is how one sees this. Applied to the combinations ax + by, it makes the greatest common divisor a combination of a and b (Bézout’s theorem), and the Euclidean algorithm computes it. Multiplying that combination by a third integer gives Euclid’s lemma, that a prime dividing a product divides one of the factors, and with it the uniqueness of prime factorization and the lowest terms of a rational number. The second half returns to the clock of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.5. There, and again for 
Z and 
Q in Chapter 2, each sum and product of classes was checked separately to be well defined. Section 3.4 makes the check once, for the quotient of any commutative ring by an ideal, and 
Z/n
Z becomes a commutative ring with n elements on which, for n \ge 2, no order fits. In it the classes that can be divided by are exactly the classes of the integers coprime to n. So 
Z/p
Z is a field with p elements for every prime p, and two congruences with coprime moduli have exactly one class of solutions modulo the product of the moduli, the Chinese remainder theorem. The quotient by an ideal is the pattern that Chapter 5 follows to build 
R from Cauchy sequences, and that Algebraic Preliminaries, Chapter 5 follows for polynomials modulo a polynomial. Two integers, one theory. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2 proved its facts about divisibility for the school integers, from school facts such as the closure of 
Z under +, - and \cdot (@fd2:prp-integers-closed). This chapter keeps their definitions of divisibility, prime and congruence (@fd2:def-divides, @fd2:def-prime, @fd2:def-congruence), read word for word on the ring of Chapter 2, and proves the results again; no proof in it cites a result of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality about integers. Each such result has a twin here, named in the section that proves it: division with remainder (@fd2:thm-division-algorithm) and the antisymmetry of divisibility on 
N (@fd2:prp-divides-partial-order) in Section 3.1; a prime factor of every n \ge 2 (@fd2:thm-prime-factor) and lowest terms (@fd2:lem-lowest-terms) in Section 3.3; and the arithmetic of congruence classes (@fd2:prp-congruence-arithmetic) in Section 3.4. Nothing earlier was circular: the earlier chapters used these facts about the school integers as stated facts, and this chapter proves them for the constructed ones. What you need. Chapters 1 and 2, chiefly Section 2.3, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 1–3, chiefly Sections 2.2 and 2.5. From Chapter 2: the commutative ring 
Z and its algebra (@def-commutative-ring-and-field, @thm-integers-commutative-ring, @prp-ring-algebra), its order, the rules for inequalities and discreteness (@prp-ordered-ring-rules, @thm-integers-ordered-ring), the least element of a set of integers bounded below (@prp-integer-least-element), the copy of 
N inside 
Z (@prp-naturals-embed-integers), the lemma that a rule on classes is a function when equivalent inputs give equivalent outputs (@thm-well-defined-on-classes), the two-element field that cannot be ordered (@exm-finite-ring-not-orderable), and the field 
Q with 
Z inside it, its order, reciprocals and integer part (@def-rational-operations, @thm-rationals-field, @prp-integers-embed-rationals, @thm-rationals-ordered-field, @prp-reciprocal-order, @prp-rational-integer-part). From Chapter 1, the citing rule of Section 1.7 (@cor-omega-identification), by which induction (@fd1:ax-induction) and the recursion theorem (@fd2:thm-recursion, @thm-omega-recursion) apply to 
N; and powers and parity on 
N (@prp-omega-powers-parity), compared with in Section 3.1 and used in review exercise R2. From Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.2, the definitions of divisibility and prime (@fd2:def-divides, @fd2:def-prime); from Section 2.3, finite products (@fd2:def-sum-product), used in Section 3.3 as a pattern for products of lists; from Section 2.5, equivalence relations, classes and quotient sets (@fd2:def-equivalence-relation, @fd2:def-quotient-set, @fd2:thm-classes-partition) and congruence (@fd2:def-congruence); from Section 2.6, suprema and the divisibility order (@fd2:def-order-supremum, @fd2:exm-divisibility-lcm), in a remark of Section 3.2 and in Section 3.3’s B2. From Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1: products, equality of functions and bijections (@fd2:def-cartesian-product, @fd2:prp-function-equality, @fd2:def-bijective); and from its Section 3.1, finite sets and equinumerous sets (@fd2:def-finite, @fd2:prp-equinumerous-properties), to count 
Z/n
Z, with more on finite sets (@fd2:prp-subset-finite, @fd2:cor-finite-size-unique, @fd2:thm-finite-no-proper-copy, @fd2:exr-finite-sets-c2, @fd2:cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets) in Section 3.5’s B3 and C2. From Logic and Proof, Chapter 5, the catalogue of what a proof may not do (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue), for Section 3.3’s B1 and C2 and Section 3.5’s C2. A few results are compared with and not used: the twins listed above; a rule on classes that is not a function (@fd2:exm-ill-defined-class-map) in Section 3.4’s C1; lowest terms in Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.2’s C2 (@fd2:exr-induction-in-practice-c2) in Section 3.3; and, in the review exercises, the countable product of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 3.2 (@fd2:exr-countable-sets-b2, @fd2:thm-product-countable) in R2, the two proofs that \sqrt 2 is not rational (@fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational, @thm-no-rational-square-two) in R3. Review exercise R1 also returns to the integers as classes of pairs (@def-integers-as-classes). Time. About 25 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 30 hours for everything. Roadmap - Divisibility and Division with Remainder. Divisibility and primes read on the constructed 
Z, the rules for divisibility proved from the ring and its order, division with a unique quotient and remainder from a least element, the quotient as the integer part  loor{a/n}, even and odd integers, and the small-primes remark that 2, 3, 5 and 7 are prime. - The Greatest Common Divisor, Bézout, and the Euclidean Algorithm. The combinations a
Z + b
Z and the multiples n
Z, the greatest common divisor with \gcd(0, 0) \coloneqq 0, Bézout’s theorem (the least positive combination is the gcd, and every combination is a multiple of it), coprime integers, and the Euclidean algorithm as a recursion that keeps the set of combinations fixed, with back-substitution for the coefficients. - Euclid’s Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. Euclid’s lemma from the Bézout identity, a prime dividing a product of primes equal to one of them, coprime divisors, the least divisor above 1 as a prime, existence and uniqueness of non-decreasing prime factorizations by comparing the largest primes, a monoid in which factorization is not unique, and lowest terms in 
Q. - Ideals, Quotient Rings, and the Integers Modulo n. Ideals as the subsets that a quotient needs, the quotient ring R/I of a commutative ring by an ideal, the failure for 
Z \subseteq 
Q, the ideals of 
Z as the sets n
Z, and 
Z/n
Z as a commutative ring with n elements that no order fits when n \ge 2. - Units, Prime Moduli, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem. Units of a commutative ring, the units of 
Z/n
Z as the classes coprime to n with inverses from back-substitution, 
Z/n
Z a field exactly when n is prime, and the Chinese remainder theorem for two coprime moduli, with the failures when the moduli share a factor; the review exercises reach back to Chapters 1 and 2, Logic and Proof, Chapter 2, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 3. Named moves - Least positive element, then divide. Take the least positive element d of a set of integers closed under integer combinations; divide any element of the set by d; the remainder lies in the set and is smaller than d, so it is 0. This proves Bézout’s theorem in Section 3.2 and the description of the ideals of 
Z in Section 3.4, and Section 3.3’s B2 and Section 3.4’s C2 use it for common multiples and for sets closed under subtraction. - Multiply the Bézout identity. From 1 = ax + by, multiply by c: c = acx + bcy, and read off what divides c. It turns a statement about common divisors into an equation, and it gives Euclid’s lemma in Section 3.3; in Section 3.5 the same identity, read modulo n, gives inverses, and read modulo m and modulo n at once, the Chinese remainder theorem. - Compute on representatives; the ideal absorbs the change. An operation on classes a + I is well defined because a change of representative is an element of I, and multiplying it by the other argument keeps it in I. This is Chapter 2’s check one argument at a time, now made once for every commutative ring and every ideal.

title: 3.1 Divisibility and Division with Remainder
content:
Divisibility and Division with Remainder Chapter 2 built 
Z as an ordered commutative ring, and a Quick check in Section 2.3 showed that it is not a field: 2x = 1 has no solution in 
Z. So “a/b” is not available among the integers. What remains is a relation, “b is a multiple of a”, and the next best thing to division: dividing with a quotient and a remainder. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.2 defined the relation and proved division with remainder for the school integers. This section does both again for the integers of Chapter 2, where every step must come from the ordered-ring axioms and from the least-element property of 
Z. Throughout, 
Z is the ordered ring of @thm-integers-ordered-ring, with 
N \subseteq 
Z and 
Z_{>0} = \{ n \in 
Z : n > 0 \} (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)), and a - b \coloneqq a + (-b). Numerals 2 \coloneqq 1 + 1, 3 \coloneqq 2 + 1, and so on, are the natural numbers of those names, as in Section 2.6; a sum or product of numerals may be computed in 
N, because the embedding of @prp-naturals-embed-integers preserves + and \cdot, and a sign is moved by @prp-ring-algebra (c), as in (-4) \cdot 5 = -(4 \cdot 5) = -20. Divisibility on the constructed integers The definition of divisibility needs nothing that the ring 
Z lacks. We restate it, and the definition of a prime, word for word from Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.2, with 
Z now the ring of Chapter 2. Divisibility (@fd2:def-divides). Let a, b \in 
Z. Then a divides b, written a \mid b, if there exists k \in 
Z with b = ka. Then a is a divisor of b, and b is a multiple of a. We write a 
mid b when a does not divide b. Prime (@fd2:def-prime). An integer p is prime if p \ge 2 and the only positive divisors of p are 1 and p. A prime factor of an integer n is a prime p with p \mid n. Both definitions use only the multiplication of 
Z, its order \le, and the set 
Z_{>0}, and Chapter 2 provides all three. They are the same words as before; what changes is that every fact about them must now be proved from Chapter 2. Divisibility is a question about existence: is b some integer times a? Some instances. 3 \mid -12, since -12 = (-4) \cdot 3. -4 \mid 0, since 0 = 0 \cdot (-4). Even 0 \mid 0 holds, since 0 = 1 \cdot 0: the definition asks for some k, and here every k works. On the other hand 5 
mid 12. That is a statement that no k \in 
Z has 12 = 5k, and to prove it we need the theorem on division with remainder below. The relation “a \mid b” is not a fraction. It is a statement, true or false, about two integers. The expression b/a, for a 
e 0, is a rational number, and this chapter does not use it to decide divisibility. Here are the rules for divisibility that the rest of the chapter uses. Each is a short consequence of the ring laws or of the order. [Rules for Divisibility in 
Z] Let a, b, c, x, y \in 
Z. 1. a \mid 0, 1 \mid a and a \mid a. If 0 \mid a, then a = 0. 2. If a \mid b and b \mid c, then a \mid c. 3. If a \mid b and a \mid c, then a \mid bx + cy. 4. If a \mid b, then (-a) \mid b and a \mid (-b). 5. If a \mid b, a > 0 and b > 0, then a \le b. 6. If a, b \in 
N, a \mid b and b \mid a, then a = b. 7. If a \mid 1, then a = 1 or a = -1. 8. If a 
e 0, then exactly one of a, -a lies in 
Z_{>0}. Parts (a)–(d) are identities in the commutative ring 
Z: write each hypothesis as an equation b = ka and rearrange. Part (e) is the one that needs the order. If b = ka with a, b > 0, the factor k cannot be zero or negative, so by discreteness it is at least 1, and multiplying a by something at least 1 cannot make it smaller. Parts (f) and (g) then follow from (e), and (h) is trichotomy. We use the ring laws (F1)–(F9) of 
Z (@thm-integers-commutative-ring) without further mention. (a) 0 = a \cdot 0 = 0 \cdot a by @prp-ring-algebra (b) and (F6), so a \mid 0 with k = 0. Also a = a \cdot 1 by (F7), so 1 \mid a with k = a; and a = 1 \cdot a, so a \mid a with k = 1. If 0 \mid a, then a = k \cdot 0 = 0 for some k \in 
Z, by @prp-ring-algebra (b). (b) Let b = ka and c = lb with k, l \in 
Z. Then c = l(ka) = (lk)a by (F5), so a \mid c. (c) Let b = ka and c = la. Then bx + cy = (ka)x + (la)y = (kx)a + (ly)a = (kx + ly)a by (F5), (F6) and (F9), and kx + ly \in 
Z. So a \mid bx + cy. (d) Let b = ka. By @prp-ring-algebra (c), (-k)(-a) = ka = b, so (-a) \mid b; and (-k)a = -(ka) = -b, so a \mid (-b). (e) Let a 
e 0. By trichotomy (O1), exactly one of a < 0, a = 0, 0 < a holds, so exactly one of a < 0 and 0 < a does. By @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), a < 0 if and only if -0 < -a, that is, 0 < -a (here -0 = 0, since 0 + 0 = 0 and negatives are unique by @prp-ring-algebra (a)). Since 
Z_{>0} = \{ n \in 
Z : n > 0 \} (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)), exactly one of a, -a lies in 
Z_{>0}. (f) Let b = ka with k \in 
Z, a > 0 and b > 0. We show first that k > 0. If k = 0, then b = 0 \cdot a = 0 by @prp-ring-algebra (b), against b > 0. If k < 0, then ka < 0 \cdot a = 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) (multiplying k < 0 by a > 0), again against b > 0. So k > 0, and by discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c), with 0 < k) 1 \le k. If k = 1, then b = a. If 1 < k, then k - 1 > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), so (k - 1)a > 0 \cdot a = 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), that is, b - a = ka - a = (k - 1)a > 0, and a < b by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a). In both cases a \le b. (g) Let a, b \in 
N with a \mid b and b \mid a. If a = 0, then 0 \mid b, so b = 0 = a by (a). If b = 0, then a = 0 in the same way. Otherwise a, b \in 
N are non-zero, hence positive (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)), and (e) gives a \le b and b \le a. Since \le is a total order (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)), it is antisymmetric, and a = b. (h) Let a \mid 1, say 1 = ka. Then a 
e 0: otherwise 1 = k \cdot 0 = 0, against 1 
e 0 in 
Z (@thm-integers-commutative-ring). By (h), one of a, -a is positive; call it e. Then e \mid 1, by (d) if e = -a. Since 1 > 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)), part (e) gives e \le 1; and e > 0 gives 1 \le e by discreteness. So e = 1. If e = a, then a = 1; if e = -a, then a = -(-a) = -1 by @prp-ring-algebra (a). This proves the proposition. Part (f) is the antisymmetry of divisibility on 
N, @fd2:prp-divides-partial-order of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.4, now proved on 
N \subseteq 
Z for the constructed integers. On all of 
Z it fails: 2 \mid -2 and -2 \mid 2, by (d), yet 2 
e -2. That is why (f) is stated for a, b \in 
N, and why (e) needs both a > 0 and b > 0: 3 \mid -3, but 3 > -3. Which hypothesis of (e) fails for a = 3, b = 0, and is the conclusion a \le b true there? 3 \mid 0 by (a), and a = 3 > 0, but b = 0 is not positive. The conclusion 3 \le 0 is false. Every integer divides 0, so no bound of the form a \le b can hold for b = 0; that is the reason for the hypothesis b > 0. Division with remainder Now the substitute for division. Given a \in 
Z and n \in 
Z_{>0}, we want to write a as a multiple of n plus something small, and we want “small” to make the answer unique. The obvious attempt subtracts n from a until what is left lies in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}, adding n instead when a is negative. That is a process; the theorem replaces it by a least element. [Division with Remainder in 
Z] Let a \in 
Z and n \in 
Z_{>0}. 1. There are unique q, r \in 
Z with a = qn + r \quad 	ext{and} \quad 0 \le r < n . 2. Moreover q =  loor{a/n}, the integer part of the rational number a/n (@prp-rational-integer-part), so r = a - n  loor{a/n}. The integers q and r are the quotient and the remainder of a on division by n. Among the integers a - kn, k \in 
Z, look at the non-negative ones. If there is at least one, @prp-integer-least-element hands us the least, r. It must be below n: otherwise r - n would be a smaller non-negative one of the same form. Finding a non-negative a - kn is easy for a \ge 0 (take k = 0) and needs one inequality for a < 0 (take k = a). For uniqueness, two remainders differ by a multiple of n and yet by less than n, and (e) of the rules above forbids a positive multiple of n below n. Part (b) moves the inequalities qn \le a < qn + n into 
Q and divides by n. (a) Existence. Let R \coloneqq \{ a - kn : k \in 
Z \} \cap \{ x \in 
Z : x \ge 0 \} . We show R 
e \emptyset. If a \ge 0, take k = 0: a - 0 \cdot n = a - 0 = a \ge 0, by @prp-ring-algebra (b). If a < 0, take k = a: then a - an = a(1 - n) by (F7) and (F9). Since n > 0, discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)) gives 1 \le n. If n = 1, then a(1 - n) = a \cdot 0 = 0 by @prp-ring-algebra (b). If 1 < n, then -n < -1 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), so 1 - n < 0 by (O3); multiplying a < 0 by 1 - n < 0 reverses the inequality (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (d)), so a(1 - n) > 0 \cdot (1 - n) = 0. In every case R has an element. The set R \subseteq 
Z is non-empty and has the lower bound 0, so by @prp-integer-least-element it has a least element r. Write r = a - qn with q \in 
Z. Then a = qn + r and r \ge 0. Suppose r \ge n. Then r - n \ge 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), and r - n = a - qn - n = a - (q + 1)n, so r - n \in R. But -n < 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), since n > 0), so r - n < r by (O3). This contradicts the choice of r as least. Hence r < n. Uniqueness. Let a = qn + r = q'n + r' with q, q', r, r' \in 
Z, 0 \le r < n and 0 \le r' < n. Suppose r 
e r'. Exchanging (q, r) and (q', r') changes neither the hypotheses nor the goal, so we may suppose r' < r. Then r - r' = (q' - q)n , so n \mid r - r'. Here r - r' > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), and n > 0, so @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e) gives n \le r - r'. But r' \ge 0 gives r - r' \le r (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)), and r < n; so r - r' < n, a contradiction. Hence r = r'. Then qn = q'n, so (q - q')n = 0, and since n 
e 0, @prp-ordered-ring-rules (f) gives q - q' = 0, that is, q = q'. (b) From (a), 0 \le r < n; adding qn (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)) gives qn \le a < qn + n . These are inequalities between integers, and by @thm-rationals-ordered-field (b) and @prp-integers-embed-rationals they hold in 
Q as well, with the same sums and products. In 
Q, n > 0, so n^{-1} > 0 (@prp-reciprocal-order (a)). Multiplying by n^{-1} preserves strict inequalities (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)) and equalities, so q = qn \cdot n^{-1} \le a \cdot n^{-1} < (qn + n) \cdot n^{-1} = q + 1 . That is, q \le a/n < q + 1, with q \in 
Z. By the uniqueness in @prp-rational-integer-part, q =  loor{a/n}, and then r = a - qn = a - n  loor{a/n}. This proves the theorem. The hypothesis n > 0 is used three times in (a): to find an element of R when a < 0 (through 1 - n \le 0), to see that r - n < r, and to apply @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e) in the uniqueness. For n = 0 the statement fails outright: no r satisfies 0 \le r < 0. Exercise B1 handles n < 0. Uniqueness is what turns the theorem into a test for divisibility: n \mid a if and only if the remainder of a on division by n is 0. Indeed, if a = kn, then a = kn + 0 is a division with remainder, and by uniqueness it is the only one; conversely a = qn + 0 says n \mid a. For instance 12 = 2 \cdot 5 + 2 with 0 \le 2 < 5, so the remainder is 2 
e 0, and 5 
mid 12. The statement of (a) is @fd2:thm-division-algorithm of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.2, which was proved there for the school integers. The existence proof above follows the same route, with each school fact replaced by a result of Chapter 2: the closure of 
Z under +, -, \cdot by @thm-integers-commutative-ring; “a positive integer is at least 1” by @thm-integers-ordered-ring (b), (c); and the least element of a set of integers bounded below by @prp-integer-least-element. The uniqueness argument there is the one packaged here as @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e). For n = 2 and a \in 
N, (a) is @prp-omega-powers-parity (d) of Section 1.6, which we compare with but do not use. Part (b) pays a debt of Section 2.5. There, after @prp-rational-integer-part, the integer part  loor{p/q} was announced as a quotient; (b) says exactly that, and it gives a second way to compute q and r. Exercise C1 turns (b) around and proves the existence half of (a) from the integer part. Find the quotient and the remainder of a = -17 on division by n = 5, and check them against (b). q = -4 and r = 3: (-4) \cdot 5 + 3 = -20 + 3 = -17, and 0 \le 3 < 5. For (b), -4 \le -17/5 < -3, since (-4) \cdot 5 = -20 \le -17 and -17 < -15 = (-3) \cdot 5 (@thm-rationals-ordered-field (a)); so  loor{-17/5} = -4. “The remainder” means the r with 0 \le r < n. The equation -17 = (-3) \cdot 5 - 2 is true, but -2 is not the remainder of -17 on division by 5; the remainder is 3. If negative “remainders” were allowed, uniqueness would fail at once: -17 = (-3) \cdot 5 + (-2) = (-4) \cdot 5 + 3. For negative a, the quotient is not “a/n with the fraction dropped”: that would give -3 here, while  loor{-17/5} = -4. Even and odd Recall that an integer a is even if a = 2k for some k \in 
Z, that is, 2 \mid a, and odd if a = 2k + 1 for some k \in 
Z. These are the words Logic and Proof, Chapter 1 used, now read on the constructed 
Z. Section 2.6 had parity for natural numbers from @prp-omega-powers-parity (d). With n = 2, the theorem gives it for every integer, negative ones included, with one citation. [Even and Odd Integers] 1. Every a \in 
Z is even or odd, and not both. More precisely, either a = 2q for exactly one q \in 
Z and a is not of the form 2k + 1, or a = 2q + 1 for exactly one q \in 
Z and a is not of the form 2k. 2. If a \in 
Z and a^2 is even, then a is even. Divide by 2. The remainder lies in \{0, 1\}, by discreteness, and it is unique, so each integer has exactly one of the two forms. For (b), square the odd form and read off the remainder. (a) Since 2 = 1 + 1 > 0, the theorem with n = 2 gives unique q, r \in 
Z with a = 2q + r and 0 \le r < 2. Then r \in \{0, 1\}: if r 
e 0, then 0 < r, so 1 \le r by discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)); and if moreover 1 < r, then 2 = 1 + 1 \le r by discreteness again, against r < 2. If a = 2k and a = 2k' + 1 for some k, k' \in 
Z, then (k, 0) and (k', 1) would be two pairs as in the theorem, and 0 
e 1 contradicts its uniqueness. The same uniqueness shows that q is the only integer with a = 2q + r. (b) Suppose a is not even. By (a), a = 2q + 1 with q \in 
Z. Then a^2 = (2q + 1)^2 = 4q^2 + 4q + 1 = 2(2q^2 + 2q) + 1 , by @prp-ring-algebra (d) and (F5), (F6), (F9), so a^2 is odd, and by (a) it is not even. This proves (b) by contraposition. Section 2.6 proved that no rational squares to 2 by a descent on denominators (@thm-no-rational-square-two), a route that needs only the order of 
Z and adapts to other non-squares. With (b), and with lowest terms from Section 3.3, the classical parity proof of Logic and Proof, Chapter 2 can also be run on the constructed 
Q, every step citable; one of the review exercises at the end of this chapter does so. Small primes Later sections need to know that a few small integers are prime in the constructed 
Z. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.2 checked some of these after @fd2:def-prime, for the school integers; that check is not a proof about the ring of Chapter 2, so we redo it here. The small-primes remark. The integers 2, 3, 5 and 7 are prime in 
Z. Let p \in \{2, 3, 5, 7\}. Then p \ge 2. Let d be a positive divisor of p. Then 1 \le d by discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)) and d \le p by @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e), so d is one of 1, 2, \dots, p: applying discreteness repeatedly (if d 
e 1 then 2 \le d; if d 
e 2 then 3 \le d; and so on up to p) leaves no other value. Each d with 1 < d < p leaves a non-zero remainder:  egin{aligned} 3 &= 1 \cdot 2 + 1, \qquad 5 = 2 \cdot 2 + 1 = 1 \cdot 3 + 2 = 1 \cdot 4 + 1, \ 7 &= 3 \cdot 2 + 1 = 2 \cdot 3 + 1 = 1 \cdot 4 + 3 = 1 \cdot 5 + 2 = 1 \cdot 6 + 1 . \end{aligned} (For p = 2 there is no such d.) So d 
mid p for these d, by the divisibility test after @thm-integers-division-remainder: p = kd would give p = kd + 0, a second division of p by d, with remainder 0, against the uniqueness in @thm-integers-division-remainder (a). Hence the positive divisors of p are 1 and p, and p is prime. The later sections of this chapter cite this paragraph as “the small-primes remark”. The same procedure decides, for any given p \ge 2, whether p is prime; Section 3.3 shortens it. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Find the quotient and the remainder on division by n = 6 of a = 47, of a = -47 and of a = 0. 2. Where is n > 0 used in the existence half of @thm-integers-division-remainder (a)? 3. True or false, with a reason: 0 \mid 0. 4. True or false, with a reason: for all a, b \in 
Z, if a \mid b and b \mid a, then a = b. (a) 47 = 7 \cdot 6 + 5, so (q, r) = (7, 5). -47 = (-8) \cdot 6 + 1, since -48 + 1 = -47, so (q, r) = (-8, 1). 0 = 0 \cdot 6 + 0, so (q, r) = (0, 0). In each case 0 \le r < 6, so by uniqueness these are the quotient and remainder. Note (-8, 1), not (-7, -5). (b) Twice. For a < 0, the element a - an = a(1 - n) of R is non-negative because 1 - n \le 0, which comes from n \ge 1, that is, from n > 0 and discreteness. And the contradiction “r - n < r” needs -n < 0, that is, n > 0. (c) True: 0 = 1 \cdot 0, so k = 1 witnesses 0 \mid 0 (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (a)). (d) False: 2 \mid -2 and -2 \mid 2 (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (d)), but 2 
e -2. The statement is true for a, b \in 
N (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (f)). B. Practice [B1: Negative divisors] Let a, n \in 
Z with n < 0. Prove that there are unique q, r \in 
Z with a = qn + r and 0 \le r < -n. Since n < 0, -n > 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), so -n \in 
Z_{>0}. Existence. By @thm-integers-division-remainder (a) applied to a and -n, there are q_0, r \in 
Z with a = q_0(-n) + r and 0 \le r < -n. Let q \coloneqq -q_0. Then q_0(-n) = (-q_0)n = qn by @prp-ring-algebra (c), so a = qn + r. Uniqueness. Let a = qn + r = q'n + r' with 0 \le r, r' < -n. By @prp-ring-algebra (c), qn = (-q)(-n) and q'n = (-q')(-n), so a = (-q)(-n) + r = (-q')(-n) + r' are two divisions of a by -n. The uniqueness in @thm-integers-division-remainder (a) gives r = r' and -q = -q', hence q = -(-q) = -(-q') = q' by @prp-ring-algebra (a). [B2: Three in a row] Let a \in 
Z. Prove that exactly one of a, a + 1, a + 2 is divisible by 3. At least one. By @thm-integers-division-remainder (a), a = 3q + r with 0 \le r < 3, and r \in \{0, 1, 2\} by discreteness, as in the proof of @cor-integers-even-odd. If r = 0, then 3 \mid a. If r = 1, then a + 2 = 3q + 3 = 3(q + 1). If r = 2, then a + 1 = 3q + 3 = 3(q + 1). At most one. Suppose 3 \mid a + i and 3 \mid a + j with 0 \le i < j \le 2. By @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c) (with x = 1, y = -1), 3 \mid (a + j) - (a + i) = j - i, and j - i \in \{1, 2\} is positive. By @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e), 3 \le j - i \le 2, which is false. So no two of the three are divisible by 3. (Equivalently: the remainders of a, a + 1, a + 2 on division by 3 are r, and then the other two of 0, 1, 2, and uniqueness of remainders allows only one of them to be 0.) C. Z and n \in 
Z_{>0}. Prove the existence half of @thm-integers-division-remainder (a) directly from @prp-rational-integer-part, without the set R: put q \coloneqq  loor{a/n} and r \coloneqq a - qn, and show that 0 \le r < n. Say where n > 0 is used. By @prp-rational-integer-part, q \coloneqq  loor{a/n} \in 
Z satisfies q \le a/n < q + 1 in 
Q, where a/n = a \cdot n^{-1} and n 
e 0 in 
Q. Since n > 0, multiplying by n preserves the strict inequality (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)) and the equality case, so qn \le (a \cdot n^{-1}) \cdot n = a < (q + 1)n = qn + n . Subtracting qn (that is, adding -qn, (O3)) gives 0 \le a - qn < n. Here r \coloneqq a - qn is an integer, and by @thm-rationals-ordered-field (b) the inequalities 0 \le r < n, proved in 
Q, hold in 
Z. So a = qn + r with 0 \le r < n. The hypothesis n > 0 is used when multiplying by n: for n < 0, multiplication reverses inequalities (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (d)), and the same q would give qn \ge a > qn + n, so n < r \le 0 instead. (This exercise is practice with a result already proved; nothing later rests on it.)

The Greatest Common Divisor, Bézout, and the Euclidean Algorithm Section 3.1 gave the constructed integers a relation a \mid b and a division with remainder (@thm-integers-division-remainder). This section asks what two integers have in common. Here is a concrete version. A machine accepts only coins worth 12 and 42 units, and gives change in the same coins. Which amounts can be paid exactly? Paying x coins of the first kind and y of the second, with negative numbers for coins received as change, pays 12x + 42y. So 42 - 3 \cdot 12 = 6 can be paid, and hence every multiple of 6; and since 6 divides both 12 and 42, nothing else can. Why 6, and why exactly the multiples of 6? The answer is a theorem about every pair of integers, and its proof is the main move of this chapter. Integer combinations The amounts 12x + 42y form a set that deserves a name. To find coefficients x, y with \gcd(a, b) = ax + by, we run the identity of @lem-gcd-remainder-step backwards. Back-substitution. Write out the divisions x_k = q_k y_k + r_k for k = 0, \dots, K - 1, so that x_{k+1} = y_k and y_{k+1} = r_k. Start from \gcd(a, b) = x_K = 1 \cdot x_K + 0 \cdot y_K, a combination of the last pair. The pair (-35, 15). The first entry may be negative; only the second must be positive. The remainder of -35 on division by 15 is 10, not -5:  egin{aligned} -35 &= (-3) \cdot 15 + 10, \ 15 &= 1 \cdot 10 + 5, \ 10 &= 2 \cdot 5 + 0 . \end{aligned} So \gcd(-35, 15) = 5, and 5 = 15 - 10 = 15 -  igl( -35 + 3 \cdot 15  igr) = (-1) \cdot (-35) + (-2) \cdot 15 . The positive ones are at most 6 (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e)), and 6 is one of them. (The theorem does not apply directly to (0, -6), since its second entry is negative; it does apply to (0, 6), with the one division 0 = 0 \cdot 6 + 0.) \gcd(84, 35) = 7, by the chain 84 = 2 \cdot 35 + 14, 35 = 2 \cdot 14 + 7, 14 = 2 \cdot 7 + 0. Run the proof on (a, b) = (12, 42): find d, x_0, y_0, and the divisions of (b). 3. Which step fails for (a, b) = (0, 0)? 4. State the idea of the proof in two sentences. (a) Once, in (b): the remainder r of a on division by d is a combination of a and b, and if it were positive it would be an element of S smaller than d. Minimality forces r = 0. (b) The set S contains 6 = 12 \cdot (-3) + 42 \cdot 1. Every element of 12

Hence d = 6, with x_0 = -3 and y_0 = 1. The divisions of (b) are 12 = 2 \cdot 6 + 0 and 42 = 7 \cdot 6 + 0: both remainders are 0, as the proof predicts. (c) Step (a): 0

Dividing a (or b) by d leaves a remainder that is again a combination and smaller than d, so it is 0; thus d is a common divisor, and since every common divisor divides the combination d, it is the greatest. B. Practice [B1] Run the Euclidean algorithm on (1001, 357), and use back-substitution to write \gcd(1001, 357) as 1001x + 357y with x, y \in

Hence x = 5, y = -14 works. [B2] Let a, b \in 
Z. Prove that \gcd(a, b) = \gcd(-a, b), and that \gcd(a, 0) = a if a \in 
Z_{>0}. First claim. If (a, b) = (0, 0), then also (-a, b) = (0, 0), and both sides are 0 by convention. Otherwise (-a, b)

So a and -a have the same divisors, the pairs (a, b) and (-a, b) have the same common divisors, and the greatest is the same (@def-integer-gcd). Second claim. Let a > 0. Every integer divides 0 (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (a)), so the common divisors of a and 0 are the divisors of a. Among them is a itself. A positive divisor c satisfies c \le a by @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e), and a non-positive one satisfies c \le 0 < a. So a is the greatest, and \gcd(a, 0) = a. [B3: The algorithm stops quickly] In the notation of @thm-euclidean-algorithm-integers, prove that y_k \le b - k for every k \in 
N with k \le K. Deduce that K \le b: the algorithm stops after at most b divisions. We use @fd1:ax-induction (through @cor-omega-identification (b)) on k, for P(k): “if k \le K, then y_k \le b - k”. The base case P(0) is y_0 = b = b - 0. Suppose P(k), and let k + 1 \le K. Then k < K, so k \le K and P(k) gives y_k \le b - k. Hence y_{k+1} \le b - k - 1 = b - (k + 1), which is P(k + 1). With k = K: 0 = y_K \le b - K, so K \le b. Each index k < K is one division, so there are K \le b of them. C. e \emptyset. It is bounded below by 0, so it has a least element d (@prp-integer-least-element), and d = ax_0 + by_0 for some x_0, y_0 \in 
Z. d divides a and b. Divide a by d > 0 (@thm-integers-division-remainder (a)): a = qd + r with 0 \le r < d. Then r = a(1 - qx_0) + b(-qy_0) is a combination of a and b. If r > 0, then r \in S and r < d, against the minimality of d. So r = 0 and d \mid a. The same argument with b gives d \mid b. Common divisors divide d. If c \mid a and c \mid b, then c \mid ax_0 + by_0 = d (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c)). d is the gcd. d is a common divisor. A common divisor c > 0 divides d > 0, so c \le d (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e)); a common divisor c \le 0 satisfies c < d. So d is the greatest common divisor (@def-integer-gcd). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: shows S 
e \emptyset, with a reason that covers a < 0 or b < 0 (for instance, one of a, -a is a positive combination). - 1: obtains the least element by a cited well-ordering result for sets of integers bounded below. - 3: divides a by d and writes the remainder as a combination of a and b. - 2: uses the minimality of d to force the remainder to be 0, for a and for b. - 2: shows every common divisor divides d, and deduces that d is the greatest (with the case of non-positive divisors). Fatal errors (0 for the step): assuming that the gcd is a combination of a and b (circular); “d divides a because d is the least positive combination”, with no division step. A second route, through the Euclidean algorithm with back-substitution, by induction on the number of steps, maps to the same points: the invariant that each step keeps the set of combinations (or the gcd) unchanged earns the 3 points for the division, termination earns the 2 points for minimality, and the rest is marked as written.
