title: 3.3 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content:
Euclid’s Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic Section 3.2 gave every pair of integers, not both zero, a greatest common divisor, and wrote it as a combination ax + by (@thm-integers-bezout). This section spends that identity. Take 60. It splits as 2 \cdot 30, as 6 \cdot 10, as 4 \cdot 15, and every way of splitting it further, until no factor splits again, ends with the same primes 2, 2, 3, 5. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.2 proved, for the school integers, that every integer at least 2 has a prime factor, and set the uniqueness of the full splitting aside. Here we prove both, for the integers of Chapter 2. The key is a property of primes that the definition (“no positive divisors except 1 and itself”) does not obviously give: a prime that divides a product divides one of the factors. As in Section 3.1, numerals are the natural numbers of those names, and their sums and products may be computed in 
N (@prp-naturals-embed-integers (a)). Euclid’s lemma The definition of a prime p speaks about the divisors of p. The property we want speaks about the numbers that p divides. Something has to connect the two, and the connection is the Bézout identity of Section 3.2. We first prove a version for any divisor that shares no factor with one of the two numbers multiplied. Euclid’s Lemma Let a, b, c \in 
Z. If a \mid bc and \gcd(a, b) = 1, then a \mid c. The hypothesis \gcd(a, b) = 1 is a statement about common divisors, which is hard to use directly. By @cor-coprime-iff-combination it is the same as an equation 1 = ax + by, and an equation can be multiplied. Multiplying it by c writes c as acx + bcy. The first term is a multiple of a on sight, and the second is one because bc is. Suppose a \mid bc and \gcd(a, b) = 1. By @cor-coprime-iff-combination there are x, y \in 
Z with ax + by = 1. Since a \mid bc, there is k \in 
Z with bc = ka (@fd2:def-divides). Multiplying the identity by c, with (F7), (F9), (F5) and (F6), c = c(ax + by) = a(cx) + (bc)y = a(cx) + a(ky) = a(cx + ky) . Since cx + ky \in 
Z, this shows a \mid c. We call the move of this proof multiply the Bézout identity: from 1 = ax + by, multiply by c and read off what divides c. It turns a statement about divisors into an equation, which is where the work can be done. Each hypothesis has a job. Without \gcd(a, b) = 1 the conclusion fails: 4 \mid 2 \cdot 6 = 12, but 4 
mid 6, since 6 = 1 \cdot 4 + 2 leaves a non-zero remainder (uniqueness in @thm-integers-division-remainder (a)); here \gcd(4, 2) = 2. The common factor 2 of 4 and 2 let 4 divide the product without dividing 6. Lists, products and prime factorizations To say that a factorization is unique, we must first say what a factorization is. The products 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 and 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 5 \cdot 2 are equal and use the same primes, and we want to count them as one. We do so by writing the primes in order, smallest first. A factorization also has a length, and the length may be 0: the number 1 is the product of no primes at all. Products of lists are defined by the recursion of @fd2:def-sum-product. That definition was made for sequences of real numbers, and we use it as a pattern, as group (iii) of the citing rule of Section 1.7 allows. [List, Product of a List, Prime Factorization] Let k \in 
N. A list of length k in 
Z is a function p \colon \{1, \dots, k\} 	o 
Z, written (p_1, \dots, p_k) with p_i \coloneqq p(i); for k = 0 it is the empty list. Its product \prod_{i=1}^{k} p_i \in 
Z is given by the recursion \prod_{i=1}^{0} p_i = 1 , \qquad \prod_{i=1}^{j+1} p_i = \Bigl( \prod_{i=1}^{j} p_i \Bigr) p_{j+1} \quad 	ext{for } j < k , where \prod_{i=1}^{j} p_i is the product of the shortened list (p_1, \dots, p_j). A prime factorization of n \in 
Z_{>0} is a list (p_1, \dots, p_k) such that every entry p_i is prime (@fd2:def-prime), the list is non-decreasing (i \le j implies p_i \le p_j), and \prod_{i=1}^{k} p_i = n. In words: a list is a finite sequence of integers, possibly empty; its product starts at 1 and multiplies by one more entry at each stage; and a prime factorization lists primes in non-decreasing order with the right product. Why the product exists. Extend the list to a sequence  ar p on 
Z_{>0} by  ar p_i \coloneqq p_i for i \le k and  ar p_i \coloneqq 1 for i > k. Then @fd2:thm-recursion, read on 
N = \omega through @cor-omega-identification (b), with X = 
Z, starting value 1 and step g(j, x) \coloneqq x  ar p_{j+1}, gives exactly one function P \colon 
N 	o 
Z with P_0 = 1 and P_{j+1} = P_j  ar p_{j+1}; we set \prod_{i=1}^{j} p_i \coloneqq P_j for j \le k. The “Finite lists” remark after @fd2:def-sum-product shows that P_j depends only on p_1, \dots, p_j, not on how the list was extended. Its proof is an induction on j that uses only the recursion and the multiplication of the target set, so it runs unchanged with 
Z in place of 
R. In particular P_j is also the product of the shortened list (p_1, \dots, p_j), which is the displayed recursion. We cite it as the recursion of @def-prime-factorization: it peels the last entry off a product. Examples. - (2, 2, 3, 5) is a prime factorization of 60. Its entries are prime by the small-primes remark of Section 3.1; it is non-decreasing; and the recursion gives the products 1, 2, 4, 12, 60. - (5) is a prime factorization of 5, with products 1, 5. A prime p has the one-entry factorization (p). - The degenerate case: the empty list is a prime factorization of 1. Its product is 1 by the first clause of the recursion, and the conditions “every entry is prime” and “non-decreasing” hold vacuously. Without this case the number 1 would have no factorization, and the uniqueness proof below would have no base case. Non-examples by minimal change. Exchange two entries of the first example: (2, 3, 2, 5) has prime entries and product 60, but it is not non-decreasing, since positions 2 \le 3 carry 3 > 2. Merge two entries: (2, 2, 15) is non-decreasing with product 60, but 15 = 3 \cdot 5 is not prime. Why these clauses. Without “non-decreasing”, 60 would have twelve factorizations, its four primes in every order, and uniqueness could only be stated up to rearrangement, which needs a theory of permutations. Without “prime”, splitting would stop anywhere. And the requirement p \ge 2 in @fd2:def-prime is what keeps (1, 2, 2, 3, 5) out: if 1 counted as a prime, every factorization could be padded with as many 1s as we like. Find the prime factorization of 360, and check each clause of @def-prime-factorization. (2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 5). Its entries are prime by the small-primes remark of Section 3.1. It is non-decreasing. Its products, by the recursion, are 1, 2, 4, 8, 24, 72, 360. By the theorem below there is no other. Primes dividing products For a prime, the coprimality that Euclid’s lemma asks for comes almost free: a prime shares no factor with a number unless it divides that number. [A Prime Dividing a Product] Let p be prime. 1. For every a \in 
Z: p \mid a or \gcd(p, a) = 1. 2. For all b, c \in 
Z: if p \mid bc, then p \mid b or p \mid c. 3. If (q_1, \dots, q_l) is a list of primes, with l \in 
N, and p \mid \prod_{j=1}^{l} q_j, then p = q_j for some j \in \{1, \dots, l\}. For (a), the gcd of p and a is a positive divisor of p, so it is 1 or p, and the second case says p \mid a. Then (b) is Euclid’s lemma in the first case of (a). For (c), peel the last prime off the product and apply (b) to the two factors; an induction on the length handles the rest, and a prime that divides a prime is equal to it. (a) Since p \ge 2, (p, a) 
e (0, 0), so g \coloneqq \gcd(p, a) \ge 1 (@def-integer-gcd). As a common divisor, g \mid p and g \mid a. So g is a positive divisor of the prime p, and g = 1 or g = p (@fd2:def-prime). If g = p, then p \mid a. (b) Let p \mid bc. By (a), p \mid b or \gcd(p, b) = 1. In the second case @thm-euclid-lemma-integers, with a = p, gives p \mid c. (c) We use @fd1:ax-induction (through @cor-omega-identification (b)) on l, for P(l): “for every list of primes (q_1, \dots, q_l), if p \mid \prod_{j=1}^{l} q_j, then p = q_j for some j \le l”. Base case P(0). The empty product is 1 (the recursion of @def-prime-factorization). If p \mid 1, then p = 1 or p = -1 (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (g)), and both contradict p \ge 2. So the hypothesis of P(0) never holds, and P(0) is true. Step. Assume P(l), and let (q_1, \dots, q_{l+1}) be a list of primes with p \mid \prod_{j=1}^{l+1} q_j. By the recursion of @def-prime-factorization, \prod_{j=1}^{l+1} q_j = \Bigl( \prod_{j=1}^{l} q_j \Bigr) q_{l+1} , where the first factor is the product of the list of primes (q_1, \dots, q_l). By (b), p divides that first factor or p \mid q_{l+1}. In the first case P(l) gives j \le l with p = q_j. In the second, p \ge 2 > 0 is a positive divisor of the prime q_{l+1}, so p \in \{1, q_{l+1}\}, and p 
e 1; hence p = q_{l+1}. This proves P(l + 1), and with it the corollary. Part (b) is the property promised at the start of the section, and it is what makes primes the right atoms for multiplication. It fails for 6, which is not prime: 6 \mid 2 \cdot 3, but 6 
mid 2 and 6 
mid 3, since 0 < 2 < 6 and 0 < 3 < 6 rule both out by @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e). The second application of Euclid’s lemma combines two coprime divisors into one. [Coprime Divisors of a Number] Let m, n, c \in 
Z with m \mid c, n \mid c and \gcd(m, n) = 1. Then mn \mid c. Write c = km with k \in 
Z. Then n \mid km, and \gcd(n, m) = \gcd(m, n) = 1 (@def-integer-gcd), so @thm-euclid-lemma-integers gives n \mid k, say k = ln with l \in 
Z. Hence c = (ln)m = l(mn), by (F5) and (F6), and mn \mid c. The coprimality is needed: 4 \mid 12 and 6 \mid 12, but 24 
mid 12, since a positive divisor of 12 is at most 12 (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e)); here \gcd(4, 6) = 2. The least divisor is prime The existence half of unique factorization needs a supply of primes: every integer n \ge 2 must have a prime factor. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.2 proved this for the school integers by strong induction (@fd2:thm-prime-factor). On the constructed 
Z the least-element property gives a shorter route: the least divisor bigger than 1 is already prime. The Least Divisor Is Prime Let n \in 
Z with n \ge 2. The set D \coloneqq \{ d \in 
Z : d \ge 2 	ext{ and } d \mid n \} has a least element, and that element is prime. In particular, n has a prime factor. Since n \ge 2 and n \mid n (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (a)), n \in D, so D is non-empty; and 2 is a lower bound of D by its definition. By @prp-integer-least-element, D has a least element p. Suppose p were not prime. Since p \ge 2, the clause of @fd2:def-prime that fails is the one about divisors: p has a positive divisor e with e 
e 1 and e 
e p. Then e \ge 1 by discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)), and e \le p by @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e). So 1 < e < p, and e \ge 2 by discreteness again. Also e \mid p and p \mid n give e \mid n (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (b)). So e \in D and e < p, against the choice of p. Hence p is prime, and p \mid n because p \in D. This is @fd2:thm-prime-factor on the constructed 
Z, proved by a least element instead of strong induction. It also shortens the primality test of Section 3.1’s small-primes remark. If p \ge 2 is not prime, its least divisor e \ge 2 is prime by the lemma, so it is not p itself, and p = ef with f \in 
Z; then f > 0 (as e, p > 0), f 
e 1, so f \ge 2 and f \mid p, and therefore e \le f by the choice of e. Multiplying by e > 0 gives e \cdot e \le ef = p (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)). So to prove p \ge 2 prime it is enough to check that no d with d \ge 2 and d \cdot d \le p divides p. For 11 only d = 2, 3 need checking, since 4 \cdot 4 = 16 > 11. The fundamental theorem Everything is now in place for the main result of the chapter’s first half. [Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic] Every n \in 
Z_{>0} has exactly one prime factorization. Existence. Take the least n with no factorization. It is at least 2, so it has prime factors, and a largest one, p. Then n = pm with m < n, so m has a factorization. Every entry of it divides n, so it is at most p, and appending p at the end keeps the list non-decreasing. Uniqueness. Take two factorizations with the same product, (p_1, \dots, p_k) and (q_1, \dots, q_l). The largest entry p_k divides the product of the q’s, so by @cor-prime-divides-product (c) it is one of the q_j, and that is at most the largest, q_l. By symmetry q_l \le p_k. So the two last entries are equal; cancel them and induct on the length. Before reading on: why compare the largest primes, p_k and q_l, and not the first ones? Existence. Let B \coloneqq \{ n \in 
Z_{>0} : n 	ext{ has no prime factorization} \}, and suppose B 
e \emptyset. It has the lower bound 0, so it has a least element n (@prp-integer-least-element). The empty list is a prime factorization of 1, so n 
e 1; as n \ge 1 (discreteness, @thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)), n > 1, and so n \ge 2 by discreteness. The set F of prime factors of n is non-empty by @lem-least-divisor-prime. Each q \in F is positive and divides n > 0, so q \le n (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e)). By @prp-integer-least-element, F has a greatest element p. Write n = mp with m \in 
Z. If m \le 0, then mp \le 0 (m = 0: @prp-ring-algebra (b); m < 0: mp < 0 \cdot p = 0 by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)), against n > 0. So m > 0, that is, m \in 
Z_{>0} (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)). Moreover m < n: since p \ge 2 and m > 0, n = pm \ge 2m = m + m > m, by @prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) (or equality if p = 2), (F9) with (F7), and (O3). By the minimality of n, m 
otin B: let (q_1, \dots, q_l) be a prime factorization of m. If l \ge 1, the recursion of @def-prime-factorization gives m =  igl(\prod_{j=1}^{l-1} q_j igr) q_l, so q_l \mid m; with m \mid n this gives q_l \mid n (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (b)), so q_l \in F and q_l \le p. As the list is non-decreasing, q_i \le q_l \le p for every i \le l. Now let (q_1, \dots, q_l, p) be the list of length l + 1 whose first l entries are those of (q_1, \dots, q_l) and whose last entry is p. Its entries are prime. It is non-decreasing: two positions among the first l compare as before, and every entry is at most p (for l = 0 it is the one-entry list (p), and there is nothing to check). By the recursion its product is \Bigl( \prod_{j=1}^{l} q_j \Bigr) p = mp = n . So n has a prime factorization, against n \in B. Hence B = \emptyset. Uniqueness. We prove, by @fd1:ax-induction (through @cor-omega-identification (b)) on k, the statement P(k): “for every l \in 
N, if (p_1, \dots, p_k) and (q_1, \dots, q_l) are non-decreasing lists of primes with \prod_{i=1}^{k} p_i = \prod_{j=1}^{l} q_j, then l = k and p_i = q_i for every i \le k”. Two prime factorizations of the same n are such lists, so P(k) for every k gives the uniqueness. First, a non-empty list of primes (r_1, \dots, r_h) does not have product 1: by the recursion its product is  igl(\prod_{i=1}^{h-1} r_i igr) r_h, so r_h would divide 1, and r_h = \pm 1 (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (g)) contradicts r_h \ge 2. Base case P(0). If k = 0, then \prod_{j=1}^{l} q_j = 1, so l = 0 by the previous paragraph, and both lists are empty. Step. Assume P(k). Let (p_1, \dots, p_{k+1}) and (q_1, \dots, q_l) be non-decreasing lists of primes with the same product N. Since k + 1 \ge 1, N 
e 1, so l \ge 1. By the recursion, p_{k+1} \mid N = \prod_{j=1}^{l} q_j, so @cor-prime-divides-product (c) gives p_{k+1} = q_j for some j \le l, and q_j \le q_l because the q-list is non-decreasing. In the same way q_l \mid N = \prod_{i=1}^{k+1} p_i gives q_l = p_i \le p_{k+1} for some i \le k + 1. So p_{k+1} \le q_l \le p_{k+1}, and p_{k+1} = q_l (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)). By the recursion, \Bigl( \prod_{i=1}^{k} p_i \Bigr) p_{k+1} = N = \Bigl( \prod_{j=1}^{l-1} q_j \Bigr) p_{k+1} . Subtracting,  igl(\prod_{i=1}^{k} p_i - \prod_{j=1}^{l-1} q_j igr) p_{k+1} = 0 by (F9) and @prp-ring-algebra (c), and p_{k+1} 
e 0, so the bracket is 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (f)). The shortened lists (p_1, \dots, p_k) and (q_1, \dots, q_{l-1}) are non-decreasing lists of primes with equal products, so P(k), applied with l - 1 \in 
N, gives l - 1 = k and p_i = q_i for i \le k. With p_{k+1} = q_l = q_{k+1}, the two lists have the same length k + 1 and the same entries, so they are equal (@fd2:prp-function-equality). This proves P(k + 1), and the theorem. The answer to the prompt lies in the recursion of @def-prime-factorization. It peels off the last factor, so once the two last entries are known to be equal they can be canceled at once, leaving two shortened lists to which P(k) applies. And the comparison “largest with largest” needs only that both lists are non-decreasing. Comparing the first entries would also show p_1 = q_1, but removing a first entry shifts every index, and the recursion says nothing directly about that. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.2 named unique factorization as a fact it did not prove or use, and @fd2:exr-countable-sets-b2 lists, as line (vii), a step that cites it and is therefore not available there. On the constructed 
Z the fact is now proved, and Exercise R2 of Section 3.5 uses it. Uniqueness is not automatic. Let H \coloneqq \{ 4k + 1 : k \in 
N \} = \{1, 5, 9, 13, 17, 21, \dots\}. It is closed under multiplication, since (4k + 1)(4l + 1) = 4(4kl + k + l) + 1. Call h \in H with h > 1 an H-prime if it is not a product of two elements of H both greater than 1. Then 9, 21 and 49 are H-primes, and 441 = 9 \cdot 49 = 21 \cdot 21 gives two different factorizations into H-primes. What breaks is Euclid’s lemma: 9 divides 21 \cdot 21 inside H, but 9 
mid 21. The proof of @thm-euclid-lemma-integers wrote 1 = ax + by, with sums and with negative coefficients, and H is closed under neither. The proof of uniqueness above is only as good as Euclid’s lemma. Lowest terms Every rational number is a fraction in many ways: 6/4 = 3/2 = 9/6. Section 2.4 found, in its Exercise C1, a least positive denominator by the least-element property, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.2 removed common factors of 2 only (@fd2:lem-lowest-terms). With the gcd we can remove every common factor at once, and Euclid’s lemma shows that the result is unique. Recall that after the identification of Section 2.4, p/q \coloneqq pq^{-1} in 
Q for p \in 
Z and q \in 
Z_{>0}, and p/q = r/s holds if and only if ps = rq (@prp-integers-embed-rationals (b)). Lowest Terms Let x \in 
Q. 1. There are p \in 
Z and q \in 
Z_{>0} with x = p/q and \gcd(p, q) = 1, and the pair (p, q) is unique. 2. If x = r/s with r \in 
Z and s \in 
Z_{>0}, then r = tp and s = tq for some t \in 
Z_{>0}. In particular q \mid s and q \le s: q is the least positive denominator of x. For existence, divide numerator and denominator by their gcd d; the Bézout identity for d, divided by d, is a Bézout identity 1 = px_0 + qy_0 for the new pair. For (b), cross-multiplying gives ps = rq, so q \mid ps, and Euclid’s lemma removes p. Uniqueness is (b) applied to a second coprime pair. Existence in (a). By @prp-integers-embed-rationals (b), x = r/s for some r \in 
Z, s \in 
Z_{>0}. Since s 
e 0, d \coloneqq \gcd(r, s) \ge 1, and by @thm-integers-bezout (d) there are x_0, y_0 \in 
Z with d = rx_0 + sy_0. As d \mid r and d \mid s, write r = dp and s = dq with p, q \in 
Z. If q \le 0, then dq \le 0 (as in the existence proof of @thm-fundamental-arithmetic), against s > 0; so q \in 
Z_{>0}. Now d \cdot 1 = d = (dp)x_0 + (dq)y_0 = d(px_0 + qy_0) , so d(px_0 + qy_0 - 1) = 0, and since d 
e 0, px_0 + qy_0 = 1 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (f)). Hence \gcd(p, q) = 1 by @cor-coprime-iff-combination. Finally rq = dpq = p(dq) = ps, so r/s = p/q by @prp-integers-embed-rationals (b), and x = p/q. (b), for any such pair. Let x = p/q with \gcd(p, q) = 1, and x = r/s with s > 0. By @prp-integers-embed-rationals (b), ps = rq. So q \mid ps, and \gcd(q, p) = 1, hence q \mid s by @thm-euclid-lemma-integers; write s = tq with t \in 
Z. Since s > 0 and q > 0, t > 0, by the sign argument used for q above. Then q(pt) = ps = rq, so q(pt - r) = 0, and r = tp because q 
e 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (f)). As q and s are positive, q \mid s gives q \le s (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e)). Uniqueness in (a). Let (r, s) be a second pair with x = r/s, s > 0 and \gcd(r, s) = 1. By (b), r = tp and s = tq with t > 0. So t is a common divisor of r and s, and it divides \gcd(r, s) = 1 (@thm-integers-bezout (c), (d)). Hence t = 1 (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (g), with t > 0), and (r, s) = (p, q). So the least denominator N(x) of Section 2.4’s Exercise C1 is the q of (a), and every other denominator of x is a multiple of it. For example 252/198 has \gcd(252, 198) = 18 (@exm-euclidean-algorithm-run), and 252 = 18 \cdot 14, 198 = 18 \cdot 11, so its lowest terms are 14/11. The twins in Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.2 are @fd2:lem-lowest-terms, which removes only factors of 2, and @fd2:exr-induction-in-practice-c2, which asks for lowest terms in the full sense, for the school 
Q. @prp-rationals-lowest-terms is the full statement, with uniqueness, for the constructed 
Q. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These questions are about the uniqueness half of the proof of @thm-fundamental-arithmetic. 1. Why must the empty list count as a prime factorization? 2. Run the induction step on (p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4) = (2, 2, 3, 5) and a second prime factorization (q_1, \dots, q_l) of 60. Which equalities does the proof derive, and to which two lists is P(3) applied? 3. Which line of the proof uses Euclid’s lemma, and through which result? 4. Where is “non-decreasing” used? 5. Give the idea of the uniqueness proof in two sentences. (a) Without it the base case P(0) would be about nothing, and the number 1 would have no prime factorization, so the theorem would be false for n = 1. The existence proof also uses it, to exclude n = 1 from B. (b) The step first gets l \ge 1, since the product is 60 
e 1. Then p_4 = 5 divides \prod q_j, so 5 = q_j \le q_l for some j; and q_l divides 60 = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5, so q_l = p_i \le 5 for some i. Hence q_l = 5. Canceling 5 gives \prod_{j=1}^{l-1} q_j = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 = 12, and P(3) is applied to (2, 2, 3) and (q_1, \dots, q_{l-1}), which gives l - 1 = 3 and (q_1, q_2, q_3) = (2, 2, 3). (c) The lines “p_{k+1} = q_j for some j” and “q_l = p_i for some i”. They cite @cor-prime-divides-product (c), whose step uses (b), which is @thm-euclid-lemma-integers applied with a = p. (d) In q_j \le q_l and in p_i \le p_{k+1}: the entry found in the other list is at most that list’s last entry. (e) The largest prime of one factorization divides the other product, so by Euclid’s lemma it is an entry there, hence at most the other’s largest; by symmetry the two largest entries are equal. Canceling them leaves two shorter factorizations with equal products, and induction on the length finishes. B. Practice [B1: Put the proof in order] The following lines contain a proof of @thm-euclid-lemma-integers, shuffled, together with two lines that do not belong. Write the seven correct lines in an order that makes a proof, say which other orders are also admissible, and say why each of the other two lines fails. (i) Suppose a \mid bc and \gcd(a, b) = 1. (ii) There are x, y \in 
Z with ax + by = 1. (ii′) Since \gcd(a, b) = 1 and a \mid bc, we have a \mid b or a \mid c. (iii) Multiplying by c: c = acx + bcy. (iii′) Dividing 1 = ax + by by a: 1/a = x + (b/a)y. (iv) a \mid acx, since acx = a(cx). (v) Write bc = ak; then bcy = a(ky), so a \mid bcy. (vi) Hence a \mid acx + bcy. (vii) So a \mid c. An admissible order is (i), (ii), (iii), (iv), (v), (vi), (vii): Suppose a \mid bc and \gcd(a, b) = 1. There are x, y \in 
Z with ax + by = 1 (@cor-coprime-iff-combination). Multiplying by c: c = acx + bcy. Then a \mid acx, since acx = a(cx). Write bc = ak; then bcy = a(ky), so a \mid bcy. Hence a \mid acx + bcy (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c)). So a \mid c. Lines (iv) and (v) mention the x and y introduced in (ii), and (v) also uses the hypothesis a \mid bc of (i); neither uses the other or (iii). So they may be exchanged, and either may come before (iii), as long as both follow (ii). Everything else is forced: (ii) needs the hypothesis \gcd(a, b) = 1 of (i); (iii) multiplies the equation of (ii); (vi) needs both (iv) and (v); (vii) rewrites (vi) through the equation of (iii). The distractor (ii′) cites a “fact” that is not available. For a prime a it is @cor-prime-divides-product (b), which is proved from this lemma, so citing it here is circular; for a composite a nothing provides it. Either way the line uses what has not been established, which is (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. The distractor (iii′) divides in 
Z, where there is no division: 1/a is not an integer for a \ge 2, and divisibility is defined by multiplication (@fd2:def-divides), not by fractions. [B2: The least common multiple] Let a, b \in 
Z_{>0}, and let M \coloneqq \{ m \in 
Z_{>0} : a \mid m 	ext{ and } b \mid m \}. Prove that M has a least element L, and that L \mid c for every c \in 
Z with a \mid c and b \mid c. The first part of a proof is given. ab > 0 by (O4), and a \mid ab, b \mid ab, so ab \in M; and 0 is a lower bound of M. By @prp-integer-least-element, M has a least element L. Let c \in 
Z with a \mid c and b \mid c. By @thm-integers-division-remainder (a), c = qL + r with q, r \in 
Z and 0 \le r < L. Since r = c + (-q)L, and a divides c and L, a \mid r (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c)); likewise b \mid r. The last step is blank. Name the move, then complete it. The move is least positive element, then divide: the remainder lies in the set and is smaller than its least positive element, so it is not positive. Completion: if r > 0, then r \in 
Z_{>0} is a common multiple of a and b, so r \in M, and r < L, against the choice of L. Hence r = 0 (as r \ge 0), and c = qL, that is, L \mid c. The same argument proved @thm-integers-bezout (b), with the set of positive combinations in place of M. This is the twin of @fd2:exm-divisibility-lcm, now on the constructed 
Z. [B3: Two factorizations and a gcd] Find the prime factorizations of 1001 and of 2^{10} - 1, proving that each entry is prime. Then show that \gcd(1001, 1023) = 11 in two ways: from the factorizations, and by the Euclidean algorithm. Hint: the remark after @lem-least-divisor-prime shortens each primality check. Factorizations. 1001 = 7 \cdot 143 = 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13, and 2^{10} - 1 = 1024 - 1 = 1023 = 3 \cdot 341 = 3 \cdot 11 \cdot 31. So the prime factorizations are (7, 11, 13) and (3, 11, 31), both non-decreasing, once the entries are known to be prime. The primes 3 and 7 are covered by the small-primes remark of Section 3.1. For 11, 13 and 31 we use the remark after @lem-least-divisor-prime: it suffices that no d \ge 2 with d \cdot d \le p divides p. - p = 11 and p = 13: d \in \{2, 3\}, since d \ge 4 gives d \cdot d \ge 16. The divisions 11 = 5 \cdot 2 + 1 = 3 \cdot 3 + 2 and 13 = 6 \cdot 2 + 1 = 4 \cdot 3 + 1 leave non-zero remainders. - p = 31: d \in \{2, 3, 4, 5\}, since d \ge 6 gives d \cdot d \ge 36. The divisions 31 = 15 \cdot 2 + 1 = 10 \cdot 3 + 1 = 7 \cdot 4 + 3 = 6 \cdot 5 + 1 leave non-zero remainders. A non-zero remainder means d 
mid p, by the uniqueness in @thm-integers-division-remainder (a). By @thm-fundamental-arithmetic these are the only prime factorizations. The gcd from the factorizations. We do not use a rule “the gcd is the product of the shared primes”, which this chapter does not prove. We have 1001 = 11 \cdot 91 and 1023 = 11 \cdot 93. First, \gcd(91, 93) = 1: a common divisor of 91 and 93 divides 93 - 91 = 2 (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c)), so a positive one is 1 or 2 (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e) and discreteness), and 2 
mid 91 = 45 \cdot 2 + 1. By @cor-coprime-iff-combination, 91x + 93y = 1 for some x, y \in 
Z; indeed 91 \cdot 46 - 93 \cdot 45 = 4186 - 4185 = 1. Multiplying by 11, 1001 \cdot 46 - 1023 \cdot 45 = 11 . So every common divisor of 1001 and 1023 divides 11 (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c)), and a positive one is at most 11 (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e)). Since 11 is itself a common divisor, \gcd(1001, 1023) = 11 (@def-integer-gcd). The gcd by the algorithm (@thm-euclidean-algorithm-integers): 1023 = 1 \cdot 1001 + 22, 1001 = 45 \cdot 22 + 11, 22 = 2 \cdot 11 + 0. The last non-zero remainder is 11. C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: unique factorization] Prove that two prime factorizations of the same positive integer are equal: the uniqueness half of @thm-fundamental-arithmetic. You may cite @thm-euclid-lemma-integers. The proof of uniqueness in @thm-fundamental-arithmetic is a complete answer. Its steps, in order: set up P(k) for non-decreasing lists of primes of length k and arbitrary length l, with equal products; base case k = 0, where a non-empty list of primes cannot have product 1; in the step, l \ge 1, then p_{k+1} = q_j \le q_l and q_l = p_i \le p_{k+1} by @cor-prime-divides-product (c) (proved from Euclid’s lemma by induction on the length of the product) and the order of the lists; so p_{k+1} = q_l; cancel this non-zero factor (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (f)); apply P(k) to the shortened lists. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: sets up an induction on the length of one list (or a least counterexample), with the statement quantified over all lengths of the other list, and proves the base case. - 3: shows that the largest (or any chosen) prime of one list divides the other product, and identifies it with an entry of the other list by Euclid’s lemma for products of several factors, proved or cited. - 2: uses the symmetric step and the non-decreasing order to get equality of the two largest entries. - 1: justifies the cancellation by the absence of zero divisors. - 2: applies the induction hypothesis (or minimality) to the shortened lists and concludes equality of length and entries. Fatal errors (0 for the step): using the uniqueness of the factorization of a smaller number without an induction or a least counterexample set up; applying Euclid’s lemma for two factors to a product of many with no induction. Canceling a prime without noting that it is non-zero costs 1 point and is not fatal. A least-counterexample proof on n (the least positive integer with two different factorizations) maps to the same points: its set-up and the case n = 1 take the first 2, and “the cofactor m in n = m p_k has only one factorization” takes the last 2. [C2: Find the error] Here is a statement and an argument for it. Claim. Let m, n, c \in 
Z. If m \mid c, n \mid c and \gcd(m, n) = 1, then mn \mid c. Argument. (1) Write c = mk and c = nl with k, l \in 
Z. (2) Then c^2 = c \cdot c = (mk)(nl) = mn \cdot kl. (3) So mn \mid c^2. (4) Hence mn \mid c. Is the claim true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the line that fails, explain why, and give a counterexample to the step. The claim is true: it is @prp-coprime-divisors-product. The argument does not prove it. Lines (1)–(3) are correct. The failing line is (4). It rests on a general “fact”: x \mid c^2 implies x \mid c. That has not been proved, and it is false, so the line cites nothing: entry (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. A counterexample to the step: x = 4, c = 2, with 4 \mid 4 = c^2 and 4 
mid 2 (a positive divisor of 2 is at most 2, @prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e)). There is no counterexample to the conclusion, which is true. A sign that something is wrong: the argument never uses \gcd(m, n) = 1, and without that hypothesis the claim is false (4 \mid 12, 6 \mid 12, 24 
mid 12). The repair is the proof of @prp-coprime-divisors-product, which spends the coprimality in Euclid’s lemma. [C3: There is no last prime] Prove that no finite list contains every prime: for every list of primes (p_1, \dots, p_k), with k \in 
N, there is a prime that is not an entry of the list. [Hint 1] Consider N \coloneqq \prod_{i=1}^{k} p_i + 1, and ask which primes can divide it. [Hint 2] First prove, by induction on k, that every entry of a list of primes divides its product, and that the product is at least 1. A lemma on products. For a list of primes (p_1, \dots, p_k), write P_j \coloneqq \prod_{i=1}^{j} p_i for j \le k. We prove, by @fd1:ax-induction (through @cor-omega-identification (b)) on j, the statement “if j \le k, then P_j \ge 1 and p_i \mid P_j for every i \le j”. Base j = 0: P_0 = 1 (the recursion of @def-prime-factorization), and there are no entries to check. Step: let j + 1 \le k; then j \le k, so the statement holds for j, and P_{j+1} = P_j p_{j+1} by the recursion. Each p_i with i \le j divides P_j, which divides P_{j+1}, so p_i \mid P_{j+1} (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (b)); and p_{j+1} \mid P_{j+1} by @fd2:def-divides. Since P_j \ge 1 > 0 and p_{j+1} \ge 2 > 0, P_{j+1} > 0 \cdot p_{j+1} = 0 (@prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), @prp-ring-algebra (b)), so P_{j+1} \ge 1 by discreteness (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)). The new prime. Let N \coloneqq P_k + 1. Then N \ge 2, so its least divisor q \ge 2 is prime (@lem-least-divisor-prime), and q \mid N. If q = p_i for some i, then q \mid P_k by the lemma, so q divides N - P_k = 1 (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c)), and q = \pm 1 (@prp-divisibility-rules-integers (g)), against q \ge 2. So q is a prime that is not an entry of the list. For the empty list, N = 2 and q = 2. For (2, 3, 5, 7), N = 211, which happens to be prime; for (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13), N = 30031 = 59 \cdot 509 is not, and the new prime is 59. The proof promises a new prime factor of N, not that N itself is prime. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: defines N as the product plus 1 and shows N \ge 2, with a reason that the product is positive. - 2: shows that each p_i divides the product, by an induction or a cited result. - 2: produces a prime factor q of N, citing @lem-least-divisor-prime or an equivalent. - 3: shows q is not any p_i, since it would divide 1. - 1: concludes with the quantifiers in order: for every list there is a prime outside it. Fatal errors (0 for the step): claiming that N is prime; assuming “the set of primes is finite” and taking its product without a list (no list, no product).

title: 3.4 Ideals, Quotient Rings, and the Integers Modulo n
content:
Ideals, Quotient Rings, and the Integers Modulo n Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Section 2.5 turned the school integers into a clock, 
Z/n, and checked by hand that its sum and product are well defined (@fd2:prp-congruence-arithmetic). Chapter 2 made the same kind of check twice more, for 
Z and for 
Q, each time through @thm-well-defined-on-classes and a computation special to the formula. This section makes the check once, for every commutative ring and every subset of the right kind, called an ideal. The integers modulo n, now a ring, are the first example. Chapter 5 builds 
R by the same pattern, from classes of Cauchy sequences of rationals, and Algebraic Preliminaries, Chapter 5 builds rings of polynomials modulo a fixed polynomial. Throughout, R is a commutative ring (@def-commutative-ring-and-field), with a - b \coloneqq a + (-b). What a quotient needs Let I \subseteq R, and call a and b related when they differ by an element of I: a \sim_I b \quad :\Longleftrightarrow \quad a - b \in I . For R = 
Z and I the multiples of n, this is congruence modulo n. We want two things: \sim_I should be an equivalence relation, and the sum and product of classes should be computable on representatives. Each wish makes a demand on I. - Reflexivity, a - a \in I, needs 0 \in I. - Symmetry: b - a = -(a - b), so it needs I to be closed under negatives. - Transitivity: a - c = (a - b) + (b - c), so it needs I to be closed under sums. - The sum on classes. Changing a to a' changes a + b to a' + b, and the difference is a - a' again: no new demand. - The product on classes. Changing a to a' changes ab to a'b, and the difference is (a - a')b: an element of I multiplied by an arbitrary element of R. So I must swallow such products. The last demand contains the second: -x = (-1)x. Three clauses remain, and they get a name. An ideal is a set of allowed errors: it contains 0, it is closed under adding errors, and an error multiplied by anything is still an error. [Ideal] Let R be a commutative ring. A subset I \subseteq R is an ideal of R if 1. 0 \in I; 2. for all a, b \in I, a + b \in I; 3. for all a \in I and all r \in R, ra \in I. In words: (I1) and (I2) say that I contains 0 and is closed under addition; (I3), absorption, says that multiplying an element of I by any element of the ring, inside I or not, lands in I. The ring element r in (I3) ranges over all of R, and that is what separates (I3) from mere closure under multiplication, where r would have to lie in I. Two consequences are used constantly. First, an ideal is closed under negatives and differences: for a \in I, -a = (-1)a \in I by (I3), since (-1)a = -(1 \cdot a) = -a by @prp-ring-algebra (c) and (F7) with (F6); then a - b = a + (-b) \in I for a, b \in I, by (I2). Second, if 1 \in I, then I = R, since every r = r \cdot 1 \in I by (I3). Examples. - The degenerate cases: \{0\} and R itself are ideals of R. For \{0\}: 0 + 0 = 0 and r \cdot 0 = 0 (@prp-ring-algebra (b)). For R, every clause asks for an element of R. They are the two extremes: “no error allowed” and “everything allowed”. - For n \in 
Z, the multiples n
Z = \{ kn : k \in 
Z \} form an ideal of 
Z (@def-integer-linear-combinations): 0 = 0 \cdot n; kn + ln = (k + l)n; r(kn) = (rk)n. In particular the even integers 2
Z form an ideal. - For a, b \in 
Z, the combinations a
Z + b
Z form an ideal of 
Z, by the closure properties in @def-integer-linear-combinations; @thm-integer-ideals-principal below records this. Non-examples by minimal change. 
N \subseteq 
Z satisfies (I1) and (I2), but (I3) fails at a = 1, r = -1: (-1) \cdot 1 = -1 
otin 
N, since -1 < 0 (@thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)). And 
Z \subseteq 
Q satisfies (I1), (I2) and is even closed under negatives and products, but (I3) fails at a = 1, r = 1/2: (1/2) \cdot 1 = 1/2 
otin 
Z. (If 1/2 = m \in 
Z, then 2m = 1, but 1 = 2 \cdot 0 + 1 is odd and so not of the form 2m, by @cor-integers-even-odd (a).) In both cases the ring element r comes from outside the subset, which is exactly what (I3) allows. Why these clauses. Each clause was forced by one of the five wishes above, and dropping one loses its wish: without (I1) or (I2), \sim_I is not reflexive or not transitive; without (I3), the product on classes can fail, as the warning after the next theorem shows for 
Z \subseteq 
Q. The quotient ring The payoff is a single theorem that builds a ring of classes from any ideal. We write [a], or [a]_I when the ideal must be named, for the class of a under \sim_I, and R/I for the quotient set R/{\sim_I} (@fd2:def-quotient-set). [Quotient Ring by an Ideal] Let R be a commutative ring and I an ideal of R. 1. Setting a \sim_I b \iff a - b \in I defines an equivalence relation \sim_I on R, and the class of a is [a] = a + I \coloneqq \{ a + x : x \in I \}. 2. The rules [a] + [b] \coloneqq [a + b], [a] \cdot [b] \coloneqq [ab] and -[a] \coloneqq [-a] are well defined on R/I \coloneqq R/{\sim_I}. 3. R/I, with these operations, is a commutative ring with zero [0] and one [1]. The quotient map \pi \colon R 	o R/I, \pi(a) \coloneqq [a], satisfies \pi(a + b) = \pi(a) + \pi(b), \pi(ab) = \pi(a) \pi(b) and \pi(1) = [1]. 4. [a] = [0] if and only if a \in I. In particular [1] = [0] if and only if I = R. In words: (a) and (b) say that classes modulo an ideal can be added, multiplied and negated through any representatives; (c) says that the result obeys every ring law, and that passing to classes respects the operations; (d) says that the elements of I are exactly those that become 0, and that the quotient collapses to the zero ring exactly when I is everything. A change of representative is an element of I. The equivalence-relation clauses ask that such changes can be reversed and chained, which is closure under negatives and sums. (Eq1): a - a = 0 \in I, by (F4) and (I1). (Eq2): if a - b \in I, then b - a = -(a - b) \in I, since I is closed under negatives; here (a - b) + (b - a) = 0 by (F1)–(F4), so b - a = -(a - b) by the uniqueness of negatives (@prp-ring-algebra (a)). (Eq3): if a - b \in I and b - c \in I, then a - c = (a - b) + (b - c) \in I, by (F2)–(F4) and (I2). So \sim_I is an equivalence relation (@fd2:def-equivalence-relation). Then  egin{aligned} (a + b) - (a' + b) &= a - a' \in I , \ ab - a'b &= (a - a')b = b(a - a') \in I , \end{aligned} by (F1)–(F4) in the first line, and by (F9), (F6) and @prp-ring-algebra (c) in the second, where the membership is (I3) with r = b: the ideal absorbs b. title: Axiom 1.1.1 (The Axioms (Z1)–(Z6))
page: 1.1 Axioms for Sets
content: Extensionality. Sets with the same elements are equal: for all sets \(A\) and \(B\) , if \(x \in A \leftrightarrow x \in B\) for every \(x\) , then \(A = B\) . Empty set. There is a set with no elements. Pairing. For all sets \(a\) and \(b\) there is a set whose elements are exactly \(a\) and \(b\) . Union. For every set \(\sS\) there is a set whose elements are exactly the elements of members of \(\sS\) . Power set. For every set \(X\) there is a set whose elements are exactly the subsets of \(X\) . Separation. For every set \(A\) and every property \(P(x)\) there is a set whose elements are exactly the \(x \in A\) with \(P(x)\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 1.1 Axioms for Sets
content: For each of the sets \(\{\emptyset\}\) , \(\{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\}\) , \(\powerset{\emptyset}\) , \(\bigcup \{\emptyset\}\) , and \(\{ x \in A : x \notin x \}\) for a given set \(A\) , name the axioms that produce it. True or false: for all sets \(a\) and \(b\) , \(\{a\} = \{b\}\) implies \(a = b\) . Justify your answer. Prove that \(\bigcup \{a\} = a\) for every set \(a\) . Is there a set \(T\) such that \(\{x\} \in T\) for every set \(x\) ? Justify your answer.

title: Exercise (B1: Power sets and unions)
page: 1.1 Axioms for Sets
content: Compute \(\powerset{\powerset{\emptyset}}\) . Prove that \(\bigcup \powerset{X} = X\) for every set \(X\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Intersections of sets of sets)
page: 1.1 Axioms for Sets
content: Let \(\sS = \{ X, Y \}\) with \(X = \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\}\) and \(Y = \{\{\emptyset\}, \{\{\emptyset\}\}\}\) . Compute \(\bigcap \sS\) twice: once with \(A_0 = X\) in @prp-zf-basic-sets (c), once with \(A_0 = Y\) . Explain in one or two sentences why the two computations had to agree. Explain why the definition of \(\bigcap \sS\) makes no sense for \(\sS = \emptyset\) .

title: Exercise (C1: What the empty-set axiom really says; intersections as greatest lower bounds)
page: 1.1 Axioms for Sets
content: Show that (Z2) follows from (Z6), once some set \(A\) is known to exist. Let \(\sS\) be a non-empty set. Show that \(\bigcap \sS \subseteq S\) for every \(S \in \sS\) , and that every set \(C\) with \(C \subseteq S\) for all \(S \in \sS\) satisfies \(C \subseteq \bigcap \sS\) . Deduce that \(\bigcap \{A, B\} = A \cap B\) for all sets \(A\) , \(B\) .

title: Proposition 1.1.2 (The Sets Named by the Axioms)
page: 1.1 Axioms for Sets
content: There is exactly one set with no elements. It is written \(\emptyset\) . For all sets \(a\) and \(b\) the set of (Z3) is unique. It is written \(\{a, b\}\) , and \(\{a\} \coloneqq \{a, a\}\) , the set whose only element is \(a\) . For every set \(\sS\) the set of (Z4) is unique. It is written \(\bigcup \sS\) , and \(A \cup B \coloneqq \bigcup \{A, B\}\) for sets \(A\) , \(B\) , so that \(x \in A \cup B\) if and only if \(x \in A\) or \(x \in B\) . The sets \(A \cap B \coloneqq \{ x \in A : x \in B \}\) and \(A \setminus B \coloneqq \{ x \in A : x \notin B \}\) exist by (Z6). For a non-empty set \(\sS\) , the set \[ \bigcap \sS \coloneqq \{ x \in A_0 : x \in S \text{ for every } S \in \sS \} \] exists by (Z6) for any \(A_0 \in \sS\) , it does not depend on \(A_0\) , and \(x \in \bigcap \sS\) if and only if \(x \in S\) for every \(S \in \sS\) . For all sets \(a, b, c, d\) , \[ \{a, b\} = \{c, d\} \iff (a = c \wedge b = d) \vee (a = d \wedge b = c). \] In particular \(\{a\} = \{c, d\}\) if and only if \(a = c\) and \(c = d\) .

title: Definition 1.2.1 (Ordered Pair as a Set)
page: 1.2 Ordered Pairs Built from Sets
content: For sets \(a\) and \(b\) , the ordered pair of \(a\) and \(b\) is the set \[ (a, b) \coloneqq \{\{a\}, \{a, b\}\} . \] Its first coordinate is \(a\) and its second coordinate is \(b\) .

title: Example (Three Encodings That Lose Information)
page: 1.2 Ordered Pairs Built from Sets
content: Consider the claim: any set built from \(a\) and \(b\) in which \(a\) is mentioned first is an ordered pair , that is, has the characteristic property. Test it on the three encodings \[ \text{(i) } \{a, b\}, \qquad \text{(ii) } \{\{a\}, \{b\}\}, \qquad \text{(iii) } \{a, \{b\}\} . \]

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 1.2 Ordered Pairs Built from Sets
content: In the proof of @thm-kuratowski-pair , where is the hypothesis \(a \ne b\) of Case 2 used, and what replaces the argument when \(a = b\) ? Run the proof of @thm-kuratowski-pair on the equation \((\{\emptyset\}, \emptyset) = (c, d)\) : which case applies, and what does each step give? Which axioms make \((a, b)\) a set? State the idea of the proof of @thm-kuratowski-pair in two sentences.

title: Exercise (B1: Coordinates from unions and intersections)
page: 1.2 Ordered Pairs Built from Sets
content: Let \(p = (a, b)\) . Compute \(\bigcap p\) and \(\bigcup p\) , and show that, when \(a \ne b\) , the set \(\bigcup p \setminus \bigcap p\) has exactly one element, namely \(b\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Nested pairs)
page: 1.2 Ordered Pairs Built from Sets
content: Write \(((a, b), c)\) for the pair whose first coordinate is the pair \((a, b)\) . Prove that \(((a, b), c) = ((a', b'), c')\) if and only if \(a = a'\) , \(b = b'\) and \(c = c'\) . Determine whether \(((\emptyset, \emptyset), \emptyset) = (\emptyset, (\emptyset, \emptyset))\) . Justify your answer.

title: Exercise (C1: Exit check: Kuratowski pairs)
page: 1.2 Ordered Pairs Built from Sets
content: Prove that for all sets \(a, b, c, d\) , \(\{\{a\}, \{a, b\}\} = \{\{c\}, \{c, d\}\}\) if and only if \(a = c\) and \(b = d\) . You may use @prp-zf-basic-sets .

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
page: 1.2 Ordered Pairs Built from Sets
content: Here is an argument for @thm-kuratowski-pair , direction \((\Rightarrow)\) . Let \((a, b) = (c, d)\) . (2) Matching the members of \(\{\{a\}, \{a, b\}\}\) and \(\{\{c\}, \{c, d\}\}\) in the order written, \(\{a\} = \{c\}\) and \(\{a, b\} = \{c, d\}\) . (3) From \(\{a\} = \{c\}\) , \(a = c\) . (4) Then \(\{a, b\} = \{a, d\}\) , and so \(b = d\) . Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the first line that fails, the rule it breaks, and give a counterexample to that step.

title: Exercise (C3: Wiener’s encoding)
page: 1.2 Ordered Pairs Built from Sets
content: For sets \(a\) and \(b\) let \(W(a, b) \coloneqq \{\{\{a\}, \emptyset\}, \{\{b\}\}\}\) . Prove that \(W(a, b) = W(c, d)\) if and only if \(a = c\) and \(b = d\) .

title: Proposition 1.2.2 (The Product Exists)
page: 1.2 Ordered Pairs Built from Sets
content: For all sets \(A\) and \(B\) there is exactly one set \(A \times B\) whose elements are exactly the pairs \((a, b)\) with \(a \in A\) and \(b \in B\) : \[ p \in A \times B \iff \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ \ p = (a, b) . \]

title: Proposition 1.2.3 (The Working Rules from the Axioms)
page: 1.2 Ordered Pairs Built from Sets
content: The axioms (Z1)–(Z6) give the working rules (W1)–(W5) of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality , Section 1.1 in the following form. For every set \(A\) and every admissible property \(P(x)\) (one whose unwinding is a formula of the language, Section 1.1), \(\{ x \in A : P(x) \}\) is a set. For each list \(a_1, \dots, a_n\) written out in the text, entry by entry, there is a set \(\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}\) whose elements are exactly \(a_1, \dots, a_n\) . For sets \(A\) and \(B\) , \(A \cup B\) is a set. For a set \(X\) and a family \((A_i)_{i \in I}\) of subsets of \(X\) , given as a function \(I \to \powerset{X}\) ( @fd2:def-indexed-family ), the union \(\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i\) and the intersection \(\bigcap_{i \in I} A_i\) of @fd2:def-family-union-intersection are sets. For every set \(X\) , \(\powerset{X}\) is a set. For sets \(A\) and \(B\) , \(A \times B\) is a set.

title: Theorem 1.2.1 (Characteristic Property of Pairs)
page: 1.2 Ordered Pairs Built from Sets
content: For all sets \(a, b, c, d\) , \[ (a, b) = (c, d) \iff a = c \text{ and } b = d . \]

title: Axiom 1.3.1 (Axiom of Infinity)
page: 1.3 Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers
content: (Z7) There is an inductive set.

title: Definition 1.3.3 (The set of natural numbers)
page: 1.3 Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers
content: Fix an inductive set \(I\) , which exists by (Z7). Define \[ \omega \coloneqq \{ x \in I : x \in J \text{ for every inductive set } J \subseteq I \} . \] The elements of \(\omega\) are the natural numbers .

title: Definition 1.3.1 (Successor of a set)
page: 1.3 Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers
content: For every set \(x\) , the successor of \(x\) is the set \[ \mathrm{S}(x) \coloneqq x \cup \{x\} . \]

title: Definition 1.3.2 (Inductive set)
page: 1.3 Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers
content: A set \(I\) is inductive if \(\emptyset \in I\) and, for every \(x \in I\) , also \(\mathrm{S}(x) \in I\) .

title: Example (The first natural numbers as sets)
page: 1.3 Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers
content: Define \[ \begin{aligned} 0 &\coloneqq \emptyset , & 1 &\coloneqq \mathrm{S}(0) , & 2 &\coloneqq \mathrm{S}(1) , \\ 3 &\coloneqq \mathrm{S}(2) , & 4 &\coloneqq \mathrm{S}(3) . \end{aligned} \] Write each of \(1, 2, 3, 4\) as a set of the earlier numerals, and then using only \(\emptyset\) and braces. Check that \(0, 1, 2, 3\) are four different sets.

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 1.3 Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers
content: List the elements of \(3\) and of \(4\) as sets of numerals. Is \(2 \subseteq 3\) ? Is \(2 \in 3\) ? True or false, with a reason: every inductive set has \(5 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(4)\) as an element. Write “ \(J\) is not inductive” in symbols, with the negation moved inward until it stands only in front of a membership statement.

title: Exercise (B1: Intersections and differences)
page: 1.3 Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers
content: Let \(J\) and \(K\) be inductive sets. Prove that \(J \cap K\) is inductive. Is \(J \setminus \{\emptyset\}\) inductive? Justify your answer, and say which clause of the definition holds and which fails.

title: Exercise (B2: Zero or a successor)
page: 1.3 Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers
content: Prove that every \(n \in \omega\) is \(\emptyset\) or is \(\mathrm{S}(k)\) for some \(k \in \omega\) , by showing that the set \[ A \coloneqq \{ n \in \omega : n = \emptyset \text{ or } n = \mathrm{S}(k) \text{ for some } k \in \omega \} \] is inductive.

title: Exercise (C1: Two steps back)
page: 1.3 Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers
content: Prove that every \(n \in \omega\) is \(0\) , or is \(1\) , or is \(\mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(k))\) for some \(k \in \omega\) . Let \(I\) be an arbitrary inductive set. Running the argument of (a) on \(\{ x \in I : x = 0 \text{ or } x = 1 \text{ or } x = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(k)) \text{ for some } k \in I \}\) , what does it prove about the elements of \(I\) , and what does it not prove?

title: Theorem 1.3.3 (Induction on \omega)
page: 1.3 Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers
content: (Set form.) Let \(A \subseteq \omega\) . If \(0 \in A\) , and \(\mathrm{S}(n) \in A\) for every \(n \in A\) , then \(A = \omega\) . (Property form.) Let \(P(n)\) be a property, that is, a formula of the first-order language with \(\in\) and \(=\) , possibly with other variables as parameters. If \(P(0)\) holds and, for every \(n \in \omega\) , \(P(n)\) implies \(P(\mathrm{S}(n))\) , then \(P(n)\) holds for every \(n \in \omega\) .

title: Theorem 1.3.2 (The Least Inductive Set)
page: 1.3 Successors, Inductive Sets and the Natural Numbers
content: \(\omega\) is inductive. \(\omega \subseteq J\) for every inductive set \(J\) , whether or not \(J \subseteq I\) . \(\omega\) is the only set with properties (a) and (b). In particular, \(\omega\) does not depend on the inductive set \(I\) fixed in @def-omega .

title: Definition 1.4.2 (Peano system)
page: 1.4 The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano's Axioms
content: A Peano system \((M, e, s)\) consists of a set \(M\) , an element \(e \in M\) , and a function \(s \colon M \to M\) , such that: (P3) \(s(x) \ne e\) for every \(x \in M\) ; (P4) \(s\) is injective; (P5) every subset \(A \subseteq M\) with \(e \in A\) and \(s(x) \in A\) for every \(x \in A\) is equal to \(M\) .

title: Definition 1.4.1 (Transitive set)
page: 1.4 The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano's Axioms
content: A set \(x\) is transitive if every element of \(x\) is a subset of \(x\) : for every \(y \in x\) , \(y \subseteq x\) .

title: Example (Each axiom is needed)
page: 1.4 The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano's Axioms
content: Show that each of the following structures \((M, e, s)\) , with \(s \colon M \to M\) , satisfies two of (P3), (P4), (P5) and fails the third. \(M \coloneqq \{0\}\) , \(e \coloneqq 0\) , \(s(0) \coloneqq 0\) . \(M \coloneqq \{0, 1\}\) , \(e \coloneqq 0\) , \(s(0) \coloneqq 1\) , \(s(1) \coloneqq 1\) . ( The natural numbers beside a two-sided chain. ) \(M \coloneqq \omega \times 3\) , whose elements are the pairs \((n, i)\) with \(n \in \omega\) and \(i \in 3 = \{0, 1, 2\}\) ; \(e \coloneqq (0, 0)\) ; and \[ \begin{aligned} s(n, 0) &\coloneqq (\mathrm{S}(n), 0) , & s(n, 1) &\coloneqq (\mathrm{S}(n), 1) , \\ s(0, 2) &\coloneqq (0, 1) , & s(\mathrm{S}(k), 2) &\coloneqq (k, 2) , \end{aligned} \] for \(n, k \in \omega\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 1.4 The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano's Axioms
content: For each of the three structures in @exm-peano-axioms-independent , which of (P3), (P4), (P5) fails? In the proof of (P4) in @thm-omega-peano , where is @lem-omega-transitive (a) used, and where is (c)? Is \(\omega \cup \{\omega\}\) inductive? Justify your answer. Is \(\{0, 1, \{1\}\}\) a transitive set? Is it an element of \(\omega\) ?

title: Exercise (B1: Put the proof in order)
page: 1.4 The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano's Axioms
content: Let \(m, n \in \omega\) . The following lines contain a proof that if \(\mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n)\) , then \(m = n\) , shuffled, together with two lines that do not belong. Write the seven correct lines in an order that makes a proof, say which other orders are also admissible, and say why each of the other two lines fails. So \(m \in n \subseteq m\) , that is, \(m \in m\) . Suppose \(\mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n)\) . We have \(m \cup \{m\} = n \cup \{n\}\) , so \(m = n\) by canceling \({\cup}\{\cdot\}\) on both sides. Since \(n \in \mathrm{S}(n) = \mathrm{S}(m)\) , we have \(n \in m\) or \(n = m\) . Suppose \(m \ne n\) ; then \(m \in n\) and \(n \in m\) . This contradicts \(m \notin m\) ( @lem-omega-transitive (c)); so \(m = n\) . From \(m \in n\) and \(n \in m\) we get \(m = n\) , since \(\in\) is antisymmetric. Since \(m\) is transitive ( @lem-omega-transitive (a)) and \(n \in m\) , we have \(n \subseteq m\) . Since \(m \in \mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n)\) , we have \(m \in n\) or \(m = n\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Two steps at a time)
page: 1.4 The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano's Axioms
content: Let \(d \coloneqq \mathrm{S} \circ \mathrm{S} \colon \omega \to \omega\) ( @fd2:def-composition ), so that \(d(n) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(n))\) . Show that \((\omega, 0, d)\) satisfies (P3) and (P4) of @def-peano-system , and that it does not satisfy (P5). Hint: look at the set \(\omega \setminus \{1\}\) .

title: Exercise (C1: A Peano system with a different start)
page: 1.4 The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano's Axioms
content: Give an example of a Peano system \((M, e, s)\) with \(M \subseteq \omega\) and \(e \ne 0\) . Check every clause of @def-peano-system .

title: Exercise (C2: Closed subsets of the chain)
page: 1.4 The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano's Axioms
content: Let \((M, e, s)\) be the structure (iii) of @exm-peano-axioms-independent . Call \(A \subseteq M\) good if \(e \in A\) and \(s(x) \in A\) for every \(x \in A\) . Show that every good set contains \(\omega \times \{0\}\) . Show that each of the following sets is good, where \(m, k \in \omega\) : \[ \begin{aligned} G_0 &\coloneqq \omega \times \{0\} , \qquad G_\infty \coloneqq M , \\ R_m &\coloneqq G_0 \cup \{ (n, 1) : n \in \omega, \ m \in \mathrm{S}(n) \} , \\ L_k &\coloneqq G_0 \cup (\omega \times \{1\}) \cup \{ (j, 2) : j \in \mathrm{S}(k) \} . \end{aligned} \] Show that a good set that contains \((k, 2)\) contains \(L_k\) .

page: 1.4 The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano's Axioms
content:
Every \(n \in \omega\) is a transitive set. \(\omega\) is a transitive set: every element of a natural number is a natural number. \(n

title: Proposition 1.4.3 (No Pair Is a Natural Number)
page: 1.4 The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano's Axioms
content: For all sets \(a\) and \(b\) , the pair \((a, b)\) is not an element of \(\omega\) .

title: Theorem 1.4.2 (Peano’s Axioms Hold in \omega)
page: 1.4 The Natural Numbers Satisfy Peano's Axioms
content: \(0 \in \omega\) . For every \(n \in \omega\) , \(\mathrm{S}(n) \in \omega\) . For every \(n \in \omega\) , \(\mathrm{S}(n) \ne 0\) . For all \(m, n \in \omega\) , if \(\mathrm{S}(m) = \mathrm{S}(n)\) , then \(m = n\) . Every \(A \subseteq \omega\) with \(0 \in A\) and \(\mathrm{S}(n) \in A\) for every \(n \in A\) is equal to \(\omega\) . Moreover, \(\{ (n, \mathrm{S}(n)) : n \in \omega \}\) is a set, and with codomain \(\omega\) it is a function \(\mathrm{S} \colon \omega \to \omega\) , which is injective and does not take the value \(0\) .

title: Corollary 1.5.2 (Successor Cancellation)
page: 1.5 The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication
content: For all \(k, l \in \omega\) : if \(k + 1 = l + 1\) , then \(k = l\) ; and \(k + 1 \ne 0\) .

title: Definition 1.5.1 (Addition and Multiplication on \omega)
page: 1.5 The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication
content: For each \(m \in \omega\) , let \(A_m \colon \omega \to \omega\) be the function given by @thm-omega-recursion with \(X = \omega\) , \(a = m\) and \(g(n, x) = \mathrm{S}(x)\) . The sum of \(m\) and \(n\) is \(m + n \coloneqq A_m(n)\) . Thus, for all \(m, n \in \omega\) , \[ m + 0 = m, \qquad m + \mathrm{S}(n) = \mathrm{S}(m + n) . \] For each \(m \in \omega\) , let \(M_m \colon \omega \to \omega\) be the function given by @thm-omega-recursion with \(X = \omega\) , \(a = 0\) and \(g(n, x) = x + m\) . The product of \(m\) and \(n\) is \(m \cdot n \coloneqq M_m(n)\) , also written \(mn\) . Thus, for all \(m, n \in \omega\) , \[ m \cdot 0 = 0, \qquad m \cdot \mathrm{S}(n) = m \cdot n + m . \] The numerals are \(0 \coloneqq \emptyset\) and \(1 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(0)\) , \(2 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(1)\) , \(3 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(2)\) , and so on, as in @exm-von-neumann-numerals . For every \(n \in \omega\) , \(n + 1 = \mathrm{S}(n)\) ; in particular \(1 + 1 = 2\) and \(k + 2 = (k + 1) + 1\) for every \(k \in \omega\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 1.5 The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication
content: These questions are about the proof of @thm-omega-recursion . Where in the proof is \(\mathrm{S}(n) \notin \mathrm{S}(n)\) used, and what would fail without it? Run the construction for \(X = \omega\) , \(a = 0\) and \(g(n, x) = \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{S}(x))\) : write the graphs of the partial solutions up to \(0\) , \(1\) and \(2\) . Why does the uniqueness half need only an induction, while existence needs partial solutions? State the idea of the proof in two sentences.

title: Exercise (B1: Small products)
page: 1.5 The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication
content: Compute \(3 \cdot 2\) and \(2 \cdot 3\) from the defining equations of @def-omega-arithmetic alone, without using @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws . Here \(5 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(4)\) and \(6 \coloneqq \mathrm{S}(5)\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Distributivity, last step blank)
page: 1.5 The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication
content: Here is the proof of \(m(n + k) = mn + mk\) for all \(m, n, k \in \omega\) , with the last step left blank. Name the move, then complete it. Fix \(m, n \in \omega\) and induct on \(k\) . Base case: \(m(n + 0) = mn = mn + 0 = mn + m \cdot 0\) . Inductive step: suppose \(m(n + k) = mn + mk\) . Then \[ m\bigl(n + (k + 1)\bigr) = m\bigl((n + k) + 1\bigr) = m(n + k) + m = (mn + mk) + m = \underline{\hspace{6em}} . \] Justify each equality you add.

title: Exercise (C1: Exit check: addition is commutative)
page: 1.5 The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication
content: From the two defining equations of addition, \(m + 0 = m\) and \(m + (n + 1) = (m + n) + 1\) , and @thm-omega-induction alone, prove that \(m + n = n + m\) for all \(m, n \in \omega\) . Prove every auxiliary fact you need.

title: Exercise (C2: Associativity of multiplication, last half blank)
page: 1.5 The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication
content: Prove that \((km)n = k(mn)\) for all \(k, m, n \in \omega\) . The first half is given; name the move, then complete it. Fix \(k, m \in \omega\) and induct on \(n\) . Base case: \((km) \cdot 0 = 0 = k \cdot 0 = k(m \cdot 0)\) . Inductive step: \(\underline{\hspace{10em}}\) You may use (a)–(f) of @thm-omega-arithmetic-laws .

title: Exercise (C3: Doubling)
page: 1.5 The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication
content: Show that there is exactly one function \(D \colon \omega \to \omega\) with \(D(0) = 0\) and \(D(n + 1) = (D(n) + 1) + 1\) for every \(n \in \omega\) , and prove that \(D(n) = n + n\) for every \(n \in \omega\) .

title: Theorem 1.5.3 (Laws of Arithmetic on \omega)
page: 1.5 The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication
content: For all \(k, m, n \in \omega\) : \(0 + n = n\) , and \((m + 1) + n = (m + n) + 1\) ; \(m + n = n + m\) ; \((k + m) + n = k + (m + n)\) ; \(m(n + k) = mn + mk\) and \((n + k)m = nm + km\) ; \(0 \cdot n = 0\) , \((m + 1) \cdot n = mn + n\) , and \(n \cdot 1 = 1 \cdot n = n\) ; \(mn = nm\) ; \((km)n = k(mn)\) .

title: Theorem 1.5.1 (Recursion Theorem on \omega)
page: 1.5 The Recursion Theorem; Addition and Multiplication
content: Let \(X\) be a set, let \(a \in X\) , and let \(g \colon \omega \times X \to X\) be a function. Then there is exactly one function \(f \colon \omega \to X\) such that \[ f(0) = a \quad \text{and} \quad f\bigl(\mathrm{S}(n)\bigr) = g\bigl(n, f(n)\bigr) \ \text{ for every } n \in \omega . \]

title: Definition 1.6.1 (Order on \omega)
page: 1.6 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers
content: For \(m, n \in \omega\) , we write \(m < n\) if \(m \in n\) , and \(m \le n\) if \(m < n\) or \(m = n\) . As usual, \(n > m\) means \(m < n\) , and \(n \ge m\) means \(m \le n\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 1.6 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers
content: List the elements of \(\{ k \in \omega : k \le 3 \}\) . Which natural number is this set? True or false: for \(m, n \in \omega\) , \(m < n\) implies \(m \subseteq n\) . Justify your answer. Find the least element of \(\{ n \in \omega : n \cdot n > 10 \}\) , and say why it is least. Which clause of @thm-omega-order says that the notation \(\{0, \dots, n\}\) of Sets, Relations, and Cardinality , Chapter 2 still means what it meant there, and what set is it on \(\omega\) ?

title: Exercise (B1: Order as inclusion)
page: 1.6 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers
content: Prove that for all \(m, n \in \omega\) , \(m \le n\) if and only if \(m \subseteq n\) .

title: Exercise (B2: A product is at least its factor)
page: 1.6 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers
content: Prove that for all \(m, n \in \omega\) with \(n \ge 1\) , \(m \le mn\) . Show by an example that the hypothesis \(n \ge 1\) is needed.

title: Exercise (C1: Strong induction on ω)
page: 1.6 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers
content: Let \(P(n)\) be a property of natural numbers. Suppose that, for every \(n \in \omega\) , if \(P(k)\) holds for every \(k \in \omega\) with \(k < n\) , then \(P(n)\) holds. Prove that \(P(n)\) holds for every \(n \in \omega\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
page: 1.6 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers
content: Here is an attempted proof that any two natural numbers are comparable. Is the conclusion true? Is the proof correct? If not, give the first line that fails, the rule it breaks, and a counterexample to the step. Claim. For all \(m, n \in \omega\) : \(m \in n\) , \(m = n\) or \(n \in m\) . We use @thm-omega-induction (b) on \(n\) , for the property “for every \(m \in \omega\) : \(m \in n\) , \(m = n\) or \(n \in m\) ”. (2) For \(n = 0\) : every \(m\) is \(0\) or contains \(0\) , by @lem-omega-transitive (e). (3) Suppose the property holds for \(n\) , and let \(m \in \omega\) . (4) If \(m \in n\) or \(m = n\) , then \(m \in n \cup \{n\} = \mathrm{S}(n)\) . (5) If \(n \in m\) , then \(\mathrm{S}(n) \le m\) , because nothing lies strictly between \(n\) and \(\mathrm{S}(n)\) : no \(k \in \omega\) has \(n \in k \in \mathrm{S}(n)\) . (6) In every case \(m \in \mathrm{S}(n)\) , \(m = \mathrm{S}(n)\) or \(\mathrm{S}(n) \in m\) , which is the property for \(\mathrm{S}(n)\) . (7) By @thm-omega-induction (b), the claim holds.

page: 1.6 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers

title: Proposition 1.6.4 (Powers and Parity on \omega)
page: 1.6 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers
content: For all \(b, m, n \in \omega\) : \(b^{m+n} = b^m \cdot b^n\) ; if \(b \ne 0\) , then \(b^n \ne 0\) ; if \(b > 1\) and \(m < n\) , then \(b^m < b^n\) ; there is exactly one pair \((q, r)\) with \(q \in \omega\) , \(r \in \{0, 1\}\) and \(n = 2q + r\) . In particular, no \(n \in \omega\) is both of the form \(2q\) and of the form \(2q' + 1\) .

title: Proposition 1.6.5 (Tuples and Lists as Sets)
page: 1.6 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers
content: Let \(X\) be a set. For \(n = 2\) , an \(n\) -tuple in \(X\) is a pair \((x_1, x_2)\) with \(x_1, x_2 \in X\) ( @def-kuratowski-pair ), and \(X^2 \coloneqq X \times X\) . For \(n \in \omega\) with \(n \ge 3\) , an \(n\) -tuple in \(X\) is the graph \(G\) of a function \(x \colon \{1, \dots, n\} \to X\) ; with \(x_k \coloneqq x(k)\) it is written \[ (x_1, \dots, x_n) \coloneqq \bigl\{ (k, x_k) : k \in \{1, \dots, n\} \bigr\} = G . \] For \(n \ge 2\) , there is exactly one set \(X^n\) whose elements are exactly the \(n\) -tuples in \(X\) ; for \(n = 2\) it is \(X \times X\) . For \(n \ge 2\) , two \(n\) -tuples \((x_1, \dots, x_n)\) and \((y_1, \dots, y_n)\) in \(X\) are equal if and only if \(x_k = y_k\) for every \(k \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) . For \(n \ge 3\) , no \(n\) -tuple is a pair; and for \(n, n' \ge 3\) with \(n \ne n'\) , no \(n\) -tuple is an \(n'\) -tuple. For every \(n \in \omega\) ( \(n = 0, 1\) allowed) and every function \(x \colon \{1, \dots, n\} \to X\) , the list \[ \{x_1, \dots, x_n\} \coloneqq \bigl\{ y \in X : y = x_k \text{ for some } k \in \{1, \dots, n\} \bigr\} \] is a set: the image \(x(\{1, \dots, n\})\) of @fd2:def-image . For \(n \ge 3\) , no \(n\) -tuple is an element of \(\omega\) .

title: Theorem 1.6.1 (Order on \omega)
page: 1.6 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers
content: \(<\) is a strict total order on \(\omega\) : for all \(k, m, n \in \omega\) , never \(n < n\) ; if \(k < m\) and \(m < n\) , then \(k < n\) ; and exactly one of \(m < n\) , \(m = n\) , \(n < m\) holds. For \(m, n \in \omega\) , \(m < \mathrm{S}(n)\) if and only if \(m \le n\) . Hence no \(k \in \omega\) satisfies \(n < k < \mathrm{S}(n)\) . Every \(n \in \omega\) is the set of the natural numbers less than it: \(n = \{ m \in \omega : m < n \}\) . Hence \(\{0, \dots, n\} \coloneqq \{ k \in \omega : k \le n \}\) equals \(\mathrm{S}(n)\) . \(0 \le n\) for every \(n \in \omega\) ; if \(n \ne 0\) , then \(1 \le n\) ; and \(0 < 1\) . For \(n \in \omega\) , \(\{1, \dots, n\} \coloneqq \{ k \in \omega : 1 \le k \le n \}\) equals \(\mathrm{S}(n) \setminus \{0\}\) .

title: Theorem 1.6.2 (Well-Ordering of \omega)
page: 1.6 Order and Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers
content: Every non-empty subset \(A \subseteq \omega\) has a least element: an \(a \in A\) with \(a \le x\) for every \(x \in A\) . The least element is unique.

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 1.7 All Peano Systems Are Alike
content: These questions are about the proof of @thm-peano-categoricity . Where in the proof is (P5) for \(M\) used, and where are (P3) and (P4) for \(M\) used? Where is (P4) for \(\omega\) used? (It is not visible in the proof itself.) Run \(\varphi\) of part (a) for the system \((\omega \setminus \{0\}, 1, \mathrm{S})\) on \(0\) , \(1\) and \(2\) , from the two equations alone. State the idea of the proof of (a) and (b) in two sentences.

title: Exercise (B1: The even numbers)
page: 1.7 All Peano Systems Are Alike

title: Exercise (B2: The identification at work)

Compute \(\varphi(2 \cdot 3)\) in two ways: from (a) of the corollary, and by unwinding \(2 \cdot 3\) in \(\omega\) to a numeral first.

title: Exercise (C1: Writing out categoricity)
page: 1.7 All Peano Systems Are Alike

title: Exercise (C2: Without induction, no recursion)
page: 1.7 All Peano Systems Are Alike
content: Let \((M, e, s)\) be structure (iii) of @exm-peano-axioms-independent , the natural numbers beside a two-sided chain: \(M = \omega \times 3\) , \(e = (0, 0)\) , \(s(n, 0) = (\mathrm{S}(n), 0)\) , \(s(n, 1) = (\mathrm{S}(n), 1)\) , \(s(0, 2) = (0, 1)\) and \(s(\mathrm{S}(k), 2) = (k, 2)\) . Show that there is no function \(f \colon M \to \omega\) with \(f(e) = 0\) and \(f(s(x)) = \mathrm{S}(f(x))\) for every \(x \in M\) . Which Peano axiom, missing in \(M\) , is responsible?

title: Exercise (R1)
page: 1.7 All Peano Systems Are Alike
content: Prove that \(\omega\) is infinite.

title: Exercise (R2)
page: 1.7 All Peano Systems Are Alike
content: Show that the successor function \(\mathrm{S} \colon \omega \to \omega\) has a left inverse and no right inverse. Write a left inverse down explicitly. Is it the only one?

title: Exercise (R3)
page: 1.7 All Peano Systems Are Alike
content: Let \(M = \{0, 1\}\) , \(e = 0\) and \(s(0) = s(1) = 1\) . Show that there is no function \(f \colon M \to \omega\) with \(f(0) = 0\) and \(f(s(x)) = \mathrm{S}(f(x))\) for every \(x \in M\) . Which of the Peano axioms play the part, for definitions on \(\omega\) , that a theorem about reading formulas plays for definitions on formulas?

title: Exercise (R4)
page: 1.7 All Peano Systems Are Alike
content: For \(n \in \omega\) , compute \(\bigcup \mathrm{S}(n)\) and \(\bigcup n\) . Then find a set \(x\) with \(\bigcup \mathrm{S}(x) \ne x\) .

title: Proposition 1.7.2 (Isomorphisms Preserve Arithmetic and Order)
page: 1.7 All Peano Systems Are Alike
content: Let \((M, e, s)\) be a Peano system, and let \(\oplus, \otimes \colon M \times M \to M\) be functions such that, for all \(x, y \in M\) , \[ \begin{aligned} x \oplus e &= x, & x \oplus s(y) &= s(x \oplus y), \\ x \otimes e &= e, & x \otimes s(y) &= (x \otimes y) \oplus x . \end{aligned} \] Let \(\varphi \colon \omega \to M\) be the bijection of @thm-peano-categoricity . Then for all \(m, n \in \omega\) : \(\varphi(m + n) = \varphi(m) \oplus \varphi(n)\) ; \(\varphi(m n) = \varphi(m) \otimes \varphi(n)\) ; \(m < n\) if and only if \(\varphi(n) = \varphi(m) \oplus z\) for some \(z \in M\) with \(z \ne e\) .

title: Theorem 1.7.1 (Categoricity of the Peano Axioms)
page: 1.7 All Peano Systems Are Alike
content: Let \((M, e, s)\) be a Peano system. There is exactly one function \(\varphi \colon \omega \to M\) with \(\varphi(0) = e\) and \(\varphi(\mathrm{S}(n)) = s(\varphi(n))\) for every \(n \in \omega\) . This \(\varphi\) is a bijection. For any two Peano systems \((M, e, s)\) and \((M', e', s')\) there is exactly one bijection \(\psi \colon M \to M'\) with \(\psi(e) = e'\) and \(\psi(s(x)) = s'(\psi(x))\) for every \(x \in M\) .

title: Theorem 2.2.1 (Functions on Classes)
page: 2.2 Well-Definedness, and the Arithmetic of the Integers
content: Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on a set \(X\) , and \(\approx\) an equivalence relation on a set \(Y\) . Classes are taken for \(\sim\) in \(X\) and for \(\approx\) in \(Y\) . Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function such that, for all \(x, x' \in X\) , \(x \sim x'\) implies \(f(x) \approx f(x')\) . Then there is exactly one function \(F \colon X/{\sim} \to Y/{\approx}\) with \(F([x]) = [f(x)]\) for every \(x \in X\) . Let \(g \colon X \times X \to X\) be a function such that, for all \(x, x', y, y' \in X\) , \[ \begin{aligned} x \sim x' &\implies g(x, y) \sim g(x', y) , \\ y \sim y' &\implies g(x, y) \sim g(x, y') . \end{aligned} \] Then there is exactly one function \(G \colon (X/{\sim}) \times (X/{\sim}) \to X/{\sim}\) with \(G([x], [y]) = [g(x, y)]\) for all \(x, y \in X\) . Let \(S \subseteq X\) be such that, for all \(x, x' \in X\) , \(x \sim x'\) and \(x \in S\) imply \(x' \in S\) . Let \(\bar S \coloneqq \{ [x] : x \in S \} \subseteq X/{\sim}\) . Then, for every \(x \in X\) , \([x] \in \bar S\) if and only if \(x \in S\) .

title: Definition 2.3.1 (Commutative Ring, Field)
page: 2.3 The Integers as an Ordered Ring
content: A commutative ring is a set \(R\) with two functions, addition \(+ \colon R \times R \to R\) and multiplication \(\cdot \colon R \times R \to R\) (written \(a \cdot b = ab\) ), such that clauses (F1)–(F7) and (F9) of the following list hold; clause (F8) is used only for fields. \(a + b = b + a\) for all \(a, b \in R\) . \((a + b) + c = a + (b + c)\) for all \(a, b, c \in R\) . There is an element \(0 \in R\) with \(a + 0 = a\) for every \(a \in R\) . For every \(a \in R\) there is an element \(-a \in R\) with \(a + (-a) = 0\) . \((ab)c = a(bc)\) for all \(a, b, c \in R\) . \(ab = ba\) for all \(a, b \in R\) . There is an element \(1 \in R\) with \(a \cdot 1 = a\) for every \(a \in R\) . For every non-zero \(a \in R\) there is an element \(a^{-1} \in R\) with \(a a^{-1} = 1\) . \(a(b + c) = ab + ac\) for all \(a, b, c \in R\) . A field is a commutative ring in which, in addition , \(1 \ne 0\) and (F8) holds. We write \(a - b \coloneqq a + (-b)\) , and in a field \(a / b \coloneqq a b^{-1}\) for \(b \ne 0\) .

title: Definition 2.3.2 (Ordered Ring, Ordered Field)
page: 2.3 The Integers as an Ordered Ring
content: An ordered commutative ring is a commutative ring \(R\) ( @def-commutative-ring-and-field ) together with a relation \(<\) on \(R\) such that, for all \(a, b, c \in R\) : (trichotomy) exactly one of \(a < b\) , \(a = b\) , \(b < a\) holds; (transitivity) if \(a < b\) and \(b < c\) , then \(a < c\) ; (addition) if \(a < b\) , then \(a + c < b + c\) ; (multiplication) if \(0 < a\) and \(0 < b\) , then \(0 < ab\) . An ordered field is a field that is an ordered commutative ring. We write \(b > a\) for \(a < b\) , and \(a \le b\) for “ \(a < b\) or \(a = b\) ” (likewise \(b \ge a\) ). An element \(a\) is positive if \(a > 0\) , negative if \(a < 0\) , and non-negative if \(a \ge 0\) .

title: Proposition 2.4.1 (Cross-Multiplication Is an Equivalence Relation)
page: 2.4 The Rationals as Classes of Fractions
content: The relation \(\sim\) on \(\nZ \times \nZ_{>0}\) given by \[ (p, q) \sim (r, s) \iff ps = rq \] is an equivalence relation ( @fd2:def-equivalence-relation ).

title: Theorem 2.4.3 (The Rationals Form a Field)
page: 2.4 The Rationals as Classes of Fractions
content: \(\nQ\) , with the operations of @def-rational-operations , is a field ( @def-commutative-ring-and-field ), with zero \([(0, 1)]\) and one \([(1, 1)]\) . A rational number \([(p, q)]\) is zero if and only if \(p = 0\) . If \(p > 0\) , its inverse is \([(q, p)]\) ; if \(p < 0\) , its inverse is \([(-q, -p)]\) .

title: Proposition 2.5.5 (Integer Part of a Rational)
page: 2.5 The Rationals as an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property
content: For every \(x \in \nQ\) there is exactly one \(m \in \nZ\) with \(m \le x < m + 1\) . It is called the integer part of \(x\) and written \(\floor{x}\) .

title: Proposition 2.5.2 (Reciprocals Reverse Order)
page: 2.5 The Rationals as an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property
content: Let \(F\) be an ordered field and \(a, b \in F\) . If \(a > 0\) , then \(a^{-1} > 0\) . If \(0 < a < b\) , then \(0 < b^{-1} < a^{-1}\) , that is, \(0 < 1/b < 1/a\) .

page: 2.5 The Rationals as an Ordered Field; the Archimedean Property
content: For every \(x \in \nQ\) there is \(n \in \nN\) with \(x < n\) .

title: Exercise (B1: Put the proof in order)
page: 2.6 The Gaps in the Rationals
content: Here are lines of a proof of @thm-no-rational-square-two , shuffled, together with two lines that do not belong. Write the lines of a correct proof in a correct order, and say what is wrong with each line you leave out. Set \(p' \coloneqq 2q - p\) and \(q' \coloneqq p - q\) ; both are positive integers, by the two inequalities between \(p\) and \(q\) . Write \(x = a/b\) with \(a, b \in \nZ_{>0}\) ; then \(a^2 = 2b^2\) . Since \(p^2 = 2q^2\) , we have \(p < q\) . Since \(q' = p - q < q\) , this contradicts the choice of \(q\) ; so no rational squares to \(2\) . Suppose \(x \in \nQ\) has \(x^2 = 2\) ; replacing \(x\) by \(-x\) if necessary, take \(x > 0\) . \(p < 2q\) , since \(p \ge 2q\) would give \(p^2 \ge 4q^2 > 2q^2\) . Choose such an \(x\) with the least positive value. Among all pairs \((p, q)\) of positive integers with \(p^2 = 2q^2\) , choose one with \(q\) least ( @prp-integer-least-element ; \(b\) is such a \(q\) ). Expanding, \(p'^2 - 2q'^2 = 2q^2 - p^2 = 0\) , so \(p'^2 = 2q'^2\) . \(q < p\) , since \(p \le q\) would give \(2q^2 = p^2 \le q^2\) , that is, \(q^2 \le 0\) .

page: 3.2 The Greatest Common Divisor, Bézout, and the Euclidean Algorithm

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 3.3 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content: These questions are about the uniqueness half of the proof of @thm-fundamental-arithmetic . Why must the empty list count as a prime factorization? Run the induction step on \((p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4) = (2, 2, 3, 5)\) and a second prime factorization \((q_1, \dots, q_l)\) of \(60\) . Which equalities does the proof derive, and to which two lists is \(P(3)\) applied? Which line of the proof uses Euclid’s lemma, and through which result? Where is “non-decreasing” used? Give the idea of the uniqueness proof in two sentences.

title: Exercise (B1: Put the proof in order)
page: 3.3 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content: The following lines contain a proof of @thm-euclid-lemma-integers , shuffled, together with two lines that do not belong. Write the seven correct lines in an order that makes a proof, say which other orders are also admissible, and say why each of the other two lines fails. Suppose \(a \mid bc\) and \(\gcd(a, b) = 1\) . There are \(x, y \in \nZ\) with \(ax + by = 1\) . (ii′) Since \(\gcd(a, b) = 1\) and \(a \mid bc\) , we have \(a \mid b\) or \(a \mid c\) . Multiplying by \(c\) : \(c = acx + bcy\) . (iii′) Dividing \(1 = ax + by\) by \(a\) : \(1/a = x + (b/a)y\) . \(a \mid acx\) , since \(acx = a(cx)\) . Write \(bc = ak\) ; then \(bcy = a(ky)\) , so \(a \mid bcy\) . Hence \(a \mid acx + bcy\) . So \(a \mid c\) .

title: Exercise (B3: Two factorizations and a gcd)

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
page: 3.3 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content: Here is a statement and an argument for it. Claim. Let \(m, n, c \in \nZ\) . If \(m \mid c\) , \(n \mid c\) and \(\gcd(m, n) = 1\) , then \(mn \mid c\) . Argument. (1) Write \(c = mk\) and \(c = nl\) with \(k, l \in \nZ\) . (2) Then \(c^2 = c \cdot c = (mk)(nl) = mn \cdot kl\) . (3) So \(mn \mid c^2\) . (4) Hence \(mn \mid c\) . Is the claim true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the line that fails, explain why, and give a counterexample to the step.

title: Exercise (C3: There is no last prime)
page: 3.3 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content: Prove that no finite list contains every prime: for every list of primes \((p_1, \dots, p_k)\) , with \(k \in \nN\) , there is a prime that is not an entry of the list.

title: Lemma 3.3.4 (The Least Divisor Is Prime)
page: 3.3 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content: Let \(n \in \nZ\) with \(n \ge 2\) . The set \(D \coloneqq \{ d \in \nZ : d \ge 2 \text{ and } d \mid n \}\) has a least element, and that element is prime. In particular, \(n\) has a prime factor.

title: Proposition 3.3.3 (Coprime Divisors of a Number)

content: Let \(m, n, c \in \nZ\) with \(m \mid c\) , \(n \mid c\) and \(\gcd(m, n) = 1\) . Then \(mn \mid c\) .

title: Theorem 3.4.1 (Quotient Ring by an Ideal)
page: 3.4 Ideals, Quotient Rings, and the Integers Modulo n
content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring and \(I\) an ideal of \(R\) . Setting \(a \sim_I b \iff a - b \in I\) defines an equivalence relation \(\sim_I\) on \(R\) , and the class of \(a\) is \([a] = a + I \coloneqq \{ a + x : x \in I \}\) . The rules \([a] + [b] \coloneqq [a + b]\) , \([a] \cdot [b] \coloneqq [ab]\) and \(-[a] \coloneqq [-a]\) are well defined on \(R/I \coloneqq R/{\sim_I}\) . \(R/I\) , with these operations, is a commutative ring with zero \([0]\) and one \([1]\) . The quotient map \(\pi \colon R \to R/I\) , \(\pi(a) \coloneqq [a]\) , satisfies \(\pi(a + b) = \pi(a) + \pi(b)\) , \(\pi(ab) = \pi(a) \pi(b)\) and \(\pi(1) = [1]\) . \([a] = [0]\) if and only if \(a \in I\) . In particular \([1] = [0]\) if and only if \(I = R\) .

title: Definition 3.5.1 (Unit of a Commutative Ring)
page: 3.5 Units, Prime Moduli, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem
content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring ( @def-commutative-ring-and-field ). An element \(u \in R\) is a unit of \(R\) if there exists \(v \in R\) with \(uv = 1\) . The set of units of \(R\) is written \(R^{\times}\) . For a unit \(u\) , the element \(v\) is unique ; it is written \(u^{-1}\) and called the inverse of \(u\) .

title: Theorem 3.5.1 (Units Modulo n)
page: 3.5 Units, Prime Moduli, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem
content:
Let \(n \in 
Z_{>0}\) and \(a \in 
Z\) . Then \([a]\) is a unit of \(
Z/n
Z\) if and only if \(\gcd(a, n) = 1\) . In that case, for any \(x, y \in 
Z\) with \(ax + ny = 1\) , \([a]^{-1} = [x]\) .
